en: The Compendium of the Six Pāramitās, Scroll One, translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of Kangju during the Wu Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Pāramitā of Dāna (Generosity). This chapter contains ten sections.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha,
together with five hundred arhats and one thousand bodhisattvas, all seated in assembly.

Among them was a bodhisattva named Aniruddha; whenever the Buddha preached the sutras and the Way, he would always listen with a tranquil mind and deep sympathy, remaining silent and free from discursive thought, his mind fixed steadily upon the scripture.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, spoke for them:
"The Bodhisattva’s six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are unsurpassed practices that are difficult to attain; by practicing them, one swiftly becomes a Buddha.
What are these six?..."
First is giving; second is observing the precepts; third is patience; fourth is diligence; fifth is meditative concentration; and sixth is the sublime practice of the Perfection of Wisdom.
"As for the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), what are its principles?

It nurtures all beings with loving-kindness, takes pity on the multitudes of the heterodox, rejoices in the accomplishments of the worthy, protects and rescues sentient beings, and its vast moisture transcends heaven and earth, overflowing like great rivers and seas."

He bestowed gifts upon sentient beings: providing food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing for the cold, and cool relief for the heat; he provided medicine to alleviate the sick. As for carriages, horses, boats, and carts, as well as various treasures, rare jewels, wives, children, and kingdoms—whenever they were requested, he granted them with generosity.
It was like Prince Sudāna, who gave alms to the poor and destitute as if nurturing his own children; though his father the king banished him, he felt compassion rather than resentment.

(1) [The Jātaka of the Bodhisattva] (1): "In the past, the Bodhisattva’s mind was attuned to the truth; beholding the impermanence of the world and that life and glory are difficult to preserve, he gave away all his wealth in charity."

Śakra, Lord of Devas, beheld the Bodhisattva’s compassionate nurturing of all beings and his practice of giving to relieve the multitudes; seeing that his meritorious achievements were towering and his virtue weighed heavily upon the ten directions, he feared the Bodhisattva would usurp his own position. Consequently, he transformed himself into a hell and appeared before him, saying:
"One who practices giving to relieve the multitudes shall, at the end of life, have their soul enter the Great Mountain Hell, where they are scorched and boiled by ten thousand poisons."
"Is it that giving brings about harm? Is this what your kindness has wrought?
The Bodhisattva replied, "How could there be such a thing as practicing the virtue of giving and yet entering the Great Mountain Hell?"
The Śākya said:
"If you do not believe me, you may ask the one who was executed.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"For what reason do you dwell in this hell?

The sinner replied, "In my past life in the world, I emptied my own house to relieve the poor and rescued many from their misfortunes; yet now I undergo this heavy retribution, dwelling in the prison of Mount Tai."
The Bodhisattva asked:
"If benevolence and kindness bring about misfortune, what becomes of the one who receives the gift?
Śakra replied:
"The benefactor shall ascend to heaven at the end of his life.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"My relief and salvation are intended solely for all sentient beings."
If you say, "I truly desire this," then I shall certainly do it for you,
even if it means that my compassion and kindness bring me retribution.
To endanger oneself to save the multitude is the supreme aspiration of a Bodhisattva.
The Śākya asked:
"What is your aspiration that you still pursue such lofty conduct?
He replied:
"I wish to seek Buddhahood, to uplift and deliver sentient beings, and cause them to attain Nirvana so that they no longer undergo birth and death.
When Shi heard of this holy aspiration, he bowed his head and said:
"In truth, there are none who practice giving to compassionately save sentient beings; rather, those who distance themselves from merit and receive calamity shall enter the prison of Mount Tai."
Your virtue moves heaven and earth; fearing that you would usurp my position, I merely displayed the hells to delude your resolve.
To deceive a sage out of folly—consider the gravity of such an offense.
Having finished repenting for his transgressions, he prostrated himself and withdrew.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Compassionate Benevolence in bestowing gifts. 2.

[The Jātaka of King Śvāpada] (II): “In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king named Śvāpada. He bestowed gifts upon sentient beings according to whatever they sought, and out of compassion for those in distress and difficulty, he was always filled with sorrowful pity.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld that the King’s virtue of compassion and bounty had spread throughout the ten directions; thus the devas, spirits, and nāgas all spoke in unison:

"The exalted position of Śakra is never permanently held by one person. He who is complete in precepts, lofty in conduct, and abundant in the merit of compassion and bounty shall become the Lord of Devas when his life ends and his spirit departs."
Fearing that his own throne might be usurped, he wished to go and test him in order to discern the truth from falsehood.
The Emperor commanded the Border King, saying:
"Now this king of men possesses a compassionate and pervasive grace, and his merit and virtue are towering; I fear that in his pursuit of his aims, he may seek to usurp my imperial throne."
"You shall transform yourself into a pigeon and hasten to the king's presence; feigning terror, you shall beg for mercy from that king.
That king is benevolent and compassionate, and he will surely grant you refuge;
I shall follow behind and demand you back from the king."
"The King will certainly not return; he must surely purchase meat to take its place.
If my deception does not stop him, yet the King’s intent is pure and sincere, and he has promised never to go back on his word, he will surely cut flesh from his own body to weigh against it."
"If one weighs meat while it still possesses its own weight, once the meat is exhausted, the body will ache and one will surely regret it.
If there is regret in one's mind, what one aspires to will not be accomplished.
Śakra then transformed himself into a hawk, and the King of the Borderlands transformed himself into a dove.
The pigeon flew swiftly toward the king’s feet and, in terror, cried out:
"Great King, have mercy on me!
My life is at its end!"
The king said:
"Do not fear, do not fear!
I shall now save you."
The hawk soon arrived and said to the king:
"That pigeon has come here; the pigeon is my food. I pray that Your Majesty will return it to me.
The king replied:
"The pigeon has come to seek refuge in my life; having accepted its surrender, I am a man of my word and shall not deviate from it from beginning to end.
If you truly obtain the meat, I will provide for you myself, making it a hundredfold more than what you require."
The hawk said, "I desire only this pigeon and have no need for other meat; I hope Your Majesty will grant me this favor.
Why then do you snatch away my food?"
The King said:
"I have already accepted his surrender; I hold the heavens and earth in high esteem—what heart could I have to go back on my word?
What object should I give you so that you may set the pigeon free with joy?"
The hawk said, "If Your Majesty,
out of compassion and benevolence, will surely save this living being by cutting flesh from your own body to equal the weight of the pigeon, I shall joyfully accept it."
The King said, "Very well!
and immediately cut flesh from his own thigh, weighing it until it equaled the weight of the pigeon; he then gave it [to the hunter].

The pigeon exceeded its own weight; it continued to cut itself until its flesh was entirely exhausted, yet still did not equal the weight of the scales, and the pain of its bodily wounds was immeasurable.
With a heart of compassion and patience, the King wished for the pigeon to live, and he commanded his close minister, saying:
"Kill me quickly and weigh my marrow until it equals the weight of the pigeon."

I have served the Buddhas and received the profound and true precepts; I rescue sentient beings from peril and distress. Though there may be the afflictions of many heterodox influences, they are like a gentle breeze—how could they move Mount Tai?
"King Śyāmaka remained firm in his resolve to uphold the Way and was difficult to match in his compassion and benevolence; thus, each returned to their original forms.
Śakra and the frontier king prostrated themselves upon the ground, saying:
'Great King!'"
"What aspirations do you hold that cause you such distress and suffering?

The King of Men replied, "I do not aspire to the rank of Śakra, Lord of Devas, nor to the position of a Cakravartin Emperor. I see sentient beings submerged in blinding darkness, neither beholding the Triple Gem nor hearing the Buddha's teachings; they indulge their hearts in malevolent and calamitous conduct, casting themselves into the Avīci Hell."
Beholding this ignorance and delusion, he was moved with compassion.
He made a vow to seek Buddhahood, to rescue sentient beings from their distress and enable them to attain Nirvana.
The Heavenly Emperor said in astonishment:
"The fool says, 'The Great King wishes to seize my position; that is why he disturbs me.
What instructions do you have for him?
The King said:
"May my bodily sores heal and return to their former state, and may my resolve for generosity and my conduct in aiding the multitude exceed what they are now.

The Heavenly Emperor then had celestial physicians apply divine medicine, and his bodily sores healed; his complexion and strength surpassed his former state, and his sores were completely cured in an instant.
Having prostrated himself in homage and circumambulated the king three times, he departed with great joy.
From that time forward, his practice of giving surpassed his former efforts.
Such was the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Perfection of Giving through compassionate benevolence.

3. [The Jātaka of the Poor Man] (III): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was exceedingly impoverished. He traveled to another country together with a group of merchants; all of them were resolved to have faith in the Buddha, practicing generosity toward the destitute to deliver sentient beings."
The people all said, "Everyone here is compassionate and benevolent; what will you bestow?
He replied:

"Indeed, among those things that are merely borrowed for the body, there is none that is not eventually cast aside. As I observe the fish in the sea, where the large devour the small, my heart is filled with sorrow.
I shall offer my own body as a substitute for one of the smaller ones, so that it may obtain a brief respite of life."
He immediately threw himself into the sea.
The large fish were satiated, while the small ones were able to survive.
His soul was transformed into the king of the *zhān* fish, his body spanning several *lǐ* in length.
"On the seashore there is a country that has suffered from a drought; its people are famished and devour one another.
A fish wept and said:
'The sentient beings are in such turmoil; how great is their suffering!'"
"My body has flesh measured in *li*, sufficient to provide for the needs of the common people for ten days or a month.

He then cast himself from his own body onto the shore of the kingdom; the entire nation devoured it to preserve their lives, yet the fish remained alive even as they carried away the flesh for several months.
A deva descended and said:
"You endure this suffering; how can you possibly bear it?
Why do you not relinquish your life-span so that you may be free from this pain?"
The fish said, "I shall take my own life so that my spirit departs and my body rots; lest the people suffer famine hereafter and devour one another, which I cannot bear to witness.
His heart was moved by this sentiment. Then Heaven said:
"The Bodhisattva’s embrace of compassion is difficult to equal.
The deva, his heart grieved, said:
"You shall surely attain Buddhahood and deliver my sentient beings."
"A man then struck off its head with an axe, and the fish died instantly.
Its spirit was immediately reborn as the crown prince of a king.
From birth, he possessed the brilliance of a supreme sage; his fourfold benevolence and vast compassion moistened all things like the two polarities of heaven and earth."
Compassionate toward the people’s poverty and distress, he spoke with a voice choked with emotion.
Yet the state was still suffering from drought; so he composed his mind in solemnity, withdrew from meals and ceased all offerings, and prostrating himself, repented of his faults, saying:
"The people’s lack of goodness is my own fault. I pray that I may lose my life to benefit the people with timely rain."
Day after day he mourned with deep sorrow, like a filial son who has suffered the loss of a saintly father.
His sincerity reached far and wide, and immediately five hundred Buddhas arrived within his realm.

Upon hearing this, the King’s heart rejoiced; he was so filled with joy that he felt as if his body no longer existed. He went out to welcome them and prostrated himself, inviting them to return to the main palace.

The Queen and the Crown Prince were all equally solemn and reverent; they offered him the finest dharma-robes and provided whatever he lacked. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they bowed their heads and wept, saying:

“Our minds are defiled and our conduct turbid; we have not conformed to the teachings of the Triple Gem and the Four Debts of Gratitude. We have oppressed and cruelly treated the people, and our sins deserve to be punished by ourselves.”
"The suffering has spread even to the lowliest, with drought persisting for many years; the common people suffer from famine, their resentment and grief wounding their hearts.
We pray that you remove this calamity from the people by casting the misfortune upon me.
Each of the Buddhas replied:
"You are a benevolent ruler, compassionate and kind, whose virtue equals that of Śakra; this is known by all the Buddhas.
Now I bestow blessings upon you; be careful not to feel sorrow."
He then swiftly issued an edict to the people, commanding them all to plant grain.

The King acted according to these instructions; men and women applied themselves to their labors, and there was no household that did not cultivate. Yet the rice transformed into gourds, and the agricultural minister reported this to the King.
The King said, "It must ripen.

Then the melons and fruits covered the entire kingdom, all containing unhusked rice within; each could hold several *hu* measures, their flavor was exquisite and fragrant, and their aroma spread throughout the nation.
The entire nation rejoiced and sighed in praise of the king’s virtue.
Hostile nations on all four frontiers all declared themselves his subjects; the common people gathered like clouds, and the borders of the kingdom expanded daily.
Throughout the land, all maintained the precepts and took refuge in the Triple Gem. After the king, his ministers, and the people passed away, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said, “The poor man at that time was my own self.

Through many kalpas, I have practiced benevolence and compassion to rescue and aid sentient beings; this merit has not gone to waste, and now I have attained Buddhahood, am titled the God among Gods, and act as the hero of the three realms.”
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and benevolence (maitrī-karuṇā-pāramitā) practices giving.

4. [The Jātaka of the Bodhisattva] (IV): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a *śramaṇa* who constantly dwelt in mountain marshes, single-mindedly and diligently contemplating the Way and refraining from all evils."

He ate fruit and drank water, storing not even the slightest surplus. Out of compassion for sentient beings who were deluded and self-decayed, he would always rescue those he saw in peril by risking his own life.
While traveling in search of fruits and melons, he encountered a nursing tigress on the road.
After suckling her cub, the tigress was exhausted and lacked food; her hunger and distress agitated her mind, and she desired to return and devour her own offspring.

When the Bodhisattva beheld this, his heart was moved with profound sorrow. He lamented that the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings dwelling in the world are immeasurable, and that the pain of mother and child devouring one another is beyond words. He choked with emotion and shed tears.
He turned his body and looked in all four directions, searching for something with which to feed the tiger and save his son’s life.
Seeing nothing at all, he thought to himself:
"The tiger is a creature that feeds on meat."
He reflected deeply and profoundly:

"I have established my resolve to study the Way solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings who are submerged in heavy suffering, so that they may be freed from calamity and their lives may find eternal peace."
"After I have grown old and died, this body will inevitably be cast aside; it would be better to benefit the multitude through compassion and kindness to achieve virtue.
He then threw his own head into the tiger's mouth.
By giving his head, he intended for the tiger to die quickly so that it would not feel the pain.
The tiger mother and cub were both present.

The Buddhas praised his virtue, and the supreme sages matched him in merit; among the devas, nāgas, benevolent spirits, and those with the aspiration for the Way, there was none who did not feel profound sorrow.

There were those who were practicing for, or had attained, the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, or those who had resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

With this fierce resolve, he transcended all other bodhisattvas by nine kalpas; he vowed to become a teacher of gods and humans amidst the five turbidities, delivering those who are rebellious and evil so that they may falsely conform to the Way.
"Thus did the Bodhisattva practice the perfection of giving through his compassionate benevolence.

5. [The Jātaka of King Kaniṣka] (V): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king; his kingdom was named Kaniṣka, and his title was Priyadarśin. He was wise within and benevolent without; his countenance was harmonious and upright. The people followed his transformation, and there were no prisoners in his jails. When the common folk were impoverished, they were allowed to seek whatever they desired. His compassionate benevolence was so moistening and his kindness like that of Śakra."

"The people of other lands were moved by his sincerity and submitted to his benevolent generosity, which accorded with the desires of the multitude. Yet, a host of wicked and envious men, jealous of him, sought to destroy the true with the false; they went to the palace gate and said:
'We have heard that the enlightened king relieves the hardships and deprivations of the common people, just as the moisture of Heaven covers all things universally.'"
He said to the guards,
"Can you hear him? When the attendants reported this, the King appeared immediately.
Shixin appeared and said:

"The benevolent grace of Your Majesty’s enlightened rule extends to the four quarters; among all sentient beings, there are none who do not sigh in admiration. I venture to present my wish for Your Majesty’s imperial hearing."
The King said,
"Excellent! Śreṇika said:
"The Heavenly King is fond of giving; when one requests, he never refuses.
Now, it is appropriate for me to employ my own head for this purpose; I pray that you will grant me your head to fulfill our hopes.
The King said:
"What is so desirable about my head that you wish to obtain it?
I possess many treasures; I shall bestow them upon you in addition.
Śyāma refused to accept them. The king then had craftsmen fashion seven-jeweled heads, numbering several hundred, and gave them to Śyāma.
Śyāmaka said,
"I desire only the king's head.
Since the king had never before opposed anyone, he immediately descended from the palace, wrapped his hair around a tree, and said:
"I shall offer my head to you, Master.

Shixin drew his sword and advanced with rapid strides. Upon seeing this, the tree spirit was incensed by his lack of propriety; it struck him on the cheek with its hand, whereupon Shixin’s body twisted and contorted, his face turned backward, and his hand fell as the sword dropped from his grasp.
The King attained peace and well-being, and his ministers and subjects offered him long life; grief and joy mingled within him as the devas praised his virtue—this may be called "internal giving"!

Protected by the Four Kings, all poisons were extinguished; the realm was free from disease, the five grains ripened in abundance, prisons were broken open and destroyed, and both ruler and people rejoiced heartily.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The King of the country of Kāśī at that time was none other than myself;
Śreṇika was Devadatta."
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and generosity is practiced through giving. 6.

[The Jātaka of the King] (Sixth): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king who governed his people with compassion, extending his own self-understanding to others. Month after month, he traveled among the poor and destitute, providing relief to widows and orphans, and supplying medicine and congey for the sick."
Whenever he went on tours of inspection, he would order his rear carriage to carry various treasures, clothing, and medicines, and he would bury those who had died along the way.
Whenever he saw impoverished people, he would immediately reproach himself, saying:
"Your Majesty lacks virtue, and thus the people are destitute."
"If you are rich in virtue, the people's households will have sufficient means.
Now that the people are poor, I am poor as well.
The King’s compassion was such as this, and his fame spread throughout the ten directions.
As Śakra sat for the second time, he was overcome by its heat; his heart was immediately filled with fear, and he said:
"His virtue is so lofty that he will surely seize my position.
I must frustrate his resolve; otherwise, his journey will be completed!"
He then transformed himself into an old brahmin and begged the king for one thousand silver coins; the king immediately granted them to him.
He said, "I am traveling to the west, and I fear people might steal them."
"I wish to entrust it to Your Majesty.
The King said,
"In my kingdom, there are no thieves."
He spoke again, saying,
"I entrust it to Your Majesty.
The King then accepted it.
The deva again transformed himself into a brahmin and went to the palace gate; when the attendants announced his arrival, the king immediately granted him an audience.
The brahmin sighed in admiration, saying:
"Great King, your fame and merit spread throughout the eight directions, and your virtuous conduct is rare indeed."
"I have now come from afar wishing to beg for something.
The king said, "Excellent!"
He said, "In my past lives, I was of meager merit and born among the common people; I longed for noble honor and wished to beg for this kingdom.
The king said:
"Excellent! he exclaimed, and immediately gave the carriage to his wife and children, departing on foot.
The Heavenly Lord then transformed himself into a brahmin and begged the king for the carriage.
He bestowed chariots and horses upon him as gifts.
Accompanied by his wife and children, he set out on the road and halted for the night near a mountain.

A Daoist master of the Five Paths, who was a friend of the king, remembered the king’s virtue and looked up toward the place where he was staying. Seeing that he had lost his kingdom, the Daoist calmed his mind through dhyāna and observed the Heavenly Lord Śakra; he saw that Śakra, driven by greed and envy, had seized the kingdom, leaving [the former king] exhausted and emaciated.
The Daoist, by means of his supernormal power, suddenly appeared before the King and asked,
"What do you seek that you have exerted your will so greatly?
He replied:
"What my mind intends, you know it all," the Daoist said.
He then transformed into a single-axle chariot to escort the King back; by dawn, they had parted ways.
The deity transformed himself into a brahmin and begged for his chariot again, so he gave it to him once more.
Having traveled further, but not yet reached that country by some tens of li, the deity again transformed himself into the previous brahmin and came to demand silver coins.
The king said, "I have bestowed the kingdom as a gift upon the people; I have inadvertently forgotten your money.
The brahmin said:
"I must have my money back within three days.
The king immediately pledged his wife and himself to separate families as collateral, obtaining one thousand silver coins to return to the brahmin.

The wife served as a handmaid in the family where she was held as collateral; while bathing, she removed her pearls, necklaces, and various jewels and hung them on a rack. A celestial being transformed into a hawk, snatched the clothes and jewels, and flew away.
The woman said,
"This slave has stolen!
and she was arrested and imprisoned.
The boy lay down to sleep with the son of the host family; during the night, the deity went and killed the host's son.

The family of the deceased took the boy and delivered him to prison; both mother and son were bound together. Emaciated by hunger and famine, they wailed for help in vain, lamenting and weeping all day long until their crimes were proven and they were abandoned at the marketplace to die.

The king hired himself out for one thousand silver coins to ransom his wife and children; as he passed through the marketplace and beheld them, he immediately brought to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions and repented, saying:
"How could the evil karma of my past lives have led to this!"
With a tranquil mind, he entered meditative absorption, and through the clarity of his supernormal powers, he beheld what the gods were doing.
A voice from the air said:
"Why do you not kill him quickly?"
The King said:

"I have heard that Śakra universally relieves all sentient beings with a sincere heart of compassion, nurturing them beyond what a loving mother does; there are no blood-bearing creatures who do not receive his protection. Have you obtained this imperial throne through no evil causes?"
Śakra harbored heavy malice, and his evil having ripened, his transgression was completed; he entered Mount Tai alive.
Among devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts, there were none who did not praise this as virtuous.
"The King, Lord of the Earth, shall immediately pardon the offenses of Śakra’s wife and son."
When the two kings met, they immediately inquired into the origins of these events; as each recounted the circumstances in full detail, there was no one, whether high or low, who did not shed tears.
The sovereign king of the host country divided his realm to govern it [with the guest];
thus the ministers and people of the former kingdom sought out the king’s location and led the entire land to welcome him.
"The rulers and people of the two kingdoms were thus one in sorrow and one in joy.
'The King at that time was I myself;
the wife was Jiuyi.'"
The son was Rāhula;
the Lord of Devas was Devadatta;
and the brahmin in the mountains was Śāriputra.
The king of that country was Maitreya.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassion and benevolence.

7. [The Jātaka of the Former King] (VII): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king who governed his people with righteousness and impartiality, yet he did not go out for excursions or spectacles."
The Prime Minister petitioned, saying,
"I wish to go out on an excursion.
The King said:
"Excellent! On the following day, he departed.

The people were joyful and content, each finding their proper place. Beholding the wealth of the nation and the exquisite elegance of the residences, with roofs of gold and silver and garments that illuminated the roads, they exclaimed:
"How abundant is my kingdom!
he thought, his heart filled with great joy.
Returning to the palace, he recalled this and said:
"What benefit do these householders bring to the state?
he asked, and issued an edict to confiscate their wealth for the military reserves.
There was one householder whose private fortune amounted to thirty million [units], yet he maintained a distant relationship with the reigning king.
The King said in anger,
"How dare you deceive me to my face? He replied:
"Since I first began managing my livelihood, whatever private wealth or treasures I have within my home are subject to division among the five families;
they are not mine. He asked, "What do you mean by 'private wealth'?"

He replied: "In my heart I mindfully contemplate the Buddha's deeds, in my mouth I proclaim the Buddha's teachings, and in my body I perform the Buddha's works. I relinquish my share of the five families to establish the ancestral temple of the Buddha; I reverently serve the assembly of the worthy by providing them with food and clothing; and I compassionately nourish all classes of beings, from those that fly and wriggle to those that crawl.

I do not inflict upon others anything that would cause unease in my own heart. This merit and virtue follow me wherever I go, just as a shadow follows a form; this is what is called 'private wealth.'"
The five parties that divide [one's property] are:
first, water; second, fire; third, thieves; fourth, the authorities; and fifth, the exhaustion of one’s life.

When the body reaches its end, the family treasures are abandoned in this world; one must depart alone, and as the destination of misfortune or fortune remains unknown, one views the world as an illusion and therefore does not dare to possess anything.
"Calculating the five households, they would amount to one billion; this is a nest of calamity, and I am constantly afraid it will endanger me. How could I dare to possess such wealth?
I pray that you, my fellow monks, carry it away to remove my anxiety."
The king said, "Truly indeed these words.
He then immediately sent him away.
He retired to his meditation chamber and concentrated his mind in profound reflection, whereupon he awoke to this realization:
"If one cannot even preserve one's own body, how much less can one expect the long-lasting endurance of kingdoms, wives, children, and all such things?"

He immediately compiled and recorded the sūtras and their commentaries, whereby the defilements of his mind were illuminated and removed. He promoted upright ministers who offered loyal admonitions, granted a general amnesty throughout the kingdom, returned treasures to the people, reorganized the various officials, and deliberated upon policies of leniency and rectitude.
He said to his ministers:
"Those who do not behold the wondrous meaning of the Buddha’s sutras and the gravity of the precepts are truly deaf and blind!
While they are wealthy householders, I alone am poor!"

He immediately issued an edict throughout the realm to distribute wealth and treasures, providing relief to the poor and destitute according to their every desire; he established Buddhist temples and monasteries, hung silk banners, burned incense, provided meals for the śramaṇas, and personally observed the six days of fasting.

Thus, for three years, the four borders were peaceful and tranquil; bandits and thieves completely ceased their activities, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the people suffered neither hunger nor cold.
When the king later reached the end of his life, he was immediately reborn in the second heaven.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The king at that time was myself;
the householder was Śāriputra."
"The one who exhorted the king to observe his kingdom was Ānanda.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of compassion and benevolence in bestowing gifts.
8. [The Jātaka of the Householder Śānta] (8): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great householder named Śānta, whose wealth was beyond counting."

Having beheld the Buddha’s luminous scriptures, he realized that the world is impermanent, that life and its honors cannot be preserved, and that wealth does not belong to oneself; only the merit of giving remains indestructible.
He then addressed the common people, saying:
"If there are those who are poor or in want, let them take as much as they desire."
After several months had passed in this manner,
the administration was lenient and the people were wealthy, with none suffering from a lack of resources.
The seer sighed and reflected, saying:
"I shall simply purchase medicine to provide for and protect the many who are ill.
He immediately procured excellent medicines to save the lives of the multitude; his compassionate nurturing reached everywhere, and his kindness was all-encompassing.

The grace of many years has spread its fragrance afar; sick people from the four quarters hasten here, praising its vast and moistening influence from beginning to end, for his virtue matches that of Heaven.

When his wealth was entirely exhausted, he went out himself to gather treasures. Having traveled more than a hundred li from home, he encountered several carriages on a river carrying those who were gravely ill.
He asked them, "Where are you going?"
He replied, "I shall go to the place where the Immortal Xiantan resides, hoping to preserve my remaining life.
Xiantan immediately returned and borrowed five hundred taels of gold from the king; he purchased medicine with it to treat the patient, and the illness was completely cured.
He had previously gone to sea with merchants to gather treasures, obtaining a vast amount.

Upon returning to his country, he set aside his boat and traveled on foot; being exhausted on the road and lacking water, the Immortal sighed and caused a well of water to appear. He called out for people of equal status to draw the water, while he himself took some to drink.

When the merchants saw the white pearl he had obtained, its brilliance surpassing all others, their greed became especially malignant; they slandered the sage, harmed the benevolent one, and together they pushed the Immortal Xian into the well.
The benevolent virtue of the Bodhisattva moved the spirits and shook the earth; the celestial deities received and supported him so that he suffered no injury.
When the merchants returned to their country, the king asked, "Where has the Rishi Khanda gone?"
He replied,
"I left the state and parted from them, but I do not know where they have gone.
The Master said:
"Did you then kill him? He replied, "No."
The seer sighed as he looked at the empty space beside the well’s opening; following it, he entered the house’s well and, traveling for seven days, reached his own country.
The king asked, “For what reason have you returned empty-handed?”
He replied, "I have not.
The King reflected quietly and said:
"There must be a reason for this!
He summoned the merchant and asked:
"If you truly confess, you shall live; if you lie, you shall die."
They immediately all confessed, and were handed over to the prison for sentencing.
The Immortal sighed and wept; he hurried to the palace gate, prostrating himself with his forehead on the ground to beg for forgiveness.
The King said:
"This contradicts the proper governance.
He then requested again, saying:
"The foolish have inverted views; it is not yet sufficient to hold them fully accountable."
"Tracing it back, it was due to his ignorance.
The King admired the immortal for his benevolent compassion and, considering the merchant's grave offense, issued an order to return the goods.
The merchants all said:
"Xian Tan, how could one who does not serve the Buddha possess such benevolence?
Each then selected a famous treasure to return to him.
Xian Tan accepted half from each, whereupon the merchants prostrated themselves and said:
"Having been preserved by your divine protection, I wish to offer it all back to you.
Thereupon, he accepted it and returned it to the King, who then practiced great acts of charity.

From the King down to his ministers and subjects, they all followed one another’s example in receiving the precepts. Sons were filial and ministers were loyal; the celestial deities provided protection, the land became abundant, and the people lived in peace. The four borders submitted to his virtue, and there was none who did not praise him well.
The Buddha said:
"The seer named Uttara at that time was my own self.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassionate benevolence."
9. [The Jātaka of the Merchant Leader Viśvantara] (IX): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born into one of the four castes; as soon as he touched the ground, he said:
'Among the myriad calamities of sentient beings, I shall deliver them.'"

They have not beheld the deportment of the Buddha, nor have they heard the luminous Dharma; I shall open their eyes and ears, remove their blindness and deafness, and cause them to behold and hear the Unsurpassed, Right, and True—the King of all Sages and the Source of the Luminous Model.
He enticed and encouraged them with gifts until none failed to submit.
His nine relatives were startled and said, "From the beginning of antiquity, we have never heard of an infant speaking such words; could this be the spiritual power of a deva, a nāga, or a spirit?"
"You should divine about this.
He then replied to his parents:
"I have been transformed by the Supreme Sage and embrace the spontaneity of universal illumination; these are not those common demons, so please have no doubts."
Having finished speaking, he fell silent.
His father said, "My son possesses a will as vast and nourishing as heaven and earth; he shall surely not be an ordinary man!"
He named his son Pushi (Universal Giver).

When the boy reached the age of ten, he had mastered all the Buddhist scriptures as well as the various arts and techniques of the secular world; he took leave of his parents to aid the multitude by giving alms to the poor and destitute.
The father said, "I possess the supreme name of greatest merit; you may freely bestow alms upon the many poor.
He replied:
"It is not enough.
He requested to become a śramaṇa, saying:
"Grant me dharma robes, an alms bowl, and a staff; to use these to aid the multitude is my lifelong aspiration."
The mother remembered the vow her son had made at birth and, having no words to refuse him, immediately granted his wish and allowed him to become a śramaṇa.

As he traveled about to teach and transform others, he passed through a great kingdom. In that kingdom there was a man of noble lineage who was also learned in many scriptures. Upon seeing the majestic and radiant countenance of Puṣya, whose nature was serene and pure like celestial gold and who bore the marks of a supreme sage, [the nobleman realized] he would surely become a Hero of the World.
He said to Pushi:
"I have something I wish to tell you; may the Holy One deign to accept it. I have an humble daughter whom I wish to offer for the service of sweeping and winnowing.
He replied:
"Excellent! Wait for me to return.

He then proceeded to the seashore, boarded a vessel to cross the sea, disembarked, and entered the mountains. Reaching a desolate place, he beheld from afar a silver city and palace, radiant and beautiful.
At that time, there was a venomous serpent that had encircled the city seven times; its body was as thick as a hundred spans. Seeing Viśvantara approaching, it raised its head high.
Viśvantara thought to himself:
"This creature harbors poison and must surely have a malicious intent; I shall arouse boundless compassion to neutralize its venom."
“Now, fierceness is fire, and compassion is water. To extinguish fire with water—how could it not be extinguished!

He then sat down and entered the meditative concentration of compassion, vowing: “May all sentient beings quickly leave the eight difficulties; may their minds abandon evil thoughts so they may encounter the Buddha and see the Dharma, meet with the śramaṇas, and hear the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of illumination. May their minds open and their defilements be extinguished, just as I have seen.”
As he gave rise to this concentration of loving-kindness, the snake’s venom was immediately extinguished; it lowered its head and fell asleep.
Viśvantara stepped upon its head and entered the city. Within the city there was a deva who, seeing Viśvantara approaching, spoke with great joy:
"I have long revered your holy virtue, and now that you have come to alight here, my original wish is fulfilled."
"I pray that you will remain for a period of ninety days.
Pushi granted his permission.

The Heavenly King then entrusted the affairs of state to his subordinate ministers and personally provided the meals, maintaining a reverent disposition morning and evening as he received the sublime practices of the Buddhas—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—and the illuminating Dharma for saving sentient beings.
At that time, when the meal was finished, Pushi set out on his journey. The Heavenly King presented him with a single bright moon pearl, saying:
"Carry this pearl with you; its radiance will extend for forty li."
He made this vow: "May my aspirations be fulfilled with every kind of treasure.
When I later attain Buddhahood, may you become my disciple and personally attend at my side.
Pushi replied, "So be it."

He proceeded further and beheld a golden city, its adornments surpassing those of silver; moreover, a venomous serpent encircled the city fourteen times, its massive body twice as large as before and its head raised several fathoms high.
Pushi further contemplated the samādhi of vast compassion; the snake venom was immediately neutralized, and it lowered its head and fell asleep.
As he ascended [the snake] and entered the city, a celestial being beheld Pushi and said with joy:

"I have long admired your spiritual brilliance. It is most excellent that you have alighted here. I pray that you remain for two seasons, one hundred and eighty days; I wish to provide for all your needs, provided only that you leave behind your majestic spiritual power."
He immediately consented, remained to preach for him the unsurpassed clarity of practice, and upon its conclusion, took his leave.
The deva further presented him with a divine pearl that shone for eighty *li*; whatever treasures he desired, they filled the entire distance of those eighty *li*.
"If you attain the Way, I wish to become your disciple, for your spiritual power shall be unsurpassed.

He accepted the divine pearl and immediately continued on his journey. He beheld a city of lapis lazuli, its radiance surpassing that of the previous one; moreover, there was a venomous snake of immense body coiled twenty-one times around the city, with its head raised and eyes glaring at the city gate. [The Bodhisattva] again sat in deep meditation upon the Samādhi of Universal Compassion, vowing to deliver all sentient beings; the poison subsided, and the snake lowered its head.
He ascended it and entered the city.
A celestial being greeted him with words of joy as before, saying, "Please stay for three seasons; I wish to provide for all your needs. When the appointed time had ended, he took his leave;

the deity further presented him with a divine pearl that shone for one hundred and sixty li. Wherever the pearl was located, various treasures followed and filled its luminous sphere. Whatever one desired, there was nothing they could not obtain through their will.
"If you should attain the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true awakening, I vow to become your disciple, possessing the most brilliant wisdom.
He replied,
"Your wish shall surely be fulfilled."
Pushi said regarding the jewel,
"This is sufficient to relieve the destitution of sentient beings," and returned to his former dwelling.
The dragon deities of the ocean all held a council, saying:
"In our great ocean, these three jewels alone are our glory.
Now that the Daoist has obtained them all, what glory shall we have?"
"Though we have lost all other treasures, we have not lost this pearl.
The sea deity transformed into an ordinary man and stood before Pushi, saying, "I have heard that you, O Benevolent One, have obtained a treasure of the world; may I behold it?"
He immediately showed it to him.
The spirit struck his head and seized the pearl. Pushi said:

"I have traversed perilous obstacles and crossed over vast oceans only to obtain this treasure, intending to rescue and relieve the destitution of sentient beings; yet it has been snatched away by this deity?"
He said, "Return my pearl to me; otherwise, I shall dry up your sea.
The Sea God replied:
"What you say is false!
This great ocean is so deep and vast that it is difficult to fathom; who could ever exhaust it?
The sun and moon might fall, and the great winds might be turned back, yet the ocean is as difficult to drain as space is difficult to destroy."

Puśya said: "In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I vowed to attain the power of the Way such that I could overturn the oceans, lift up Mount Sumeru with my finger, shake heaven and earth, and shift other buddha-fields."
The Buddha has granted my resolve and fulfilled my vow; I have now attained it.
Now, you ghosts and spirits with your hair-thin, demonic powers—how could you possibly obstruct my righteous and true momentum?
He then spoke: The sutra says,

"Since I have come from incalculable kalpas ago, the milk I have drunk from my mothers' breasts, the tears I have shed in weeping, and the blood that flowed when my bodies died, would not be contained even by the oceans."
Affection is difficult to sever, and birth-and-death are difficult to bring to an end; yet I still desire to cut off the root of affection and bring the spirit of birth-and-death to a halt.
If I cannot exhaust this task in this life, I shall exhaust it through every successive life.
He immediately stood with his two feet together and, using a ladle, scooped up seawater and cast it beyond the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
A deva named Viśuddha heard of this from afar and reflected deeply within himself:
"In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I heard that this man would fulfill his vow and surely become a World-Honored One to deliver my sentient beings."
The deva immediately descended and assisted in bailing out the water, removing eight-tenths of it.
The ocean deity, filled with regret and fear, said:
"Who is this person?"
"And yet, there is this spirit of the Infinite!
Now that these waters have run dry, my dwelling will be destroyed.
He then brought forth various treasures and emptied all his storehouses to give them away in universal charity.
Viśvantara would not accept it, saying,
"I only wish to have my pearl.
The deities returned his pearl, and Viśvantara returned the water.

Upon returning to his native land, he traveled along the way practicing giving; in every country he passed through, there were no longer any impoverished people. In each of these lands, the rulers did not fail to reform their conduct by adopting the five precepts and ten wholesome actions as the basis of state governance. They opened the prisons and issued great pardons, so that their grace reached all sentient beings, until they finally attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
“The one who was Viśvantara was I myself;
his father was King Śuddhodana.”
The mother was none other than my own mother, Śrīmitrā.
The daughter of the Daoist was none other than Jīvaka.
At that time, the deity within the silver city was none other than the present Ānanda.
The deity in the golden city was Maudgalyāyana;
the deity in the lapis lazuli city was Śāriputra.
For kalpas on end, these bodhisattvas diligently practiced the four debts of gratitude, vowing to seek buddhahood and rescue all sentient beings.
"Thus did the Bodhisattva practice the perfection of giving through his compassionate benevolence. 10.
[The Jātaka of King Dīrghāyu] (10): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king named Dīrghāyu, and his crown prince was named Jīvaka."
That king was compassionate and always harbored a heart of sorrow, taking pity on sentient beings and vowing to deliver them with tireless diligence.
He did not employ the sword or staff, yet his ministers and subjects felt no resentment; winds and rains fell in their proper seasons, and precious grains grew in abundance.
The neighboring small king was of violent and cruel character, making greed and cruelty his law; the country was desolate and the people impoverished. He said to his ministers:
"I have heard that the Land of Longevity is wealthy and abundant, not far from here; its ruler cherishes benevolence and does not kill, nor does he maintain preparations for war."
"I wish to seize it; can it be captured?
The ministers replied, "It can."
He then raised up warriors and reached the borders of the great kingdom.
The frontier officials galloped to report the situation, praying for preparedness.
Chángshòu then assembled his ministers and deliberated, saying:
"That king who comes seeks only the many people, treasures, and wealth of my nation.
If I were to fight him, I would surely cause loss to our people's lives; to benefit oneself while harming the people is greedy and uncompassionate, and I shall not do it."
The ministers all said in unison:
"We have long practiced military strategy and the art of war; we request to destroy it ourselves, so that Your Majesty need not trouble your holy mind.
The King said:

"If we are victorious, they will die; if we are weak, we shall perish. Both their soldiers and our people were nurtured by Heaven; they all value their bodies and cherish their lives—who would be otherwise?"
"To harm the people for the sake of oneself is something the worthy do not do.
The ministers went out and said,
"This ruler of celestial benevolence must not be lost."
He personally marshaled his forces and used his troops to resist the rebels.
Changshou became aware of this and said to the Crown Prince:
"They covet our kingdom and have come here harboring malice."
"The ministers, by means of my single person, wish to destroy the lives of the people.
Now, if I abdicate the state, I may hope to preserve the whole populace.
Is this not righteous?"
The Prince replied, "So be it.
Father and son then leaped over the city wall, immediately changing their names and clans, and went into hiding among the mountain grasses.

Thereupon, King Greed entered the kingdom; the ministers and the common people, having lost their former sovereign, were like filial sons mourning for a parent—their wailing and leaping for joy in grief was such that there was no door where it did not occur.
King Greed offered a reward of a thousand *jin* of gold and ten million coins.

"When Changshou went out and sat beneath a tree by the roadside in deep contemplation, he took pity on the sentient beings who toil in the suffering of birth and death; they do not perceive impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self, and being deluded by desire, their suffering is beyond measure."
A brahmin from a distant land, having heard that the king delighted in giving alms and saving the lives of sentient beings, traveled far to seek refuge and rested beneath a tree.
They greeted one another with inquiries after each other's welfare and each related their respective backgrounds and circumstances.
The brahmin was startled and asked,
"For what reason is the Heavenly King in such a state?
Shedding tears, he spoke of his own circumstances:
"My remaining years are few; therefore, I have come to beg for alms, hoping to preserve my life.
Now that Your Majesty has lost your kingdom, my own life is at its end.
Having said this, he wept with great sorrow.
The king said, "You have come to me in your distress at a time when I myself have lost my kingdom; that I am unable to assist you—is this not painful!
Wiping away his tears, he said:
"I have heard that the new king has offered a very heavy reward for my head; if you take it, you may obtain a great bounty. He replied, "Not so."

From afar, I have admired how the Heavenly King’s benevolence relieves all sentient beings, with its moisture equaling that of Heaven and Earth; therefore, I have left my native land in the hope of attaining salvation for myself.
Now, though you command me to behead me, I dare not obey your decree.
The King said:
"The body is but a decaying vessel; how could one dare to preserve it?
Birth is followed by death; who can remain forever?"
"If you do not take [this child], he will surely turn to ashes and dust.

The Brahmin said, "Your Majesty has spread the grace of celestial benevolence; since you are determined to sacrifice your own life to save one so lowly, I only pray that you release my hands so that I may depart."
The king immediately followed him to the old city gate and ordered him to be bound and brought before him.
When the people of the kingdom saw the king, they wailed with grief, shaking the land;
the brahmin received his reward.
King Greed ordered that he be burned alive at a crossroads.
The ministers petitioned him, saying:
"Our former lord is about to pass away; we beg you to provide a modest meal as an offering for his deceased spirit."
King Greed replied, "So be it.
The officials and the common people were so overcome with grief that they blocked the roads; they leaped and rolled about in mourning, and there was none who did not cry out to Heaven.
The Crown Prince Changsheng also feigned the sale of firewood and stood before his father.
When his father saw him, he looked up to heaven and said:
"To disobey my father’s final instructions, to harbor ferocity and cherish malice, and to harbor deep resentment—bringing calamity for ten thousand years—is not the way of a filial son."

The moisture of the Buddhas' fourfold universal compassion is so vast that its virtue encompasses heaven and earth. Seeking this Way, I would sacrifice my own life to save the multitude; yet I still fear that I may fail to practice even the subtle deeds of filial piety—how much more so for one who commits atrocities and seeks vengeance?
"To not abandon my words may be called filial piety.
The son, unable to bear watching his father die, returned to the deep mountains.
"The King’s life has ended," the Crown Prince cried out in grief, blood flowing from his mouth as he said:
"Although my lord has left instructions to practice benevolence to the end of his life, I must certainly disobey them; I shall execute those who used poison and gall.
He then went out to seek employment, working as a subject to plant vegetables for his master.
While I was strolling through the garden, I observed that the vegetables were exceptionally fine and inquired about the circumstances.
The garden supervisor replied,
"I hired a man from the market who is a master at gardening."
The minister Xian asked,
"Are you capable of all these?
He replied:
"Among the artisans of a hundred crafts, I am the foremost.
The minister then requested that the king order the preparation of a superior meal, one surpassing even those of the Grand Kitchen.
The king said:
"Who prepared this food?
The minister answered with the circumstances.
The king immediately took him and appointed him as the superintendent of the kitchen.
As he was capable in every matter, he was promoted to a high minister, and the king addressed him, saying:
"The Prince of Changshou is my bitter enemy; I now appoint you as a bulwark against him."
He immediately replied, "So be it.
The King said:
"Do you enjoy hunting?
He replied, "I do enjoy it."

The king immediately went out to hunt; as he galloped his horse in pursuit of game, he became separated from his retinue and was left alone with Changsheng for three days in the mountains. Eventually, they grew so hungry and exhausted that the king untied his sword and gave it to Changsheng, then lay down to sleep with his head resting on Changsheng’s lap.
Changsheng said,
"Have you been caught now? He drew his sword,
intending to strike him down, but suddenly remembered his father’s command and said:
"To disobey my father's instruction would be unfilial.
He sheathed his sword and desisted.
The King awoke and said:
"Chushou Mengchang wishes to cut off my head; what shall I do?
[The King] replied:
"The mountains have powerful ghosts who delight in inflicting burning heat; as your servant attends you, what need is there for fear?"
The king lay down again, and this occurred three times. Finally, he threw down his sword and said, "I am your benevolent father; I grant you your life.
The king then awoke and said:
"I saw 'Long Life' in my dream; it is my own life.
The Prince said, "That which is 'Long Life' is this very body of mine."
I now remember my father’s pursuit of vengeance even unto this day.
Yet, as my father was passing away, he left behind a benevolent admonition, instructing me to follow the path of the Buddhas’ forbearance—to meet evil with goodness.
Yet I possess a nature of extreme folly and wished to pour two poisons upon one another.
Having reflected three times upon my father’s admonition, I have thrice laid down my sword.
I pray that Your Majesty will swiftly eliminate this grievous affliction; when the body dies and the spirit departs, no evil intent shall remain.
The king repented his error, saying:
"I have been violent and tyrannical, failing to distinguish between the good and the bad.
Your late father’s lofty conduct was pure and complete; though the state perished, his integrity did not perish—he may truly be called a supreme sage!"
If you preserve your father and complete your conduct, you may truly be called filial!
I am a wolf or a jackal who would ruin my life merely to satisfy my appetite; now that your life rests with me, I have pardoned you rather than executing you—how could I ever go back on this?
"Now I wish to return to my country; by which path shall I go?
He replied, "That which causes confusion regarding the Way is my own doing."
He led the king out of the forest to meet with his ministers.
The king asked:
"Gentlemen, do you know of one who has attained immortality?"
They all replied,
"We do not know.
The King said:
"This is indeed the way to attain longevity!
Now that you have returned to your kingdom, I shall return to my own abode.
From this day forward, let us be brothers; we shall share equally in both misfortune and fortune."
On the day the crown prince was installed, throughout the land grief and joy were mingled; all offered congratulations on his longevity.
King Trana returned to his kingdom, where subjects again presented offerings to one another, leading the realm to a state of great prosperity and peace.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The King Dīrghāyu at that time was I myself;
the crown prince was Ānanda."
The greedy king was Devadatta.
Throughout successive lifetimes, Devadatta harbored poisonous intentions toward me, yet I always rescued him.
Ānanda and Devadatta had no prior enmity; therefore, they did not harm one another.

Throughout my successive lifetimes, I have endured what is unbearable, restraining my mind and establishing my conduct; therefore, I have now attained Buddhahood as the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Giving through compassionate benevolence.
The Compendium of the Six Pāramitās, Volume One.
The Compendium of the Six Pāramitās, Volume Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of Kangju during the Wu Dynasty.
Chapter on the Perfection of Giving: This consists of four sections. 11. The Sūtra of King Pāyāsa [The Jātaka of King Pāyāsa] (11).

The Sūtra of King Pāyāsa: "In the past, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Pāyāsa. He governed the kingdom with benevolence; weapons were laid aside, the use of the staff and cane ceased, and prisons were demolished. There were no cries of lamentation on the roads, and all living beings found their proper place. The land was abundant and the people flourished, so that the various devas praised his benevolence."

The royal city was four hundred li in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand six hundred li. Every day the king provided meals for the people within it, all according to their wishes.
When neighboring countries heard that his kingdom was abundant and its calamities had been extinguished, they consulted with their ministers, saying:
"That country is prosperous and its myriad people are wealthy and happy; we wish to seize it, for if we go there, we will surely conquer it."
The ministers and ladies all said,
"We joyfully follow the King's wish," and they immediately raised an army and marched upon the kingdom of Ren.
"The ministers of your benevolent state have reported this, wishing to resist them.
Your benevolent king, however, said with a sorrowful countenance:

'To slay the bodies of ten million people for the sake of my single person, or to cripple the lives of ten million people to preserve my single life—is it worth contending with the times over a single mouthful of food twice a day or a few garments for one body?'"
Shall I discard the virtue of spring and adopt the cruelty of jackals and wolves?
I would rather forfeit the lives of a single generation than abandon my great resolve; to extend compassion to oneself and bring peace to all living beings is surely the benevolence of Heaven.
The Regent said to his ministers, "Each of you withdraw;
we shall deliberate further tomorrow.
That night, he scaled the city wall and fled into the mountains, where he sat beneath a tree.
"A brahmin came, sixty years of age, and asked the king:
'Is that benevolent king well and free from ailment?
He replied:"
"The king has already passed away.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin fell to the ground in a state of profound grief.
The king asked him:
"How profound is your compassion?
He replied, "I have heard that the King’s benevolence extends to all living beings and his grace is like that of Śakra; therefore, I have hastened here to take refuge."
"But now that he has perished, I am old and destitute.
The King said,
"That benevolent king was none other than I."
When the king of a neighboring country heard that my kingdom was prosperous and abundant, its people numerous, and its treasures plentiful, he commanded his warriors, saying:
"To whoever captures my head, I shall grant a reward of one thousand male and female servants, one thousand horses, one thousand oxen, and one thousand pounds each of gold and silver."
"Now, take my head, along with the golden crown and sword as clear evidence, and go to that king; you shall receive a great reward, which can serve as a legacy for your descendants."
"My heart is filled with joy.
He replied,
"To act unrighteously and oppose the Way— I would rather die than do so."
The king said, "This old man relied upon me for his livelihood; how could I let him fall into poverty?
I shall now bestow my head upon you, so that you may be free from guilt."
Rising up, he prostrated himself toward the ten directions and, shedding tears, made this vow:
"For those among the multitudes of living beings who are in peril, I shall bring them peace;
for those who turn their backs on the Truth and follow what is false, I shall cause them to take refuge in the Triple Gem."
"Now, by using my head to extricate your son from his peril, I shall ensure that you remain free of guilt.
Having said this, he drew his sword and offered to sacrifice himself to rescue the other from his distress.
The Brahmin then took his head and the sword and went to the king's presence. The king questioned his former minister:
"How could the benevolent king’s power, which was sufficient to match a thousand men, have been captured by this son?
The former ministers prostrated themselves, falling to the ground, so overcome with grief and pain that they were unable to respond.
He questioned the brahmin further, who then related the matter from beginning to end.
The common people leaped in the streets and wailed in the alleys; some spat out blood, while others collapsed with their breath cut off, staring like corpses.
From that king down to his ministers and warriors, there was not one, great or small, who did not wail in grief.
The king looked up to heaven and sighed deeply, saying:
"I am indeed without the Way!"
"Can Tian is a benevolent son.

He took the corpse and head of Renwang, joined them together with gold leaf, and placed the body seated upon the throne. He served as the Son of Heaven for thirty-two years, after which he established his son as king.
"The neighboring countries did not fail to cherish him as their own child.
When this benevolent king’s life ended, he was reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The benevolent king was I myself.
The king of the neighboring country was Maudgalyāyana.
The ministers of that kingdom are the bhikṣus here today."
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving through his compassionate benevolence. 12.

The Sūtra of the King of Vārāṇasī [The Jātaka of King Kālaṅga] (12) "The Sūtra of the King of Vārāṇasī: Long ago, the crown prince of the King of Vārāṇasī was named Kālaṅga. There were two brothers; when their father, the king, passed away, they offered to abdicate the kingdom to one another, yet there was no one to whom it could be entrusted."
The elder brother took his wife and fled deep into the mountains to study the Way, settling by the banks of a river.

At that time, there was a criminal from another country whose hands and feet had been severed and his nose and ears cut off by the state’s administration; he was cast into a ruined boat and set adrift upon the current.
The sinners cried out to Heaven in unceasing succession.
Hearing this, the Daoist was moved to sorrow and spoke with deep lamentation:
"Who are these people?"
His distress was most extreme.
Now, to extend great compassion and self-forgiveness, risking one's own life to rescue the perils of all living beings—this is the vocation of a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

He threw himself into the water, surging against the waves and cutting through the current to pull the boat to the shore. Carrying it back to his dwelling, he nurtured and protected it with diligent care until the wound healed and its life was restored.
For four years she nurtured him with compassion and never grew weary.
Her wife was promiscuous and knew no bounds, consorting with criminals and plotting to murder her husband, saying:
"If you kill him, I shall live with you."
The criminal said, "That man is a worthy one; how could I kill him?
His wife spoke as she had before, and the criminal said:
"I have no hands or feet; I cannot kill him," [the husband] said.
His wife replied, "Sit down, sir; I have my own plan."
Feigning a headache, she said to her husband:
"This must be the work of a mountain spirit; I wish to dispel it.
Tomorrow, I shall follow you to seek blessings."
The husband replied, "Excellent!
The next day they set out for a mountain ridge forty *li* high, with three sides rising like sheer walls; all who beheld it were struck with fear.
The wife said, "According to the ritual method, you, my son, stand facing the sun while I perform the sacrifice.
The husband immediately faced the sun; his wife then feigned circumambulating him several times before pushing him over the mountain.

Halfway up the mountain there was a tree with leaves that were dense, thick, and soft; the Daoist climbed its branches and stood upon them, and by eating the sweet and delicious fruits of the tree, he preserved his life.
Beside the tree was a tortoise that also ate fruit daily; seeing a person at the tree, it feared him and did not dare approach.
After five days of hunger, it ventured out to seek the fruit; neither was harmed, and they eventually drew near to one another.
The Daoist leaped up and mounted the tortoise, causing it to startle and leap down to the ground;
the heavenly deities protected them, so that neither was harmed.
He then returned to his native country, where his younger brother yielded the kingdom to him.
The elder brother, exercising great compassion by extending to others the same leniency he shows himself, rescued and sustained all living beings.

When the king governed his kingdom, he practiced giving from sunrise; within four hundred li, people, carriages, horses, various treasures, and food were provided freely, and he bestowed such benevolent nourishment upon those in the east, west, south, and north.
The King’s fame and merit were renowned throughout the world, and his virtue was praised in the ten directions.
His wife believed her husband was dead; since no one in the country recognized her, she carried her husband—who sat upon a wooden stump—into the kingdom and declared:

"Since we were bound in marriage, our family has encountered the decay and chaos of the age, and my person has become withered and ruined. Having received the compassionate kindness of the Heavenly King, I have come to beg for alms."
The people of the country admired him for this and instructed him, saying:
"The Heavenly King is universally compassionate, nurturing all living beings; tomorrow he shall go out through the eastern gate to practice giving."
"If you oppose him, I shall value your virtuous conduct and surely bestow many rewards upon you.
The next day, he begged from the king; the king silently took note of this and related the full background of his wife to his ministers.
One minister said,
"We should burn it.
Another minister said:
"Execute him! The Minister of Justice replied:
"Indeed, there is no crime greater than abandoning the righteous and entering into depravity, committing acts of rebellion and perversity."
"Let us nail the malevolent man to the back of the female sorceress so that she must carry him forever.
The ministers all said, "Excellent!"
"By following what they prefer, one's governance becomes clearly manifest.
The King transformed the people through the ten wholesome deeds, and there were none who did not rejoice and revere him.
The King, along with his ministers and subjects, was reborn in the heavens for the rest of their lives.
"The criminal couple died and entered hell.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was myself."
The sinner was Devadatta; his wife was the woman Huaiwan.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassion and kindness.

13. The Sāhvanta-rāja Sūtra [The Jātaka of King Sāhvanta] (13) The Sāhvanta-rāja Sūtra: "In the past, there was a king named Sāhvanta, which is explained as 'One Who Gives All. Whatever was requested of him, he never went against the wishes of others."
His practice of giving was such that the king’s name spread throughout the eight directions, known by all without exception.
At that time, Mañjuśrī wished to go and test him; he transformed himself into a young Brahmin and approached the gate of the royal palace from a foreign land, saying to the gatekeeper:
"I have come from afar, wishing to see the Great King."
At that time, the gatekeeper reported these words to the king.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately went out to welcome him, like a son seeing his father; he prostrated himself before him and invited him to be seated.
He inquired after him, saying:
"Whence have you come, O practitioner?
Having traveled these roads, I trust you are not fatigued?"
Śyāmaka said:
"I was in another country when I heard of the King’s virtues, so I have come to see you; now I wish to beg for alms.
The King said:
"Excellent! Regarding that which you wish to obtain, do not harbor any doubt or hesitation.
My name now is 'The Giver of All'; what is it that you seek?"
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not want anything else; I wish to have the king's body as my slave, and the king's queen as my maidservant."
"If you can do so, then follow me.
The king was greatly pleased and replied, "Excellent!"
"My own person can certainly be obtained; I wish to belong to you, O man of the Way, to serve and attend to your every command.
As for his wife, she is the daughter of a great king; we should go and inquire of her."
Then the king entered and said to his wife:

"There is now a man of the Way, young and handsome, who has come from afar wishing to beg for my person to serve as a slave; he now further seeks you as well to be his maidservant. What should we do?"
The queen asked,
"What was the King’s reply?
The king said:
"I have already consented to make him my slave; I have not yet consented to you.
Then the lady said, "The King has abandoned me, and you alone have gained your advantage, yet you do not consider to deliver me."
At that time, the queen immediately followed the king out and said to the practitioner,
"I pray that you may accept my person to serve as your attendant.
Then the brahmin spoke again to the king:
"Is this truly so?
I wish now to depart.
The king addressed the practitioner, saying:
"I have given alms throughout my life without ever having regretted it; I have received them only from those who follow the Way. Śreṇika said:
"You must follow me, all of you barefoot and not wearing sandals; you must act according to the law of slaves and not fail to cover yourselves."
The King and his consort both replied,
"Yes, we obey.
We shall follow your instructions and dare not disobey your command."
At that time, the brahmin took his slaves and servants and departed on the road.
Mañjuśrī then manifested transformation-beings to take the places of the king and the queen, managing the affairs of state so that they remained as they were before.

"The King's consort was originally the daughter of a great king; she was peerless in her beauty, with hands and feet so soft and supple that, having been raised in the deep palace, she had never experienced cold or hardship."

Furthermore, she was heavily pregnant for several months; as she followed the master on foot, her entire body ached, and with the soles of her feet wounded and bleeding, she could no longer proceed, falling far behind from sheer exhaustion.
Then the brahmin looked back and scolded her, saying:
"Now that you have become a maidservant, you should behave according to the manner of a maidservant; you must not maintain the demeanor you had in your former life."
The lady knelt upright and said,
"I dare not!
I have merely become slightly exhausted and am staying here to rest."
He shouted, "Come quickly! Hurry and follow behind me!
They proceeded to the marketplace of the kingdom and sold the slaves separately, each going their own way with their respective master at a distance of several li.
"At that time, a householder purchased this slave and made him guard this house; he was ordered to collect taxes from all those who buried things there and was not permitted to act otherwise.
As for the maidservant, her mistress was extremely jealous and compelled her to work from dawn until night without a moment's rest."
A few days later, the maidservant gave birth to a son; the lady, filled with rage, said, "You are but a servant—how could you have such a child?
She ordered him to be seized and killed immediately.
Following the master's instructions, she immediately killed her son, carried him away, and buried him.
She then went to where the slave was and, upon meeting him, said:
"I gave birth to a son today, but he has already died."
"I did not bring any money; can we now simply bury him here in Tang?
The servant replied, "The master is in great haste!"
"Those who have heard of this will hold me in no small measure of blame.
Your Majesty, take her away at once and seek another location; she must not remain here.
Although the King and his consort were thus able to see one another, they did not speak of their hardships, and each harbored no resentment toward the other.

In the brief moment it took for these words to be spoken, everything became as if in a fleeting dream; the king and his consort naturally found themselves back in their own kingdom, seated upon the main throne of the inner palace exactly as before, with no difference. All the ministers, the ladies of the harem, and the court attendants were likewise restored to their former states, and the newborn prince was also naturally restored to life.
The king and his queen felt doubt within their hearts, wondering by what cause this had come to pass.
Then Mañjuśrī appeared in the air, seated upon a lotus flower made of the seven precious gems, manifesting his physical form and features, and praised them, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Now your generosity is as sincere as this.
The king and his consort leaped for joy and immediately prostrated themselves before him.

Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma for them; the three thousandfold world-system shook violently, and all the people of the kingdom were covered by this event, each of whom gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. At that moment, the king and his consort attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The king at that time was none other than myself.
The queen at that time is now Sujātā."
"The Prince at that time was none other than Rāhula now.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

In my past lives, I practiced giving in this manner; for the sake of all people, I did not begrudge even my own body or life, and throughout countless kalpas, I felt no resentment or regret, nor did I harbor any hope for worldly glory, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment by myself.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving through the power of his compassionate benevolence. 14.

The Sūtra of Sudāna [The Jātaka of Prince Sudāna] (14) The Sūtra of Sudāna: "In the past, there was a king of the kingdom of Śrāvastī named Śibi; he governed the realm with righteousness, and the common people harbored no resentment."

The king had a crown prince named Sudāna, whose countenance and deportment illuminated the world; his compassion and filial piety were beyond compare, he protected all beings with the four immeasurables, and his speech never caused harm to others.
The king had a son whom he cherished immeasurably; the crown prince served his parents as if they were celestial beings.

When he reached the age of understanding, he made this vow: "I constantly wish to practice giving to rescue and deliver all living beings, so that in my future lives I may receive inexhaustible blessings."
The fool does not perceive the transformation of impermanence and claims that things can be preserved;
the wise person illuminates the five families [of transmigration] and thus prizes the practice of giving.
"The Buddhas of the ten directions, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Arhats—all praise giving as the world’s most precious treasure.
Thereupon, the Prince expanded his universal charity, extending its benefits to all sentient beings.

To those who desired clothing or food, he granted them at the mere sound of their request; as for gold, silver, various treasures, carriages, horses, fields, and houses, there was nothing he would not give upon being asked.
