His radiant fame spread afar, and throughout the four seas, all sighed in admiration.

The father king possessed a white elephant, fierce and martial in its power, capable of throwing down sixty other elephants; whenever a hostile kingdom came to wage war, this elephant invariably achieved victory.
The kings deliberated and said:
"The crown prince is a sage and worthy one, who bestows his bounty upon all who seek it."
He dispatched eight Brahmins to the Prince’s residence, ordering them to beg for the white elephant.
"If you can obtain it," he said, "I shall reward you handsomely.

Having received their orders, they set out immediately; clad in deer skins, wearing sandals, and carrying water jars and staffs, they traveled far across many provinces and commanderies for over a thousand li until they reached the kingdom of Yebha. There, they all leaned on their staffs and stood before the palace gate with one foot raised, addressing the guards:
"I have heard that the Crown Prince bestows alms upon the poor and needy, extending his grace to all living beings; therefore, he has traveled from afar to beg for what I lack.
The guards immediately entered and reported the matter to the King as it had occurred.
Upon hearing this, the Crown Prince joyfully galloped out to meet him; like a son beholding his father, he prostrated himself at his feet and comforted him, saying, "From where have you come?
How is your body faring?"
"Would you stand on one foot for as long as it takes to seek what you desire?

He replied, "The Prince’s radiant virtue is heard throughout the eight directions; it reaches upward to the azure heavens and downward to the Yellow Springs. Majestic as Mount Tai, there is no one who does not sigh in admiration."
"You are the son of gods and men; whatever you utter must be true.
If you truly cherish the practice of giving and do not go against the wishes of the multitude, I now wish to beg for the white elephant that walks upon lotuses, whose name is Rājavṛṣabha."
The Prince said: "Excellent!
You may take as much gold, silver, and various treasures as you desire; do not hesitate."
He immediately commanded his attendant to quickly saddle a white elephant with a gold and silver harness and bring it forth.
Holding the elephant’s harness in his left hand and a golden pitcher in his right, he washed the brahmin’s hands and, with compassionate joy, presented him with the elephant.
The brahmin was greatly delighted; having finished his incantations and prayers, he mounted the elephant together with the others and departed with a smile.
The Chancellor and the hundred ministers were all filled with regret, and they said in unison:
"This elephant is a paragon of fierce strength; the state relies upon it for its peace. When enemies engage in battle, it invariably causes them to tremble and flee."
"Now that you have bestowed this upon a hostile nation, what will we rely upon?
They all appeared before him and said:
"As for the white elephant, its strength is capable of throwing sixty elephants; it is the treasure of this kingdom used to repel the enemy."

Yet the Crown Prince honors his enemies with such great kindness that the royal treasury is depleted day by day; the Prince bestows gifts at will without ceasing, and within a few years, we ministers fear that the wives and children of the entire kingdom will surely become objects for his charity.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with sorrow for a long time and said:
"The Crown Prince delights in the Buddha-way; providing for the destitute and aiding the needy, he compassionately nurtures all living beings—this is the foremost of his practices."
"Even if they were to prohibit it or even detain and punish them, this would be an act of unrighteousness.
The hundred ministers all said, "The teachings of refinement and admonition have not been lost; to detain and punish them would be cruelty—how could we, your ministers, dare to hear of such a thing?"
"Drive him out of the country and place him in the wilderness; that within ten years he may feel shame and repent is our wish.
The King immediately dispatched a messenger to address him, saying:
"The elephant is a national treasure; why do you seek to harm your benefactor?"
"I cannot bear to inflict punishment upon him; I shall depart from this country with haste.
The messenger, having received these instructions, delivered the message accordingly.
The Prince replied:
"I dare not disobey the mandate of Heaven.
I pray that you grant me seven days of alms to relieve my destitution; then I shall leave the country with no regrets.
The messenger reported this to the king, who said:
"Leave at once; I will not permit you to stay.
The messenger returned and said, "The King's command cannot be disobeyed."
The Prince spoke again:
"I dare not disobey the mandate of Heaven.
I possess private wealth and shall not venture to encroach upon the state's resources."
When the messenger heard this again, the king immediately granted his request.
The prince joyfully commanded his attendants:

"Should there be any among the common people in the kingdom who are impoverished or in need, urge them to come quickly; let them have their desires fulfilled to their heart's content, without any hindrance."
"Kingdoms, official ranks, fields, houses, wealth, and treasures—all things such as these, like illusions and dreams, shall without exception perish.

Thereupon, the myriad people, both great and small, rushed to the palace gate; the Prince, having bestowed food, drink, clothing, and the various rarities of the seven treasures according to the people's desires, completed his acts of charity so that the poor were all made wealthy.

His wife was named Manjī, the daughter of various kings; her countenance was radiant and brilliant, peerless in the entire land, and from head to foot she was adorned with necklaces of the seven treasures.
He said to his wife:
"Arise and listen to my words. The Great King has banished me to Mount Tāṇḍya, with a limit of ten years.
Do you understand?"
The wife rose in alarm and, seeing the Prince with tears falling from his eyes, said:
"What crime have you committed that you are thus driven away, abandoning the dignity and glory of the kingdom to dwell in the deep mountains?"
He answered his wife, saying:
"Because my acts of giving have exhausted the resources of the kingdom, and because I gave away the war-elephant, a treasure, to an enemy,
the King and his ministers have driven me out in anger."
The wife then made this aspiration:

"May the land be abundant with harvests, and may the king, his ministers, and the myriad people enjoy boundless wealth and longevity; may you alone resolve to attain the Way in those mountain marshes through your great vows."
The Prince said:
"Only in those mountain marshes and places of terror are tigers, wolves, and predatory beasts difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, there are venomous insects, *wangliang* spirits, and murderous ghosts, as well as thunderbolts, lightning, wind, rain, clouds, and mist; these are most truly fearsome."
When cold and heat become excessive, trees provide little shelter; thorns and pebbles are not for you to endure.

You are the son of a king, born in splendor and raised within the inner palace; your garments have been fine and soft, your food sweet and delicious, your bed was draped with curtains and canopies, your ears were filled with manifold music, and your every wish was granted according to your heart’s desire.
"Now that we dwell in the mountains and marshes, sleeping on straw mats and eating only fruits and gourds—this is something no one could endure; how can you bear it?
His wife replied, "What benefit do fine silks, precious jewels, curtains, and sweet delicacies bring to oneself?"
"Are you living in separation from the Crown Prince?

When the Great King goes forth, he takes the banner as his sign; fire takes smoke as its sign; and women take their husbands as their sign. I rely upon the Crown Prince as a child relies upon its parents. While the Crown Prince was in the kingdom bestowing gifts upon those far and wide, I always shared in that same aspiration."
Now that you must traverse these perilous passes yet still remain here to guard your glory—is this truly the way of benevolence?
Should there be one who comes to beg for your life and does not behold his father, his heart will be so utterly shattered that he will surely die; of this there is no doubt.
The Prince said:
"A man from a distant land has come to beg for my wife and children;
I have no heart to refuse him. Yet you, out of affection, might oppose this path of grace, thereby severing great benefit and destroying my heavy responsibility."
The wife said, “The Prince’s generosity is rare in this world; you must fulfill your great vow and be careful not to grow weary.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, no one like you shall attain the heavy responsibility of Buddhahood; I dare not disobey you.”
The Prince said,
"Very well!
He then took his wife and children to see his mother for leave, prostrating himself on the ground and bidding her farewell with deep compassion, saying:

"I pray that you will set aside these grave reflections and preserve the safety of your precious person. State affairs are already overwhelming; I hope you will frequently accept my compassionate admonitions and not, in the name of personal freedom, wrong those subjects of Heaven.
You must endure what is difficult to endure, holding patience as your treasure."

Upon hearing these parting words, the mother looked back at her attendants and said, "My body is like stone and my heart is as hard as steel; yet now that I have this one son who is being driven away, what heart do I have left?"

Before I had a son, I made a vow to seek an heir; on the day I conceived, it was like a tree holding its blossoms, for which I daily awaited its fruition. May Heaven not frustrate my vow and grant me this child; now that he has been nurtured to maturity, must I be separated from him at birth?
The ladies of the court and their attendants, those who were jealous, felt joy at this and no longer showed him respect.

The Crown Prince’s wife and children prostrated themselves and withdrew; from the highest officials to the lowliest within the palace, none failed to choke with emotion. As he went out to bid a sorrowful farewell to the ministers and the common people, they all departed the city together, each whispering to themselves:
"The Crown Prince is the spiritual sage of the nation and the most honored among all treasures; what heart could his parents have that they should banish him?"
The Crown Prince sat outside the city to bid farewell to those who had come to see him off, and sent them back to their homes.
The myriad people prostrated themselves and collectively wailed; some leaped about in grief and cried out to heaven, the sound of their lamentation shaking the kingdom.
Accompanied by his wife, he proceeded on the road; realizing he was far from his native country, he sat beneath a tree.

A brahmin came from afar to beg, so he took off his precious garments and gave them, as well as the pearls and jewels of his wife, bestowing them all upon him. He then had his wife mount the carriage and, holding the reins himself, they departed.
Just as he was about to set out on his journey, he encountered a brahmin who came to beg for his horse;
he gave the horse to him and pulled the cart himself from the axle to proceed on the road.
Again, he encountered a brahmin who came to beg for his cart; he immediately brought down his wife and children and gave the cart to him.

The Prince’s chariots, horses, robes, furs, personal treasures, and miscellaneous belongings were all exhausted without remainder; he left his wife and infant daughter behind while he himself carried their son.

During his time in the kingdom, he had bestowed upon others famous elephants, various precious chariots, and horses; yet when he was met with ruin and exile, he never felt resentment or regret, but followed along with a harmonious mind, entering the mountains with joy.
After twenty-one days—three times seven—he arrived at Mount Dantaka.

The Prince beheld the mountain’s trees and vegetation in full bloom, with flowing springs, fine water, and an abundance of sweet fruits; wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks frolicked among them, while hundreds of birds warbled in harmony with plaintive cries.
The Crown Prince beheld this and said to his wife:

"Behold these mountains; their trees reach toward the heavens with few broken or injured branches. Flocks of birds cry out in sorrow, and there are springs at every spot, with an abundance of fruit for food and drink.
Let us devote ourselves solely to the Way, so as not to violate our vow."
The mountain recluses all maintained their integrity and delighted in learning; among them was a recluse named Ajita, who had long dwelt in the mountains and possessed profound and wondrous virtue.
He immediately went with his wife and children to visit him, prostrated himself, and then stood with palms joined, addressing the Daoist:
"I have brought my wife and children here to study the Way; I pray that you will bestow upon us your great compassion and instruct us so that we may fulfill our aspirations."

The Daoist instructed him, and the Prince followed his example: he built a hut of brushwood and grass, bound his hair in a topknot, and wore coarse garments; he ate fruit and drank from mountain springs.
The son was named Yeli, who wore small grass robes and accompanied his father in and out;
the daughter was named Jienayen, who wore a deer-skin robe and accompanied her mother in and out.
While staying overnight in the mountains, the heavens caused springs to swell with water of profound sweetness, and medicinal trees and famous fruits grew lush and abundant.

Later, there was an old and poor brahmin named Kauṇḍinya; his wife was advanced in years, yet her complexion was radiant and her features were upright and beautiful as she carried a pitcher to draw water.
On the road, he encountered a young man who blocked his path and taunted him, saying:
"You live in poverty and have nothing with which to sustain yourself; you covet that old man's wealth in the hope of having a place to settle.
That elder studies the Way, yet internally he is obstructed and lacks penetration; regarding the principles of transformation and instruction, he hopes to bring but a single person to completion."
You are exclusively foolish and obstinate; what is it that you covet?

Your facial features are ugly and dark, your nose is flat and crooked, your body is contorted, your face is wrinkled and your lips are pursed [dīng], your speech is stammering, and both eyes are blue; your appearance is like that of a ghost. With nothing good about your entire person, who would not loathe you?
"As you have become a householder, will you not feel shame or weariness?
When the wife heard her husband's teasing, she shed tears and said,
"I see that old man’s beard and hair are pure white, like frost upon the trees."
"Day and night I have directed my heart toward this, wishing for his early death.
Since he has not yet yielded to my wish, there is nothing I can do.
She returned to her husband and recounted the matter in full, saying:
"You have male servants to employ, yet you do not send your concubines to fetch water.
If things remain as they are now, I shall leave you.
Her husband said:
"I am poor; might I obtain employment as an attendant?
His wife said, "I have heard that the Supreme Being of Almsgiving named Sudāna is exhausting his kingdom with vast compassion to save the multitudes."
"The king and his ministers shall be exiled to the mountains.
As for his two sons, I will grant them to you as alms.

Although his wife had spoken these words many times, he found it difficult to go against his love for her; thus, he followed her advice and went to the kingdom of Yebapo, where he approached the palace gate and said:
"Is the Crown Prince at peace?
the guards reported upon hearing this.
When the King heard these words, his heart was constricted and his mind blocked; tears flowed profusely as he said after a moment:
"The Crown Prince was driven away solely because of these people;
how is it that they have come back now?
Please show us some hospitality and ask them why they have returned."
He replied, "The Prince’s virtue is so fragrant that those far and near sing his praises; therefore we have come from afar to take refuge in him, hoping for our own relief.
The King said:
"The Prince has exhausted his treasury of jewels in almsgiving; now dwelling in the deep mountains, he lacks even sufficient food and clothing. With what, then, can you bestow upon me?

He replied, "Your virtue is most lofty and sublime; from afar I have exhausted myself in longing for it. To behold your radiant countenance is my noble fortune, and I shall have no regrets until the end of my days."
The king sent men to show him the way. On the road,
he encountered a hunter who said,
"As you have traveled through these mountains, have you perhaps seen the Prince?"
The hunter, who had long known the reasons for the Prince’s exile, suddenly burst out with a curse:
"I shall cut off your head! What do you know of the Prince?
The brahmin, filled with shame and fear, said:
"I shall surely be killed by you!
I must seize the opportunity and deceive you. He said:
"The King and his ministers have sent word to summon the Crown Prince to return to the kingdom to serve as king.
He replied, "Very well!"
Pleased, he pointed out the location.
"In the distance they saw a small hut, and the Prince also beheld them approaching.
Upon seeing him, the two boys were struck with inner terror, and both brothers said:"
"Our father was fond of giving, and now this man has come; our wealth is exhausted and there is nothing left to match it, so he will surely bestow us brothers upon him.
With these words, they took each other's hands and fled together.
The mother intentionally dug a pit large enough to contain a person; the two children entered it and covered themselves with firewood on top, warning each other:
"If our father calls, do not answer."
The Prince looked up and questioned him, inviting him to sit before him and placing fruit juice before him.
After he had finished eating the fruit and drinking, the Prince comforted him, saying:
"You must be exhausted from traveling such a long distance!"
He replied:
"I have come from that place with my entire body in agony, and I am also greatly hungry and thirsty.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“In the past, there was a king named Sādhūmukha. The king practiced benevolence and impartiality, loving his people as if they were his own children; he ruled the country with the True Dharma, so that the people harbored no resentment.”

That kingdom was vast with many prefectures and counties; its borders were flourishing, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the land was free from calamities and pestilence. The lifespan of its people was eighty thousand years.

King Harmony-Silence issued clear edicts throughout the palace, instructing the queen, noble ladies, the hundred officials, attendants, and ministers who upheld the fundamental principles to govern their respective jurisdictions according to the True Dharma.

The King constantly regards all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness, feeling compassion for those who, out of folly and delusion, fall into madness and perversity. He seeks to preserve the source of the Way, and his joy knows no bounds; he protects and pities sentient beings like Śakra, Lord of Devas. Such evils as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, frivolous chatter, jealousy, anger, and ignorance—none of these wicked things remain in his mind.

Be filial and obedient to one’s parents and respectful and affectionate toward one’s nine relations; seek out and follow the worthy, honor and revere the sages, and have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the words of the śramaṇas. Believe that good brings blessing and evil brings calamity; through such loyalty and integrity, practice these ten wholesome dharmas clearly within yourself.

I further command the empresses and consorts down to the humble concubines that they all shall honor and uphold these teachings, leading one another toward goodness; let this be proclaimed to the officials and citizens of the four frontiers, great and small alike, so that all may wear the scriptures upon their persons, recite them, hold them in their hearts, and practice them.

"In a state there are those who are poor; unable to endure their destitution, they lose their sense of propriety and commit theft. If the owner of the property catches them, he shall report the matter to the King.

"Those among my people who are hungry, it is I who have starved them; those among my people who are cold, it is I who have left them naked."
He spoke again, saying, "My power is such that I can ensure there are no poor people in this land; the happiness or suffering of the people rests with me alone.

The entire nation is harmonious and joyful; the whip and staff are not employed; enemies submit as vassals; weapons of war rot in their arsenals; prisons hold no prisoners; the people acclaim this goodness, saying, "How fortunate we are to have been born in such a time!"

16. The Discourse on the Four Castes (16). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the families of the four castes suffered the calamities of their past karma; they were so impoverished and distressed that they lived upon grass mats and grass seats, subsisting on a gruel of vegetables.

Although they were in extreme hardship, their feet never trod upon the dwellings of the unrighteous, nor did their hands accept the gifts of the unrighteous. Their will and conduct were pure, and no multitude of evils could defile their minds.

Receiving instructions in the morning and discussing them in the evening, he never ceased reciting the sutras and precepts from his mouth. Praised by the World-Honored One and revered by the wise, although he could not provide sufficient clothing or food for his own body and mouth, he served the holy assembly with whatever vegetables, gruel, and straw mats his household possessed, never neglecting this for even a single day.
The śramaṇas said:
"The four castes are impoverished and often have the appearance of hunger; we must not accept their regular offerings.

The Sūtras state that a śramaṇa maintains the truth with a single mind, is complete in precepts, and is lofty in conduct; his will is like celestial gold, he prizes neither wealth nor beauty but regards only the Sūtras as treasure, and because he has severed the six types of hunger, he vows to eliminate poverty. Why should he feel ashamed to go on alms-rounds and not practice them?"
Together they went to where the Buddha was and related the matter from beginning to end.
The World-Honored One remained silent.
On a later day, the four castes went in person to the vihāra; having prostrated themselves, they sat to one side.
The Buddha, mindful of the matter previously reported by the śramaṇas, asked the four castes:
"Do you daily provide compassionate offerings and support to the bhikṣus?
They replied:
"Indeed it is so.
Our household provides daily offerings, yet we regret our poverty; with only vegetable gruel and straw mats, we have unworthily burdened the Holy and Wise One with our silence.
The World-Honored One said:

"The practice of giving depends solely upon four mental states: directing a mind of loving-kindness toward others, following them with compassion, rejoicing in their attainment of liberation, and protecting and rescuing all sentient beings."

Although their giving was meager, the two realms in which they were subsequently born—among gods and among humans—were constant; their wishes were spontaneously fulfilled, and regarding the objects of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—fine garments for the body and the mind—they were always joyful and never feared lack.
If one gives meager offerings and their heart is not joyful, yet later obtains blessings, these will be meager among blessings.
Though they may attain official rank and the seven treasures, they find no cause for glory;

dwelling in such meagerness, their hearts remain stingy and parsimonious, not daring to eat or wear fine clothing. They are anxious and uneasy, never knowing joy; with hungry bellies and cold bodies, they resemble beggars. Their lives are lived in vain and they die in vain, having no good deeds to protect themselves.

If one gives with fine things but without sincere heart, being arrogant and self-reliant, failing to show reverence in person, seeking only for a flowery reputation and desiring to spread one's own fame far and wide;
Later, when they possess little wealth, people vainly praise them as possessing billions;
yet inwardly fearing robbery, their clothing is always coarse and thin, and their food is never sweet—thus they live in vain and die in vain.
The bhikṣu has never set foot at his gate; he remains far removed from the Triple Gem and constantly draws near to evil paths.

Bestow excellent things upon him, honoring him with the four immeasurables, personally serving him with your own hands, and keeping the Triple Gem in your thoughts. Vow that all sentient beings may encounter the Buddhas and ascend to heaven, that their bitter poisons be extinguished, and that in future lives they shall have no wish unfulfilled. That they encounter the Buddhas and be born in heaven shall surely accord with these aspirations.

(17) Long ago, there was a brahmin named Vimala, who held a position of great honor and was a sovereign emperor who could travel through the air. His wealth was beyond calculation, and he delighted in practicing charity:
he gave away beautiful women of exquisite complexion whose finery illuminated the world;

There were cauldrons for food made of gold and silver, containing a hundred flavors;
the oxen of the Qin waters all had their hides covered in gold, and each single-horned ox yielded four sheng of milk daily;
they were all accompanied by their calves, who wore robes woven from precious materials with bright pearls set as ornaments.
The couches and curtains were draped with jeweled hangings that dazzled the eyes;
there were famous elephants and fine horses with saddles and bridles of gold and silver, encrusted with various precious gems;
and there were various chariots with ornate canopies and seats made of tiger skin, featuring every kind of exquisite carving and engraving.
From his own daughter down to the precious chariot, there were one thousand eight hundred and four items for each, all of which he bestowed as gifts upon others.
Because of Vimalakīrti’s compassionate kindness, the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits of the eight directions, above and below, all rejoiced in his merit.

"To provide for the common people with the generosity of Vimalakīrti, exhausting one's entire lifespan without a day of weariness or indolence, is not as meritorious as feeding a single woman of pure faith who observes the precepts for a single day; the latter’s merit is double that of the former and cannot be calculated."
Furthermore, the aforementioned offerings made by a hundred laywomen (*upāsikā*) are not equal to a single meal for one layman endowed with the precepts (*śīlavat*).
A hundred such men endowed with the precepts are not equal to a single meal for one woman who has entered the stage of the *srotāpanna* (*āhāra-vinaya*).
A hundred female *śrāmaṇerīs* are not equal to the meal of a single high-conduct *śrāmaṇera*.
A hundred *śrāmaṇeras* are not equal to a single *śramaṇa* who is fully ordained and practices the precepts, whose mind is free from defilement and who is pure both internally and externally.
Ordinary people are like tiles and stones, while those who possess the precepts and practice lofty conduct are like the bright moon pearl;
though tiles and stones may fill the four continents, they are not equal to a single genuine pearl.
"Furthermore, even as much almsgiving as Vimalakīrti has performed, and even the giving of many who have attained the full precepts, is not equal to a single meal given to a Srotāpanna.
A hundred meals for Srotāpannas are not equal to one for a Sakṛdāgāmin."
"One hundred *sakṛdāgāmin*s do not equal one *anāgāmin*.
One hundred *anāgāmin*s do not equal a single *arhat* to whom one offers food.
Furthermore, the previous offerings made by Vimalakīrti and his feeding of the various worthies and sages do not equal filially serving one's own parents."
Filial piety consists in exhausting one's heart without any external selfishness.
A hundred generations of filial service to one's parents is not equal to feeding a single Pratyekabuddha.
One hundred Pratyekabuddhas [are not equal to feeding one Buddha].
It is not as good as providing a meal for one Buddha;
feeding a hundred Buddhas is not as good as establishing one shrine and maintaining the three refuges—refuge in the Buddha, refuge in the Dharma, and refuge in the Sangha of Bhikṣus.

To be entirely benevolent and refrain from killing, to maintain purity and refrain from stealing, to uphold integrity and refrain from violating another’s wife, to honor faith and refrain from deception, to be filial and obedient and refrain from intoxication—to observe these five precepts and the six monthly fasts—their merit is so towering that it surpasses the gift of ten thousand kinds of famous objects to the Vimalakīrti Garden, as well as the feeding of sages and worthies; it is truly beyond calculation.
"Maintaining the precepts is not as meritorious as cultivating a mind of equanimity to compassionately nurture sentient beings; such merit is inexhaustible.

Even if one subsists on vegetable gruel and grass mats, yet upholds the Three Refuges, harbors the four immeasurable minds, and fully observes the five precepts—the weight of mountains and seas may be measured, but this merit is difficult to calculate."
The Buddha told the four castes:
"If you wish to know who Vairaṇyā was, it was I myself.
Having heard this sutra, the four castes were greatly delighted in their hearts; they paid homage and departed.

18. [The Jātaka of the Deer King] (18): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a deer king; his body was tall and large, his fur was five-colored, and his hooves and antlers were extraordinary and elegant. Thousands of deer followed him in submission, forming a great herd."

The king went out on a hunt, and the herd of deer scattered; they threw themselves over cliffs and fell into pits, were dashed against trees and pierced by thorns, suffering many casualties and deaths.

Seeing this, the deer king choked with emotion and said, "As the leader of the multitude, I ought to have exercised clear foresight and chosen a place for our roaming. If we have come here merely for the sake of fine grass, causing such decay and ruin to my young followers, the fault lies with me."
He proceeded directly into the kingdom; when the people of the land saw him, they all said, "Our king possesses the virtue of supreme benevolence, for the divine deer has come to alight here.
Regarding this as an auspicious omen for the state, no one dared to disturb it.
He then went before the palace hall, knelt down, and said:
"This humble creature, greedy for life, has taken refuge within your borders.
Suddenly encountering a hunter, the insects have scattered in all directions; some have lost one another while still alive, and others lie dead in a chaotic heap."
Your Majesty’s benevolence extends to all creatures, and they are truly pitiable.
We pray that you allow us to select among ourselves daily to provide for the Imperial Kitchen; we beg only that you know our number, so that we may not dare deceive Your Majesty.
The king was greatly astonished and said, "The Chief Cook uses no more than a single day's supply; I did not know that you all had killed and died in such great numbers.
If it is truly as you say, I swear never to hunt again."
The Deer King retreated and summoned all the deer, fully explaining his intention and demonstrating their respective fortunes and calamities.
The herd of deer listened with bowed heads and assigned themselves their places in order.
Whenever those who were destined to die first approached their deaths, they would take leave of the king; the king would weep for them and instruct them, saying:
"Behold, all in this world must die—who can escape it?"
"Seeking the path while reciting the Buddha’s name, with benevolence, instruction, and a compassionate heart, you must be careful not to harbor resentment toward that king of men!
Thus it was day after day.
Among them was one who was due to travel but whose body was heavy with child; she said:
"I dare not avoid death; I beg to take her place in pregnancy.
He then sought out the next person in line to substitute for her, but that person bowed his head and wept, saying:
"I must surely face death;
yet there remains one day and one night of life, a brief span of existence. When the time comes, I shall have no regrets.
The Deer King could not bear that his life be taken unjustly, so the following day he left the herd and went in person to the Grand Cook.
The kitchen attendants recognized him and immediately reported the matter to the king.
When the king asked for the reason, they answered as described above.
The king was moved with grief and shed tears, saying:
"How could there be such a beast that harbors the benevolence of Heaven and Earth, sacrifices its own life to save the multitude, and practices the conduct of the ancient sages' vast compassion!
As a ruler of men, I daily take the lives of sentient beings to fatten my own body."
"Am I so fond of cruelty that I would still cherish the conduct of a jackal or a wolf?
Even a beast can practice such benevolence; it possesses the virtue of serving Heaven.
The King sent the deer away to return to its original dwelling and issued a decree throughout the realm:
"If there be anyone who offends against the deer, they shall be punished the same as a human.

From that time forth, the king and his ministers led by example, and the common people followed the Way of Benevolence and refrained from killing. This grace extended even to the grasses and trees, and the kingdom subsequently attained great peace.
"Throughout successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva risked his own life to save sentient beings; as his merit was perfected and his virtue flourished, he eventually became a venerable hero.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the deer at that time was my own self."
The king was Śāriputra. Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassion and benevolence.
19. [The Jātaka of the Crane] (19): "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was a crane, he had three sons."
At that time, the country suffered a great drought, and there was nothing with which to sustain their lives. [The mother] tore the flesh from beneath her own armpits to save them.
Her three sons were filled with doubt and said, "The scent and flavor of this meat are identical to the scent of our mother's body; could it be that our mother has fed us her own flesh?"
The three sons were deeply moved with grief and sorrow.
They further said,
"We would rather lose our own lives than harm our mother's body."
Thereupon, he closed his mouth and refused to eat.
Seeing that he would not eat, his mother went out to search for more food.
The deva sighed and said:
"The mother's compassionate kindness is beyond compare; the son's filial piety is rare indeed.
The various devas will protect him, and his wishes shall be fulfilled at once.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The mother of the cranes was my own self;
the three sons were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassionate benevolence."

In this chapter, according to a separate edition, it follows after the "Vimalakīrti Chapter" [the twenty-first]. (20) "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a peacock king; he left behind his former mate and, leading five hundred wives, desired the wife of a blue pheasant."
The blue pheasants feed exclusively on sweet nectar and fine fruits, which the peacock, acting as their husband, goes daily to gather for them.
The king’s consort fell ill and, in a dream, beheld a peacock, who said that its flesh could serve as medicine.
Upon waking, he reported this to the King, who ordered his hunters to go quickly and search for her.
The lady said,
"Whoever can find her shall be married to my youngest daughter and granted one hundred jin of gold."

"The hunters of the kingdom were distributed and went out to search; they saw the Peacock King at his usual feeding place with a single green parrot. They immediately smeared honeyed flour on trees in every location, so that the peacock would take it to provide for his wife."
The archery master smeared his body with flour and lay down as a corpse; the peacock took the flour, and the man was about to seize it.
The peacock said, "Your diligent labor must surely be for the sake of profit."
"I shall show you a mountain of gold that can serve as an inexhaustible treasure; you must grant me my life.
The man said, "The Great King has granted me a hundred catties of gold and given me his youngest daughter in marriage."
"How can I believe your words?
He then presented it to the King.
The peacock said:

"Your Majesty cherishes benevolence, and your grace reaches everywhere; I pray that you will accept my humble words. I beg for a small amount of water, and by means of compassionate incantations, I shall cause your illness to be cured immediately.
If it proves ineffective, it will not be too late to receive punishment."
The king complied with her wish; the lady took it, and all her ailments were cured. Her complexion became radiant and brilliant, and the same occurred for all the palace women.
The entire nation marveled at the king’s vast compassion, noting that by sparing the life of the peacock, he had secured the longevity of the whole country.
The sparrow said:
"I wish to cast myself into that great lake and consecrate its waters with a mantra, so that the myriad ailments of the common people throughout the land may be healed.
If you harbor any doubt or suspicion, I pray you strike my feet with your staff."
The king said,
"Very well.
The sparrow then recited a spell over it.
The people of the country drank the water, and those who were deaf heard, the blind saw, the mute spoke, and the crippled extended their limbs;
all manner of ailments were thus cured. When the people’s illnesses were removed, they all attained freedom from disease and harbored no ill will toward the peacock.
The sparrow understood this and addressed the king, saying,
"Having received the grace of Your Majesty’s life-sustaining moisture, I shall repay it by saving the lives of the entire kingdom.
Having finished his report, he requested to withdraw, whereupon the king said:
"Very well," the sparrow replied,
and immediately it soared up into the tree, saying again:
"In the world there are three kinds of fools."
The king asked, "What are these three? [The minister replied:
"First is my own folly; second is the folly of the hunter; and third is the folly of Your Majesty."
The King said,
"I pray that you release him.
The sparrow said:
"The Buddhas revere the precepts, regarding physical form as fire—the source from which one's body is consumed and one's life endangered.

I abandoned five hundred wives who provided me with offerings, yet I craved a green pheasant; I sought food to provide for it as if it were a servant, only to have it caught in a hunting net, nearly endangering my own life."
"This was my folly.

As for the hunter's folly, it was my own sincere words that led him to abandon gold from a mountain and discard treasures beyond measure, only to believe the deceptive frauds of this lady and hope for her daughter as a wife; all the mad and ignorant people of the world are of this same sort."

To cast aside the precepts of sincere devotion to the Buddha and instead believe the deceptions of ghosts and demons, indulging in wine, music, and lewdness—this may lead to the calamity of one's family line being destroyed, or to death and entry into Mount Tai with its countless sufferings. To hope to return to human form from such a state is like a bird without wings wishing to soar into the heavens; how could it not be difficult?
The seductive charms of a lewd woman are like those of malevolent spirits; there is nothing that ruins a state or endangers a person that does not stem from this, yet the foolish revere them.
Of ten thousand words, not one is sincere, yet the master archer believes them.
This is what is called the folly of the hunter.

The King obtained a celestial physician who eradicated the diseases of the entire nation; all poisons were extinguished, and his countenance became like a flower in full bloom. Both the great and the small rejoiced and relied upon him, yet the King released him.
"This is what is called the folly of a king.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"From that time forward, King Peacock traveled throughout the eight directions, constantly using divine medicines to bestow gifts with a compassionate heart, thereby curing the illnesses of the multitude."
The peacock king was myself;
the king was Śāriputra.
The hunter was Devadatta;
the lady was Devadatta’s wife.
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and benevolence practices giving. [21] The Jātaka of the Rabbit King (21).

"In the past, there was a brahmin one hundred and twenty years of age who maintained his integrity and remained unmarried. He was utterly free from lust and lewdness; he dwelt in quietude amidst mountains and marshes, taking no pleasure in worldly glory. He made his hut of reeds and his mat of thistle and mugwort; he sustained his life with mountain springs and wild fruits. His resolve was vast and his conduct sublime, such that the whole world marveled at his virtue."

King Ping appointed him as his minister, but he was resolved upon the Way and would not serve in office; he dwelt among the mountains and marshes for over several decades, and his benevolence reached all living beings, such that even birds and beasts relied upon him.
At that time, there were four animals—a fox, a otter, a monkey, and a rabbit—who said:
"We shall provide offerings to the Daoist master, so that we may settle our minds and listen to the sutras."
After many years had passed, the mountain fruits were completely exhausted. The Daoist practitioner wished to move elsewhere to seek out where the fruits abounded.
The four beasts said with concern:
"Though there may be the flourishing and elegant scholars of an entire kingdom, they are like turbid water filling the ocean; they are not worth even a pint or a quart of nectar."
"As for those Daoist practitioners who have departed, they have not heard the sacred scriptures; am I not declining?
Let each of you seek out food and drink as appropriate to provide for these Daoist practitioners, and I entreat you to remain on this mountain so that we may hope to hear the Great Dharma."
They all said in unison, "It can be done.
The monkey sought fruit; the fox transformed into a human and obtained a bag of flour; the otter caught a large fish. Each said:
"It will suffice for a month's provisions.
The hare reflected deeply within himself:
"By what means shall I provide for this practitioner?"
He replied:
"Indeed, birth is followed by death; the body is a decaying vessel that must eventually be cast away.
To feed ten thousand ordinary people is not as meritorious as feeding a single practitioner of the Way."
He immediately went to gather firewood and burned it into charcoal,
then said to the Daoist, "Though my body is small, it may serve as provisions for one day.
Having finished speaking, he threw himself into the fire, but the flames would not ignite him.
When the Daoist observed this, he was moved by such a sight; the Buddhas praised his virtue, and the heavenly deities nurtured him with compassion.
The Daoist then remained there, daily expounding the wondrous sutras, while the four beasts received his instruction.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The brahmin was Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
the hare was my own self."
The macaque was Śāriputra; the fox was Ānanda;
and the otter was Maudgalyāyana.
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and benevolence (maitrī-karuṇā-pāramitā) practices giving.

22. [The Jātaka of the Householder] (22): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great householder who accumulated treasures equal to those of a kingdom. He always delighted in relieving the poor and bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings; he received the refuge of all, just as the ocean contains all flowing streams."
At that time, there was a friend's son whose dissolute conduct had exhausted the family wealth.
His mother-in-law took pity on him and instructed him, saying:
"Manage your livelihood through the Way, and your blessings and profits will be inexhaustible."
"I shall give you one thousand taels of gold as capital.
The son replied,
"I respectfully accept."
"I dare not disobey your clear instructions," he said, and immediately set out as a traveling merchant.

By nature he was inclined toward depravity and fond of the strange; he served ghosts and demons, indulged in lewdness, wine, and music, until his wealth was exhausted and he fell into further destitution.
Having exhausted his wealth through these five activities, he returned to his original state of poverty and remained there.
At that time, there was a dead mouse on the dung outside the householder’s gate;
the householder pointed it out and said, "A wise and virtuous man can use even this dead mouse to establish a livelihood and maintain his dwelling."
"Though you possess a thousand ounces of gold, are you still in poverty?
Now I shall give you another thousand ounces of gold.

At that time, there was a beggar who, hearing these instructions from afar, was moved with deep emotion. He continued to beg for food as before, but returned to take away the mouse; following those sublime instructions, he begged for various ingredients, seasoned and roasted them, and sold them for two coins.
He subsequently turned to selling vegetables until he had amassed more than a hundred head of livestock.
By progressing from the humble to the prominent, he eventually became a wealthy family.
While living in retirement, he recalled:
"I was originally a beggar; by what cause have I come to possess such wealth!
Upon waking, he said:
"It was because the virtuous householder instructed that stubborn boy that I have come to possess these treasures."
"To receive kindness and fail to repay it is called turning one's back on the light.
He then fashioned a silver tray and a golden rat, filling its belly with various rare treasures, and displayed them upon the tray.
Furthermore, adorning its borders with various precious necklaces and providing all manner of sweet delicacies, he paid homage to that householder and explained his purpose:
"I now respond to the celestial moisture."
The householder said,
“How virtuous you are, O noble sir!
You may indeed serve as an example for instruction.”
He immediately gave him his daughter as a wife, entrusted him with his various residences and domains, and said:
"You shall be my successor; you must revere the Triple Gem of the Buddha and rescue and deliver all sentient beings with the four immeasurable minds."
He replied,
"I shall certainly cultivate the Buddhist teachings.
Later, he became the successor to a householder and was renowned throughout the land for his filial piety.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The householder was I myself;
that profligate was Devadatta."
The one who became wealthy by means of mice was the bhikṣu Pāṇṭaka.
Devadatta harbored my sixty million fascicles of sūtras; though his words were compliant, his actions were contrary, and after death he entered the Great Mountain Hell.
The bhikṣu Pāṇṭaka, by cherishing a single phrase from me, attained transcendence in the world.
Now, to have words without practice is like using oil to extinguish its own light; this is the wisdom of the petty person.
When speech and conduct support one another, their clarity is like that of the sun and moon; embracing all sentient beings and bringing salvation to all things—this is the brilliance of a great man.
Conduct is the earth, from which all things arise.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and benevolence practices giving. 23.
[The Jātaka of the King] (23): "In the past, there was a widow who worked as a domestic servant for a householder, guarding his fields and gardens."
The host was in a state of agitation, and the time for his midday meal had already passed.
When it was time to eat, the śramaṇa came to beg from him.
The host’s mind turned toward this man, who had severed desire and abandoned depravity, whose conduct was pure and true.
"It is not as good to relieve the hunger of those in the four seas as it is to bestow even a small portion of the pure precepts upon a true sage.
Having placed his entire share of food into the bowl, he offered a single lotus flower upon it as a gift!
The practitioner of the Way manifested his supernormal powers and emitted radiance;
the mother joyfully exclaimed, "Truly, he is what is called a divine sage!
I pray that in my future lives I may give birth to a hundred sons such as this."
When his mother’s life ended and her spirit departed, she was destined to become the successor to a brahmin.
Her spirit gathered at the place where the brahmin urinated; a doe happened to urinate there as well, and through this, she conceived.
When her term was full, she gave birth to a daughter, whom the brahmin raised.
When she was over ten years old, she possessed a radiant appearance and a dignified gait; she tended the dwelling and guarded the sacred fire.
While playing with the deer, she did not notice that the fire had gone out.
Her father became angry once more and ordered her to go out and seek fire.
When the girl reached a place where people were gathered, a lotus flower sprang up at every step she took.
The master of the fire said:
"Go around my dwelling three times, and I shall give you fire.
The woman immediately obeyed his command; flowers grew upon the dry land surrounding the house in three concentric circles.
As the practitioner stood there, all were struck by its exquisite and marvelous beauty.
"News of this proclamation reached the king of that country, who ordered a skilled physiognomist to examine [the child] for signs of nobility or lowliness.
The master said:
'He shall certainly have a holy successor, and his legacy shall be passed down without end.'"
The King commanded his worthy ministers to go and welcome her with full ceremonial rites; her beauty was radiant and peerless among the palace women.
When her pregnancy had reached its full term, she gave birth to one hundred eggs.

From the principal consorts down to the concubines, none were free from jealousy; they had previously carved images of ghosts out of plantain wood, and upon reaching the time of childbirth, they covered the faces of these figures with hair and smeared them with lochia, then presented them to the King.
The various demons obscured the light, and the King was deluded enough to believe them.
A multitude of wicked ones placed eggs in a jar, sealed its mouth tightly, and cast it into the current of the river.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended and sealed the mouth with his seal; the gods provided protection, causing the vessel to stop in the current as firmly as a pillar planted in the ground.

In a country downstream, its king was gazing from atop a terrace when he saw a jar floating down the river; it shone with a brilliant luster as if possessed of some numinous spirit, so he took it to examine it.
Upon examining the inscription on the seal, he discovered one hundred eggs and had one hundred women carry and nurture them with warmth.
When the time was full and their bodies were formed, they gave birth to one hundred sons.

From birth, they possessed the wisdom of supreme sages; it was self-evident without being taught. Their countenances and radiance transcended the world, and their marks and signs were rare and extraordinary. Their strength, vigor, and prowess were a hundred times that of ordinary men, and the resonance of their voices was like the roar of a lion.

The king immediately provided one hundred white elephants, each equipped with saddles and harnesses made of the seven treasures, to serve his noble successor and command him to campaign against neighboring states;
thus the four borders were brought under submission, and all acknowledged themselves as subjects and handmaidens.
Furthermore, when he attacked the country from which he had been born, none among the people, whether high or low, failed to tremble with fear.
The King asked:
"Who is there capable of repelling this enemy?"
The lady said, "Great King, do not fear.
Observe from where the enemy comes and by which side they are attacking the city.
I shall ascend the tower to observe them and bring about your victory."
The king immediately went to the place where his enemy had passed and stood there watching.
His mother ascended the tower and raised her voice, saying:
"There are three things that constitute the greatest of rebellions."
To not distance oneself from the multitude of evils and thus invite calamities in both worlds—this is the first.
To be born without recognizing one's kin and thereby act in opposition to filial piety—this is the second.
To rely on power to kill one's parents and direct poison toward the Triple Gem—this is the third.
"Having harbored these three perversions, their evil is beyond measure.
Now, as you open your mouths, the proof shall manifest this very day.
The mother grasped her breasts, and by the power of the heavens, the milk sprayed forth, filling the mouths of all one hundred sons.
Moved by such sincere devotion, and feeling deep sorrow as they drank her milk, they all said in unison, "This is our mother.
With tears streaming down their necks,
they joined their palms and stepped forward, prostrating themselves to repent for their transgressions.
When the imperial successor first met him, there was none who did not grieve with profound sorrow.
The two nations were harmonious, their affection surpassing that between uncles and nephews.
People from all quarters rejoiced, and there was none who did not praise this excellence.
"The sons beheld the impermanence of the world as being like an illusion; they took leave of their parents to study the Way, distancing themselves from worldly defilements.
Ninety-nine of the sons all attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
Ruling the state as the son of a single child, he ascended the throne upon the demise of his father, the King.

He issued a general amnesty for all crimes, demolished prisons, breached embankments to release stagnant waters, and granted freedom from servitude to slaves. He comforted those who were filial and fraternal, nurtured the orphaned and the solitary, opened the treasuries for great acts of charity, and provided for the people according to their wishes.
They took the ten wholesome actions as the national law; every person recited them, and every household had filial sons.

They established stupas and monasteries and made offerings to the śramaṇas. As they recited the sūtras and śāstras, their mouths were free from the four evils; all poisons were extinguished, and their lifespans increased.
"The Heavenly Emperor nurtured and protected him as if he were his own son.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The one who remained to be king was my very self."
The father-king was the present King Śuddhodana;
the mother was Māyādevī.
Such was the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of giving through compassion and benevolence.
24. [The Jātaka of the Brahmin] (24): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was once a brahmin; he was profoundly learned and erudite in the scriptures, and the people of the land took him as their teacher."
He had five hundred disciples, all of whom possessed Confucian virtue; they were naturally inclined toward generosity, yet remained as self-guarded as one protects their own body.

At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, the Honored One of True Reality and Supreme Enlightenment, who led those within the three realms back to the fundamental non-being of the spirit.

When the Bodhisattva beheld the Buddha, he joyfully took refuge in him and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to remain at his home for seven days, providing them with offerings according to the rites.
The disciples of the Brahmin each disputed over whom they should serve as their master.
A certain person was young; when the Master sent him on an errand, he returned and requested to perform some work.
The Master said, "If there is work to be done for which you have no specific task, you shall take charge of it."
The youth replied,
"Only a lamp has no master.
The Master said:
"Excellent!
The disciple filled a jar with sesame oil and ointment, bathed himself thoroughly, wrapped his head in a clean white cotton cloth, and set it ablaze with his own hand.
When devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts beheld such fierce resolve, there was none who did not clap their hands in astonishment and sigh in admiration:
"This is unprecedented in the world; he must surely be a Buddha.

The Buddha praised him, noting that his head remained uninjured throughout the clear night, as his mind remained fixed on the sutra, free from all thought, for seven days without a single moment of weariness.
The Buddha then bestowed upon him the prediction:
"After incalculable kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara.
With radiance emanating from each side of your neck and shoulder, you shall teach and deliver beings, and those who attain liberation through you shall be immeasurable."
When the devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons heard that he was to become a Buddha, there were none who did not rejoice and prostrate themselves in greeting and congratulation.
The Brahmin thought to himself:
"If he attains Buddhahood, I shall certainly attain it as well; I must receive my prediction [of enlightenment]."
The Buddha then departed.
[The man] bowed his head to the ground before him and said:
"I have now prepared this meager offering with all my heart; I pray that you grant me a prediction of my future destiny."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"When the youth becomes a Buddha, he shall grant you the prediction of your future enlightenment.

Upon hearing that he was destined to become a Buddha, the brahmin was so filled with joy that he forgot his own physical existence. From that time forward, he practiced great generosity, providing food for the hungry, clothing for the cold, and medicine for the sick; even for the smallest creatures that fly, crawl, or wriggle, he provided sustenance according to their needs at the proper times.
"In the lands of the eight directions, he was called the Benevolent Father.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The youth was Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
"The Brahmin was my own self.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Compassionate Benevolence when he performed acts of giving.

25. [The Jātaka of the Householder] (25): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great householder. His accumulated wealth amounted to billions; he constantly served the Triple Gem and extended compassion toward all sentient beings."
While observing the marketplace, he saw a turtle and felt compassion for it; he asked its price, whether it was high or low.

The owner of the turtle, knowing that the Bodhisattva possessed the virtue of universal compassion and was intent on saving sentient beings, and that his wealth was beyond counting such that no price would be refused, replied:
"It costs one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. It would be well if you could take it; otherwise, I shall cook it."
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Very well! He then paid the agreed price, took the turtle home, washed and tended its wounds, and released it into the water.
Beholding him as he departed, she was moved by both sorrow and joy, and vowed:

"May all beings such as those in the hungry ghosts realm of Mount Tai and those in the prisons of worldly lords be swiftly delivered from their hardships; may they find peace of body and preservation of life just as you do now."
He prostrated himself toward the ten directions and, with palms joined, made this vow:

"Sentient beings are in turmoil, their suffering immeasurable. I shall act as heaven and earth for them; I shall provide moisture for the drought and rafts for those adrift; I shall be food for the hungry and drink for the thirsty; I shall be clothing for the cold and coolness for the heat;
I shall be a physician for the sick and light for the darkness. Should there come a time of turbid age and perversion, I shall become a Buddha therein to deliver those sentient beings."
The Buddhas of the ten directions all approved of his vow and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! You shall surely attain your aspiration."
Later that night, the turtle came and gnawed at his gate. Finding the gate making a noise, he went out to look and saw the turtle; returning, he reported what had happened as it was.
The Bodhisattva looked at it, and the turtle spoke in human speech, saying:
"I have received profound kindness and my body has been preserved whole; yet I have no way to repay this kindness."
"The creatures dwelling in the water know the ebb and flow of the waters; when the flood is about to arrive, it will surely cause great destruction.
I pray that you quickly prepare your boat so that we may meet you at the appointed time.
He replied:
"Excellent! At dawn the next morning, he went to the gate and reported the matter to the king as it had occurred.
Because the Bodhisattva had long possessed a reputation for goodness, the king trusted his words.
"Move from the low ground to the high ground.
When the time came, a turtle approached and said, "The great flood is arriving;
you may quickly unload your goods and follow where I go, and you shall obtain safety without harm."
The boat followed after it, when a snake approached the vessel;
the Bodhisattva said, "Take it.
The turtle said:
"Excellent! he said.
Then, seeing a floating fox, he said, "Take it."
The turtle also said,
"Excellent.
Then it saw the drifting man slapping his cheeks and calling out to Heaven, pleading for pity and rescue from its life, saying:
"Take it! The turtle said, "Be careful not to take it!
For the hearts of men are deceitful; rarely do they maintain faith to the end. They turn their backs on kindness and pursue power, delighting in committing violence and rebellion."
The Bodhisattva said:
"To save such creatures as insects while regarding human beings as lowly—is this truly benevolence?
I cannot bear it."
Thereupon, he took it.
The turtle said,
"What a regret!"
He then departed for the fertile lands.
The turtle took his leave, saying,
"My debt of gratitude having been repaid, I beg to withdraw."
He replied,
"Once I have attained the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I shall certainly deliver you.
The turtle said:
"Excellent! The turtle withdrew, and the snake and fox each departed.
The fox, which had made its dwelling in a burrow, discovered a hidden treasure of a hundred *jin* of famous purple-polished gold left by an ancient; delighted, it said:
"I must repay that kindness.
He hurried back and said,
"This tiny insect has received my moisture and been saved from its precarious life."

"Insects are creatures that dwell in burrows, seeking holes for their own security. To find a hundred jin of gold within such a hole—this hole is neither a tomb, nor a home, nor a site of plunder, nor a place of theft.
This is the result of my own sincerity; I wish to present it to a worthy man."
The Bodhisattva reflected deeply:
"To not take it would be a mere waste, providing no benefit to the impoverished;
to take it and give it as alms so that sentient beings may obtain relief—would that not be excellent!"
He immediately went to take it.
When the man drifting on the water saw him,
he said, "Give me half."
The Bodhisattva immediately gave him ten jin of it.
The man adrift said, "You have dug up a grave and plundered gold; what shall become of your transgression and merit?"
"I shall not divide it; I must inform the authorities.
He replied, "The poor are in dire straits; I wish to distribute this equally."
"Is it not biased for you to wish to monopolize it?

The boatman then reported this to the authorities, and the Bodhisattva was arrested. Having no one to whom he could appeal, he took refuge solely in the Triple Gem, repented his transgressions with self-reproach, and made a compassionate vow:
"May all sentient beings quickly escape the eight difficulties, and may none harbor resentment as I do now."
The fox said to the snake,
"What shall we do about this matter?
The snake replied:
"I shall rescue him. Thereupon, he carried excellent medicine in his beak, opened the prison gate, and entered the cell.
Seeing the Bodhisattva’s form, his countenance marred, he was moved with deep sorrow and compassion, and said to the Bodhisattva:
"Carry this medicine with you; I shall bite the Prince, and its venom will be so extreme that none can save him.
If the worthy one lets me hear of it and applies the medicine, he will be cured."
The Bodhisattva remained silent.
As the serpent had said, the Prince’s life was about to perish. The King issued a decree:
"Whoever can save him shall be enfeoffed as Chancellor of State; I shall share the governance of the realm with him."
When the Bodhisattva heard this above, he applied it and the man was immediately healed.
The King, filled with joy, asked how it had happened, and the prisoner recounted the details from beginning to end.
The King, feeling despondent, reproached himself, saying:
"How deeply ignorant I am! he exclaimed.
He immediately executed the boatman, granted a general amnesty throughout the kingdom, and appointed the man as his minister. Taking him by the hand, he entered the palace and sat with him, saying:
"What scriptures does the worthy one recite?"
"What path do you embrace,
that you possess the benevolence of the Two Polarities and extend your grace to all living beings?
He replied:
"To preach the Buddha’s sutras is to cherish the Buddha’s Way.
The King asked,
"Does the Buddha have a definitive teaching?"
He replied: "There is.
The Buddha taught the four marks of impermanence; for those who abide by them, all calamities are extinguished and auspicious blessings flourish."
The King said:
"Excellent! I pray that I may obtain its fruit."
He said:

"At the time when heaven and earth come to an end, seven suns will appear simultaneously, and the great ocean will be completely exhausted. Heaven and earth will blaze intensely, Mount Sumeru will collapse and be destroyed, and the lives and bodies of devas, humans, ghosts, dragons, and all sentient beings will suddenly be consumed by fire until nothing remains."
That which was once flourishing is now in decline; this is what is called impermanence.
The enlightened person maintains the mindfulness of impermanence, saying: "If even heaven and earth are thus, how could official rank, noble title, or territory endure for long?"
"One who attains this mindfulness possesses the resolve for universal compassion.
The King said,
"If even heaven and earth are thus, how much more so the realm?"
"The Buddha has taught that all things are impermanent; my heart believes this.
The householder further said:
"The most grievous suffering, Your Majesty, you ought to know."
The King said,
"I wish to hear your clear admonition.
He replied:

"The consciousness-spirit of sentient beings is subtle and difficult to know; it has no form when viewed and no sound when heard. It is vast throughout the world, lofty beyond covering, boundless and unfathomable, revolving without limit."

Yet, they hunger and thirst for the six desires, just as the ocean is never filled by its many tributary streams; because of these, they undergo the various sufferings of being burned and boiled on Mount Tai and subjected to manifold poisons.
Sometimes they become hungry ghosts, with molten copper poured into their mouths and forced to labor on Mount Tai;
sometimes they become animals, slaughtered, carved, flayed, and torn apart, dying only to be struck again by blades, enduring immeasurable pain.

If one attains human birth, one dwells in the womb for ten months; at the time of birth, one is squeezed with urgency as if being bound by a rope constricting the body. The pain of falling to the ground is like being dropped from a great height, or being blown upon by wind, or as if one’s own body were being burned by fire. Washing with warm water is like having boiling molten copper poured over oneself; rubbing the body with the hands is like being flayed by a blade. Such various pains are so extremely bitter that they are difficult to describe.

After reaching old age, all the faculties have matured; the hair at the head turns white and the teeth fall out. Internally and externally, one is depleted and exhausted. Thinking of this, the heart is filled with sorrow, and it develops into a grave illness. As the four great elements seek to separate, every joint aches; one requires assistance for sitting or lying down, and the arrival of a physician only adds further distress.
When life is about to end, all the winds arise together; they sever the tendons and shatter the bones, completely blocking the orifices.
The breath ceases and the spirit departs, following the path it has traveled.

Even if one ascends to heaven, there are still distinctions of poverty and wealth, nobility and meanness; though one’s lifespan may be extended, when merit is exhausted and sin arrives, one descends into the Great Mountain Hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm—this is what is called suffering.
The King said: "Excellent!
The Buddha has spoken the essential truth of suffering; my heart believes it!"
The householder spoke again:

"That which exists must necessarily be empty, just as when two pieces of wood are rubbed together to produce fire; the fire then consumes the wood, and once both fire and wood are exhausted, both things are empty."
"The palaces and subjects of the ancient former kings have now perished; one no longer sees where they have gone—this too is empty.
The King said, "Excellent!"
"The Buddha has taught the essentials of emptiness; my heart believes it!
The householder spoke again:
"The body consists of earth, water, fire, and wind: that which is solid is earth, that which is moist is water, that which is hot is fire, and that which is the breath is wind."
"When life ends and the spirit departs, the four great elements disperse; nothing can preserve them as a whole.
Therefore, it is said that this is not the self. The King said, "Excellent!"
"The Buddha has taught that there is no self; my heart believes this!
If one cannot even preserve the body, how much less can one preserve a kingdom?
Alas for our former kings, who did not hear the teaching of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True, Most Perfect Enlightenment—that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self!"
The householder said:
"Heaven and earth are impermanent; who can guarantee the preservation of a kingdom?
Why not empty your treasuries and bestow them as alms upon the poor and the hungry?"
The king said:
"Excellent! How delightful is the instruction of a wise teacher!"

He immediately emptied all his treasuries to bestow upon the poor and destitute, providing husbands for widows and fathers for orphans. The people were moved by this magnificent display; rich and poor became equal and harmonious. The entire nation rejoiced, walking about with smiles upon their faces, and looking up to heaven, they sighed in wonder, saying:
"Has the spiritual transformation of the Bodhisattva reached such a state?"
"The four quarters praised his virtue, and thus peace was established.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The householder was my own self."
The king was Maitreya;
the turtle was Ānanda;
and the fox was Śāriputra.
The snake was Maudgalyāyana;
the drifting man was Devadatta.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through compassionate benevolence.

26. [The Jātaka of the Śramaṇa] (26): "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was practicing as a śramaṇa, he constantly dwelt in mountain forests. With a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he thought: 'Sentient beings have long suffered, transmigrating through the three realms; how may I deliver them?'"
He settled his mind in contemplation, seeking the vast source of the Way in order to rescue all beings.

However, there were lice in his robes; his body itched and his mind was disturbed, so that his resolve for the Way could not be established. Reaching out his hand to search for them, he immediately found a louse.
Feeling deeply pained at heart, he sought a way to comfort it.
There happened to be some animal bones; he slowly placed them in the center.
Having obtained seven days' worth of food, the louse finished eating and then departed.
"Transmigrating through birth and death, the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood to weave the fabric of teaching and transformation.
At that time, a great snow fell, cutting off the paths of travelers; a householder in the kingdom invited the Buddha and several thousand bhikṣus to receive offerings for seven days.
His heart was solemn and reverent, and the entire imperial clan was of one mind; yet the snow had not yet melted.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Command all the śramaṇas to return to their viharas."
Ānanda said, “The host is reverent and solemn, and his mind has not yet been overcome; the heavy snow has not ceased, so there is no place to go for alms.
The World-Honored One said:
"The host's intention has been fulfilled; he will no longer provide offerings.
The Buddha then led Fa-mai away, and the śramaṇas followed as attendants back to the vihāra.
The next day, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You shall go from the master's house to beg for alms.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went and arrived at the master’s gate.
When the gatekeeper saw him, he did not inquire as to his purpose.
After a short while, he returned, prostrated himself, knelt for a long time, and reported the matter as it had occurred.
He further questioned him about its origin: "That man's mind was not constant; why did it change so rapidly?"
The Buddha then explained it to him in detail as above.
He further said:
"Ānanda!..."

With a compassionate heart, I rescued the tiny life of a louse and bestowed upon it my own decaying bones and seven days' worth of food; now I have obtained this offering, the finest tribute from the entire world.

Because the grace of my past-life charity was equal to those seven days, its influence has ceased and no longer continues as before—how much more so when one directs a compassionate heart toward the Buddha and the assembly of śramaṇas?

To uphold the precepts with purity, to practice lofty conduct free from desire, to rectify one's own mind within, and to manifest compassionate transformation outwardly—to respectfully bestow kindness upon even a single bhikṣu of such lofty conduct exceeds the merit of giving to ordinary people throughout the accumulation of kalpas with all one’s heart.

Why is this so? Because the bhikṣu embraces the Buddha’s sutras, possessing the seeds of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; by means of these five virtues, he compassionately guides sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from the calamities of the myriad sufferings within the three realms.
Ānanda said:
"How fortunate is this householder!

To have personally encountered and received the compassionate nurture of the Tathāgata—the One Free from Attachment, the Truly and Perfectly Enlightened One, the Charioteer of the Dharma, the Teacher of Gods and Humans—along with the assembly of śramaṇas, some of whom are srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, or arhats, and others who are bodhisattvas who have established great and vast compassion to lead all sentient beings!"
"This merit is difficult to measure, like the ocean;
it is difficult to praise, like the earth.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Excellent, Ānanda! It is just as you have said.”

"A Buddha is difficult to encounter; the sutras and Dharma are difficult to hear; and a community of bhikṣus is difficult to find for making offerings to, occurring only once in a while, like the udumbara flower.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus rejoiced, bowed their heads in prostration, and respectfully set out to practice it.
The Bodhisattva’s perfection of loving-kindness and benevolence (*maitrī-āramitā*) consists in practicing giving (*dāna*) in this manner.

Chapter Two: The Perfection of Precepts (Śīlapāramitā). This chapter contains fifteen sections.
Regarding the Perfection of Precepts, what are its principles?

They are crazed, foolish, and cruel, delighting in taking life; they are greedy and prone to theft, lewd and impure, double-tongued, abusive, deceitful, and frivolous in speech; their minds are characterized by envy, malice, and delusion.

To endanger one's parents, slaughter the sages, slander the Buddha, and disrupt the worthy; to seize the objects of the ancestral temple and harbor such ferocity and rebellion as to destroy the Three Honored Ones—such a primary evil would rather face being sliced for meat or minced into pickled sauce in the marketplace than ever commit it.
One who truly believes in the Triple Gem of the Buddha shall universally deliver the four debts of gratitude.

27. [The Jātaka of the Lay Devotee] (27): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a lay devotee (*upāsaka*). In the kingdom where he resided, the king’s conduct was upright; he exhorted his ministers and subjects to know the Triple Gem. Those who upheld the precepts and observed the fasts were exempted from taxes and corvée labor.
When the common people, both great and small, saw that the king honored the worthy, many feigned goodness while secretly practicing evil."

The king, observing the conduct of the people through the lens of the Buddha’s precepts, saw those who were outwardly virtuous but inwardly corrupt, thereby contravening the Buddha’s pure transformation. He immediately issued a provisional decree, commanding:
"Whoever dares to follow the Way of the Buddha shall be punished by execution."
Among those who feigned virtue, there were none who did not abandon the truth and indulge their own minds by following their original depravity.
When the Bodhisattva reached an advanced age, he harbored the vast and brilliant illumination of the true and correct; hearing this command, he was startled and said:
