"To abandon the truth and follow depravity in order to obtain the status of a sovereign—wherein one’s lifespan equals that of the two polarities and one’s wealth and honor are boundless—with the six pleasures arising from the mind—I shall never do such a thing."
"Though my life may last but a single meal, if I am granted the opportunity to behold the transformation of the Three Honored Ones, the Most True, I shall joyfully accept it.

Yet, though one might possess tens of billions of scrolls of worldly records, dwell in a celestial palace, and enjoy a lifespan as vast as the heavens, if one remains ignorant of the Three Honored Ones and hears not the Buddha’s scriptures, I would have no desire for such a state."
To receive the Buddha’s word and immediately face the calamity of execution—this I accept with a willing heart.

As the Sūtra says: “It is difficult for sentient beings to cast themselves into the three miserable realms; it is difficult to obtain a human rebirth; it is difficult to dwell in a central land; it is difficult for the six sense faculties to be complete; it is difficult to be born in a land where the Way exists; it is difficult to encounter a Bodhisattva as a kinsman; it is difficult to behold the sūtras and believe them; it is difficult to penetrate the profound and understand the subtle; it is difficult to meet a śramaṇa of noble conduct and provide offerings with a pure mind; and it is difficult to encounter a Buddha and receive his prediction of enlightenment.”

"Because my past merits are manifest, I now behold the Buddhist scriptures and have been granted the privilege of serving the Triple Gem. Even if I were to encounter the cruelty of being pickled and minced under an unrighteous ruler, or the horrors of boiling water and fire, I would never abandon the正道 (Correct Path) to follow those demonic and sorcerous ways."

The King then commanded his officials to investigate those who had disobeyed his orders and execute them in the marketplace. When the investigators saw that the Bodhisattva’s resolve was firm and unshakable, and that he served the Triple Gem with such sincere devotion that his purpose remained unimpaired, they immediately seized him and reported it to the King.
The king said,
"Execute him in the marketplace. In secret,
he dispatched men to follow and observe what was being said.
The Bodhisattva, facing death, instructed his son, saying:

"Since the beginning of heaven and earth and the arrival of humanity, sentient beings dwelling in the world have had their six sense-faculties lead them into chaotic conduct worse than that of the mad or intoxicated; they rarely behold the Three Honored Ones who guide through the transformation of clarity and purity."
Since you fortunately understand the Dharma, be careful not to abandon it.
For if one forsakes the practice of the Buddha-dharma to adopt the deceptions of demonic spirits, the ruin of the state is certain.
"I would rather sacrifice my body than depart from the truth.
Your Majesty is now acting perversely and erroneously; you must not follow him.
The upright official reported this to the king.
The King, knowing that Xingzhen was genuine, immediately welcomed him with joy and took his hand as they ascended the throne hall, saying:
"You may truly be called a disciple of the Buddha.

He appointed him as State Chancellor and entrusted him with the administration of the government; furthermore, he exempted those who had abandoned worldly affairs for the pure transformation of the Buddha from taxes and corvée labor. Consequently, throughout the realm, none vied more than to practice goodness.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"The king at that time was Maitreya.
The lay follower..."
"I am that very person.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Conduct through the Firm Resolve of Observing the Precepts.

28. [The Jātaka of the Elephant King] (28): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of elephants. His mind was vast and far-reaching; he clearly perceived that there is a Buddha, there is the Dharma, and there is the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. He constantly took refuge in these three, and at all times rescued and sustained sentient beings with universal compassion, vowing that upon attaining Buddhahood, he would deliver all beings."
The elephant king had two wives among his five hundred elephants.
While in the water, he found a lotus flower of exquisite color and gave it to his principal wife.
The principal wife obtained the flower and, filled with joy, said:
"The ice is exceedingly cold; by what cause has such a flower appeared?
The junior wife, driven by greed and jealousy, spoke in anger and made this vow:
"Zhang Hui will kill you with a potent poison," he said, and [the man] died of a constricted heart.
His spirit was transformed into a girl of the four noble clans;

her beauty surpassed that of ordinary women, her intellect and insight were flowing and penetrating, she possessed broad knowledge of antiquity and the present, and by observing the celestial phenomena above, she clearly understood the rise and fall of the times.
When the King heard that she was like this, he betrothed her as his consort.
Upon her arrival, she set forth the principles of governing the state; her righteousness accorded with those of a loyal minister, so the King delighted in and respected her, following her every word.
The lady said, "In my dream I beheld an elephant with six tusks; my heart desires its tusks to serve as pendants for my hairpins.
If the King does not procure them, I shall die."
The King said, "There are no such things as demonic words; people would merely laugh at you if they heard them.
The Queen said:
"Linked by these signs, my mind has become bound with anxiety.
The King summoned four ministers for consultation and recounted his dream, saying:
"Has there ever been such a phenomenon in the past or present?"
One minister replied,
"There is none. Another minister said:
"The King did not dream," [another] minister said.
"I have heard that such things exist; the more distant the place, the more likely it is."
One minister said,
"If one can bring him here, Śakra will now alight here.
The four ministers immediately summoned the archery masters from the four directions and questioned them.
The Master from the South said:
"My late father often used to say: 'There is.'"
"However, he is far away and difficult to reach.
The minister reported to the Emperor, saying:
"This man knows of him."
The King immediately revealed it to her.
The Queen said:
"Traveling straight south for three thousand li, you will reach a mountain; enter the mountain and travel for about two days, and you will arrive at the place where the elephant is."
"Dig a pit by the side of the road, shave off his hair and beard, dress him in the robes of a śramaṇa, and shoot him from within the pit.
Cut out his tusks and bring those two tusks here."
The Master acted according to his instructions; he went to the elephant’s dwelling place, first shot the elephant, donned the Dharma robes, and took up his alms bowl, standing still within the pit.
When the elephant king saw the śramaṇa, it immediately lowered its head and said:
“Homage to you, O Master!”
"What matter do you intend to use to harm my life?
He replied,
"I wish to obtain your tusks."
The elephant said:
"My pain is unbearable; quickly take away my tusks so that you do not disturb my mind and cause evil thoughts to arise.
Those whose will and thoughts are evil die and enter the realms of the Great Mountain (Mount Tai), hungry ghosts, and animals."

To harbor patience and practice compassion, responding with goodness when evil comes, is the supreme conduct of a Bodhisattva; even if one's bones were placed on a carving board and their flesh sliced for meat, they would never deviate from this practice.
"One who practices this path will ascend to heaven upon death and swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*.
The man then bit off his own teeth, and the elephant said,
"A practitioner of the Way should walk backward, so as not to leave footprints for the herd of elephants to follow."
When the man had gone some distance away, the elephant’s pain became unbearable; it collapsed to the ground, cried out loudly, and died suddenly, immediately being reborn in the heavens.
The herd of elephants came from all four directions and all said, "Who has killed our king?"
Having searched for it without success, he returned to guard the king, wailing in grief.
"The Master has returned the tusk.

When the king beheld the elephant's tusk, his heart was immediately stricken with anguish and terror. As the queen placed the tusk in her hand and was just about to look at it, thunder and lightning struck her; she spat blood and died, falling into hell.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"At that time, the elephant king was I myself;
the chief wife was Sujātā."
The hunter was Devadatta;
the junior queen was Śīrṣabhadra.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve (Adhyāśaya-pāramitā) when he practiced the precepts.
29. [The Jātaka of the Parrot King] (29): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a king of parrots; he constantly honored the teachings of the Buddha and took refuge in the Triple Gem."
When his death was imminent, he did not commit the ten evil deeds even as he died; instead, he taught with a compassionate heart, making the six perfections his primary practice.

At that time, the king was fond of eating parrots, and hunters vied with one another to seek them out. Upon seeing a flock of parrots, they captured them with a net and obtained the entire group to present to the Grand Cook.
The steward collected them; those that were fat were cooked to serve as delicacies.

The King of Parrots reflected deeply: "Sentient beings, in their frantic turmoil, rush toward hell and lose their lives; it is invariably because of food that they wander through the cycle of the three realms."
He told his attendants:
"If one eliminates greed and renounces food, though the body may suffer slight affliction, life may still be hoped for.
The fool is gluttonous and lacks foresight; he is like a stingy man who covets the scant honey upon a blade, unaware of the calamity of having his tongue cut off."
"I am now restricting my food; you all should do likewise.
Because the Parrot King grew thinner day by day, he leaped out through the opening of his cage and stood upon the top of it, saying:
"Indeed, great is the evil of greed, and supreme is the goodness of desirelessness!"
He spoke again:
"The Buddhas regard greed as a prison, as a net, as poison, and as a blade; you all should diminish your food just as I have.

From that time on, even when acting as an ordinary person, the Bodhisattva provided for his life with coarse food and covered his body with tattered clothes; he maintained this resolve against greed every single day.

When one possesses the fortune of an emperor, one should immediately employ the wisdom of the Buddha to contemplate the burdens of the state. Though such fortune may be lofty, vast, and abundant, it is difficult to calculate its true nature.
It is not eternal and lacks solidity; there is only suffering and no joy. All that exists perishes; the body is a deceptive illusion, as fragile as an egg and as difficult to nurture as a wolf.
Those who have eyes to behold him cannot help but tremble with awe.

Throughout his successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva practiced with the precepts as his conduct, until he finally became the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the parrots at that time was I myself;
the king of men was Devadatta."
"Thus does the Bodhisattva, firm in resolve, practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

[The Jātaka of Prince Dharmadatta] (30) "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the crown prince of a king, named Dharmadatta. His inner mind was pure and his outer conduct was clean; he constantly guarded his heart against the calamities of following the path of error, honoring the sages and being filial toward his parents, while compassionately rescuing all sentient beings."
Whenever the Crown Prince went to pay his respects at court, he invariably required the presence of the Chancellor; his every movement followed the rites, and he never failed in decorum.

A favorite concubine of the King, harboring illicit lust within her heart, came out to seize the Crown Prince; the Prince struggled with all his might and managed to escape, striking the Chancellor’s head and saying, "Begone!"
His crown fell to the ground, and his head was seen to be hairless; the concubines laughed at him, and he was ashamed and harbored resentment.
The concubine wept before the king and said, "Though I am humble and lowly, I am still your queen; the Crown Prince is insolent and has lustful designs upon me."
The King said:

"The Crown Prince’s conduct is such that he thinks nothing except the Buddha's intent, speaks nothing except the Buddha's teachings, and practices nothing except the Buddha's Way. The eight directions praise his virtue, and no other kingdom can equal him; how could there be anything wrong with him?"
The slanderous words were frequent and insistent, intended to delude the king’s mind.
The king said, "To harm one's own flesh and bone is called rebellion and treachery; I shall not do such a thing."
He was appointed as a frontier king, eight thousand *li* from his home country, and was told:

"As you govern the lands beyond the borders, practice benevolence in accordance with the Way; do not take the lives of the people wantonly, nor covetously oppress the common folk. Treat the elderly as your own kin and love the people as your own children; carefully cultivate the Buddhist precepts and guard the Way until death."
"The world abounds in deceit and falsehood; it is only through the teaching of the tooth-seal that one may find faith.
The Prince bowed his head to the ground and said with tears:
"I dare not disregard your venerable instruction."

He immediately took up the governance of the land, establishing the five precepts and ten virtues, and transforming the people through compassion. Within one year of occupying the throne, the distant populace was drawn by his influence; they returned to his rule in clouds, increasing the number of households by more than ten thousand. When this report was submitted to the imperial court, it was remarked that the King’s virtuous influence had shone so far as to cause this result.
The King and his Queen Consort were delighted and sighed with admiration.

A concubine, however, harbored deep resentment; she conspired with him to eliminate the Crown Prince. Watching for a moment when the King was asleep, she took his seal, pressed it with wax, and forged a letter: "You have committed the crime of insolence toward Your Majesty.
Unable to execute you in person, I have written this letter: as soon as it reaches you, quickly remove the pupils from your eyes and deliver them to the messenger to be returned to your own country."
The messenger arrived, and the assembled ministers all said, "This is a messenger of demonic chaos; he does not come from Your Majesty.
The Crown Prince said:
"Great King, your former teeth have now truly appeared.
To love one's own body while abandoning one's kin is called a great rebellion.

He then rejoiced with his ministers for three days, traveled throughout the realm to provide for the destitute and relieve the needy, and used the Buddha’s shadow image to instruct the people with a heart of compassion.
He issued a proclamation seeking anyone capable of removing an eye; the boy who sold the fodder immediately had his eyes extracted and handed over to the messenger.
The messenger placed them in a casket and hurried back to his native land, where the Chancellor presented them to his favorite concubine. The concubine hung them before her bed and scolded, saying:
"Did you not follow my will? Is it pleasant to have one's eyes gouged out?"
"The Great King dreamed that a snake and a bee stung the Crown Prince’s eye;
upon waking, he choked with emotion and said, 'Will there be some misfortune for my son?
A favorite concubine replied:"
"The King’s arrival is imminent; this dream was merely a premonition, and there will surely be no other outcome.
The Prince used the music of his lute to seek food and sustain his life, traveling from country to country until he reached the kingdom of his consort’s father, the King.
The king possessed a marvelous lute; he summoned [the musician] to play it.
Its sound sighed in praise of the virtues of the former kings, rather than being a mournful tone of lament for an orphan without kin.
His consort, understanding the sounds [of his distress], choked with sobs and said,
"My lord is in dire straits!
The King said:
"What do you mean?
The consort related the matter in detail and took leave of her kin, saying:
"This is simply my destiny; for a woman to have two surnames is not virtuous."
"Please invite a gentleman of filial piety to accompany us.
When the two parents raised their voices in mourning, the consort took the Crown Prince and returned to his native land.
"The King, having heard that there was one skilled at the lute, summoned him to perform it."
His appearance was haggard and emaciated, and the king recognized him only by his voice.
The king said,
"Are you my son, Dharmaśreṣṭha?"
The Crown Prince prostrated himself on the ground, choking with sobs.
The Queen, the palace attendants, and everyone throughout the kingdom, high and low, were moved to profound grief.
The Consort then related the matter from beginning to end.
The King said:
"Alas! Women are devoid of benevolence, like rice mixed with poison.
Is it not fitting that Buddhism distances itself from them?"

He immediately seized the Chancellor and his favorite concubine, flogging them with thorny whips; he poured molten lac into their wounds, which blistered and split open, and he buried them alive in a pit.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In a previous life, the Prince once sold white pearls. At that time, that concubine was the daughter of a wealthy family traveling by carriage on the road, and the Prime Minister was the charioteer."
He called out to the pearl-selling boy, saying,
"Bring your pearls here for me to see.
Without purchasing the pearls, he gazed lustfully at him and spoke with lewd words.
The youth said in anger, "You have not returned my pearl and instead cast lustful glances at me; I shall gouge out your eyes!
The woman and the charioteer both said:
"Would it be right to bind you with thorns and whips, smear you with sticky resin until your flesh is torn, and bury you alive?

For once good or evil has been committed, calamity or fortune follows of its own accord, just as a shadow is bound to a form. When evil ripens and guilt is established, it is like an echo responding to a sound."
To desire that evil deeds bring no calamity is like sowing seeds while hoping they will not sprout.
When a Bodhisattva receives the pure precepts of the Buddha, it would be better for them to lose their sight and die than to live by committing sexual misconduct.
At that time, the Prince Dharma-dāna was none other than myself.
The Prime Minister was Devadatta.
And the favorite consort was Devadatta’s wife.
"Thus does the Bodhisattva, firm in resolve, practice the perfection of ethical discipline.

31. [The Jātaka of the King] (31): "In the past, there were three brothers who were Bodhisattvas. During a time of drought that had befallen the world, the common people were devouring one another; they all went out to seek food in order to sustain their fragile lives."
After traveling through mountainous and perilous terrain for several days without food, his two elder brothers each said,
"Would it be permissible to save our lives by using our wife?
The eldest brother first killed his own wife and divided her body into five portions.
The younger brother was moved by compassion and would not eat out of grief.
When the middle brother killed [the animal] again, the younger brother was particularly choked with emotion.
When the two elder brothers wished to kill his wife, the younger brother said:
"Killing another to save oneself is not the benevolent path of the Buddha; I shall not do it.
He took his wife into the mountains to gather fruit for their sustenance.
After many years had passed in the mountains, there was a lame man who had a secret affair with the wife; they conspired to kill her husband.
She feignedly said, "It is my duty to provide labor and support, yet you are performing it for me; tomorrow I shall follow as your attendant, wishing to share in these hardships together.
She said:
"The mountain is extremely treacherous; you must not go there.
Although he declined three times, she would not listen, and so they set out together.
Seeing the height of the mountain and the depth of the valley, the wife pushed her husband over the precipice.
By the water’s edge there was a deity, who received them and settled them in peace.
The woman was delighted to have found a place and returned with her husband, who was still lame, to live together.
The husband subsequently traveled along the river and encountered some merchants; he then related the whole matter from beginning to end.
The merchant took pity on him and carried him to the kingdom of Feng.
The king of that country had passed away, yet there was no crown prince; the ministers yielded to one another, and there was no one suitable to be installed.
He ordered the brahmins to perform a divination, saying, "Should any traveler appear who possesses the auspicious marks, establish him as king.
When the brahmins beheld the Bodhisattva, they immediately said, "Excellent!"
"This is a ruler who possesses the Way; he can provide the people with the protective canopy of supreme benevolence!
The assembled officials and the common folk shed tears and sighed in admiration, all of whom offered him blessings of long life.
He was escorted into the palace and invested with the imperial throne; he immediately nourished the people through the four means of governance and abolished all heterodox arts.
He bestowed the five precepts and proclaimed the ten wholesome actions, so that throughout the land everyone observed the precepts.

Thereupon, the Lord of Devas protected that kingdom; demons and malevolent spirits fled in all directions, poisonous vapors dissipated, and grains and fruits ripened in abundance. Neighboring states were transformed by its rectitude, former enemies became closer, and people gathered like clouds, carrying infants in their arms.
“The wife and infant were lame, and their husband entered the state to beg for alms, explaining that he had previously fled the calamities of his time as a suitor.
Now he has come to submit to Your Benevolence.
Among the people, both high and low, there was none who did not regard him with refined wonder; they all said:”
"A virtuous wife may be recorded," the lady said.
"She should be granted a generous reward."
The king immediately saw his wife and asked,
"Do you recognize the Son of Heaven?
The wife, terrified, bowed her head to the ground.
The King recounted the matter from beginning to end to his palace attendants, and the Minister of Rectitude said,
"This man deserves execution.
The King said:
"The Buddhas regard benevolence as the supreme treasure of the three realms; I would rather sacrifice my life than depart from the path of benevolence.
The king then sent men to drive him out of the country and sweep away his footprints.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The king was I myself;
the lame man was Devadatta."
"The wife" refers to Hao-shou (Good Head).
"Thus is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Perfection of Conduct through the Firm Resolve of Observing the Precepts. 32.

[The Jātaka of the Ordinary Man] (32): "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was an ordinary man, he studied the Buddhist scriptures extensively and deeply understood the nature of sin and merit. Regarding the various paths of learning, medical arts, and even the cries of birds and beasts, there was nothing he did not clearly comprehend."
Beholding the world’s turmoil and defilement, he withdrew from office and did not serve; he revered the Buddha’s precepts and followed only what was correct.
Living in poverty and hardship, he worked as a merchant carrying loads on a pole.
As they passed by a riverbank where food was being served, a flock of crows screeched together; the merchant became terrified, his hair standing on end with dread, yet the Bodhisattva laughed at him.
Having finished his meal, he departed immediately and returned to his own land.
He paid the man his wages and said, "When the crow cawed and you laughed, was there some reason for it?
The man replied:
The crow said:
"He possesses a white pearl of immense value.
Kill him and take the pearl; I wish to eat his flesh."
"Therefore, I merely smiled at him.
[The other] asked,
"Did you not kill him?"
He replied:
"Those who have not studied the Buddhist scriptures commit sins as vast as the heavens, yet they claim there will be no retribution; this is nothing but self-deception."

I have beheld the scriptures of the Unsurpassed True Reality and observed the pure benevolence of the Bodhisattvas; they cherish even the smallest creatures that fly, crawl, or wriggle and do not kill them, nor do they take what belongs to others, regarding even grass and weeds as not their own.

Those who delight in killing are not benevolent; those who delight in taking what is not theirs are not pure. In my previous life, I committed the defilement of taking what was not mine, and now I have reaped its calamity: dwelling in wretched poverty, I am a hired laborer for my son.
If I were to commit this again now, I would plant immeasurable sins and cease to be a disciple of the Buddha.
"I would rather die poor and lowly while upholding the Way than live wealthy and honored while lacking the Way.
The host said, "Excellent!"
"Only the Buddha’s teaching is true.
Thus did the Bodhisattva practice the perfection of ethical discipline with such firm resolve. 33.
[The Jātaka of the Poor Merchant] (33): "In the past, the Bodhisattva lived in poverty in this world. He worked as a hired laborer for a merchant and entered the sea to gather wealth."

The ship remained stationary and could not move forward; the merchants, both great and small, were filled with fear and did not fail to pray to the gods and spirits, while those above and below provided mutual relief.
The poor man, however, relied solely on the Three Refuges, observed the precepts without transgression, and repented and reproached himself three times each day and night.
He made a compassionate vow:
"May no sentient beings in the ten directions experience fear as I do today;
when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall deliver such beings."
Even after seven days had passed, the ship did not move forward; the sea deity then falsely appeared in the merchant's dream and said, "If you abandon this poor man, I will take you away."
When the merchant received the dream, he was deeply moved with sorrow and discussed it in private.
The poor man observed this subtly and fully understood the reason for it, saying:
"Do not sacrifice the lives of the multitude for the sake of my single body."
The merchant owner built a raft, provided him with provisions, placed him upon the raft, and pushed it away.
The great fish overturned the ship and devoured all the merchants, while the poor man, carried by the wind, reached the shore and returned to his native land, where his nine clans rejoiced.

The poor man obtained this merit by taking the three refuges, observing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, maintaining the fasts, repenting, and directing loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
That poor man was none other than myself.
"Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Willingness when he practiced the precepts.

(34) [The Jātaka of the Poor Brahmin] (34): "In the past, the Bodhisattva lived in seclusion observing the precepts, having no desire for worldly glory. He relied on the support of the four castes to tend their graves; whenever there were funerals or burials, he would immediately lend his strength to assist them."
The presiding mourner was moved by this and bestowed the treasures upon him as a gift; however, whatever he obtained, he immediately returned to the four families.
The four families said, "You exerted great effort to acquire these treasures; why do you return them to us?"
The Daoist said, "I guard your wilderness, yet he is buried in your land; according to the principles of great righteousness, the treasure belongs to you.
The four castes sighed and said:
"Excellent! How could the sages of antiquity surpass you?
He then selected from among his maidservants one who possessed both virtuous conduct and beautiful appearance, and gave her to him as a wife, dividing his family wealth to establish her household.
The Daoist said,
"Advance your practice and elevate your virtue.
At that time, the poor Daoist was none other than myself.
"The wife was Jiu-yi.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Willingness in maintaining the precepts. 35.
[The Jātaka of the Boy] (35): "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was an ordinary man, he took refuge in the Triple Gem and observed the precepts without fail."
He traveled together with his maternal uncle, supporting himself by selling goods as they went toward a foreign land.
The uncle crossed the river first and stayed at the house of a widow; she had a young daughter who said to her mother, "There is a basin behind us;
we can trade it for white pearls with that merchant."

The mother complied with her daughter's wish and showed it to the merchants; they scraped it with knives to examine it and saw that it was genuine treasure, yet they feigned throwing it to the ground, saying, "It has defiled our hands!"
They immediately set out on their way, and both mother and son were ashamed.
When the youth arrived later, the woman again requested the pearl, and her mother said,
"The shame of our previous conduct should serve as a warning for now."
The girl said, "Observe this young boy;
he possesses the marks of a benevolent man and is not the greedy and cruel one from before.
She showed him again.
The young boy said, "This is purple-gold; may I trade all my goods for it?
His mother said:
"Yes," the youth said,
"will you ferry me across for two of my gold coins?"
The maternal uncle soon returned and said, "I now bestow these few pearls upon you; bring the tray back.
His mother said:
"There was a noble youth who offered me his finest pearls in exchange for my golden plate; yet I still deplored that they were so base.
If you do not depart at once, I shall further strike you with my staff."
When the uncle reached the water’s edge, he stamped the ground and cried out,
“Give me back my treasure!
In his haste, he beat his breast until he vomited blood and died.
The nephew returned the gold, but having already witnessed his uncle’s death, he choked with emotion and said:
"Greed has even led to the loss of one's life!
The Bodhisattva maintained his integrity to obtain the treasure, while Devadatta lost his life through greedy deception.
The youth was my own self;
the uncle was Devadatta.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Willingness when he practiced the precepts.
36. [The Jātaka of the Elder Brother (the Monkey)] (36): "In the past, during countless kalpas, there were two brothers who sought wealth and profit to support and honor their kin."
He went to a foreign land and had his younger brother present the pearl to its king.
When the king beheld his brother’s radiant countenance, he was delighted and gave his consent, promising him his daughter in marriage, provided he were asked for ten million pearls.

The younger brother returned and informed his elder brother; the elder brother pursued him to the king’s presence. Upon seeing the elder brother’s majestic and dignified countenance, and hearing how his speech was always in accord with the sacred scriptures, the king found his noble appearance beyond compare.
The King highly esteemed her and offered his daughter in marriage to her.
The woman’s feelings were wavering and indecisive, so her elder brother said to her with deep concern:
"An elder brother-in-law is as a father, and an elder sister-in-law is as a mother; this constitutes the bond of parent and child—how could there be the propriety of marriage between us?"
"This king occupies the honored position of a sovereign, yet he behaves like a beast.
She then led her younger brother away.
As the woman ascended the terrace and looked out, she said:
"I am a *jing-gu* spirit; would it be acceptable for me to eat my elder brother's liver?
Thus they transmigrated through birth and death: the elder brother became a macaque, while she and her younger brother both became turtles.
The female turtle was ill and craved the liver of a macaque; her mate went out to seek it for her.
Seeing a macaque drinking at a watering place, the turtle said, "Have you ever witnessed joy?"
He replied, "Not yet. He asked:
"I have a sublime joy within my house; do you wish to behold it?
He replied, "Indeed."
The turtle said,
"Mount upon my back and I shall take you to see it.
He mounted its back and followed after it.
Midway across the stream, the turtle said,
"My wife longs to eat your liver.
What pleasure is there in being in the water?"
The monkey felt a sense of shame in his heart and said,
"Now, observing the precepts is the constant way of guarding goodness, while expedient means is the great method for rescuing those in distress. He continued:
"Why did you not say so sooner?
I have already hung my liver upon that tree.
The turtle believed him and returned.
The monkey climbed onto the shore and said, "You dead turtle-worm! How could there be a liver inside your belly that should be hanging from a tree?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The elder brother was none other than myself; though I constantly maintained purity and never committed sexual misconduct, I have fallen among the monkeys due to the lingering karmic retribution of my past."
The younger brother and the king’s daughter both received the bodies of turtles; the male was Devadatta, and the female was Devadatta’s wife.
Such was the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of resolve (adhyāśaya-pāramitā) in the observance of the precepts.
37. [The Jātaka of the Householder] (37): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was traveling by ship across the sea to gather jewels and relieve the destitute."
On the seashore there was a city, complete with gardens and groves. A beautiful woman stood by the water's edge and called out to her companions, saying:
"This country is rich and fertile; one may seek out treasures at will. You should deign to enter the city and observe whether the people possess anything of value."
The merchants, deluded by the seductions of the malevolent spirit, remained to live there for five years.

The Bodhisattva, feeling longing for his two parents and his native land, left the city and climbed a mountain where he gazed far and wide. There he beheld a man within an iron city, wearing a celestial crown and sitting with solemn dignity, who said to the Bodhisattva:
"Are you all so deluded?"
To take a malevolent spirit as a wife, abandoning the deep bonds of your parents and nine generations of kin—only to be swallowed by a ghost—is this not delusion?
Do not sleep; examine the truth of this matter!
Now there is a divine horse soaring here to deliver the masses; you may mount it and return to your dwelling to preserve your life and limb.
If you dote upon your bewitched wife, you will die and enter this city, where all manner of poisons will be inflicted upon you, and even then, regret will be of no avail.
The Bodhisattva accepted the command and feigned sleep to observe her; seeing the words "True Suchness" (Tathatā), his heart was filled with dread.
The next day he secretly informed the others, and they all agreed. Each watched for their wives to transform into the bodies of foxes, competing to devour people.
Everyone was filled with dismay and said,
"We are lost! Alarmed by one another,
they were so preoccupied with their own preparations that they neglected their vigilance and were thus destroyed.
The Horse King Zhen said, "Who is there dwelling apart from home who, with a heart longing for their kin, has come swiftly to this place? I shall deliver you.
The merchants rejoiced and said:
"This must surely be the work of Heaven," they cried,
and the multitude galloped back to take refuge in him.
His wife immediately embraced their child and followed his tracks in mournful lamentation, her words saying:
"Alas for the Sovereign Heaven! For many years she was my wife, yet now she has become a ghost.
Her mournful cries were heart-wrenching.
She went before the King and spoke as follows: "Now I am in great distress and have no means of relying upon myself; I only pray that Your Majesty will compassionately attend to my circumstances."
The king summoned the Bodhisattva and questioned him regarding the cause of these events; he then related the beginning and end of what he had witnessed.

Upon seeing the beauty of her form, the king hurriedly sent his son-in-law away and took her into the inner palace, where she gave herself up to licentious excess, causing the state to fall into great disorder.
The ghosts transformed into foxes, roaming by day to devour people; their harm was thus extreme, yet the King remained unaware.
Later, each reached the end of their lives and transmigrated through the cycle of birth and death. Through the accumulation of merit, the Bodhisattva eventually attained Buddhahood.
A fox-spirit, having been reborn through transformation in the household of a brahmin, possessed an exquisite beauty.
At that time, the Buddha was seeking alms in the district of Dharmāraṇya; having finished his meal, he left the city and sat beneath a tree.
The brahmin beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence; his complexion was like refined gold, and a halo of light radiated from his neck like the moon among the stars.
Seeing the Buddha in this way, his joy was immeasurable, and he returned to tell the boy’s mother:
"My daughter has found a husband who is a Hero of the World."
"Quickly clothe yourself in the name [of this practice] and possess all the worldly excellences.
The Brahmin and his wife took their daughter to offer her to him; on the way, they saw his footprints.
His wife said:
"This divine hero is free from desire; how could he allow licentiousness or depravity to disturb his resolve?
The father said, "My daughter is the most exquisite flower of the kingdom; why does she possess such high virtue yet fail to turn his heart?"
The wife then versified its meaning, saying:
"The lustful man walks with trailing feet; The angry man walks with clenched toes;
The fool stamps the earth with his feet; These are the tracks of those honored by gods and men."
"Do not bring shame upon yourself.
His father said,
"Your wisdom is shallow."
He turned away and departed, offering his daughters to me.
The World-Honored One said:
"The sixth Māra-heaven offered me three daughters, who were transformed into hungry ghosts."
"Now you, a sack of excrement, have come here again for what purpose?
The brahmin was abashed, and his wife further humiliated him.
At that time, there was a mendicant who stepped forward, bowed his head, and said:
"I pray that you grant it to me.
The World-Honored One admonished him, saying:
"In the past, when you were a king, she was a female ghost; she deceived you with her beauty and devoured all your subjects. Are you not weary of this?"
The bhikṣu was ashamed; he withdrew to meditate and attained concentration, thereby realizing the stage of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"After the Bodhisattva had received the precepts from the people in the city, he returned home and took refuge in the Triple Gem, making this vow:”
"Thinking, 'When my time comes to die, even in death I shall no longer transgress the pure and weighty precepts of the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha,' he accumulated vast merit through his observance of the precepts, and thus the Way of the Buddha was eventually accomplished."
At that time, the elder was myself;
the king was this present bhikṣu;
and the ghost was the brahmin’s daughter.
The celestial being within the city was Śāriputra.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Precepts when he resolved his will upon the infinite.
38. The Sūtra of Prince Mūpaka [The Jātaka of Prince Mūpaka] (38). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the śramaṇas:

"In the past, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī. The king had a crown prince named Mūpaka, who possessed infinite wisdom from birth; regarding all matters of the past, present, and future, his knowledge was unimpeded. He was upright and radiant, like the moon among the stars."
The king had only one son, whom the entire kingdom loved; yet at the age of thirteen, he remained silent and spoke not, as if he were mute.
The king and queen were filled with anxiety and summoned the brahmins to inquire into the cause of this.
He replied, "This is an ill omen. Though upright and silent, what benefit does he bring to Your Majesty?
Since there are no heirs in the inner palace, could this not be his doing?"
"It is fitting that the Dharma should bury him alive; he will surely have a noble successor.
The King was immediately struck with remorse and entered to consult his Queen. From the Queen down to all the palace attendants, there was none who did not mourn bitterly, sighing and saying:
"How tragic it is that the Crown Prince’s merit is so meager that he has met with such calamity while still living!"
Mourners blocked the road as if there were a great national mourning.
He was fully attired in precious garments and entrusted to the funeral attendants.
The attendants stripped him of his noble robes and prepared a tomb for him together.
Mupò thought to himself:
"The King and the people of the state believe me to be truly mute.
He then silently adjusted his robes, entered the water to bathe, anointed his body with incense, and donned his precious garments; approaching the tomb, he called out:
"What are you doing? he asked.
They replied, "The Crown Prince is mute and deaf, and the kingdom has no heir. The King has ordered us to bury him alive, hoping that an excellent successor might be born."
He replied, "I am the spirit of the tomb.

When the bereaved husband looked at the carriage, it appeared suddenly empty and void; yet observing his appearance, it was radiant with light, its brilliance extending far and wide across the fields like the clarity of the sun. Such was the vast power of his sage-like spirit, moving the divine and the numinous.

In mourning for their husband, there was no one, whether high or low, who was not struck with terror; they looked at one another in pairs, their complexions turning yellowish-green, and even when their words formed elegant prose, everyone feared them.
They looked up to heaven and said:
"The spiritual virtue of the Crown Prince has reached this state!"
He immediately prostrated himself with his head to the ground and said,
"I pray that Your Majesty will return to the kingdom so that the people may not lament.
The Prince said:
"Go quickly and inform the King, saying that I am able to speak.

The man immediately galloped to report this; the King, his consorts, and the myriad people were greatly amazed by what had occurred. Their hearts rejoiced as they praised it as excellent, and there was none who was not delighted. Chariots raced and men ran, crowding the roads until they were completely filled.
Mupò said,
"Would it not be excellent for me to attain the practice of emptiness and stillness as a śramaṇa? At this,
his intention first inclined toward that course.
Śakra immediately transformed himself into a garden with ponds and trees such as the world had never beheld, and he changed his many precious robes into a *kāṣāya*.

When the King arrived, the Prince prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs and paid homage according to the rites. As the King took his seat and heard the Prince’s voice, the majesty and spiritual power of his light and shadow caused both heaven and earth to tremble. The King was filled with joy and said by way of praise:
"Since you were born, the entire kingdom has held you in reverence and love; you shall succeed to the celestial throne and become the father and mother of the people."
He replied:
"I only pray, Great King,
that you will compassionately heed these humble words."

In the past, I was once the king of this land, named Susīma. For twenty-five years I ruled the kingdom and governed the people; I personally upheld the ten wholesome paths and nurtured the people with compassion. The use of whips, staves, and all weapons of war completely ceased and was no longer practiced; there were no prisoners in the jails, and not a sound of resentment or lamentation was heard on the roads. My benevolent gifts were distributed far and wide, providing moisture that reached everywhere without exception.
Yet, because he went out on excursions with a vast retinue of attendants, his guides and ministers galloped ahead to clear the way, causing the common people to tremble with fear;
in the end, he entered Mount Tai to be roasted, boiled, and dismembered for sixty thousand years, unable to seek death and crying out in lamentation without rescue.

At that time, with nine kinds of relatives within and subjects and citizens without, possessing billions of years' worth of wealth and enjoying boundless pleasures, how could one have known that I would enter the Mount Tai hell to undergo the infinite suffering of being burned and boiled?
Regarding the glory of existence—wife, children, and subjects—who among them can share away one’s sufferings?
Only those various poisons are immeasurable; every time I recall them, my heart is pained and my bones ache, my body breaks into a cold sweat, and my hair stands on end.

They say that when misfortune departs, calamity follows like a shadow; though they wish to speak, they fear incurring further blame. The suffering of Mount Tai is difficult to endure a second time; therefore, they shrink back their tongues and desire to remain entirely silent.
It has been thirteen years since the sorcerer-master ordered Your Majesty to bury me alive.
Fearing that Your Majesty might incur the calamity of Mount Tai, I have ventured to speak these words once more.
"Now I wish to become a śramaṇa and maintain the practice of desirelessness; seeing that the gates of manifold calamities lie open, I shall no longer be king.
I pray you do not find this strange.
The King said:

"You are a benevolent ruler whose conduct is noble and whose virtue is honored; you lead the people according to the Way. Any transgressions were but as fine as a hair or a thread, things not even remembered by others. How can it be that for this you have incurred such a cruel and severe punishment!"
"If I am now the ruler of men and follow my own desires without upholding the True Dharma, where will I ultimately go?
He then permitted himself to study the Way.
The King returned to governing the state with rectitude rather than wickedness, and consequently brought about abundance and joy.

Mupò immediately disciplined his emotions and severed his desires; with a resolve to advance toward the true Way, he eventually attained Buddhahood. He extensively expounded upon exemplary models to rescue and deliver sentient beings until they reached nirvana.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who was the tomb-ghost at that time was my own self.
The father king was the present King Śuddhodana."
As for "mother," it refers to my mother who has now abandoned this world of wonders.
Indeed, worldly splendor, beauty, and perverse pleasures are the furnaces that incinerate the body;
purity and detachment are the home free from affliction.
If one wishes to avoid calamity and escape transgression, one must not fail to follow the Buddha’s teaching.

Although practicing the Way is arduous, it is still superior to dwelling within the three miserable realms; as a human being, one stays far removed from poverty and does not encounter the eight difficulties.
"The resolve to study the Way should be like the conduct of the Buddha; those who wish to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, an Arhat, or Nirvana can obtain it by taking this path.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the śramaṇas were filled with joy and prostrated themselves in worship.
39. The Milinda Sutta (The Birth Story of King Milinda) (39). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the śramaṇas dwelt in seclusion and reflected deeply:
"The people of the world practice heterodoxy and indulge in desire; from beginning to end, there is no one who tires of the five pleasures.
What are these five pleasures?"
The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and fragrances, the tongue and flavors, the body and tactile sensations—
regarding these five desires, how could anyone ever grow weary of them by the time their life comes to an end?
After midday, they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand aside, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Only the ignorant among the world are deluded by the five desires; until the end of their lives, do they ever feel weariness toward them?"
The Buddha told him: "Behold the world;
there is no satisfaction in those five worldly pleasures.
Long ago, there were five hundred merchants who went to sea to gather wealth. Among them was a wise man named Mīḷha, who served as their leader."
In the sea there is a divine fish named Makara; it struck and wrecked their ship, and everyone on board perished, except for Miliṇa, who barely escaped by clinging to a plank.

Driven by the wind, he was cast onto a shore; the place was named Bimā. Having ascended the bank, he wandered about in hopes of finding some relief. He discovered a narrow path and followed it forward.
From afar, he saw a city of silver with lush, flourishing trees, and within it were bathing pools surrounded on all four sides, encircled by sweet water.
There were four beautiful women, whose appearance equaled that of celestial maidens; they came forward to welcome him, saying:
"Having traversed the vast ocean, your toil has been great; we offer our congratulations on this auspicious arrival."

Now, within this silver city, there are many treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and giant clam shells—with which the palaces are adorned. We four daughters shall serve you as your attendants, retiring late and rising early, following whatever commands you give; we pray that you do not wander elsewhere.

Milaṇa entered the city and ascended the palace of the seven treasures; there he enjoyed pleasures according to his desires, and there was nothing he wished for that was not provided. He remained there for over a thousand years.
Milaṇa thought to himself:
"Is there some karmic connection that prevents these jade maidens from allowing me to depart?"
He waited until the four women were asleep, then stole away in haste.
From afar he beheld a golden city where eight jade maidens met him; their greetings were as before, and the jade maidens' exquisite beauty surpassed that of the four women.

In the city was a jeweled palace named Kṣema, where the brilliance of the moon, pearls, and various gems surpassed those of the former [palace], and his lifespan lasted for many tens of millions of years.
He then wondered:
"Is there a reason why these eight daughters do not allow me to depart?"
Watching for him to fall asleep, he stealthily and swiftly departed.
Again, he beheld a city of crystal, where sixteen jade maidens came out to welcome him; their words were as before, inviting him to enter the city and ascend the seven-jeweled palace.
The palace of the city was composed of various jewels, and the splendor of the jade maidens surpassed that of before; he resided there for many tens of millions of years.

Yet, his mind remained unsatisfied, so he waited until the maidens were asleep and fled. He beheld again a city of lapis lazuli, its radiance shimmering brilliantly, where thirty-two maidens came out to meet him, kneeling and prostrating themselves with reverent words as previously described.

He was invited into the city and ascended the Palace of Seven Jewels, named Uttara. Within it, the various jewels, musical performances, delicious foods, and female beauty surpassed those of the previous palace; he dwelt therein for a long duration of years, as described above.
Furthermore, while observing the women as they lay asleep, he departed and fled. From afar he beheld an iron city, yet there was no one to welcome him.
Milaran thought to himself:

"The silver city had four women, the golden city eight, the crystal city sixteen, and the lapis lazuli city thirty-two; these jade maidens, whose radiance illuminates the world, have practiced devotion to welcome me. That they do not welcome me now—is it because of my noble status?"

After circumambulating the city once, a spirit opened the gate. As Māluṅkyaputta entered the city, he immediately saw that spirit; the spirit’s name was Kūṭadanta. A glowing iron wheel was spinning upon its head. The spirit who guards those who commit transgressions took that wheel from its own head and placed it upon Māluṅkyaputta’s head; his brain flowed out and his body was scorched.
Mila wept and said:
"From four to eight, from eight to sixteen, and from sixteen to thirty-two; I have dwelt in the Hall of Glory, the Hall of Fragments, and the Hall of Utmost Joy."
"Because I practice the conduct of non-satisfaction, I have obtained this.
When shall I be free from this affliction?
The guardian spirit replied:
"The number of years for this retribution has been as long as you have lived; you shall be spared from this calamity.
Thus, the wheel of fire remained above Māluṅkyaputta's head for sixty million years before he was finally released.
The Buddha said to the śramaṇas:
"Milaṇa was none other than myself. Why is this so?"

Before I had reverently taken refuge in the Triple Gem, I was deluded by folly and believed in heterodox teachings; while my mother was bathing, putting on new clothes, and lying down, I stepped upon her head. For this reason, Mount Tai rolls its wheel of fire over my head.

Furthermore, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he once observed the eightfold precepts with a heart full of joy; consequently, he attained a precious city and a lifespan of billions of years, such that his every wish was fulfilled according to his mind, and there was nothing he sought that he did not obtain.
"Beholding the world, one finds no satisfaction; only upon attaining the Way does one come to rest.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"Milaṇa has emerged from the prison of Mount Tai; he has closed his mind to the three evil realms, sealed his mouth against the four blades, and restrained his body from the three faults."

Be filial and obedient to your parents; personally serve the Three Honored Ones. Wear the precepts as your crown, don the precepts as your robe, cherish the precepts as your sustenance, and savor the precepts as your delicacy. Whether eating, resting, sitting, or walking, do not forget the Buddha’s precepts. In every step you take, accomplish yourself through the virtue of the precepts, until you naturally attain Buddhahood.

In the conduct of ordinary people, those who are unfilial toward their parents and fail to honor and revere their teachers see their own future bring upon them grave offenses; Mīḷha is surely of that sort!
"Indeed, when one commits evil, calamity follows as surely as a shadow pursues the body; by severing depravity and revering the Truth, all misfortunes will naturally perish.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the śramaṇas rejoiced and paid their respects.
40. The Sūtra on King Māndhātṛ [The Previous Life of King Māndhātṛ] (40). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Ānanda was dwelling in seclusion and reflected deeply:
"From beginning to end, few among sentient beings grow weary of the five desires.
After midday had passed, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and having withdrawn, addressed him, saying:
"O World-Honored One!
While sitting in leisure, I reflected deeply:
'Among sentient beings, those who know contentment are few, while those who do not weary of the five desires are many.'"
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said."
Why is this so? In ancient times there was a king named Mūrdhaja, to whom all the lands of the east, west, south, and north were subject.
This king possessed seven treasures:
The power of the flying golden wheel, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, the bright moon pearl, the jade maiden wife, the noble minister, and the minister of the military—
these seven treasures of the king are rare to behold in the world.
Furthermore, he had a thousand sons, handsome and elegant, intelligent and profoundly wise, whom the world acclaimed as sages;
they possessed fierce strength that subdued all others, like lions.
The King was both sagely and benevolent; all under heaven delighted in his rule, and his lifespan numbered in the hundreds of millions.
The King thought to himself:

"I possess the continent of Aparagoyānī, a land thirty-two thousand li in length and breadth. Its inhabitants are flourishing, its five grains are abundant and fertile, and every household is immensely wealthy—a rarity in this world—and my kingdom encompasses it all."
Even if this were so, would it not be excellent if that august Heaven were to rain down gold and silver coins for seven days and seven nights, bestowing such bounty upon me?
The deity granted his wish, raining down two kinds of precious coins that filled his realm; the brilliance of these celestial jewels shone resplendently throughout the kingdom.
The king rejoiced immeasurably, and all under heaven offered their congratulations.
The King rejoiced together with his ministers, and the people all praised him, attaining boundless joy for many tens of millions of years.
The King thought to himself again:

"I possess the western lands, spanning three hundred and twenty thousand *li*, with the splendor of the seven treasures and a thousand sons illuminating the kingdom; it has never been before in this world that the heavens have rained down precious coins."

Although this may be so, I have heard that in the south there is Jambudvīpa, a land twenty-eight thousand li in breadth and length, where the populace is vast and one cannot fail to obtain whatever one seeks.
"Would it not be a joy for me to obtain that land?
As the King’s thought first arose, the golden wheel turned southward; the seven treasures and the four armies rose lightly into flight and together arrived at that land.
The king’s ministers and subjects followed him with joy; the ruler and the people of that land were filled with delight all day long.
The king continued his teaching and transformation for a number of years as mentioned above.
The king thought again:
"I possess the Western Lands, and now I have acquired the Southern Lands; among gods and men and all manner of treasures, what is there that I do not have?

Now I hear that in the East lies Pūrvavideha, a land thirty-six hundred thousand *li* in extent. Its sovereign and its people, its jewels, grain, and various rarities—there is nothing one could wish for that is not found there."
"Would it not be a joy for me to obtain that land?

As soon as these words left his mouth, the golden wheel turned toward the east, and the seven treasures and the four armies arrived by flight together; from the sovereign and ministers to the common people, there was none who did not rejoice in their allegiance.
Furthermore, he governed his subjects with the benevolent transformation of the True Dharma; for as many years as mentioned above, every household cherished his virtue.

The King thought again: "I possess the western lands, the southern lands, and the eastern lands; among the gods and men, there is no precious treasure I do not have. Now I hear of the land of Uttarakuru in the north; would it not be excellent if I were to obtain its kingship?"
Upon opening his mouth to make this vow, the golden wheel turned northward, and the seven treasures along with the fourfold army all flew forth as before.
As he first entered that realm, he beheld from afar that the ground was green like the color of emerald feathers.
The King asked,
"Do you all see the green ground?
They replied:
"I see it," he replied.
"This is the land of Uttarakuru."
Again [the Buddha] asked, "Do you see the white ground?
He replied, "I see it."
He said, "This is pounded rice; you all should eat it.
Furthermore, he saw various jewel trees upon which were hung many soft and exquisite garments, armlets, rings, necklaces, and various rare ornaments, saying:
"Did you see him?
He replied, "Indeed, I did!"
He said, "You all shall wear these.
The King governed with benevolence and transformed the people through forbearance; he resided there for many years, their number being as stated above.
Again, he gave rise to this thought:
"I possess the three worlds, and now I have acquired forty thousand *li* in the north; I desire to ascend to the abode of Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
The King’s mind was finally convinced; the golden wheel turned upward, and the seven treasures and four armies flew through the air into heaven, entering the palace of Śakra.
Seeing the King arrive, Śakra welcomed him joyfully, saying:
"I have long admired your lofty reputation and have desired to meet you for a long time; how wonderful it is that you have come here!"
Taking his hand, he sat together with him, offering him half of his own seat.
The king looked around to his left and right and beheld celestial palaces made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and pearls; seeing them, his heart rejoiced.
He then thought again:
"I possess four kingdoms and countless treasures; such glory is beyond words.
Yet it would cause the Heavenly Emperor to perish."
"If I occupy this position, would that not be my highest wish?
As this evil thought arose, his supernatural powers were extinguished; Śakra returned him to his former palace, where he immediately fell gravely ill.
A minister asked, "The King’s illness is grave;
should you pass away before our eyes, will there be a final testament?
The King replied:
If someone were to ask, "Why did the king lose his life? one should answer according to what was observed:
he contracted a disease because of greed, which ultimately led to the loss of his life.
Greed is the blade that severs life and the foundation upon which nations perish.
There is nothing—from abandoning the Three Honored Ones to dwelling in the three miserable realms—that does not stem from it.
I warn future descendants: greed and delusion are the very fires that incinerate the self; be careful not to succumb to greed.
"Indeed, for those who possess great honor and status, their calamities are lofty; for those who possess many treasures, their resentments are numerous.
After the King passed away, his descendants recited this precept on greed, transmitting it as a treasure through the generations.

"The people of the four continents revere his benevolent transformation; they honor the Triple Gem, practice the ten wholesome deeds, and take these as their method of governance, thereby attaining eternal blessings.
The World-Honored One said:

"In observing the world, those few who are able to abandon glory and nobility and cast off the five desires are only those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, Arhat, or Pratyekabuddha. Only one who has attained the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path, the Most Perfect Enlightenment, the Charioteer of the Dharma, and the Teacher of Gods and Humans is able to sever them completely."

That the Celestial Emperor (Shengxing Huangdi) exists and fulfills his vows without failing his heart is brought about by the practice of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom in past lives; it is not obtained in vain.
"King Mūrdhaja was none other than myself.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha. 41.
The Sutra of King Samantaprabha [The Jātaka of King Samantaprabha] (41). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“In the past, there was a Bodhisattva who was a great king named Samantaprabha. His compassionate benevolence radiated far and wide, and his excellence was sung of throughout the ten directions. The people relied upon his prosperity, just as a loving child brings peace to his parents.”
A neighboring kingdom had a king who governed with justice; his strength was like that of a lion, such that he could run and seize birds in flight.

Once, when the cook lost some meat, he rushed to the market at dawn to search for it. On the road, he saw a fresh corpse and took it to prepare as a dish, the flavor of which surpassed that of ordinary animal flesh.
On a later day, he prepared a meal, but its flavor was not as good as that one.
The King reprimanded the Grand Cook, and the cook returned in sincerity, prostrating himself and confessing.
The King felt ashamed and said:
"Is human flesh sweet?
he asked, and silently commanded the executioner to make this his regular practice.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One.

"Those who are excessively attached to flavors find the Way of Benevolence (ren) thin; when the Way of Benevolence is thin, the hearts of jackals and wolves arise. Now, as for the wolf, it greedily craves the taste of flesh and robs the lives of creatures; therefore, the world holds it in enmity."
The cook received the command and silently went about killing people to satisfy the king’s desires, while the subjects and citizens groaned in distress.
When the report reached the king and he sought out the culprit, the king said, "It is only right."
He secretly warned the cook, saying,
"Be careful! The official caught him.
The rebel said,
"The King has commanded you.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:

"Your servant has heard that only one who possesses the virtue and benevolence of a King, the spiritual brilliance of a Sovereign as clear as the sun and moon, whose bounty equals the moisture of the Earth and the harmony of Heaven and Earth, and who embraces all sentient beings like the vast void—only such a person may become the King of the world."
To violate benevolence and follow cruelty is to belong to the class of jackals and wolves;
to leave light for darkness is to be among the ranks of the blind;
to abandon the means of rescue and sink oneself is to be of the same category as those who wrecked their boats.
To release moisture while nourishing the parched is the calamity of fire and drought;
to turn one's back on the void and face the obstructed is the heart of a stone man.

Now, the predatory cruelty of the wolf, the blindness of the blind man, the fragility of unbaked clay, and the burning of a stone man’s nature—such conduct cannot serve as a model for overseeing men; how much less could it serve as the way for a king of the world?
"If one honors superior virtue, the state prospers; if one delights in cruelty and slaughter, it perishes.
Between these two principles—one good and the other evil—upon which will Your Majesty rely?
The King said:
"Is it permissible to deprive a child of its milk?
He replied, "It is not."
The King said,
"I am like him. The assembled ministers all said:
"A jackal or wolf cannot be raised; one who lacks the Way cannot be a ruler.
With one heart and one voice, the ministers and subjects pursued him.
The King fled into the mountains, where he beheld a divine tree. He prostrated himself before it and addressed it, saying:
"Let me return to my kingdom and offer the hundred kings as tribute to the gods.

Having completed his vow, he set out immediately; spying when the kings emerged, he suddenly leaped into the crowd and seized them—just as a hawk or a falcon snatches a swallow or a sparrow—and captured ninety-nine kings.
The tree spirit manifested a human form with a countenance of extraordinary splendor and said to Aqun:
"You have lost the king’s glory through your lack of the Way; now you again commit extreme cruelty—what do you hope to gain from this?"
"Aqun stepped forward toward him, but he suddenly vanished.
At that time, King Puming went out to inspect the suffering and happiness of his people; on the road, he encountered a brahmin, who said:
'Great King, please return to the palace; I have something to say.'"
The King said, "I was ordered to go out yesterday; it is difficult to go back on one's word.
Let the Daoist sit forward, and I shall return immediately."
He was subsequently captured by Aqun, who threw him beneath a tree. The king said, "I do not fear the loss of my life;
I only regret that my word of honor has been violated. Aqun said:
"What do you mean? the king asked.

The practitioner explained in detail the vow he had seen and expressed his wish to behold him once more, receive his profound precepts, and offer him rare treasures; he added that he would die without regret upon returning home.
Aqun released him, and upon returning he saw the Daoist personally arranging a high seat. As the Daoist ascended the seat, he immediately spoke these verses:
"When the kalpas have reached their end, Heaven and earth blaze in conflagration;
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans Are all reduced to ashes and embers."
When the merit of devas and nāgas is exhausted, they wither and perish therein;
if even the two polarities of heaven and earth must fall, how can there be permanence in a kingdom?
Birth, old age, sickness, and death revolve without end.
When reality contradicts one's wishes, sorrow and grief become a source of harm.
When desire is deep, calamity is high; there is no external thing that is not a festering sore.
The three realms are entirely suffering—what reliance can there be in this world?
That which exists has its origin in non-existence; through causes and conditions, all things are formed.
That which flourishes must inevitably decline; that which is substantial must inevitably become empty.
Sentient beings, in their restless confusion, all dwell within an illusory realm.
Both sound and resonance are empty; the lands are likewise so.
Consciousness has no form, yet it rides upon the four serpents;
with the precious elephant of ignorance, it makes its pleasure-carriage.
"The form has no permanent master, and the spirit has no permanent home;
the three realms are all illusions—how could there be a kingdom?
Having finished receiving these verses, he immediately offered twelve thousand gold coins.
The brahmin admonished him again, saying:
"If you maintain awareness of the four signs of impermanence, its calamities will surely be extinguished.
The king said:
"I respectfully accept [your command] and dare not neglect your clear admonition.
He then proceeded to the tree, walking with a smile.
Ajita said:
"My life is in peril this very moment; why do you rejoice and laugh?
He replied, "The words of the World-Honored One are rarely heard even within the three realms."
"I now cherish this; what is there in the fate of a kingdom that is worth grieving over?
Ajuna replied sycophantically, "I wish to hear your honored instruction."
The King then bestowed these four verses upon him, and with surprise and joy, he exclaimed:
"How majestic is the World-Honored One, who proclaims the four states of impermanence! Indeed, not to hear or behold this is what is called perversity and madness."
He immediately released the hundred kings, each ordering them to return to their own kingdoms.

Aqun repented his errors and renewed himself; he made his dwelling beneath a tree and daily contemplated four verses. When his life ended and his spirit departed, he was reborn as the crown prince of a king, yet he remained impotent even after taking a wife.
The king was deeply distressed by this and consequently recruited a woman from the royal harem to transform him into a man; subsequently, he became licentious and abandoned the True Way.
The king grew indignant at him and had him flayed and displayed at the crossroads, commanding passersby:
"Strike his head with your fingers; thus shall you humiliate him."
Just as the ninety-ninth person arrived, the Prince passed away.
His spirit underwent transformations and transmigrated without end until, meeting the Buddha while he was in the world, he was born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having lost his father at an early age, he lived in solitude with his mother.

He served a *brahman* teacher, being sincere by nature and truthful in speech; his physical strength was such that he could tear apart an elephant. The master loved him and his friends respected him; he was praised as a man of virtue both far and near, and whenever the master traveled abroad, he would invariably entrust the care of his household to him.
The teacher’s wife harbored illicit desire; she took his hand and seduced him with lewd words.
Aqun declined, saying, "In this world, among long-standing friends, a man is regarded as my father and a woman as my mother; how much more so for one whom my teacher reveres?"
"You may follow his example in burning your body, but you shall not dare to comply with this disorder.
The master’s wife felt abashed and withdrew to contemplate how she might bring about a change.
When her husband returned, the wife said:
"Your son praised that worthy man; was that not sufficient to illuminate your own failings?
He then detailed all of his transgressions.
The female spirit appeared so real that the Brahmin believed her.
The Master said to Aqun,
"Do you wish to become an immortal?
He replied:
"Yes," he replied. [The other] said:
"You killed a hundred men, cut off their fingers, and now you have attained the way of the divine immortals."
Receiving this command, he took up his sword and killed whoever he encountered, obtaining ninety-nine fingers; the multitude fled in terror and the kingdom trembled.
Seeing his mother, he said joyfully:
"The required number has been reached; I shall now become an immortal."
The Buddha thought:
"These heterodox paths delude the masses; such is the state of affairs throughout the world.
He transformed himself into a śramaṇa and walked before them, saying:
"The number of people is sufficient.
As he pursued from behind and could not catch up, [the king] said:
"Śramaṇa, you may stop!"
He replied:
"I have resided here for a long time; it is only you who have not. He said:
"What is the meaning of 'stopping'? He replied,
"My evils have all been stopped, whereas your evils are blazing."
Aqun’s mind opened and was suddenly cleared like clouds dispersing; he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and bowed his head in repentance for his transgressions.
Joining his palms, he followed [the monk] back to the vihāra, where he immediately became a śramaṇa.

The Buddha explained his past conduct to him and manifested the four signs of impermanence; [the youth] attained the stage of Stream-enterer, withdrew beneath a tree, closed his eyes with hands joined in prayer, refined away remaining defilements, and advanced to attain non-attachment.
"The King summoned tens of thousands of military strategists and warriors to search for and capture the demonic rebels, but they did not know where they had gone.
As they passed by the Buddha's dwelling, [the King] asked: 'From where have you come?'"
His body was covered in dust and soil.
He replied, "There is a demonic rebel in our kingdom who has killed innocent people; we are now searching for and pursuing him."
The World-Honored One asked:
"If the people first cultivate virtue but later turn to honor the heterodox, what should be the method for the governance of the state?
He replied:
"If one was noble before but becomes base later, the True Dharma shall govern them.
[The other] asked, "But if one previously harbored the mind of a beast yet later conceives the virtue of a sage, where would the True Dharma go?
He replied:
"Those who were previously base but later become noble are rewarded by the True Dharma.
He replied:
"The thief has already abandoned evil and revered the truth; he is now a śramaṇa."
The King sighed in admiration and said: "Excellent!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Supreme Guide of the Dharma—how wondrous and sublime is his transformative power that it has reached such a state!"
"Once you were a jackal or a wolf, yet now you have attained heavenly benevolence.
He bowed his head at your feet and sighed again, saying:
"This transformation is marvelous; I wish to behold it once."
The World-Honored One said,
"It may be so. Thereupon,
the king and his officials went to him and said:
"May the virtuous and worthy one deign to open his eyes and grant me an audience?
He asked this three times.
The reply was:
"My eyes shine so brightly that they are difficult to behold.
The king bowed his head and said, "Tomorrow I shall prepare a modest meal; I pray that you will deign to look upon me."
He replied,
"I go to the latrine, but not to the palace.
The king said:

"Only as you command. Upon his return, he tore down the latrine and dug up the ground to renovate it. He used the timber of *candana*, *tsi*, and *liu* trees for its pillars and beams; the floor was drenched with fragrant water. He blended *candana*, *sugandha*, and *uragasāra* incenses into a paste for the plaster. He fashioned seats and mats from fine woolens and various silks, adorned them with intricate carvings and engravings, and beautified them with a multitude of precious gems.
Brilliant and resplendent, it surpassed even the palace halls.
On the following day, the King himself held an incense burner and went out to welcome him.
Once Āgnyagātra had taken his seat, the King knelt and crawled forward on his knees, and having completed the offerings, he immediately preached the sutra, saying:
"How can one eat from what was defiled the day before at the latrine?
He replied, "It cannot."
He asked,
"Is it possible now?
He replied:
"Very well," [the Emperor] replied. Aqun said:

"Before I had beheld the Buddha, I served those demonic sorcerers; my mind, speech, and body were devoted to all manner of perversity. These heterodox paths and defiled transformations were as foul and filthy as a latrine."

Excrement can be washed away, but defilement is difficult to remove. Fortunately, by virtue of past merit, one is born into the age of a Buddha; by bathing in the pure transformation, one discards foul odors and embraces fragrance, becoming inwardly and outwardly pure like a celestial mani-jewel.
