Those who do not behold the Buddha and do not understand the four marks of impermanence—observing their inclinations—are like the insane who intoxicate themselves with wine. To not associate with the assembly of the virtuous and instead rely upon the ten evil deeds is no different from being confined in a cage with jackals and wolves!
The King said: "Excellent!
How marvelous is the supreme transformation wrought by the Buddha, for he has caused the stench of the latrine to be transformed into sandalwood!"
When he had finished preaching the sutra, he immediately set out through the marketplace and heard that there was a woman giving birth against nature, her life hanging by a thread.
He returned and reported the matter as it was; the Buddha said, "Go and assist her in childbirth."
Aqun felt ashamed.
The World-Honored One said:
"You expected to give birth [to a son] and said:..."
"Since my birth, I have directed compassion toward all sentient beings, moistening and sustaining heaven and earth.
Now, both you, mother and child, are complete.
Having received these instructions, he went forth to proclaim the Buddha's grace, and thus both mother and child were born together.

Returning along the path, he was filled with doubt, thinking that while he had been cruel enough to commit murder, he now spoke of universal compassion; thus, he bowed his head and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ajñāta Kauṇḍinya:
"The day when an ordinary person's mind opens and they receive the Way may be called their 'new birth.'"
Not beholding the Three Honored Ones and not yet having received the grave precepts, one is like a child in the womb; though such a one possesses eyes, what can they see?
Though they possess ears, what can they hear?
"Therefore it is said: 'It has not yet arisen.
At these words, Aqun’s mind was opened and he immediately attained the path of Arhatship (*arhat*).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who was Puming in former times was my own self.
In a previous life, I bestowed upon him four verses, which enabled him to save hundreds of kings; now he has caused them to attain the Way and shall not suffer heavy retribution."

In a previous life, Aqun was once a bhikṣu who carried a bushel of rice to a monastery and presented a knife to the Master; filled with joy and admiration for his honor, he prostrated himself and departed.

Carrying rice, one gains great strength; climbing a blade, one gains many jewels; rejoicing, one gains a handsome appearance; praising the Honored One, one becomes a king; and because of performing prostrations, one is venerated by the people of the land.
Ninety-nine people struck him on the head until he eventually lost his life; thus, he killed his former enemies and cut off their fingers.
When the next person wished to strike him, seeing that he was already dead and beholding the śramaṇa, he felt even greater compassion.

Because his mother first conceived an evil intent, Aqun’s initial disposition was likewise wicked; yet because he beheld the śramaṇa with even greater compassion, upon seeing the Buddha, he immediately became filial.

Planting the pure yields the pure; planting the mixed yields the mixed. Once good or evil has been sown, calamity or fortune follows it accordingly. Like a shadow following a body or an echo responding to a sound, everything has its cause; it is not merely a matter of spontaneity.
The bhikṣu made a vow, saying:
"May you encounter a Buddha and attain the Way.
As he had vowed, he obtained it.

If one makes offerings to the Triple Gem even as small as a strand of hair, and a śramaṇa utters compassionate blessings for the donor, then what is spoken shall be obtained exactly as said; there is not one in ten thousand cases where it fails.
"Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s resolve for the Perfection of Precepts.
*The Compendium of the Six Perfections*, Volume Four;
*The Compendium of the Six Perfections*, Volume Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of the Kingdom of Kāñcī in Wu.
Chapter Three: The Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣāntipāramitā). This chapter contains thirteen sections.
As for the principle of the Perfection of Forbearance, what is it like?
The Bodhisattva reflects deeply:

"The consciousness of sentient beings is obstructed by ignorance; they are arrogant and conceited, constantly desiring to surpass others, and wish to monopolize for themselves official rank, territory, and the pleasures of the six sense-faculties."

If one perceives that [the self] exists, the fool immediately becomes greedy and envious; greed and envy dwell within, while hatred dwells without. Giving does not lead to cessation, and thus he remains intoxicated by madness, dwelling long in blinding darkness.
"Transmigrating through the five realms, one is scorched and boiled in Mount Tai, or becomes a hungry ghost or an animal; the accumulated suffering is immeasurable.
Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva immediately awakened and sighed with regret:

"The reason sentient beings suffer the ruin of states and families, the peril of their persons, and the extinction of their clans—why they encounter such calamities in life and the retribution of the three miserable paths after death—is entirely due to their inability to embrace patience and practice compassion, which causes it to be so."
The Bodhisattva, awakening to this, made a vow to himself:
"I would rather undergo the cruelty of boiling water and fire or the suffering of being minced into sauce than ever inflict the poison of anger upon sentient beings."
"Indeed, the endurance of what is unbearable is the source of all blessings.

Since his awakening, he has practiced compassion in every lifetime; even when sentient beings reviled him, beat him with sticks, stripped him of his wealth, treasures, wife, children, and kingdom, or endangered his body and life, the Bodhisattva would immediately use the merit of the Buddhas' power of endurance to suppress their venomous anger. Out of compassionate pity, he would pursue them to rescue and protect them, and if they were spared from their transgressions, he would rejoice on their behalf.

42. [The Jātaka of the Bodhisattva] (42): "In the past, the Bodhisattva beheld that the world was defiled and turbid; kings and ministers were unrighteous, turning their backs on the truth and following what is false, making them difficult to guide and transform. Therefore, he concealed his brilliance and hid his form, dwelling among the tombs to practice the conduct of patience."

In a cemetery there was a cow with a calf that constantly took its dung and urine for food and drink; thus, its life was exposed to the elements as it focused its thoughts on this practice, its appearance becoming so ugly and dark that all people loathed it.
The people of the country saw this and told one another,
"There are ghosts in this land.
None of those who saw it failed to spit upon and revile them, or to pelt them with earth and stones.
The Bodhisattva harbored not even a hair’s breadth of anger; with a heart of compassion and pity, he said:
"How tragic it is that this person, failing to see the Buddha's sutras, commits such evil.
He then made a vow:
"I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I shall certainly deliver them across this [suffering].
Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) when practicing forbearance.

43. [The Jātaka of the Seer Śyāma] (43): "In the past, there was a Bodhisattva whose name was Śyāma. He constantly harbored universal compassion that moistened all sentient beings; he felt pity for the ignorant masses who did not perceive the Three Honored Ones."

He settled his two parents in the mountains and marshes; as his parents were advanced in years and both had lost their sight, Śyāma was filled with grief and sorrow, weeping whenever he spoke of them.

He rose three times every night to check whether they were cold or warm. Through such supreme filial conduct, the fragrance of his virtue pervaded heaven and earth, becoming known to the terrestrial deities, the sea dragons, and the people of the land.

They reverently uphold the Buddha’s ten wholesome actions: they do not kill living beings; they do not pick up lost items on the road; they maintain chastity and do not marry. Thus, physical calamities are entirely stilled. They sever all verbal transgressions—double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, and frivolous talk—as well as slander, calumny, and deceitful falsehoods. Within their minds, all manifold defilements—the stains of envy, anger, greed, and gluttony—are entirely pacified.
Faith in the good brings blessing; doing evil brings calamity.
Using thatch and weeds for a hut and tares and brambles for a mat, one remains pure and free from desire, with a will as steadfast as celestial gold.

On the mountain there was a flowing spring from which lotuses grew; various sweet fruits surrounded its banks. Rising early to gather fruit, he never tasted them first himself; his benevolence shone afar, and birds and beasts relied upon him for protection.

At that time, his two parents were thirsty, so Śyāma went to fetch water. A king of the Kāśī kingdom had entered the mountains to hunt; drawing his bow and releasing an arrow, he shot at a deer on the mountain, but by mistake struck Śyāma in the chest. The poison from the arrow spread through his body, and the pain was beyond words.
Looking around to left and right, he wept and spoke in a loud voice:
"Who is there who can kill three Daoist masters with a single arrow?
My parents are advanced in years and both have lost their sight; were I to perish this very day, they would surely all lose their lives."
He raised his voice in lamentation, saying:
"The elephant dies for its tusks, the rhinoceros for its horn, and the peacock for its plumage; I have no tusks, horns, or beautiful eyes and feathers—by what means shall I die?"
Upon hearing this piteous cry, the king dismounted from his horse and asked,
"Are you from the deep mountains?
He replied:
"I shall take my two parents to dwell in these mountains, rid myself of the world's manifold defilements, and advance in my resolve for the Way.
When the King heard Śyāma’s words, he choked with emotion and shed tears, mourning him with profound sorrow.
He said:
"I have committed acts of non-benevolence, cruelly ending the lives of creatures, and furthermore, I have killed one of supreme filial piety.
He then raised a lament, saying:
"What shall we do with this? The ministers, from the highest to the lowest, were all choked with sobs.
The King spoke again, saying:
"I will ransom your life with an entire kingdom; I pray you show me where my parents are, for I wish to confess my transgressions.
He replied, "Follow this small path; not far from here there is a humble thatched hut, and my parents are within it."
"Explain to my parents that from this point on we shall be parted forever; may they live out their remaining years in peace, and pray they do not grieve for me with longing.
Shi then raised his voice in lamentation once more, and suddenly passed away.
The king and his retinue were once again overcome with grief; following the indicated path, they arrived at the place where their kinsmen were.

As the king’s large entourage passed through, the grasses and trees rustled with a solemn sound. Hearing this, the two parents suspected it was some extraordinary being and asked, "Who is this traveler?"
The king said,
"I am the King of Kāśī.
His kinsman said:
"It is most excellent that Your Majesty has come here. There is this grass mat upon which you may rest and cool yourself, and sweet fruits to eat; my son shall fetch water. For now, please return."
When the king saw his kinsmen treating their son with such compassion, he choked back his sobs once more.
The king said to the kinsmen, "I see these two practitioners treating their son with such compassion; my heart is deeply grieved, and my pain is immeasurable."
"The Daoist's son, Shan, has been killed by my arrow.
His parents cried out in shock and distress, saying,
"What crime has our son committed that you should kill him?"
"Your son possesses benevolence and compassion; when he treads upon the earth, he always fears it might cause pain. What crime has he committed that Your Majesty would execute him?
The King replied, "A filially pious son is truly the most excellent of men; I merely mistook him for a deer and shot him by accident!"
He said: "You have already died; what can you rely upon?
I am now dead."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will lead my two elderly parents to the place where your son’s corpse lies; there we shall surely meet our end together, so that we may all alike turn to ash and dust.
Hearing these words from his kinsmen, the King was once again overcome with profound grief and lamentation; he personally led his parents to the site of the corpse.
The father placed his head upon his knees, while the mother cradled his feet; they both kissed his mouth and sucked his feet, each using one hand to stroke the wound from the arrow.

Beating their breasts and slapping their cheeks, they looked up and cried out: "O gods of heaven and earth, gods of the trees and waters! Our son, Śyāma, revered the Buddha and believed in the Dharma; he honored the worthy and was filial to his parents. He harbored a great benevolence that knew no bounds, its moisture reaching even to the grasses and trees."
He said again:

"If your sincere devotion to filial piety toward the Buddha has truly reached the heavens, then the arrow shall be extracted, the heavy poison shall be extinguished, and you shall survive to complete your practice of ultimate filiality.
If it is not so, my words shall prove untrue, and I shall consequently perish, and we shall both become mere ashes and dust."
When Śakra, Lord of Devas, the Four Great Kings, the terrestrial spirits, and the sea dragons heard the sound of his piteous lamentation, they believed his words and were all moved with agitation.
Śakra descended from his celestial form and said to his attendant,
"This son of supreme filial piety, I can restore to life.
He poured divine elixir into Śyama’s mouth, and suddenly he regained consciousness.
The parents and Śyāma, the king and his retinue of ministers, were filled with a mixture of grief and joy, and they all wailed once more.
The king said:
"The virtue of supreme filial piety in honoring the Buddha has reached such an extent as this."
He then commanded his ministers:
"From this day forward, let all the people throughout the land revere the goodness of the Buddha’s ten virtues and cultivate the practice of Shian’s supreme filial piety."
When this was practiced throughout the entire kingdom, the state subsequently became prosperous and the people lived in peace, eventually leading to a Great Peace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“In life after life, I have served the Buddhas with the practice of supreme filial piety; my virtue was lofty and my blessings abundant, until I became the God among Gods, peerless throughout the three realms.”
At that time, Śyāma was my own self; the king was Ānanda;
and Śyāma’s father was my father of today.
The mother was my own mother, Śrīmatī;
the Lord Śakra was Maitreya. Such was the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) when he cultivated forbearance in this manner.

44. [The Jātaka of the Brahmin Kṣāntivādin] (44): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a brahmin named Kṣāntivādin. He dwelt in mountain marshes, practicing intense meditation beneath a tree, subsisting on fruits and spring water."
With internal defilements extinguished and abiding in empty stillness, he extensively illuminates and attains the full knowledge of the six supernormal powers.

His wisdom is like the fragrance of incense that wafts through the eight directions, above and below; all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Arhats do not fail to praise him with admiration.

Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the sea dragons, and the terrestrial deities, morning and evening, with solemn piety join their palms and bow their heads; receiving his transformation and following his influence, they protect his kingdom. Winds and rains accord with the seasons, the five grains ripen in abundance, poisons are eliminated and calamities extinguished, and both ruler and ministers flourish in prosperity.
The king, named Kali, entered the mountains to hunt; pursuing the deer, he followed their tracks until he came before the Bodhisattva.
The king asked the practitioner, "These animal tracks pass by here; how did they come to be thus?"
The Bodhisattva thought silently to himself:
"Sentient beings are in turmoil, seeking only their own bodies and lives; they fear death and crave life—how is my mind any different?
If I were to speak to the king, his cruel killing would be unrighteous, and my sin would be equal to his."
"If you say you do not see it, then I am being deceived.
Feeling ashamed in his heart, he lowered his head and said nothing.
The King then said angrily:
"The beggar who is about to die—when I, the honored sovereign of an entire kingdom, questioned him, he failed to answer at once and merely feigned a downward gaze?

The land was named *Te-zhi-shou-zhao-wei-bu* (The Land of Plucking the Fingernails and Saying No). The Bodhisattva was filled with sorrow; because the people of that land plucked their fingernails and said "no," he showed the king [the beggar] as if he had not seen him.
He said, "The tracks of the beast have passed this way, yet you say it is not seen; the King’s power is absolute—is it that you are unable to execute him?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I shall listen to you, O King.
The king asked, "Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am a man who practices patience.
Enraged, the king drew his sword and severed his right arm.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"My resolve is set upon the Supreme Way, and I do not contend with the times. If even this king adds his blade to mine, how much more so will the common people?
I vow that when I attain Buddhahood, I shall deliver him first, lest the masses follow his example in committing evil."
The king asked, “For whom was it? He replied:
"I am a person who practices patience.

Again, his left hand was severed; for every question, one limb was cut off—his feet were severed, his ears were severed, and his nose was severed. His blood flowed like a spring, and his pain was immeasurable. Heaven and earth shook, and the sun became darkened.
"The Four Great Heavenly Kings all arrived together and, with one voice, cried out in indignation:
'This king is cruel and tyrannical; his deeds are beyond compare!
They said to the Daoist master:"
"Do not let your hearts be defiled.
We shall execute the king along with his wife and children, and annihilate the entire kingdom to manifest his evil.
The Daoist replied:
"What does this mean?

This calamity arises because in my previous life I did not honor the Buddha's teachings and instead inflicted poison upon others; having committed evil, the retribution follows me like a shadow that is bound to its form."

In the past, what was sown was small, yet now what is harvested is vast. If I were to comply with this fate, the calamity would be as great as heaven and earth; suffering retribution for many kalpas, how could it ever come to an end?
When the common people witnessed these transformations, they rushed to him to confess their transgressions, speaking with one voice:
"The Daoist Master dwells here, bestowing auspicious protection and nourishing the state, averting calamities and extinguishing pestilence;
yet this most ignorant ruler, failing to discern right from wrong and lacking clarity regarding what to abandon or pursue, has heaped malice upon the Original Sage."
"We only pray that the Holy One will not report us to the Supreme Deity.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The King has inflicted innocent and grievous suffering upon my body; my heart feels compassion for him, just as a loving mother grieves for her infant."
"What fault have the common people committed that they should resent him?
If you have any doubts or expectations, seize my arm and cut it off and bring it here!
The people immediately seized him, and milk and blood flowed together.
He said, "I have felt the grief for my compassionate mother, and now its truth is manifest here.
When the people beheld this profound sincerity, there was none who did not submit to his transformation; they withdrew with joy and gladness.

The Bodhisattva had a younger brother who had likewise perceived the source of the Way; he resided on a different mountain and, using his divine eye to see through all things, observed the assembly of devas, spirits, and nāgas discussing the king’s wickedness, none of whom failed to harbor resentment.
Fearing that his brother might harbor thoughts detrimental to his virtue, he used his supernormal power to go to his brother's side and asked,
"Have you suffered any injury?"
He replied:
"No. You wish to test my faith."
"Take these severed hands, feet, ears, and nose and place them back in their original positions; if they are restored, you shall have my trust.
When the younger brother rejoined them, they were immediately restored.
The elder brother said, "My faith in universal compassion is now manifest."

The heavenly deities and terrestrial spirits were all moved by both grief and joy; they bowed their heads in homage and praised him well, exhorting one another to advance toward lofty conduct, and having received the precepts, they withdrew.

From that time forward, the sun and moon lost their radiance, the five planets strayed from their courses, and portents of calamity followed one after another. Droughts caused grain prices to soar, leaving the people in distress and resentful toward their king.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, Kṣāntivādin was none other than myself;
his younger brother was Maitreya."
"The King was the Arhat Kauṇḍinya.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in exercising forbearance. 45.

[The Jātaka of the Boy] (45): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born into a poor family. As the poor family could not raise him, they wrapped him in a rag and, when the night was quiet and no one was about, silently placed him at the crossroads, leaving a thousand coins beside his path."

According to the customs of the country, this day is regarded as an auspicious one; people from all over the land gather in the fields and wilds, where both gentlemen and commoners, each with their own kind, partake in sumptuous feasts and enjoy themselves.
The brahmin, witnessing the performance, praised those gathered, saying:
"Oh, those gathered today!
There is another who is like pure white non-glutinous rice, unadulterated and whose fragrance is most exquisite."
"Now, as for those born today, whether male or female, they shall be noble and virtuous.

Among those seated was a householder who was childless; hearing this, he rejoiced silently and dispatched people in all directions to search for anyone who had abandoned a child, instructing them to ask passersby:
"Have you seen anyone who has abandoned a child?"
The traveler said,
"There is a widow who takes them.
He sent someone to search for her and found her location, saying:
"I am of the four castes, wealthy yet childless; if you offer this boy as a tribute, you may obtain many treasures.
The mother said, "You may leave money behind to send for the boy, so that he may seek goods according to his desire."
The mother’s wish was fulfilled.
After raising the child for several months, his wife became pregnant and said, "I raised this child of a different surname because I had no offspring;
now that Heaven has granted me a blessing, what shall I do with this child?"
He wrapped the child in a cloth and placed it in a cesspool at night.
A domestic sheep went there daily to suckle; a shepherd, searching and observing, saw the child and sighed, saying, "For what reason has the Supreme Lord caused his son to fall here?"
He took [the child] back and raised him with goat’s milk.
When the four castes discovered this, they rebuked him, saying:
"Did you steal the milk?"
He replied,
"I obtained a son left behind by Heaven and have nourished him with my milk.
The four castes were filled with regret.

After he had been raised for several months, the woman eventually gave birth to a son; her evil thoughts arose once more, and she again wrapped him in rags as before and placed him in a carriage rut. The child’s mind remained fixed on the Triple Gem, and his compassion was directed toward his parents.

"At dawn, several hundred merchants traveling in carriages passed by this very road; their oxen stumbled and would not move forward. The merchants investigated the cause and, seeing the boy, cried out in alarm:
'Son of the Heavenly Emperor, by what means have you come to be here?'"

Cradling the child in his arms, he placed him in the carriage; the oxen moved forward as if flowing with ease. After traveling twenty li, they stopped beside a rest-house for oxen. There was a widowed mother who addressed the merchant, begging him, saying:
"Please grant me this child to relieve my old age and poverty."
He then gave her to him.
Not long after his mother had raised him, the four castes heard of this and said with deep sorrow:
"Was our lack of benevolence a violation of Heaven’s virtue?"
Furthermore, using various treasures, he invited his son back home; choking with sobs, he reproached himself and raised both sons equally.
Within a few years, observing his son’s intelligence—extraordinary, versatile, and all-encompassing—an evil thought arose again, and he said:
"This boy's brilliance exceeds all bounds; my own son is no match for him. I must surely seize him."
He wrapped the child in his robes and entered the mountains, discarding it among the bamboo and refusing food, certain that he would perish.
The child conceived a thought of compassion and said:
"When I later attain Buddhahood, I shall surely deliver all beings from suffering."
The mountain was near a mountain stream; the boy, exerting his own strength, shook himself off and fell from the bamboo to the ground, rolling until he reached the water’s edge.

Twenty li away from the water stood a funeral bier carrying a corpse, with people passing by gathering firewood. Seeing the small boy from afar, they approached to look at him and sighed, saying, "Has the Supreme Deity dropped his son?"
He took [the child] home and raised him. When the four castes heard this, their resentment was as before;

they requested his return with various precious jewels, weeping piteously. [The child] was taught writing, arithmetic, astronomy, divination, and the arts of the various paths; he could master them upon a single glance. By nature benevolent and filial, his every word guided and transformed others. The people of the country hailed him as a sage, and Confucian scholars gathered like clouds.

A malevolent thought arose in his father; his nature was deeply corrupt. There was a smith seven *li* from the city whose house he approached, intending to kill his son. He wrote an instruction to the smith, saying:
"In the past, I raised this child; since he entered my household, pestilence has followed one after another, my wealth has been exhausted, and my livestock have died."
The Grand Diviner’s prognostication stated:
"The child has brought about this calamity.
Upon receiving the letter, he seized it with extreme urgency and cast it into the fire.

Feigning illness, he called his son and said, "My years are drawing to a close and I am afflicted by a grave illness; go to the smith's and carefully calculate the money and treasures there—they shall be your wealth for the rest of your life."
The son received his command and went forth; within the city gate, he saw his younger brother playing with his companions at tossing walnuts.
The brother said, "It is my good fortune that you have come, elder brother; please break some more for me."
The elder brother said,
"I must carry out my father's command.
The younger brother said:
"I beg leave to go," he said,
and took the letter to the master smith.
The master smith received the letter and threw his younger brother into the fire.
The father’s heart was agitated with fear, and he dispatched a messenger to seek his son. Upon seeing the elder brother, the messenger asked, "What has become of your younger brother?
The elder brother answered according to the facts.
The elder brother returned and reported this; his father sent a messenger on horseback to pursue his son, but the boy had already been reduced to ashes.
The father threw himself down, crying out to Heaven, until his vital energy became internally blocked, resulting in a chronic illness.
Furthermore, a poisonous thought arose within him:
"Since I have no heir, shall I not take this child as my own?
I must kill him."
The father had a storehouse located a thousand *li* from the capital; he then dispatched this son, saying:
"He is dissipating my wealth; you must go there to audit it.
I now give you a letter for the storehouse, sealed with wax and placed in a bag; you must set out at once."
In secret, he wrote an instruction saying:
"When this child arrives, quickly bind a stone around his waist and sink him into a deep abyss.
Having received the command, the boy bowed his head and proceeded on light horseback for half the distance.
There was a brahmin on the road who was a distant relative of his father; they were constantly exchanging gifts and letters and frequently visited one another.
This brahmin had a daughter who was both virtuous and wise, possessing profound knowledge of auspicious and inauspicious signs, astronomy, and divination.
When the boy arrived at the brahmin’s residence, he said, "The brahmin who is a close relative of my father is currently staying right here."
He said to his attendant, "I wish now to go and pay my respects; would that be permissible?
The attendant replied:
"Excellent!
he said, and immediately went to pay his respects.
The brahmin was delighted and said:
"Brother, our son has arrived!

he exclaimed, immediately summoning scholars, Confucian students, and men of venerable virtue from the four neighboring districts to gather like clouds. They feasted and enjoyed themselves in merriment, consulting together on all their doubts; there was no one who did not rejoice, remaining so until the end of the day and deep into the night, when each grew weary and fell asleep.

The woman secretly observed the man; seeing that he wore a pouch upon his belt containing a sealed letter, she silently untied it, took it back, and having read its contents, sighed with regret, saying:
"What kind of malevolent demon is this, to have harmed my virtuous son to such an extent?"
He tore up the letter and rewrote it, saying:

"My years are at their end, and my grave illness grows more severe by the day. That Brahmin is a dear friend of mine; his daughter is both virtuous and wise, and she is fit to be my son's match for all time. Prepare a full array of precious silks for the betrothal gifts, ensuring the minor rites are exhaustive and the major betrothal is magnificent. On the day of taking her as wife, act according to these instructions."
When he had finished writing it, he opened the door and returned [the letter].
At dawn, as they set out on their journey, the brahmins and scholars all followed along, sighing in admiration.
Upon receiving the letter at the guest house, they followed the instructions and went to the brahmin’s residence with full ceremony.
The Brahmin couple deliberated, saying:

"In the rites of marriage, one begins by selecting a partner of virtuous conduct and inquiring into their faults through divination of omens; if they are well-behaved and the ceremonies are complete, we shall grant our consent."
"Now that you are currently a man, you have not sought a match through a go-between, yet a bride has already arrived; how could he possibly be acting with arrogance?
She then withdrew for a banquet and rest, saying:
"That men and women become a couple is as it has been since antiquity."
"A man so virtuous and a woman so chaste are truly difficult to encounter.
He then accepted the marriage proposal from the Zong family, and his nine branches of kin sighed in admiration, saying,
"This glory shall be passed down through the generations."
When the ceremony for taking a wife was completed, the news was dispatched to his residence; upon hearing this, the four clansmen fell gravely ill.
When the son heard of his relatives' illness, he spoke with a choked voice:
"Life is difficult to preserve; it is like an illusion and not real."

The Brahmin wished to select an auspicious day to send him back, but the Bodhisattva, suffering inwardly, would not comply with his words. His family hurried home, where he ascended the hall and bowed his head; his wife followed by prostrating herself twice, advancing three steps while weeping as she bowed again, and calling out his name: "I am the wife of your son, [Name]. You have personally summoned me for such-and-such a purpose; I shall serve as the vessel for the ancestral lineage and fulfill my filial duties with all propriety."

"I only pray that the Great Man may recover swiftly and fortune arrive, that he may preserve his life forever without end, and allow him to fulfill his heart's desire and attain the virtue of a filial wife.
Having spoken, the four castes were filled with resentment; their inner blockage caused them to perish.

The Bodhisattva performed the funeral rites with compassion and deep mourning; the entire kingdom praised his filial piety, and after the period of mourning ended, he practiced the Way, his fragrance spreading throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The youth was none other than myself."
The wife was Jīvī; the four castes were Devadatta.
Such was the Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) when he cultivated forbearance in this manner.

46. [The Jātaka of the King] (46): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king who constantly nurtured and protected all sentient beings with the four immeasurables; his fame resounded far and wide, and there were none who did not praise his excellence."
His maternal uncle was also a king, residing in a foreign land; he was greedy by nature and shameless, regarding cruelty as valor.
Kaishilin sighed, saying:
"The Bodhisattva harbors the benevolence and kindness of Heaven and Earth."
They spread false accusations and slander, fabricating grounds for grievance, and raised an army intending to seize the Bodhisattva’s kingdom.
The Bodhisattva’s ministers all said:
"We would rather be lowly under a heavenly benevolence than hold high rank under a beast of prey."
The people said, "We would rather be the livestock of a ruler who possesses the Way than be the subjects of one who lacks it.

The king selected his warrior elite and arrayed his troops for inspection; ascending the terrace to observe the military situation, he saw the vast multitude and wept with tears streaming down, his face pressed against the railing as he lamented.

"If I were to sacrifice my single person for the lives of the myriad people, the state would perish and be difficult to restore, and a human body is difficult to obtain again. If I withdraw and flee, the borders of the state will all be peaceful and healthy; who then would suffer?"
The King and the Empress both abdicated their thrones and perished.

The maternal uncle entered and took control of the kingdom, governing with greed and cruelty; he executed the loyal and upright while promoting the sycophantic and treacherous. Governance became oppressive and the people were reduced to misery; their cries of resentment followed one after another, and they longed for the former ruler as a filial son yearns for a compassionate parent still living.

"While the King and his principal consort were dwelling in the mountain forests, there was a wicked dragon in the sea who, coveting the Consort’s radiant countenance, transformed himself into a brahmin. He feigned [piety] by joining his palms, sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture with his head bowed and mind stilled in contemplation, appearing exactly like a practitioner of the Way absorbed in meditative concentration."
The king beheld this with joy and daily gathered fruits to offer as sustenance.
One day, while the king was away on his rounds, the dragon seized the queen and fled, intending to return to his abode in the sea.
On his way, he passed through a narrow path between two mountains where a giant bird spread its wings to block the passage; there, it fought a battle with the dragon.
A dragon manifested as a thunderbolt and struck the bird, causing its right wing to fall off; it was thus captured and returned to the sea.
When the king returned from gathering fruit and did not see his consort, he said with regret:
"Has my past conduct been contrary to the Way, that such calamity has now befallen me?"
Thereupon, taking up his bow and holding his arrows, he traveled across various mountains in search of his principal consort.
Upon seeing a flowing stream, he followed it to its source and beheld a giant monkey who was wailing in deep grief. The King, moved with sorrow, said:
"What is it that you mourn?"
The monkey said, "I served as king alongside my maternal uncle; yet he used his power and influence to seize my subjects. Alas, there is no one to whom I can appeal!
By what means do you now soar over this rugged mountain?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"My grief is equal to yours!
I too have lost my consort, and I do not know where she has gone."
The monkey said,
"If you assist me in battle and restore my troops,
I shall search for them for you; you will surely find them in the end."
The king agreed, saying, "So be it.

The next day, the monkey fought with his uncle. The king then drew his bow and notched an arrow; his limbs tensed in a display of martial prowess. The uncle, struck with awe from afar, hesitated and fled in haste. The monkey king and his followers turned back, and he then commanded his host, saying:
"The Chief Consort of the Human King is lost on this mountain; you all must search for her.
The monkeys dispersed in various directions and saw a bird with injured wings.
The bird asked, "What do you seek?"
They said, "The King of Men has lost his principal consort; we have come to search for her.
The bird said:
"The dragon has stolen it!
There is nothing I can do; it is now upon a great island in the midst of the ocean.
Having finished speaking, the bird vanished.
The Monkey King led his host along a path to the seashore, anxious that there was no means to cross.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately transformed himself into a monkey with a body afflicted by scabies and came forward, saying:
"With such a vast multitude of soldiers as you have, more than the sands of the sea, why worry about not reaching that island?"
"Now let us each carry stones back to fill the sea; it can be made into a high mountain, not merely a passable islet.

The Monkey King immediately appointed him as Overseer, and the multitude followed his plan. Once the task of carrying stones was accomplished, the multitude gained passage, and the islet became surrounded by layers upon layers of earth.
The dragon created a poisonous mist, and the entire troop of monkeys fell ill, none of whom failed to collapse to the ground.
The two kings were filled with sorrow and lamentation, whereupon the young monkey spoke again, saying:
"Let the multitude’s illness be healed; there is no need for your holy concern."
He then applied celestial medicine to the nostrils of the multitude; they then cleared their noses and rose up, their strength and momentum exceeding what it had been before.

The dragon immediately raised wind and clouds to shroud the sun, flashing lightning across the sea of light, while its fierce rage sent thunderbolts crashing, shaking the heavens and rattling the earth.
The young monkey said:
"O King of Men, you are a master archer. That which flashed like lightning was surely a dragon.
By discharging your arrow to eliminate this evil and summon blessings for the people, all the sages will have no cause for resentment."
As a flash of lightning struck, the king released his arrow, which pierced the dragon’s chest directly; the dragon was shot dead, and the monkey host acclaimed it as well done.
A young monkey extracted the key to the gate, opened the door, and brought out the queen, to the joy of both gods and spirits.
The two kings returned together to their respective mountains and took leave of one another with humble grace and mutual deference.

Upon learning that his maternal uncle had died without an heir, the king’s subjects rushed forth to seek out their former sovereign. Amidst the mountain passes, the ruler and his ministers met; they wept together as they returned, and along with recovering their uncle’s kingdom, the myriad people rejoiced, crying out "Long live the Emperor for ten thousand years! A general amnesty was proclaimed and governance was made lenient; the hearts of the people were filled with joy, and they walked along with smiles upon their faces.
The King said:
"If a wife leaves her husband and travels alone for a single night, the people harbor doubts and suspicions; how much more so after ten days or a month?
Returning to your own clan accords with the rites of antiquity."
The consort said, "Though I dwell in this den of foul insects, I am like a lotus flower situated in the mud.
My words are true; the earth shall split asunder."
When he had finished speaking, the earth split open, and it was said:
"My proof has appeared.
The king said:
"Excellent! Indeed, integrity and purity are the conduct of a śramaṇa.

From this kingdom onward, merchants yield their profits, scholars decline official positions, the powerful can endure the lowly, and the strong do not oppress the weak—such is the transformation wrought by the King's influence.

"The lewd woman changed her ways; those in perilous situations maintained their integrity; the deceitful became trustworthy; and the crafty returned to sincerity—this was the transformation brought about by the Chief Consort.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was I myself."
The queen was Jīvī;
the maternal uncle was Devadatta;
and the Lord Śakra was Maitreya.
"Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) through the exercise of forbearance.

47. [The Jātaka of the Monkey] (47): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a monkey. His physical strength was peerless among his kind, and his wisdom surpassed that of men; he constantly harbored universal compassion to rescue and deliver all sentient beings."

While staying in the deep mountains, he climbed a tree to gather fruit and beheld a person in a remote ravine who was unable to escape. For several days, the man had been wailing and crying out to heaven, begging for his life.
Hearing their lamentation, the monkey was moved with sorrow and shed tears, saying:
"I have vowed to seek the Buddha solely for the sake of these beings.
If I do not rescue this man now, he will surely perish in misery."
"I shall seek out a valley below the bank and carry you out.
He then entered a secluded valley, had a man carry him, and climbing the mountain by grasping at the grass, he placed him on level ground.
Showing him the path, he said, "Go where you must; after we part, take care never to do evil."
Exhausted from his journey, he went to a secluded place to lie down and rest.
A man said to him, "In the valley you suffered from famine; now that you have come out, it is the same. What difference is there?"
He thought to himself:
"I shall kill this monkey and eat it to sustain my life.
Would that not be appropriate?"

He struck the monkey’s head with a stone until blood flowed, staining the ground crimson. Startled from his sleep, the monkey staggered and fell, then scrambled up a tree; yet he harbored no thought of malice. Feeling compassion and pity for the creature who had conceived such evil intent, he thought to himself:
"Though it is beyond my power to deliver him, I pray that in future lives he may always encounter the Buddhas, faithfully receive their teachings, and practice them until he attains liberation."
"In life after life, may no one harbor such evil thoughts as this man.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The monkey was my own self."
"The one who lived among the people of the valley was Devadatta.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) when he practiced forbearance. 48.
[The Birth Story of the Dragon] (48): "In the past, the Bodhisattva and Ānanda were both born as dragons after their karmic retribution had ended. One of the dragons said:"
"I have traveled with you throughout the great ocean, seeing all manner of things; would it not be fitting for us to go together onto dry land to enjoy ourselves?
He replied, "The people on dry land are wicked; encountering them would lead to unforeseen calamities, so we must not go out."
The first dragon spoke again:
"It has merely transformed into a small snake.
If there is no one on the road, it will seek out the main thoroughfare to play."
"If we hide whenever we encounter people,
what have we to worry about?
Thereupon, they agreed with one another and ascended together to go sightseeing.

Not long after emerging from the water, they encountered a venomous viper on the road. Upon seeing the two snakes, the viper gave rise to a malevolent intent; with the aim of attacking and harming them, it spat out poisonous foam upon the two snakes.
One snake conceived the thought of using its supernatural power to kill this venomous viper;
another snake, with a heart of compassion, endured it and admonished him, saying:
"One who acts as a noble person should forgive the many ignorant. To endure that which is unbearable—this is the true and supreme precept of the Buddha."
He then spoke in verse:
"Those driven by greed are like madmen; They possess no heart of benevolence or righteousness.
Out of jealousy they wish to harm the Sage; Only silent forbearance brings peace."
Those who act contrary to the Dharma and follow no discipline lack compassion within;
stingy and malicious, they obstruct the practice of giving, finding peace only in silent forbearance.
These heedless people who possess no precepts harbor a thief’s heart and inflict cruel harm.
Not following the Way and virtue, but finding peace only in silent endurance;
being ungrateful and lacking reciprocity, practicing hypocrisy and deceit—
this is the height of folly, yet finding peace only in silent endurance.
One snake then praised the virtue of patience and spoke a verse to explain its meaning; the other snake respectfully accepted it and consequently did not harm the viper.
The first snake said, "Shall we return to the ocean?"

They agreed and departed together, exerting their majestic spiritual power so that heaven shook and earth trembled; they raised clouds and sent down rain, manifesting transformations and dragon-like brilliance that terrified both humans and ghosts. The serpent was thus filled with dread and fear, staring at its own corpse as if unconscious, abstaining from food for seven days.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the one who wished to kill the venomous dragon was Ānanda.
The one who preached the Dharma of patience was my own self."
The venomous viper was Devadatta.
Wherever the Bodhisattva was born from lifetime to lifetime, he practiced patience; even while dwelling among birds and beasts, he did not forget his practice.
Such is the practice of patience by the Bodhisattva in the *Dharmakṣānti-pāramitā*.

49. [The Jātaka of King Dhanu] (49): "In the past, there was a kingdom named Mālava, and its king was named Dhanu. His learning was as profound as that of the gods, and there was no hidden truth he did not perceive. Realizing that the world is impermanent, he said:
'My body shall surely decay into the filth of the earth; what kingdom can one truly preserve?'"

Having renounced glory and abandoned pleasure, he donned the dharma-robes of a Mahāsattva; content with a single bowl of food, he received the śramaṇa precepts and dwelt in mountain forests for thirty years.
Beside the tree was a pit, thirty fathoms deep.
At that time, a hunter, while galloping in pursuit of a deer, fell into the pit.
There were also a bird and a snake, each one, who likewise fell in alarm; their bodies were all mangled and wounded, and they were both exhausted.
They looked up at the sky and wailed in grief, their voices filled with the sound of solitary misery.
The Daoist was moved by compassion; when he shone his torch upon them, he saw them weeping with their necks joined together. Standing at the edge of the pit, he told them:
"Have no fear; I shall deliver you from this heavy calamity."
He immediately fashioned a long rope and suspended it for them to climb; the three creatures either bit onto it or held onto it, and thus they all preserved their lives.

They bowed their heads together in gratitude, saying, "Our lives were as precarious as a flickering candle. Your Reverence’s benevolence is vast and immeasurable, allowing us to behold the light of heaven once more."

"I vow that throughout this life I shall provide for the deficiencies of the multitude, thereby repaying your profound kindness with my meager means; ten thousandfold it would not equal even one part of your grace.
The Daoist said, "I am a king of a nation;
my country is vast and its people numerous. My palaces, treasures, and court ladies are the finest in all lands. My wishes are fulfilled at once like an echo—what could I not obtain?"

I regard my kingdom as a den of enmity; I consider sensory forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, fine garments, and perverse thoughts to be six swords that sever my body and six arrows that pierce my frame. Because of these six perverted wheels, I transmigrate and undergo suffering—the fierce and unbearable torments of the three miserable realms. I am utterly weary of them.

Having renounced the kingdom to become śramaṇas, you vowed to attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śāstā of Deva-manuṣyas, and Lord of the Dharma, in order to transform all living beings and lead them back to their original source; how could this concern only the three of you?
"Return each to your former dwellings to see your relatives, and cause them to take the Three Refuges so that they do not violate the Buddha’s teachings.
The hunter said, "I have lived in this world for many years;

though I have seen Confucian scholars accumulate virtue and perform good deeds, how could there be disciples of the Buddha like these—who, out of compassion for themselves and others, rescue the masses while remaining in seclusion and not seeking fame?"
"If a Daoist possesses this, I pray that he will come to my home to receive a modest offering.
The crow said, "My name is Bo.
If the Daoist encounters difficulty, I pray that he will call upon my name; I shall then hasten there."
The snake said, "My name is Chang.
If you, O Daoist, should ever fall ill, I pray that you call my name; I shall surely come to repay your kindness.
Having finished these words, they each withdrew.
On another day, the Daoist went to the hunter’s dwelling. Seeing him approaching from afar, the hunter said to his wife, “That inauspicious person is coming;
I command you to prepare a meal for him.”
He prepared the meal slowly; once midday had passed, he stopped eating.
When his wife saw the Daoist’s face suddenly flush with anger, she feigned a desire to keep him for a meal and engaged in empty talk until past noon.
The Daoist withdrew and, returning to the mountain, saw a crow; he called out its name, saying, "Pātra.
The crow asked:
"From where have you come?
He replied,
"I have come from where the hunters are."
The crow asked,
"Have you eaten?
He replied:
"He withdrew because the midday had passed and it was not the proper time for him to eat before his meal was prepared.
The crow said, "Wicked and calamitous ghosts are difficult to save through compassion; to violate benevolence and turn one's back on gratitude is the height of treachery."
"I have no food or drink with which to make offerings.
Remain here for a moment while I return.
He flew to the kingdom of Pañcāla and entered the king’s inner palace; there he saw the king’s consort lying down, and within her head ornaments was a bright moon pearl.
A crow flew back carrying [the object] and presented it to the Daoist master.
When the lady awoke from her sleep and sought it but could not find it, she immediately reported this to the King.
The King issued an edict to his ministers and subjects:
"The one who captures it shall be rewarded with a thousand catties each of gold and silver, and a thousand head of cattle and horses;
those who fail to present it shall suffer the grave penalty of extermination of their clan.
A Daoist priest took pity on a hunter, but the hunter bound him and reported his whereabouts.
The king asked,
"From where did you obtain this treasure?
The Daoist reflected deeply:
"To describe it by its appearance, all the crows of this entire kingdom would have perished;
to say that a thief obtained it is to claim he was not a disciple of the Buddha.
He accepted his interrogation in silence, enduring thousands of blows from the staff and cudgel without resenting the king or seeking vengeance against the other, making a vow of great compassion:
"May I attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings from their sufferings.
The King said, "Seize the Daoist and bury him, leaving only his head exposed; execute him tomorrow."
The Daoist then called to the snake,
saying, "Chang.
The snake replied:
"There is no one in the world who knows my name except for this Daoist.
That he raised his voice to call out to me must surely have a reason.
He hurried forward; seeing the Daoist as described, he prostrated himself and asked:
"How did you come to this?
The Daoist fully explained the circumstances of how it had come to pass.
The snake wept and said:
"If even a Daoist as benevolent as Heaven and Earth still encounters calamity, how much more so for one who lacks the Way—who will protect him?

Heaven is benevolent and harbors no resentment; this king has only one son, the Crown Prince, with no other heir apparent. I shall enter the palace and bite the Crown Prince to death, and by applying my divine medicine to him, he will immediately recover."
That night, a snake entered the palace and bit him, and he immediately died.
His body lay in state for three days, and a proclamation was issued:
"To whoever can restore the Crown Prince to life, I shall divide the kingdom and share its governance with them."
They placed him among the mountains, intending to cremate him there.
As they were traveling along a path past a Daoist master's dwelling, the Daoist said,
"Why has the Crown Prince fallen so ill as to bring about his own death?"
"Furthermore, there is no burial!
I can restore him to life.
When his attendants heard these words, they galloped back to report them to the Emperor.
The king’s heart was filled with both sorrow and joy; overcome once more by grief, he said:
"I pardon your crime and shall divide the kingdom for you to rule as king.
The practitioner applied medicine to his body, and the prince suddenly rose up, saying:
"Why am I here? he asked. His attendants fully explained the reasons for his presence.
When the Prince returned to the palace, everyone, great and small, danced with joy.
"I offered him the division of my kingdom as a gift, yet he accepted nothing at all.
The King awoke and said:
'If he would not accept the division of my kingdom, how could he possibly be a thief?'"
He asked: "Of what country are you?
By what view do you consider yourself a śramaṇa?"
"From where did you obtain this pearl?
Only one of such lofty conduct could have done so; yet now you have suddenly met with this calamity—by what means will you recover from it?
The Daoist then related the matter from beginning to end, and the King was moved to such grief that tears flowed down his face.
The king said to the hunter, "You have rendered meritorious service to the state; summon all your kinsmen, and I shall bestow upon them a generous reward.
Whether great or small, all the relatives came to the palace gate, and the king said:
"Those who are unbenevolent and turn their backs on kindness are the foremost of evils.
He slaughtered them all.
As for the Daoist who entered the mountains to study the Way, practicing with diligence and without weariness, he was reborn in the heavens upon the end of his life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The ascetic at that time was I myself;
the crow was Śāriputra."
The snake was Ānanda; the hunter was Devadatta;
and his wife was the woman Huáipán.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Perfection of Great Benevolence, the practice of Forbearance, is infinite.

50. [The Jātaka of the Nāga King Paṇḍaka] (50): "In the past, there was a king of the city of Kauśāmbī named Uggata. His kingdom was vast and its people were numerous; he governed the state with righteousness and did not oppress the myriad subjects."
The king had two children, one son and one daughter; the son was named Sudatta and the daughter was named Anjanā. Their conduct was pure, and the king held them in high esteem.

He created a golden pond for them; the two children entered the pond to bathe. In the pond there was a tortoise named Jin, which was blind in one eye; it was also playing in the water when it touched the bodies of the two children, causing them to startle and cry out loudly!
The king then asked for the reason,
and they replied:
"There is something in the pond that terrifies us whenever it touches us."
The king said in anger, "The pond was established for my son; what creature dwells therein that would frighten him?
He ordered nets to be cast to capture it, and because the ghost-dragon was so strange and marvelous, they succeeded in catching it immediately.
The fisherman caught the tortoise, and the king asked:
"How should it be killed?
Some of the ministers said:
"Behead them," some said;
"Burn them alive," others said.
Or some said:
"Chop it up and make a soup.
One minister said:
"This killing is not cruel; only casting one into the great ocean is what is called cruelty.
The turtle laughed and said, "Only this is truly cruel."
The king ordered her to be thrown into the river.
Having escaped, the tortoise hurried joyfully to the abode of the Dragon King and reported:
"The daughter of King Uggada is of such exquisite beauty and radiant splendor that she is a match for a celestial maiden."
"The human king is thus earnest in his heart; Your Majesty wishes to form an alliance of friendship by giving me your daughter as a consort.
The dragon asked, "Are you sincere?"
The tortoise replied,
"Indeed. He then prepared a sumptuous feast for the tortoise using entirely precious vessels, whereupon the tortoise said:
"Send forth wise ministers at once to seek him out; our King wishes to obtain his decision.
The dragon dispatched sixteen wise ministers who followed the tortoise to the moat beneath the human king’s city.
The tortoise said, "Stop here!"
"I shall go up and report this.
Thereupon, the tortoise fled and did not return.
The sixteen ministers, filled with resentment and distress, entered the city together to see the king, who said:
"Why have you nāgas come?
They replied, "Your Majesty has received us with benevolence and kindness. Your Majesty wishes to take your noble daughter as our queen; therefore, we have been sent to welcome her."
The king said in anger,
"How could there be a daughter of a human king who would take a serpent-dragon as her mate?
The dragon replied:
"The Great King previously dispatched the divine tortoise to proclaim his command; we have not come in vain.
The king did not grant their request.
The dragons manifested transformations, causing all the objects within the palace to become dragons, which shone and circled before and behind the king.
The king cried out in fear!
The ministers were struck with astonishment and all went before the dais to inquire as to the reason.
The king related the circumstances in detail, and the assembly of ministers said in unison:
"How can a kingdom be lost for the sake of a single woman?
The king and his ministers escorted the girl to the water's edge to see her off; she subsequently became the consort of a dragon and gave birth to two children, a son and a daughter.
The man’s name was Pāṇḍu; when the Dragon King died, the man succeeded him and became king.

Desiring to abandon the defilements of worldly glory and cultivate the resolve for noble conduct, he had ten thousand wives who all followed him in his quest; yet even though they fled into remote and hidden places, they could not escape him.
He landed beneath a *śirīṣa* tree, where he became invisible and transformed into the body of a coiled serpent.

At night, there was the brilliance of lamps numbering in the tens under that tree; day after day, it rained various kinds of flowers, their colors radiant and their fragrance exquisite, such as had never been seen before in the world.

"There is a man among the people of this country named Pitu who can subdue dragons; he has gone into the mountains seeking a dragon to use for his alms-rounds and, upon seeing a cowherd boy, asked him whether there were any."

The boy said, "I saw a snake coiled and lying beneath this tree; at night, there were dozens of lamps upon the tree, their radiance brilliant and dazzling. Beneath the flowers was what seemed like snow, its color radiant and its fragrance exquisite beyond compare. I pressed my body against it, yet it had no intent to harm me."
The sorcerer said, "Excellent!
My wish has been fulfilled."
The sorcerer then smeared poison on the dragon’s teeth, causing them all to fall out; he beat it with a staff until its skin was wounded and its bones were broken.

As the sorcerer stroked the dragon from head to tail with his hand, the pain was immeasurable, yet the dragon harbored no resentment. It reproached itself, saying that its past karma had not yet been exhausted when it met with such calamity, and it made this vow:
"May I attain Buddhahood to rescue and deliver all living beings, bringing them all to peace and security, never again to suffer as I do now."
The sorcerer took the dragon and placed it inside a small casket; carrying it upon his shoulder, he went about begging for alms.
In every country he reached, he would have the dragon dance, and there were none among the ministers or the common people of those lands who did not stand in awe of him.
The sorcerer said:
"I beg for a thousand units each of gold and silver, a thousand male and female slaves, and a thousand of each of elephants, horses, oxen, carriages, and various other livestock.
Whenever he arrived at various kingdoms, what he obtained was always as stated.

He entered the realm of his maternal grandfather, the Dragon King; his mother and the dragon brothers all sought him on land, where he had transformed into a flying bird and was hovering about the royal palace.

When the sorcerer arrived, the Dragon King transformed himself into five heads; just as he was about to emerge and dance, he saw his mother, brother, and sister, and out of shame and contempt, he recoiled and no longer emerged to dance.
The sorcerer called out to him five or six times, whereupon the dragon finally prostrated itself.
The mother resumed her human form and met with the king, recounting the events from beginning to end.
The king, his ministers, and the common people were all moved to grief; the king wished to execute the sorcerer, but the dragon entreated him, saying:
"What I have sown through my past deeds, I shall now receive as retribution; it is not fitting to kill him to increase future enmity, so I shall grant him whatever he requests."
"With such vast compassion, the Way of the Buddha can be attained.
The king then took another country as an example and bestowed upon him everything he desired.

Having obtained these precious treasures, the sorcerer departed from the kingdom in great joy; however, upon reaching the borders of another country, he encountered bandits, whose hands were hacked to mincemeat and whose wealth was completely plundered.
The dragon mother and her son took their leave of the king, saying, "If Your Majesty remembers us and calls our names, we shall come; do not let yourself grow weary or distressed.

The king, along with his ministers and the common people, went to the riverbank to see them off; the entire nation was so overcome with grief that there were none who did not fall to the ground in lamentation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Nāga King Pāṇḍaka was I myself;
the King of Uggada was Ānanda."
The mother was my mother of the present day.
The younger brother was Śāriputra.
The younger sister was the laywoman Utpalavarṇā.
At that time, the one who was the cruel dragon was Devadatta. Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s boundless great compassion and the perfection of patience. 51.

The Sūtra of the King of Sparrows [The Jātaka of the King of Sparrows] In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as the king of sparrows. With a compassionate heart, he rescued the multitudes, holding them dear as a mother cherishes her child. He felt sorrow for their hardships as if they were his own separation from kin; seeing the multitude receive the Way brought him joy as if his own peace were restored. He nurtured and loved all living beings as if protecting the wounds upon his own body.
There was a tiger that had been eating wild beasts; a bone was stuck in its teeth, and it was suffering from the affliction, on the verge of death.
Seeing this, a sparrow felt compassion and sorrow, saying:
"The Buddhas have taught that food is a source of calamity; this is indeed the case."
He entered the mouth and pecked at the bone, doing so day after day in this manner.
The sparrow’s mouth grew sores and its body became emaciated and withered, yet the bone emerged and the tiger revived.
The sparrow flew up into a tree and recited a Buddhist sutra, saying:
"Killing is a cruel act; there is no evil greater than it.
If another were to kill you, would you take pleasure in it?
You should judge others by the same standard as yourself, and therein lies the benevolence of spring."
The benevolent person’s universal compassion brings blessings that respond like echoes;
the cruel and tyrannical person who harms the masses is pursued by calamity as surely as a shadow follows its form.
Consider these words of mine.
Upon hearing the sparrow’s admonition, the tiger became suddenly enraged and said,
"Have you just left my mouth and already dared to speak so much?
Seeing that he could not be transformed, the sparrow felt a deep sense of pity for him and immediately flew away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of sparrows was I myself;
the tiger was Devadatta."
The Bodhisattva, from lifetime to lifetime, rescues the multitude with a compassionate heart, regarding this as his primary concern just as he would care for his own body.
Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in practicing forbearance.

52. The Sūtra on the Land of the Naked [Shusheng] (52). The Sūtra on the Land of the Naked: "In the past, there were two brothers, a paternal uncle and a nephew, who each took provisions of national wealth and traveled together to the land of the naked."
The younger brother said:
"Those with abundant merit find clothing and food provided spontaneously; those with meager blessings must exert their own physical strength.

Now, that land of the naked has no Buddha, no Dharma, and no community of śramaṇas; it may be called a wilderness devoid of people. For us to go there and submit to their ways—would this not be difficult?"

"Entering a country, one must follow its customs; advancing or retreating, one must observe its protocols. To soften one's heart and speak with humility, to conceal one's brilliance and praise the simple-minded—this is the deliberation of a Great Man.
Bo said, "Rituals must not be deficient, and virtue must not be diminished. How could I expose my body naked and destroy my ancient traditions?"
The younger brother said:
"The former sages maintained their integrity even at the cost of losing their lives, yet they did not let their conduct falter; this was the constant rule of their precepts.
To have gold within but copper on the outside, to discard ritual forms while conforming to the times, and to first criticize and later praise—this is the greatness of the path of expedient means!"
They then proceeded together to that place.
The elder said,
"You go in first now to observe their success or failure, and dispatch a messenger to convey our sincere message."
The younger brother said,
"I respectfully accept.
Within ten days, he sent a messenger back to inform the elder brother, saying:
"One must surely follow worldly etiquette.
Bo Bo replied with a sudden burst of indignation:
"For a person of the Śākya clan to follow the ways of beasts—is this truly the conduct of a gentleman?"
"Uncle, what you have done is not right!

"In the custom of that country, on the night of the fifteenth day at the end of the month, they always hold festivities: they smear their heads with sesame oil and fat, paint their bodies with white earth, wear necklaces of various bones, strike two stones together, and men and women join hands, strolling, singing, and dancing;
the Bodhisattva joined them, and the people of the country rejoiced and sighed in admiration."
The king loved his people and honored his guests, waiting for them in continuous succession; he took all their goods and paid them tenfold as wages.
When Boche entered the state with his carriage, he spoke of enforcing strict laws, which immediately went against the will of the people.
The king was incensed by the people’s arrogance; he confiscated their wealth and beat them with clubs.
Only after Shu pleaded for them were they released, and they returned together to their home country.
Those escorting Shu lined the roads, while those reviling Bo were deafening to the ear.
Bo Chi said in anger:
"What kinship do they have with you?
What enmity do they have with me?"
"Your kindness in seizing me—is this not slanderous speech?
He then bound Shu Dai, saying:
"From this day forward, for generations to come, we shall treat you with relentless cruelty; you shall never be pardoned."
The Bodhisattva, moved with deep sorrow, shed tears and made this vow:

"May I, in every lifetime, encounter the Buddhas, behold the Dharma, and personally serve the śramaṇas; may the four debts of gratitude universally cover and sustain all sentient beings; and may I honor my elder brother as I do myself—may I never fail this oath."
"From that time forward, whenever the elder brother was about to strike the younger, the younger would always save him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The younger brother at that time was I myself."
The "Heir Apparent" was Devadatta. Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Compassion and Gentleness in the exercise of patience. **53.

The Sūtra on Enduring Six Years of Fasting to Expiate Sin [The King’s Jātaka]** In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king. He took refuge in the Triple Gem and fully observed the ten wholesome paths of action. His virtue extended far and wide; there were none who did not submit to his influence. Weapons were not employed, and prisons did not exist. Rain and wind came at their proper seasons, the land was abundant, and the people were wealthy. All within the four borders enjoyed peace and rest; there were no sighs of resentment upon the roads. Flowery falsehoods and petty writings were silenced throughout the nation, while all people recited the true transformation of the six perfections.
At that time, there was a brahmin of pure conduct who dwelt in seclusion among the mountains and forests, avoiding the ways of the world and devoting himself solely to virtue.
One night, thirsty, he went to drink water and by mistake reached the lotus pond planted by a man of the kingdom. Having finished drinking, he realized his error and thought:
"That man purchased this pond to offer its flowers to the Buddha temple and to provide its fruits and water for his own use."
I drank this water without informing its owner; this is precisely theft.
Now, as for the calamity of theft: first one enters Mount Tai, then one becomes an animal, being slaughtered and sold in the marketplace to repay former debts.
"If I were to obtain human birth, I would surely become a slave.
It would be better for me to bring this matter to an end now, so as not to leave a source of future suffering.

He went to the palace gate and declared his own crime of theft, saying, "I only pray that Your Majesty will punish me according to the law; let me finish this now and grant me no further reproach hereafter."
The King said, "This is natural water, a thing of no value; what crime could there be in this?
They replied:
"One who buys a house possesses its well; one who occupies a field values its thatch. To draw water or cut fodder without being informed is not permitted.
If I drink from this well without being informed, is this not theft?"
"I pray that Your Majesty will dwell there.
The King said, "My state affairs are many and complicated; for now, sit within the garden."
The Prince had him placed deep within the park, and as the King’s affairs were manifold and pressing, he forgot about him for six days.
Suddenly, he realized and said:
"Is the brahmin still there?"
"Come quickly!
The brahmin, having observed his precepts for six days of hunger and thirst, stood before the king; his body was emaciated and frail, and he staggered as he rose to his feet.
Seeing him, the king wept and said, "My transgressions are grave."
The Queen laughed at him.
The King sent someone to bathe the Brahmin and prepared a full array of delicacies; he personally made offerings and prostrated himself to repent, saying:
"As a sovereign, when my people are hungry, I am hungry myself; when they are cold, my own clothes are thin—how much more so for a man who cherishes the Way and bestows virtue?"

The merit of all the virtuous men of a nation does not equal the virtue of a single person of lofty conduct and worth. That the state is tranquil, the people are at peace, the four seasons proceed in harmony, and the harvests are abundant—whom else but the virtue of the precepts could have brought this about?
He said to the Daoist:
"If failing to report the drinking of water results in such a crime, how much more so must there be a grave guilt for actual theft?
Since I have pardoned you for this, you shall certainly face no further trouble."
The brahmin said,
"Excellent! I have received the king's great bounty."

"From that time onward, he transmigrated through the cycle of birth and death without end, until he reached the point of attaining Buddhahood after six years of fasting. Once his karmic retribution was exhausted and the Way was perfected, he released himself from Gopikā, and Rāhula was born."
When the Crown Prince abandoned his kingdom to devote himself to the mountain forests, those of heterodox views all declared him to be mad and deluded; such slanderous voices were manifold.

Upon hearing this, the Prince endured these insults and slanders, pursuing his goal with compassionate salvation. His merit flourished and his Way was perfected; the various devas gathered like clouds, bowing their heads to receive his influence, and among kings, emperors, ministers, and commoners, there were none who did not take refuge in him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was none other than myself;
the queen was Gopī."
The Crown Prince was Rāhula. Indeed, when one honors evil, calamity follows;
when one bestows virtue, blessing returns. How can one not be cautious!

The King forgot the instructions of the Daoist and left him to starve for six days; consequently, he suffered the retribution of a six-year famine. Only after those six days had passed did the famine finally subside. Because the King personally made offerings to him [the Daoist] on that sixth day, his six years of misfortune have now ended and he has attained the Way.
Gopī laughed at this; now she carries Rāhula while suffering from a grave illness for six years.
Because the Brahmin was deeply attached to the inner garden, the Prince remained in darkness for six years.

Fools, shrouded in deep darkness and lacking clarity regarding what to adopt or abandon, direct evil intentions toward the Buddha, śramaṇas, and brahmins; those who cut off hands or pull out tongues suffer only the miseries of this single lifetime.

But those who falsely strike with their hands or vainly slander with their mouths will, upon death, enter Mount Tai. There, the ghosts of Mount Tai pull out their tongues and place them upon hot sand, plowing over them with oxen; furthermore, they drive glowing nails into their five limbs, yet they cannot seek death.
The calamities and evils are such as these; therefore, one should practice in accordance with the right path without deviation.
Such is the practice of patience within the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-pāramitā of patience.

54. The Scripture on the Śākya Family Completing Their Karmic Retribution (54). The Scripture on the Śākya Family Completing Their Karmic Retribution: "In the past, the Bodhisattva maintained the precepts and practiced purity, accumulating merit and virtue until he attained the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, dwelling and traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī."

Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, as well as emperors, kings, ministers, and subjects—all without exception—turned to him as their spiritual source. When the baleful arts and heterodox techniques encountered the flourishing majesty of the Buddha’s shadow, they were eclipsed just as fireflies vanish when the sun shines with brilliant intensity.

As greed and envy arose, they failed to perceive the fire that would consume their own bodies; thus, a faction of the heterodox conspired and incited a female disciple named Haoshou to slander the Honored One.
Among the people of the land, those who had not yet attained the True Dharma harbored lingering doubts; they were suspicious of the śramaṇas, and the King likewise found them strange.

Those who practiced sorcery and were greedy and corrupt, who contended over wealth and brought accusations against one another, saw their impurity manifest and calamity return to them, leading to their immediate downfall. When the pure truth was revealed, gods and humans marveled at its excellence!

The King went to the monastery and prostrated himself to repent his transgressions. Because the King possessed a sense of shame, he sent an intermediary to inquire and request the Buddha’s sister in marriage, seeking to establish a firm bond of kinship to sever the enmity between the royal house and the Śākya clan.
The World-Honored One said, "I have left my home to become a śramaṇa and do not participate in worldly affairs; matters of marriage shall be entirely at the discretion of my father, the King.
Thereupon, he dispatched a messenger to pay his respects and convey words for forming an alliance.
The Śākyas did not grant permission, and the King said:
