"The Buddha resides in our kingdom, yet you come and go there; the wise harbor no resentment, while only the foolish have enemies.
This girl is the daughter of my humble concubine—how could she be worth such hatred?"
The king consented, saying,
"So be it," and thus the marriage was consummated.
There was an only son who requested to visit his maternal uncles and went to the kingdom of the Śākyas.

At that time, the Buddha was about to return to convert the Śākyas; the Śākyas were filled with joy and constructed a vihāra for the Buddha. They dug the earth to a depth of three feet and filled it with sandalwood incense. They gathered the various treasures of the nation to build the Buddha’s vihāra, which was so brilliantly radiant it resembled a celestial palace; when the neighboring kingdoms heard of it, there were none who did not leap for joy.
Before the Buddha had yet taken his seat, the illegitimate son entered the hall and remarked,
"The craftsmanship of this vihāra and the excellence of its myriad treasures can only be matched by the palace of the Heavenly Emperor."
He said, "The Buddha has not yet alighted here; even if I were to sit upon this seat until the end of my life, I would have no regrets.
His favorite friend, a younger brother, named Tukkha-ma, replied:
"What loss could there possibly be?
he said, and immediately ascended his seat.
A heroic disciple of the Śākya clan then rebuked him with a powerful voice, saying:
"The seat of the World-Honored One is not one for the Lord of Devas to occupy; how dare the son of a slave-girl ascend it?
He tore his seat apart and rose up again.
The illegitimate son went out and said to his friend:
"This humiliation is beyond measure!
If I become king, do not forget this.
The friend said:
"So be it," he replied.
He then attended to his mother with the intent of making her a queen for the crown prince; the mother, however, sought through sorcery and charms that her son's wish be granted.
The King said:
"Never heard of such a thing in antiquity!
To utter such reckless words is to invite shame upon oneself.
While the seductive sorceress resided within and the sycophantic ministers employed their clever rhetoric, they subsequently established two heirs apparent to divide the people and govern the state.

"When the Great King passed away, the two states were established; the people followed according to their inclinations, with the benevolent and the cruel parting ways. The benevolent then honored the elder brother, while the cruel hastened to the uncle."
The friend served as the Chancellor; he maintained the weapons of war and prepared all military provisions, reporting on matters based on established precedent.
The King said, "It may be done."
He immediately favored a heroic warrior and set out on the road; there he beheld the Buddha sitting by the side of the path beneath a tree that was half-dead.
The King approached and prostrated himself, saying, "The Buddha does not sit under a tree that is entirely living while dwelling under one that is half-dead; is there a reason for this?"
The World-Honored One said:

"This tree is named 'Śī' (Release). I cherish its name because it signifies using the Way of Benevolence to rescue those in distress, nourishing the withered and bestowing kindness upon all living beings."
The king, filled with despondency and inward shame, said:
"The Buddha’s benevolence is vast and universal; his grace extends even to grasses and trees, let alone to human beings.
Thereupon, he withdrew his army.
The Chancellor looked upward at the celestial phenomena and observed that the stars of the Śākya clan portended the exhaustion of their blessings and the rise of calamity; he reported this once more.

The army set out again, and when they were but a few li from the city of the Śākyas, the sound of bows and crossbows within the city was like wind and rain. Banners, streamers, and parasols had their poles broken and their shafts severed; armor was split and bridles cut asunder. Soldiers and horses fled in a panicked stampede, none of them losing their composure.
The king fled back once more.
A follower of Śākya informed the Buddha:
"What should we do with those bandits?"
He replied,
"Secure the gates and destroy the bridges over the moats.
The King again dispatched his army, and Maudgalyāyana addressed him, saying:
"I wish to use the majestic spiritual power of an Arhat to transform myself into a celestial net, covering the city for forty li on all sides; what can the King do against the people of the Śākya?
The World-Honored One said, "What can he do against their transgressions?"
Again he asked:
"Will you leap to another buddha-field?
He replied:
"What can be done about these offenses?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I am able to dispel that which has form, but what can be done about offenses that are formless?"
The World-Honored One said:
"When evil is sown, calamity arises; who can ward it off?
Take one son of the Śākya clan and place him beneath my alms-bowl to verify this truth."
Maudgalyāyana followed the command.
The Śākyas, the elders, received the instruction and guarded the gate. Māra transformed himself into an elder and rebuked the Śākyas, saying:
"The King has taken the road to some destination; you must block his way, lest it increase your future remorse."
"Can a disciple of the Buddha act like this?
The Māra exerted his power, pulled out the key, and forced open the door so that the soldiers entered, like water gushing from a breached dam.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra was the Great General; he had studied under the same teacher as the former king and shared a vow of lifelong friendship. He said to the king:
"Stay for the duration of one meal, O fierce man, and allow the people within the city to escape with their lives.
The King said, "So be it."
The Great General stood by the water facing the Buddha, prostrated himself with tears streaming down his face, and said:

"I beg with my humble life for those few men; I pray that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may uphold the Buddha's teachings, taking themselves as a measure to save others, so that their benevolence may harmonize Heaven and Earth, and that they no longer act like this unrighteous king, who, like a venomous wolf or viper, cruelly harms living beings."
Entering the water, he wrapped his hair around the roots of a tree; after a short while, he passed away.
The king dispatched a messenger to inspect him, who returned and reported the matter exactly as it had occurred.
The soldiers entered and dug the ground, half-burying the Śākya man.
Timbers were laid across like a trap to ensnare him, and he was struck down by either the hoof of a horse or the blade of a weapon.
At that time, the Buddha suffered from a headache, the pain of which was difficult to describe;
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings all stood in attendance with palms joined, their hearts pained for him.
Among the Śākyas, there were those who took refuge in the Triple Gem, those who recited the sūtras, and those who gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

The Śākyas had three cities; as the campaign was not yet concluded, the King remembered how Śākyamuni had sacrificed his own life to save the lives of the multitude, and he was moved with deep sorrow. He immediately withdrew his forces and disbanded the army, dispatching an envoy to pay his respects, saying:
"The troops are exhausted; let us return to our kingdom to rest the army."
On another day, he presented his offerings and bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha declined the gift, saying, “May Your Majesty take care of yourself.
When the messenger withdrew, the Buddha looked upon him.
Ānanda adjusted his dharma robes, prostrated himself, and said:
"The Buddha does not look upon things in vain; there must surely be a cause for this.
The World-Honored One replied:
"When the expiation for sins is completed, the king's own transgressions will arise.

Seven days hence, the ghosts of Mount Tai shall burn the king, his ministers, and his subjects with fire; the king’s sins will be difficult to save from, just as the calamity of release is difficult to avert."
The Buddha had Ānanda lift the bowl, and the person beneath it also died.

The Buddha led the śramaṇas to the hall where the brahmins lectured; on the way, they passed through the burial ground of the Śākyas, where there were those already dead, and others whose arms, thighs, or shins were broken. Seeing the Buddha approaching, some beat their cheeks and groaned, saying:

"We take refuge in the Buddha, we take refuge in the Dharma, we take refuge in the Noble Saṅgha! May all living beings in the ten directions attain eternal peace and prosperity, and never suffer as we do."
At that time, natural thrones emerged from the earth, and the ground became level as all the śramaṇas sat upon them.
The Buddha said:
"This King is rebellious and perverse; the offenses he has committed are vast and extensive."
He asked the śramaṇa again:
"If one sees those who slaughter animals, hunt, or cast fishing nets, will they obtain the status of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin)?
He replied:
“I do not see it.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent!”
"I also do not see it, because he lacks the four immeasurable minds to bestow grace upon the multitude of living beings.

Then, as the King traveled by the lakeside, the crowd entered the water to bathe; a deity transformed into venomous insects and stung his soldiers and attendants. As the poison spread, their bodies turned black; some died in the water, while others died at intervals of a hundred paces or a li.
Furthermore, as soon as he had entered half-way into the kingdom, malevolent spirits gathered like clouds.

Within the palace at night, the voices of people and the sounds of objects resounded; the inhabitants huddled together for support, clinging to life until dawn. The sun and moon were eclipsed, the stars lost their courses, and strange portents followed one after another—there was nothing that did not cause resentment toward the king.

When the king heard of these extraordinary transformations caused by the Buddha’s fire precept, he felt as if his inner being were seared by boiling water; he dispatched a messenger to investigate the matter.
The Buddha explained it as above, and when the messenger returned and reported the details, the kingdom trembled and collapsed like falling tiles.
The king assembled his ministers and deliberated, saying, "It may be on a mountain, or it may be by the water.
He then boarded a ship and entered the sea; those who were wealthy and powerful were able to follow him, while the poor and weak remained in the kingdom.

The women of the king’s inner palace boarded the ship and, seeing the fire, took off their garments; they removed the *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal) beads from their clothes and placed them upon the garments.
That day, clouds arose, thick and dark, and wind and rain lashed down violently; the rigging snapped and the boat was tossed about. The ministers and subjects all said:
"Because our wretched king committed an evil deed, this calamity has been brought about."

At that time, as the sun rose and shone upon the *yangsui* (sun-crystal lens), the *yangsui* was transformed into fire. Starting from the King’s boat, great mountains, ghosts, and spirits gathered like clouds amidst thunder and lightning; all living beings throughout the land entered the Great Mountain Hell.
"Those who remained on the shore were slightly frightened but remained safe.
On that day, the Buddha entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). The śramaṇas asked Ānanda, "Has the Buddha not emerged [from his meditation]?"
He replied, "A great national mourning has occurred; the Buddha has entered the samādhi of compassion, and for this reason he does not come forth.

At dawn the next morning, the Buddha emerged. All the śramaṇas prostrated themselves on the ground, as did Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the various nāgas, spirits, and deities, along with kings, ministers, and the common people, all bowing their heads before taking their seats.
Ānanda adjusted his robes and asked about the origins of the calamities and upheavals in the two kingdoms:
"I pray that you will dispel the doubts of the assembly and cause all living beings to perceive the causes from which misfortune and fortune arise.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, there were three kingdoms that bordered one another. At that time, the Buddha had been gone from the world for a long duration, and the scriptures were not being cultivated.
In the kingdom where the Bodhisattva resided, there was a lake from which countless fish were caught."
The neighboring states heard of this and were delighted; they brought wealth to purchase [the fish], but when the fish were exhausted, they returned in sorrow.
The distant states remained unaware and had no intention to buy.
Those who preyed upon the state are these three hundred million people who have now been released from death.
The person from the distant land who rejoiced at the desire to buy fish is like those people in the city today who fear they will lose their wealth in vain.
The person from the distant land who did not hear that fish had been caught is like those people within the city today who do not know that the King has arrived.
At that time, when I saw the severed fish head, I lost my composure and gave my consent;
now that I have attained Buddhahood and become the Honored One of the Three Realms, I still cannot escape the calamity of this head ailment—how much less so for ordinary people?

All you disciples: straighten your minds, cultivate virtue and kindness, and bring peace to all living beings. Practice empathy by treating others as you would yourself; be careful never to kill, steal another's property, commit adultery with those who are not your wife, engage in double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, or frivolous talk; nor harbor jealousy, anger, or delusion, nor slander the Triple Gem.
There is no calamity greater than the ten evils, and there is no honor or glory more sublime than the ten virtues.
To kill living beings is to kill oneself; to sustain living beings is to sustain oneself.

If one’s mind conceives evil, one’s speech utters evil, and one’s body performs evil, it is better to exert the mind in contemplating the Way, the mouth in speaking of the Way, and the body in practicing the Way.
When good is bestowed, blessings follow; when evil is committed, calamity ensues—just as an echo responds to a sound and a shadow follows a form.
"Those who witness this transformation must be cautious not to violate the benevolence of spring and instead emulate the ferocity of jackals and wolves.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the fourfold assembly of disciples, along with devas, nāgas, and spirits, were all filled with great joy; they prostrated themselves and departed.
The Compendium of the Six Pāramitās, Volume Five;
The Compendium of the Six Pāramitās, Volume Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of the Kingdom of Kangju during the Wu Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Perfection of Vigor. This chapter contains nineteen sections.
As for what constitutes the perfection of vigor, its principles are as follows:
He concentrated his essence upon the profound mysteries of the Way, advancing therein without weariness; whether lying down, sitting, walking, or breathing, he never ceased.
His eyes perceived, as it were, the constant vision of the numinous images and transformations of the Buddhas appearing before him;
his ears heard, as it were, the constant sound of the true and correct teachings of their compassionate voice.

Let the nose be the fragrance of the Way, the mouth the speech of the Way, the hands the service of the Way, and the feet tread upon the hall of the Way; do not let this resolve falter for even the space of a single breath.

The Bodhisattva feels sorrow and compassion for sentient beings who, throughout the long night, are tossed in a seething sea, circling in eddies and revolutions, afflicted by poisons with no means of rescue;
his grief for them is like that of a filial son at the death of a parent.

As for the path of delivering sentient beings, even if one encounters the perils of boiling water and fire, or the harms of blades and poison ahead, to cast oneself into such danger and joyfully rescue others from their hardships is a resolve that surpasses the pursuit of glory and splendor by those who dwell within the six realms of darkness.

55. [The Jātaka of the Ordinary Man] (55): "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was an ordinary man, he heard of the Buddha’s name, his marks and signs, the power of his path, and his towering merits; that all the devas revere him, and that for those who practice with high resolve, all sufferings are utterly extinguished."
The Bodhisattva, dwelling in contemplation, wept silently and said:

"Since I received the scriptures from the Teacher of Gods, I have studied and recited them, practicing them to attain Buddhahood; shall I thereby alleviate the illnesses of sentient beings and cause them to return to their original purity?"
At that time, the Buddha had passed away and there was no assembly of *bhikṣus* to receive and hear [the teachings].
A neighbor, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) by nature greedy and cruel, seeing the Bodhisattva’s diligent application and sharp resolve, said:
"I know one chapter of the Three Precepts of the Buddha; do you wish to receive it?"
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was immeasurably joyful; he prostrated at his feet, fell to the ground, and requested the precepts.
The knower of verses said:

"This is the essential teaching of the Unsurpassed, Truly Real, Most Perfectly Awakened One, the Tamer of Men and Gods, the Teacher of Devas and Humans. Do you wish to hear it in vain? How could that be so?"
He replied:
"I ask concerning the ritual of the Dharma;
what is its meaning? He said:

"If you are indeed sincere and earnest, let me prick each pore of your body with a needle; if blood flows and your body suffers pain yet your heart feels no regret, then you may hear the Honored Teaching."
He replied, "I would welcome death upon hearing the Buddha; how much more so would I endure piercing my body while remaining alive?
He then laid out needles and pierced his own body; though the blood flowed like a spring, the Bodhisattva, rejoicing at hearing the Dharma, attained a meditative state free from pain.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, beheld the Bodhisattva’s sharp resolve and was moved with compassion; he transformed the Bodhisattva’s entire body so that there was a single needle within each pore.
Seeing this, the man perceived the loftiness of his resolve and immediately instructed him, saying:
"Guard your speech, restrain your mind, and let your body commit no evil. Apart from these three practices, you shall attain the noble path of deliverance."
"This is the true exposition of the precepts by all Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Upon hearing these precepts, the Bodhisattva rejoiced and prostrated himself; looking back at his body, the needles suddenly vanished, his countenance shone with radiance, and his physical strength exceeded that of before. Among devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons, there was none who did not praise this excellence.
With a resolute will for advancement and lofty practice, following one after another like a line of footsteps, he eventually attained Buddhahood and rescued all sentient beings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The one who bestowed the verses upon the Bodhisattva was none other than Devadatta.”
Although Devadatta already knew the Buddha’s verses, he was like a blind man holding a candle to illuminate his way; since he could not see for himself, what benefit was there to him?
Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s unexcelled resolve in the perfection of diligence.
56. [The Jātaka of the Monkey King] (56): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a monkey king who constantly played with five hundred monkeys."

At that time, the world suffered from a drought and the various fruits were not abundant. The king’s capital city was not far from the mountain, separated only by a small stream; the monkey king led his troop into a garden to eat the fruit.
The park superintendent reported this to the king, who said:
"Guard him closely; do not allow him to leave."
The monkey king, understanding this, said with deep sorrow:
"As the leader of the multitude, I am the source of our fortune and misfortune; yet by greedily seeking fruit to sustain my own life, I have further brought error upon the group."
He commanded his followers, saying:
"Go out and seek out rattan vines.
When the assembly returned with the rattan, they vied with one another to link them together, binding one end to the branch of a large tree.
The Monkey King fastened his own waist and climbed the tree to leap; grasping a branch of that tree, his body hung down as the vine was too short. He commanded his followers, saying:
"Quickly climb the vine and cross over!"
When the assembly had finished their deliberation, both his armpits were severed, and he fell onto the bank by the water’s edge; having fainted, he regained consciousness.
Early the next morning, the king went out on an inspection tour and captured a large monkey that could speak human language.

The monkey prostrated itself and stated: "I am a wild beast who, craving life, relied upon your grace and attached myself to your kingdom. During a time of drought, fruit became scarce, and I trespassed upon your imperial garden. The fault and transgression lie with me alone."
"Let the rest be pardoned; this worm's body and decaying flesh may serve as a single morning meal for the Grand Cook.
The King looked up and sighed, saying, "The leader of insects and beasts has sacrificed its own life to save the multitude, possessing the vast benevolence of the sages of antiquity."
"As a ruler of men, how could I possibly do otherwise?

He shed tears, ordered his bonds to be untied, and helped him back to his place on the ground. He then issued a decree throughout the kingdom that the monkey should be allowed to eat whatever he desired, and that anyone who violated this order would be punished as severely as a common thief.
He returned to the Empress and recounted her benevolent deeds:
"The conduct of ancient sages has not equaled this; my own benevolence is but a single hair, while hers surpasses Mount Kunlun."
The Queen said:
"Excellent! How extraordinary is this insect!"
"Your Majesty should allow him to eat as he pleases and not let him suffer any harm.
The King replied,
"I have already given my command."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The monkey king was I myself; the king was Ānanda; and the five hundred monkeys were these five hundred bhikṣus.”
"Such is the diligence of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolute Zeal.

57. [The Jātaka of the Deer King] (57): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a deer king; his strength and power surpassed all others, and his benevolence covered all universally. The herd of deer followed him out of admiration, and he roamed near a royal garden."
The herder reported this to the king, who led his troops to surround and press upon them.
The deer king then realized the situation and said with tears falling:
"That you have fallen into this calamity is entirely due to my own fault."
"I shall sacrifice my life to save you, my little ones.
The deer king approached the rope, lowered his two front legs, and said, "Climb upon me and leap out; then you all may be saved."
The herd of deer followed his instructions and all were saved.
His own flesh was torn apart and his blood flowed like a spring; he collapsed to the ground and could only just breathe, his pain beyond words.
The herd of deer cried out and wandered about, refusing to leave.
Seeing their bodies mangled and the ground dyed crimson with blood, yet not seeing the rest of the herd, the king of men asked: "What is this?"
The deer king replied:
"My conduct has been unrefined and my destiny has made me a beast; seeking fine grass to preserve this fragile life, I have trespassed upon your borders, and my offense should indeed be grave."
"Though my flesh is exhausted, my two spleens and five viscera remain intact; I only pray that the Grand Cook will provide me with a single meal.
The King said, "For what reason are you like this?"
The deer king related the beginning and end of the matter, explaining his reasons.
The king was moved with compassion and shed tears for him, saying:
"Though you are a beast, you possess the vast benevolence of heaven and earth; you have sacrificed your own life to save the multitude."
"I am a ruler of men; how could I, out of greed, delight in killing and cruelly destroy what Heaven has produced?

He immediately issued a solemn decree, commanding the common people of the kingdom: "From this day forth, hunting shall cease; do not covet venison. Untie the ropes and set the deer free, placing them safely upon level ground."

When the herd of deer saw their king, they looked up to heaven and wailed in grief; each stepped forward to lick his wound, and they distributed themselves to gather medicinal herbs, chewing them and applying them to him.
When the human king witnessed this, he wiped away his tears once more and said:
"The leader cherished his subjects with the love for a son, and the subjects revered their leader with the affection for a parent; how could the way of a ruler not be benevolent?"

"From that time on, he ceased killing and honored benevolence; Heaven immediately protected him, the nation became prosperous, and the people lived in joy. Far and near, all praised his benevolence, and the people returned to him like a flowing stream.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The King of the Deer was my own self."
The five hundred deer were these five hundred bhikṣus;
the king of men was Ānanda.
Such was the bodhisattva’s indefatigable resolve and boundless diligence in the practice of *pāramitā*.

58. [The Jātaka of the Deer King Śṛṅga] (58): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a deer king named Śṛṅga; his coat was nine colors, a rarity seen in the world, and he sported by the riverbank."
Seeing a man drowning who was calling out to Heaven for mercy, the Deer took pity on him and said:
"Human life is so difficult to obtain; how can it be lost?
I would rather cast myself into danger to save him."
He immediately swam toward them and said, "Do not be afraid!
Grasp my horns and mount my back; we shall now save one another.
The man did exactly as he was told.
When the man emerged from the deer’s mouth, his breath was faint and nearly extinguished.
Overjoyed that he was alive, he circumambulated the deer three times, prostrated himself, and said:

"The human path is difficult to encounter, and one's life is most precious. You, Great Sir, have cast yourself into peril to save my precious life; your kindness exceeds that of Heaven and Earth. I shall never forget it from beginning to end. I wish to become your servant to provide for whatever you lack."
The deer said,
"Go now, and entrust my life to you for as long as you live.
Should anyone seek me out, do not say that you have seen me."
The drowning man respectfully agreed, saying,
"I shall not disobey even at the cost of my life.
At that time, there was a king named Mainguang (Māndhātṛ), whose character was pure and harmonious, and who nurtured the common people with compassion.
The King’s principal consort, whose name was Hezhi, dreamed of a deer king whose body hair was nine colors and whose antlers surpassed those of the rhinoceros.
Upon waking, she reported it, saying:
"I wish to make garments from its hide and earrings from its antlers; if I do not obtain them, I shall surely die."
The King replied gravely, "So be it.

At dawn, he described the appearance of the deer to his ministers and issued a proclamation seeking its capture: whoever obtained it would be granted a fief of one county, along with a silver bowl filled with gold grain if it were a silver bowl, or a golden bowl filled with silver grain if it were a golden bowl.
When the recruitment was thus proclaimed, the drowning man rejoiced and said:
"I shall obtain an entire commandery with gold and silver filling my bowl; this will be my joy for the rest of my life.
The deer has perished of its own accord—what concern is that of mine?"
He immediately galloped to the palace and reported the matter as it had occurred.
Within a short while, his face broke out in leprosy and his mouth became putrid and foul-smelling. He spoke again, saying:
"This deer possesses spiritual power; the King must lead his troops to capture it."
The king immediately raised an army and crossed the river to search for him.
At that time, the deer and the crow had long been close friends;
however, while the deer was lying down asleep, he did not notice the king’s arrival, so the crow said:
"Friend! The King has come to capture you!
The deer was too exhausted to hear, so he pecked at its ear and said again:
"The King has come to kill you!
Startled, the deer saw the king draw his bow toward it; it rushed forward, knelt with its knees to the ground, and bowed its head, saying:
"Your Majesty, grant me a brief moment of life so that I may state my humble thoughts."
When the king saw that it was indeed a deer, he immediately ordered his attendants to cease their pursuit.
The deer said, "Your Majesty has already shown great favor to the Queen by exerting yourself on her behalf; yet I shall ultimately not escape my fate."
"The Heavenly King dwells within the depths of his inner palace; how could he know that a tiny insect was in this place?
The king pointed with his finger and said, "A leper revealed it."
The deer said, "I was seeking fine grass to eat when I saw from afar a drowning man calling out to heaven for mercy. Moved by pity for his distress, I cast myself into danger to rescue him."
The man came ashore and, filled with joy, prostrated himself, saying:
"My life was about to perish, yet you have saved me; I pray that you accept me as your lifelong slave, providing for my water and fodder.
I replied to him:
"Go now, wherever you wish; be careful never to tell anyone that I am here.
The deer king spoke again:
"I would rather emerge from the water and float upon grass and wood onto dry land than leave the presence of one who shows no reciprocity."
"Plundering wealth and killing one's master may have some grounds for mitigating their evil;
but to plot rebellion against those who have shown one kindness—such cruelty is difficult to describe.
The King was startled and said:
"What kind of beast is this that harbors such vast compassion? To sacrifice its life to save other creatures without deeming it a hardship—it must surely be a celestial being!
The King approved of the deer’s words; filled with joy, he advanced in virtue and issued a decree throughout the kingdom:
"From this day forward, let the deer eat as it pleases. Should anyone dare to violate this, their punishment shall be death."
When the king returned, the Queen heard that he had released them; her resentment was so intense that her heart broke, and she died to enter Mount Tai.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, hearing that the king’s resolve was exalted toward benevolence and admiring him for being thus, transformed himself into a herd of deer filling the kingdom to eat the grain. He caused all the stalks of the various crops to be swept away until they were entirely exhausted, in order to observe the king’s resolve.
The common people protested against this.
The King said:
"To preserve a state through cruel falsehood is not as good as losing it by keeping one's word."
The Śākya said,
"The King truly believes.
He sent the deer away, whereupon the grain harvest increased tenfold, poisonous harms ceased, and all afflictions naturally vanished.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the deer at that time was I myself;
the crow was Ānanda."
The king was Śāriputra. The drowning man was Devadatta.
The king’s wife is now Devadatta’s wife.
"Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve. 59.
[The Jātaka of the Horse King Druma] (59): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a horse king named Druma; he constantly dwelt by the seashore to ferry people who were adrift."

At that time, on the other side of the sea, there were many female ghosts of lecherous women. Whenever they saw merchants, they would immediately transform into cities, dwellings, fields, gardens, music, and feasts, and manifest as beautiful women with radiant and exquisite countenances, inviting the merchants and entertaining them with wine and music.

When malevolent spirits bewitch humans, they invariably leave behind a mate; within one year, the lustful spirits become weary of their former companions and pierce their throats with iron pikes, drinking their blood, eating their flesh, and sucking their marrow.
The Horse King, seeing from afar a lust-demon devouring a person, wept for him.
He then flew across the sea to the other shore, where he obtained pounded non-glutinous rice; having finished eating and drinking, he ascended a mountain and called out:
"Who wishes to cross?"
This was repeated three times.
Hearing this, the merchants said with joy, "We have often heard that divine horses compassionately deliver those in peril; has their arrival finally come to pass?"
Delighted, they approached him and said,
"Pitifully deliver us!
The horse replied:
"If you go, that lust-demon will surely seize your child and show it to you, calling out as she pursues you.
Should you harbor a heart of attachment, after I have departed, the demon will surely strike your throat again with an iron mallet, drinking your blood and devouring your flesh."
If you maintain a correct mind and harbor good intentions, you shall be able to preserve your life.

Now, those who wish to return home should mount my back, grasp my mane and tail, and hold my head and neck as they please; by supporting one another in this way, you will surely survive and see your kin again.

Those merchants who placed their trust in his words all escaped with their lives to return and see their kinsmen; yet among those led astray by lust and delusion, there was no one who did not fall prey to the ghosts, demons, and sorcery.
"Indeed, by believing in what is right and abandoning what is evil, one will enjoy eternal peace in this present life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The King of Horses at that time was none other than myself."
"Such was the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve.

60. [The Jātaka of the Fish King] (60): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of fish. He had two ministers who both possessed noble conduct and constantly maintained the Buddha's teachings; they never ceased their practice even while eating or resting, subsisting on aquatic plants merely to sustain their lives.
They nurtured the small fish with compassion as if protecting their own bodies, and as they swam and played with the tides, they instructed them in the Buddha's precepts."
Unaware that a fisherman was trapping them with a net, the entire school of fish, both large and small, were filled with terror and agitation.
The king of the fish took pity on them and said, "Do not fear;

with single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha's name and wish for the peace of all sentient beings. Through this universal compassion and great vow, divine protection will follow like an echo; come quickly to seek me."
"I shall save you all.

The king of fish turned his head downward and buried it in the mud, then stayed his tail and lifted the net; the entire multitude rushed out, and the shoal of fish were saved, none of whom failed to become his devoted followers.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the fish at that time was myself.
His attendants were Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"Such is the diligence of the Bodhisattva’s sharp resolve in the perfection of transcending limits. 61.

[The Jātaka of the Tortoise King] (61): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of tortoises. Day and night he applied himself with diligence, contemplating skillful means so that sentient beings might have their spirits return to the fundamental non-being."
Furthermore, there was a king of tortoises who lived together with him in the deep mountains. They both witnessed a monitor lizard climb a tree and then throw itself down, suffering no peace.
The Bodhisattva divined, saying:
"This is an omen of peril to one's person; we should seek refuge early to ensure our safety."
"One of those turtle kings was obstinately ignorant and independent, refusing to follow the true words.
The Bodhisattva, with all his heart, rescued those who followed him and enabled them to escape the calamity."
Ten days later, as the elephant king and his herd were resting beneath the tree, a lizard leaped into one of the elephants' ears;
the elephant cried out in alarm, and the herd rushed forward in a chaotic stampede, trampling and killing many of the turtles.
The king of turtles said in anger, "Knowing that matters were such as these, yet you did not point it out—while I die and you live—is this pleasing to your heart?
For kalpas on end I have sought you; wherever we meet, you shall surely suffer mutilation and slaughter."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who was skilled at divining by tortoise shells was I myself.
The one who remained obstinate and would not leave was Devadatta."
"Such was the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve in his supreme diligence. 62.
[The Jātaka of the King of Parrots] (62): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of parrots, with a retinue of three thousand followers."

There were two parrots whose strength and vigor surpassed all others; they held bamboo stalks in their beaks to serve as vehicles for the king, upon which he rode, flying and landing at will to sport.

He constantly rode these stalk-vehicles, with five hundred parrots each on the upper, lower, front, rear, left, and right sides. With six wings of support totaling three thousand birds, they presented him with rare treasures and provided entertainment according to the season.
The king reflected deeply within himself:
"This clamor of the multitude disturbs my virtue and prevents me from attaining concentration; I shall employ a stratagem.
Feigning illness, he ceased eating and pretended to die, casting himself away from the assembly.
The flock of birds covered him with a bamboo mat and each departed;
the king arose and went in search of food.
The flock of parrots went to the abode of another parrot king on a different mountain and said:
"We have lost our king; we wish to become your subjects.
[The other replied:
"As for your king who has died, show us his corpse. If he is truly dead, we shall admit your people."
When he returned to retrieve the corpse, it had vanished without a trace. They searched everywhere until they found the king; they all paid him their respects and resumed their offerings as before.
The king said, "I have not yet passed away, yet you all have abandoned me."

The clear instructions of the Buddhas state that in observing the world, there is no relative who can be relied upon; only the Way is worthy of veneration. For a śramaṇa, the beard and hair are the defilements that disturb the will; therefore, one discards them to honor the practice of desirelessness.
"You all clamor and shout; these perverse sounds distract the mind. To be solitary and without peer is to align one's virtue with that of the Supreme Sage.

Having finished speaking, he soared away into a secluded and profound stillness. Abandoning desire and non-action, he contemplated meditative practice; all defilements were utterly extinguished, and his mind became like celestial gold.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the parrots at that time was my own self.
Such was the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve in the perfection of diligence."
63. [The Jātaka of the King of Pigeons] (63): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the king of pigeons, with a retinue of five hundred. He soared through the royal garden in search of food."

When the king beheld this, he issued an edict commanding the herdsman to lead his men to set nets and capture them; they were caught in their entirety, both large and small, with none left behind. They were confined in cages and fed with non-glutinous rice and fatty meat, which the Master of the Kitchen provided as delicacies.
When the king of pigeons was captured, he focused his mind on the Buddha, repented of his transgressions, and gave rise to compassion, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings who are bound be liberated; may they swiftly leave the eight difficulties, never again to be like me."
He said to the pigeons:
"In the Buddha's scriptures among the various precepts, greed is the foremost. To seek glory through greed is like a starving man obtaining a drink of poison."
"The joy of attaining one's ambitions lasts but as long as a flash of lightning, while the myriad sufferings that oppress us endure for billions of years.
If you all renounce food, your lives may be preserved.
To this, the multitude replied:
"Seeing that you are confined within this cage, what do you hope for?
The king said,
"Those who violate and abandon the Buddha's teachings, giving rein to their passions and greed, are without exception those who lose their lives."
He himself renounced food, his body grew emaciated day by day, and after overcoming many hardships, he managed to escape. Looking back at the others, he said:
"Only those who eliminate greed and renounce food can become like me."
Having finished speaking, he flew away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of pigeons was myself."
"Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve. 64.
*The Sūtra of the King of Bees* [The Jātaka of the Bhikṣu Vīrabhadra] (64). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
The Buddha addressed his disciples:
"You should apply yourselves with diligent vigor to hearing and reciting [the teachings], and do not be indolent or shrouded by the hindrances.

I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Sarvābhibhū-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who at that time preached the Dharma for all the devas and humans, numbering beyond measure."
At that time, there were two bhikṣus in the assembly; one bhikṣu was named Vīravādin and the other was named Guṇaratipratyayin, and they together listened to the Dharma.
Those with eloquence through diligence hear the sutra with joy and immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), becoming fully endowed with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
whereas those who delight in virtue but are drowsy do not awaken and remain solitary without attainment.
At that time, Jingzhibian (Vīryapratibhāna) said to Delezhengyan (Guṇaratnapraśastavākya):

"A Buddha is difficult to encounter; he appears but once in hundreds of thousands of millions of eons. You ought to exert yourself with vigor to serve as a foundation for the assembly; why do you sleep?"
"Sleep is the fault of the dark covering; you ought to exhort yourself and maintain a mind of awakening.

At that time, the Rectifier of Virtue and Joy (De-le-zheng), having heard this instruction, immediately began to walk in meditation (caṅkrama). While walking among the Jeta Grove, he soon fell back into sleep. Thus, being distracted and unable to settle himself, he went to the side of a spring and sat down intending to contemplate, yet he fell asleep again as he sat. Then, the Bodhisattva Vigorous Eloquence (Jingjin-bian) approached him with skillful means (upāya) and transformed himself into a king of bees, flying toward his eyes as if about to sting him.

At that time, Delezheng was startled awake and sat up; fearing this king of bees, he soon fell back asleep. Then, the king of the honey-bees flew into his armpit and stung him on the chest and abdomen. Delezheng was terrified, and his heart trembled with fear such that he did not dare sleep again.
At that time, there were flowers of various colors in the spring water—*utpala*, *kumuda*, and many other kinds, all fresh and pure.
Then, the king of bees flew and alighted upon a flower to feast on the nectar. At that moment, Śrīgupta sat upright and watched him; fearing he might fly away again, he did not dare to sleep.

The king of bees contemplated its root; though the king of bees had tasted the nectar, he did not emerge from within the flower. After a brief moment, while the king of bees was asleep, he fell into the mud.
Having bathed his body, he returned and flew back to rest upon the flower.
Then, the bee-king Delezheng addressed these verses to his subjects:
"Those who have partaken of this ambrosia Have attained peace and security within their bodies;
They should not take it back home To share it with their wives and children."
How can one fall into the mire and defile one's own body?
Such is the mark of a lack of wisdom, for it ruins the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
Furthermore, as for this flower, it is not fit to dwell within [the mire] for long.
When the sun sets, the flowers close again; One who seeks to emerge cannot do so.
Only when the light of the sun returns Can one finally emerge once more.
The exhaustion and darkness of the long night Are likewise a most grievous suffering.
Then the king of the honey-bees addressed Delezheng, replying with these verses:
“The Buddha is like nectar; one can never hear enough of him.
One should not be indolent, for such sloth is of no benefit to anyone.”
The ocean of birth and death in the five realms is like falling into foul mud;
entangled by craving and desire, one is utterly deluded by a lack of wisdom.
When the sun rises and the myriad flowers bloom, it is likened to the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya).
As the sun sets, the flowers close again; so too does the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa.
Having encountered the era of a Tathāgata, you should receive it with diligent effort;
cast off the hindrance of sloth and do not think that the Buddha will remain forever.
The essential wisdom of the profound Dharma does not rely on the causes and conditions of form;
those who currently possess such wisdom should be known as possessing skillful means (*upāya*).
That which is delivered through skillful means is beneficial and never a vain exertion.
"And yet he manifests these transformations, / Also because of all things.

At that time, Dele (Guṇarata) heard his teaching and immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). He understood the root of all dharmas, attained *dhāraṇī*, and thereby came to know diligence, eloquence, and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
He constantly practiced walking meditation alone and was no longer indolent; accordingly, he also attained the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The one named Vigorous Eloquence at that time was my very self.”
"The one whose virtue and joy were correct was Maitreya.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"At that time, I listened to the Dharma together with Maitreya; however, Maitreya fell asleep and alone gained nothing."
If I had not employed skillful means at that time to deliver them, Maitreya would still be within the cycle of birth and death today and not yet attained liberation.
Those who hear this Dharma should always be diligent, widely exhorting all others to eliminate the hindrance of drowsiness and to establish the foundation of luminous wisdom.
When these matters were spoken, countless people all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, impartial mind of universal liberation.
Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s diligence in the perfection of exertion.

65. Sūtra on the Buddha’s Smile for Three Reasons [The Previous Life of a Lay Disciple] (65) Sūtra on the Buddha’s Smile for Three Reasons: “In the past, the Bodhisattva was a lay disciple (*upāsaka*) who took refuge in the Triple Gem. His compassion was vast and his benevolence universal; he extended forgiveness to all living beings. He maintained purity and did not steal; his generosity reached the ultimate; he was chaste and pure, never licentious, and he contemplated the renunciation of internal lust. His faith was as constant as the four seasons and as steadfast as Mount Sumeru. He abstained from alcohol, never drinking it; his filial piety was honored like that toward one's own parents. On the first month, he observed the six fasts with diligent effort without weariness. In every life he encountered a Buddha, and his virtuous conduct flourished daily until he eventually became the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Lord of the Dharma, and the Teacher of Gods and Humans, whose teachings circulated throughout the world.”
As he was walking through the market, he saw an old man selling fish by the peck; he wailed in deep grief, crying out:
"Alas for the Sovereign Heaven! For what fault has my son lost his life so prematurely?"
"My son is here selling fish; how could I be so weary?
The Buddha beheld this and smiled, and light of five colors radiated from his mouth.
After passing through the marketplace for a brief moment, he again saw a large pig bathing in urine as it walked along the road, and the Buddha smiled once more.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated himself, and said:
"Just now, as there were many people present, I had no way to respectfully inquire about the cause of your smile;
yet you smile again now, which must surely be for the purpose of instruction."
"I pray that you will dispel the doubts of the assembly and serve as a model for future generations.
The World-Honored One replied, "Ānanda!"
I have three reasons for my laughter.
First, observing the folly of that old man, it is truly vast and universal.
Day after day he slaughters the lives of many creatures with his nets, yet he lacks even a hair’s breadth of compassion.
To lose one's own son through calamity and yet resent Heaven, wailing and crying out in terror—this is the conduct of the most ignorant and base;
it is neither the benevolence of the Two Polarities nor the forbearance of the sages and worthies, and for this reason, I laugh at it.

In the past, the Emperor Who Flies Through the Air planted vast and towering merit; yet his will became arrogant and his conduct dissolute, and he has now become a fish measured by the *dou*—this is the second [reason].

He did not contemplate the human or celestial realms, where a lifespan lasts eighty-four billion *kalpas*; his mind was exclusively attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), unable to realize the "emptiness of emptiness" that returns to original non-being (*mūla-abhāva*). Now that his merit is exhausted, he undergoes retribution and dwells within the *dou*—this is the third [reason].
Ānanda asked:
“The Emperor who soars through the air and even those honored devas possess such towering virtue; for what reason do they not escape from retribution for their offenses?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Calamity and fortune are not real; how could they possess permanence?
Now, one who dwells in honor and glory yet bestows the fourfold universal kindness and awakens to the four signs of impermanence may escape that calamity."

If one pursues self-indulgence because of noble status and follows deviance for the sake of gratifying the mind, when merit is exhausted one will undergo retribution; this has been so since antiquity.
Calamity and fortune follow the self like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound—how could there be any distinction between noble and base?

I recall that in a previous life I was a lay devotee. At that time, there was a neighbor who delighted in serving ghosts and using sorcery; he associated with a band of wicked men and, being faithless, committed evil deeds to which heavy calamities responded like echoes.

"Every time a day of fasting arrives, I intend to enter the temple of the Buddha’s true and correct teaching to listen as the assembly of śramaṇas expounds upon the pure Dharma, thereby establishing the root of virtue and preventing calamities; yet you, my son, are licentious and dissolute, falsely claiming that you have business to attend to."
"When I went to the Buddha’s temple, you went to disturb the path.

From that time forward, in every life I was born into, I encountered the Buddha and heard the Dharma, and my aspirations were in harmony with those of the śramaṇas. My virtuous conduct flourished daily until I eventually became the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Teacher of Gods and Men, the Lord of the Dharma, the Honored One of the Three Realms, titled the Dharma King."

A neighbor of mine was fond of demonic arts, harming and injuring living beings, indulging in licentious lust for women, and becoming intoxicated with wine and immoral; he considered himself to have attained his ambitions.
Yet, he revolves through the three realms of existence, enduring immeasurable suffering and bitterness.
"I have already become a Buddha, while you, my son, continue to be a stinking insect; that is why I laughed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Throughout many kalpas, I have received the sutras and gathered their meanings, personally delighting in the śramaṇas, and thus I have attained this majestic state."
"Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve. 66.

The Story of the Boy Who Understood the Sūtra Upon Hearing It (The Jātaka of the Boy) "The Story of the Boy Who Understood the Sūtra Upon Hearing It": Long ago, there was a bhikṣu who was diligent in upholding the Dharma. He maintained the minor precepts with such care that he never transgressed them even once; he constantly observed the holy life (brahmacarya) while residing in a monastery.

Regarding this Prajñāpāramitā which he recites, the sound with which he preaches the sutra is so sublime that none can equal it; there is no one who hears the voice of this bhikṣu who does not rejoice.

There was a young boy, seven years of age, who was herding oxen outside the city. Hearing from afar the sound of a bhikṣu reciting and expounding the sūtras, he immediately followed the sound to the vihāra. Having paid homage to the bhikṣu, he withdrew to sit at one side and listened to the words of the sūtra as they were spoken. At that time, the teaching concerned the fundamental nature of form (*rūpa*); upon hearing it, the boy understood it immediately and was filled with great joy.
When the passage of the sutra had ended, he questioned the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu was unable to provide an answer that satisfied the child's mind.
At that time, the young boy instead explained it for him; its meaning was most profound, something rarely heard in the past.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu was filled with great joy and delight, marveling that this young boy possessed such wisdom and was no ordinary person.

At that moment, the boy departed and returned to where the cattle were; the calves he was herding had scattered and fled into the mountains, so the boy followed their tracks, pursuing and searching for them.

At that time, a tiger encountered and killed this young child; his life having ended, his spirit immediately transmigrated and was reborn into the household of a householder as the son of the first wife.
"When the lady was pregnant, she was able to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* from morning until evening without ever flagging.

Since the headman’s family had never before known the Dharma, they found this woman's speech strange and considered it delusory talk; they claimed she was afflicted by a ghost-spirit and sought out every possible ritual to exorcise the calamity, yet no one could understand what was happening."
The elder was deeply distressed, not knowing how his wife had contracted this illness; everyone inside and outside the household was filled with anxiety and alarm.

At that time, a bhikṣu entered the city for alms and approached the elder’s gate; hearing the sound of the sutra from afar, his heart was filled with great joy, and he remained at the gate for a short while.
The master happened to go out and saw that this bhikṣu did not even offer him a greeting; the bhikṣu wondered at this, thinking:
"How marvelous is the excellence of the sound of the sutra being preached within this worthy man's house!"
"Now this householder does not speak with me," he thought,
and he immediately asked the householder,
"Who is it within that recites the profound sutras with such subtle and exquisite tones?"
The householder replied, "A wife in my household has contracted a demonic illness; she speaks falsely day and night, her mouth never ceasing.
Only then did the bhikṣu realize that the householder's family did not understand the Dharma, and the bhikṣu said:
"This is not a demonic affliction; it is merely that he wishes to preach the Honored Sūtra and the Great Way of the Buddha, and hopes to enter within to meet with you.
The elder said, "Excellent!"
He then led the bhikṣu into the presence of the woman.
Upon seeing the bhikṣu, the woman immediately paid him homage. The bhikṣu offered a blessing, saying:
"May you quickly attain Buddhahood."
He then engaged in debate with the bhikṣu regarding the exposition of the Dharma, analyzing and explaining it back and forth, which the bhikṣu greatly rejoiced in.
The elder asked:
"What kind of illness is this?"
The bhikṣu replied: "I have no illness;
it is only that while reciting a profound sūtra of great significance, I became suspicious that the child this lady carries in her womb might be a disciple of the Buddha."
The elder understood his meaning and immediately invited the bhikṣu to stay and provide him with food and drink.
When the meal was finished, the bhikṣu withdrew from the vihāra, and as they passed along, they said to one another:

“There is a lady of a certain elder’s household who is pregnant; it is truly extraordinary. She recites the honored sūtras from memory, speaking them like a flowing stream; her voice is exquisite and beautiful, and she explains the principles of the scriptures with profound depth.”
On a later day, the elder again invited the bhikṣus, extending the invitation to the entire Saṃgha, and prepared food and drink.
When the time arrived, they all came and took their seats; after the water and food had been served, he offered prayers for their blessing and gave the *dakṣiṇā*.

Then the lady came forth to pay homage to the assembly of bhikṣus and withdrew to sit on one side. She further expounded the Dharma for the bhikṣus with great clarity; regarding all doubts and difficulties that others were unable to resolve, she explained them fully and exhaustively for the bhikṣus. The assembly of monks rose up with joy and retired.
When the months were complete and the lady was in labor, she gave birth to a son; moreover, there was no foul discharge.
As soon as the child was born, he joined his palms, knelt upright, and recited the Prajñāpāramitā.
Once the lady had given birth, she returned to her former state and knew nothing more, just as one who has awakened from a dream finds no trace of what was perceived.
The elder then summoned the assembly of monks.
The bhikṣus gathered together and went to see the boy; as they recounted the stories from the sūtras, there was no obstacle at all.
At that time, each of the monks concentrated their minds to contemplate the boy’s origins, yet none were able to know them.
The elder asked, "What is this?
and the bhikṣu replied:
"True disciples of the Buddha, do not be startled or doubtful; cherish and protect him well.
This child shall later become a teacher for all people, and we shall all receive instruction from him."

At that time, when the boy had grown up to the age of seven, he fully understood the subtle and profound; his knowledge encompassed both the secular and the monastic, excelling far beyond the masses with boundless wisdom.
All the bhikṣus received instruction from him; wherever there were errors, omissions, or deficiencies in the sūtras, he corrected and standardized them, supplementing what was lacking.
Whenever the youth entered or left, or stopped at any place, he invariably transformed people by inspiring them toward the Mahāyāna.

Among the five hundred people—both great and small—within and without the elder’s household, all studied under the youth, resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna, and collectively performed the work of the Buddha.

Among the eighty-four thousand people who were instructed by the youth throughout the cities and market towns, all gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. Five hundred disciples followed him, and when the bhikṣus heard what the youth had said, their minds were liberated from outflows; those who sought the Mahāyāna all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The child at that time was my own self.
The bhikṣu at that time was Kāśyapa Buddha."
Thus it was, Ānanda!

In the past, upon hearing a chapter on the Mahāyāna from a certain bhikṣu, I praised it, attained understanding, and my mind was filled with joy that never wavered. With diligent application and without forgetfulness, I gained deep knowledge of my past lives and thereby attained unsurpassed, equal, and perfect enlightenment.
If the virtue of hearing it but once is already thus exalted, how much more so for one who follows and cultivates the Way all day long?
Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

67. The Sūtra on Sacrificing One’s Body to Save the Merchants [The Jātaka of the Merchant] (67). The Sūtra on Sacrificing One’s Body to Save the Merchants: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was with five hundred merchants who entered the great ocean together, desiring to gather various treasures."
Having been at sea for several months, they had obtained such treasures that their ships were heavily laden to capacity.

As they were about to return to their native land, they encountered a tempestuous wind; thunder and lightning shook the earth, and water deities gathered like a city on all sides. Fire erupted from their eyes, and surging waves overflowed the mountains.
The multitude cried out in terror, saying, "We are dead!"
Terrified and his complexion changing, he looked up to heaven seeking mercy.
The Bodhisattva was deeply moved and thought to himself:
"My quest for Buddhahood is solely for the sake of sentient beings."
The sea deity detests corpses most of all.
To risk one's life to save the multitude is the noble undertaking of a bodhisattva.
Had I not poured my own blood into the sea, the sea deity would have been repulsed by it, and I suspect the boatmen would never have reached the shore.
He said to the crowd,
"All of you, join hands and support my body.
The people obeyed his command, and the Bodhisattva immediately drew his sword and cut himself.
The Sea God detested this and drifted the boat onto the shore, where the multitude came to their rescue.
A sailor embraced the corpse and wailed to heaven, saying:
"This must surely be a Bodhisattva; he is no ordinary person."
They leaped about and wailed to heaven, saying:
"We would rather let our own lives perish here than lose a man of such supreme virtue.

Their words were so sincere that they moved the various heavens above; Śakra, Lord of Devas, beholding the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion and seeing it as something rare in the world, descended from his celestial abode and said:
"This Bodhisattva of Supreme Virtue shall become a Holy Hero; we must now restore him to life.
They poured divine medicinal herbs into his mouth and also smeared them over his corpse. The Bodhisattva immediately revived, suddenly rose to his feet, and exchanged greetings with the assembly.

Śakra filled his boat with famous jewels, a thousand times more than before, and immediately returned to his own land. There, his nine kinsmen met one another, all of whom were filled with joy; he relieved the destitute and aided the needy, extending his bounty to all sentient beings, proclaiming the Buddhist scriptures to enlighten the ignorant and deluded.

The king of that land was moved by the Bodhisattva’s virtue and went to receive his pure transformation. The ruler was benevolent and the ministers were loyal; throughout the realm, the precepts were observed, and every household had filial sons. The nation became abundant and poison was extinguished; the common people rejoiced, and upon the end of their lives, they were reborn in heaven, forever freed from all suffering.
"The Bodhisattva practiced with diligence without ceasing for many eons, until he finally attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one who sacrificed his own body to save the multitude was none other than myself."
The Deva Śakra was Maitreya.
The five hundred merchants were these five hundred *ayutya-satyas* (true persons) now seated in this assembly.
Such was the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve in his practice of diligence.

68. [The Jātaka of the Boy] (68): "In the past, the Bodhisattva was the only son of a mother. In the morning, he went to a Buddhist temple to abandon the heterodox and revere the True; he prostrated before the śramaṇas and received the divine transformation of the Buddha's teachings. Increasing his learning every morning and reciting them every evening, as the sun rose in the clear sky, he gathered and mastered the various sūtras."
The filial conduct of the ancient sages was so profoundly revered that it was like a starving man dreaming of food.

The kingdom in which he resided had a ruler who was unrighteous, greedy for wealth and obsessed with sensual pleasures, while holding the worthy in low esteem and treating the common people with contempt.
The king, contemplating impermanence, thought to himself:
"I have committed unwholesome deeds; upon death, shall I enter Mount Tai?
Why not gather gold to offer as tribute to the King of Mount Tai?"
Thereupon, he collected the gold from the people and established a severe decree, saying:
"If anyone conceals even a single *zhū* or *liǎng* of gold, their crime shall be punishable by death.
After three years like this, the people's gold was completely exhausted.
The king issued a deceptive recruitment notice, saying:
"To anyone who captures a small amount of gold to present to the king, I shall give his youngest daughter in marriage and bestow upon him the highest rank.
The boy addressed his mother, saying:
"In the past, I placed a single gold coin in my deceased father's mouth, intending it as a bribe for the King of Mount Tai; it must still be there now, so you may take it to present to the King."
The mother said,
"Very well.
The son took it and presented it to her.
The King ordered his records to be examined and asked how he had obtained the gold.

He replied, "When my father passed away, he placed this gold in his mouth, intending to bribe Mount Tai. Upon hearing that Your Majesty had established an offering to seek gold, I first dug up the tomb, removed the coffin wood, and took the gold."
The King asked,
"Has it been many years since your father passed away?
He replied:
"Eleven years have passed," he said.
"Did your father not offer bribes to the King of Mount Tai?"
He replied:
"Among the scriptures of all sages, only the Buddhist teaching is true.
A Buddhist sutra says:"
"When one performs good, blessings follow; when one commits evil, calamity follows. Calamity and blessing are like shadows and echoes.
To run away from the body in order to avoid its shadow, or to block a mountain in order to stop its echo—how could such things be achieved?
The king said,
"It cannot be. He asked:

"Indeed, the body is composed of the four great elements; when life ends, these four elements disperse. The spirit departs and undergoes transformation, following wherever its past actions lead—what gift could there possibly be?

Your Majesty practiced generosity in previous lives to cultivate virtue, and thus you have now attained the status of king. Furthermore, you revere benevolence and love, so that your grace extends far and wide. Although you have not yet attained the Way, in future lives you will surely become king once again."
The king’s heart was filled with joy; he issued a general amnesty for all prisoners and returned the seized gold.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At that time, the king intended to execute the remaining gold from the common people upon those who were innocent. The Bodhisattva beheld the people’s lamentation and wept for them; he cast his life before the tyrannical administration to rescue the people from their plight amidst the mire and ashes.”
The people were moved by his benevolence and observed the supreme precepts of the Buddha, so that the kingdom subsequently became prosperous and fertile.
At that time, the youth was none other than my own self.
Such was the vigor and diligence of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve for deliverance.

69. The Sūtra on Devadatta Teaching Others to Commit Evil [The Jātaka of the Heavenly King] (69). In the past, when the Bodhisattva held the rank of a Heavenly King, he was diligent in his subtle conduct and his will for progress flowed like a stream. On every fast day (*upoṣadha*), he would mount a horse-drawn carriage and travel throughout the four continents to proclaim the profound scriptures of the Buddha, transforming sentient beings, eliminating their defilements, and leading them to revere the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the God among Gods, the King among all Sages, the Honored One of the Way and its Teachings—one who can cause one to leave behind the source of all sufferings in the three evil realms.

Devadatta also became a Heavenly King of Māra; he traveled throughout the four continents, teaching people to do evil according to their own desires, asserting that there were no retributions for calamities and misfortunes from Mount Tai.
While traveling, he encountered a bodhisattva who asked him,
"What are you practicing? He replied:
"The teaching instructs the people to revere the Buddha and cultivate the virtue of the supreme sages.
Devadatta said,
"My teaching allows the people to indulge their desires so that they suffer no calamity in two lifetimes."
"To labor for the sake of goodness is of no benefit to oneself.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Then you must avoid my path."
He replied:
"Your doing good is like gold and silver, while my cherishing evil is like hard iron.
Hard iron can cut through gold and silver, but gold and silver cannot cut through hard iron; if you do not descend from this path, I shall slay you."
"Devadatta’s evil was so rampant that his calamity was consummated; he entered Mount Tai while still alive.

When people commit evil, they all enter the three miserable realms (trāya) after death; yet those in the three realms who embrace goodness have none who do not ascend to heaven. Thus, though one may occupy a position of honor and glory, if they harbor great wickedness, it is not as good as those in the three miserable realms who hold even a single word of the Buddha."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The heavenly king who taught others to practice goodness was I myself.
The Māra-deva who led people toward evil was Devadatta."
"Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Resolve. 70.

The Sūtra on Killing the Dragon to Save a Nation [The Previous Life of the Elder Brother] "In the past, the Bodhisattva and his elder and younger uncles were of one mind; together they practiced the Way, admiring the difficult-to-attain conduct of the Buddhas. They recited the sūtras and explained their meanings to enlighten the six realms of darkness; they refined away internal defilements and dwelt in the tranquility of śamatha and vipaśyanā."

Whenever he heard that various kingdoms were ignorant of the Triple Gem, he would invariably go there to guide and transform them, leading them to practice the sublime and true conduct of the Six Perfections.

At that time, there was a great kingdom whose king delighted in the Way; however, various demons enticed him and bestowed upon him heterodox and false teachings. The entire realm followed this trend and all practiced the way of sorcery (*gudu*). Consequently, wind and rain did not arrive at their proper times, and strange portents followed one after another.
The Bodhisattvas’ uncles and cousins said to one another:

"In our native land, the teachings of the Three Honored Ones have been practiced; people cherish the ten wholesome deeds; rulers are benevolent and ministers loyal, fathers righteous and sons filial, husbands trustworthy and wives chaste; there are sages at every door. To whom shall we go to convert them?"
In various lands, people believe in demons; dragons and serpents dwell therein, devouring the common folk, whose piteous cries go unheeded.
It is precisely for the sake of such beings that one establishes the will to seek the Buddha.
"We can transform them through the Way and instruct them with benevolence; though dragons harbor fierce venom, we shall subdue them.
Shu said, "The Buddha’s precepts regard killing as the greatest cruelty, while sparing life is the foremost principle of the Way of Benevolence."
"What shall we do with him? Bo replied,
"The one who harms a single person incurs the guilt of a hundred kalpas."
"A dragon has devoured an entire kingdom; I fear that even when the kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have ended, its calamity will not yet be removed.
If one greedily craves the fleeting benefit of a momentary taste while failing to perceive the retribution of being burned and boiled in the Great Mountain Hell, my heart is filled with compassion."

Human existence is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear; with the exception of the Kingdom of Longji, where people are guided by the noble practices of the Three Honored Ones and the Six Paramitas, their calamities are as slight as a hair or a thread, while their blessings are as vast as the two polarities of heaven and earth.
"If you transform into an elephant and I become a lion, yet neither of our lives is spared, this kingdom will not be saved.
He prostrated himself toward the ten directions and vowed:
"If sentient beings do not find peace, it is my fault."
"When I later attain Buddhahood, I shall deliver all beings.
The elephant went to where the dragon was, and the lion mounted it.

The dragon immediately exerted its power, flashing like lightning and thundering like a clap of thunder; the lion leaped and roared. The dragon’s majestic spirit and the lion’s blazing might caused the entire earth to tremble, and the dragon’s life was cut short three times over.
The devas praised them as virtuous, and there was none who did not admire their benevolence.
When the two bodhisattvas passed away, they were reborn in the fourth heaven.
The entire kingdom, having preserved its lives, embraced the corpses and wailed in grief, saying:
"This one must surely be divine!
Who could possess such benevolence?
The disciples followed after him; seeing that their Master had shown universal compassion by sacrificing his own life to save the multitude, they wailed in grief and extolled his virtue.
Each of them further propagated the Master’s teachings and transformation; only then did the king, his ministers, and the common people first learn of the Buddha.
Throughout the entire land, everyone exclaimed: "How far-reaching is the Buddha’s benevolent transformation!"
After the two corpses had been encoffined and buried, the entire kingdom was filled with grief and lamentation.
The King then issued a decree:
"Should anyone fail to uphold the Buddha’s Six Perfections and Ten Wholesome Deeds while instead serving demonic spirits, they shall be held guilty along with their entire kin."

From that time forward, thousands of śramaṇas walked side by side throughout the land; the men and women within the realm all became lay believers of pure faith and noble conduct. The four borders were peaceful and tranquil, leading eventually to a period of great peace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The elder brother at that time was I myself;
the younger brother was Maitreya."
The venomous dragon was Devadatta.
Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve and supreme diligence.

[The entire retinue acts in concert; in the Dan edition, this is identical to the section on the *teng* (dragon). **Sūtra on Maitreya Taking the Form of a Woman** [The Previous Birth of Śakra] (71) In the past, the Bodhisattva was Śakra, Lord of the Devas. His rank was honored and exalted, yet his mind constantly maintained the perception of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

When sitting, he engaged in contemplation; when traveling, he taught and transformed others. Compassionate toward the ignorant and affectionate toward the wise, he instructed them with wisdom, practicing diligence without ceasing.
He beheld a former friend who had received a female body as the wife of a wealthy clan; deluded by wealth and beauty, she failed to perceive impermanence as she sat at her stall in the marketplace.
Śakra transformed himself into a merchant and, pretending to be there for trade, stood before the woman.
The woman was delighted and sent her son to run home to fetch a single-seated couch so that he might sit upon it; the merchant then gazed intently at the woman and smiled.
The wife maintained her high principles of conduct; she found it strange that the merchant paused and laughed at an inappropriate time.
When the son took too long to fetch the bed, she struck him immediately, yet the merchant again paused and laughed.
Beside him was a boy dancing and playing with a small drum; the merchant laughed at him again.
There was another whose father was ill, and his son sacrificed an ox to the spirits; the merchant also laughed at him.

There was a woman walking through the marketplace with her child in her arms; as they passed by, the child scratched his cheeks until blood flowed down to mingle at their necks, and the merchants laughed at them once more.
Thereupon, the wife of the wealthy man asked:
"You stood before me and could not stop smiling; we were the ones beating the child, and our pleasure depended on you—why did you smile?"
The merchant said, "You are my good friend; have you now forgotten me?
The woman was despondent, her mind even more displeased, and she marveled at the merchant's words.

The merchant said again, "The reason I laughed at the boy being struck was that the boy is your father; his spirit has returned and been reborn as your son. Within a single lifetime, there are those who do not recognize their own father, so what need is there to mention the long term?"

The child who shakes the small drum was originally an ox; when the ox died, its spirit returned to become the son of the master of the house. The family used ox hide to bind this drum, and now the child plays with it, leaping and dancing about, unaware that this hide was his own former body; therefore, he laughs at it.
To slaughter an ox for sacrifice while praying for a father’s recovery from illness—seeking life by means of killing—is the height of inauspiciousness;
it is like taking aconite poison to cure a disease.
"This father has just passed away; having died, he became an ox. For generations his family has slaughtered him, and he has suffered calamity without end.
Now this sacrificial ox, at the end of its life, its spirit returns and it shall receive a human body, thereby escaping sorrow and suffering; for this reason, it laughs again."
