The mother would scratch her son's face; the son was originally the junior wife, while the mother was the senior wife. The daughter’s passion was fixed on lust, and harboring jealousy in her heart, she constantly treated her with cruel violence.

"I harbored resentment, and when my life ended, I was reborn as the son of the legal wife; now I have come to take revenge, clawing her face and wounding her body. Therefore, I dare not harbor further grievance, which is why I laugh."
Indeed, the minds of sentient beings are devoid of constancy; what was loathed in the past may be cherished now—how can there be any permanence?
This is true even within a single lifetime, where people see only the present and fail to understand; how much more so across successive kalpas?
The Sūtra says:
"Those who obstruct themselves with form are blind to the Great Way; those who focus exclusively on listening to perverse sounds do not hear the resonance of the Buddha’s voice.
It is for this reason that I laugh at them.

Worldly glory is like a flash of lightning; it vanishes in an instant. You should realize that all things are impermanent and not associate with the foolish. Exalt the cultivation of virtuous conduct and the sublime practice of the Six Perfections.
I shall now return home, but I will surely visit your gate again in the future.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished. The wife returned home with a sense of regretful longing.

She maintained her purity and focused her aspirations with such sincerity that the entire kingdom heard of it; from the king down to the various officials, there was none who did not hold him in high esteem and invite him.
Later, the merchant arrived at the gate; he appeared ugly and was dressed in tattered clothes, saying, "My friend is inside; call him out.
The gatekeeper went in and reported this, describing his appearance in full detail.
The woman came out and said,
"You are no longer my friend.
Śreṇika smiled and said:

"If you cannot even recognize me when I have changed my form and altered my clothing, how much less could you do so when passing from this life to another, casting off this body and receiving that one?
He spoke again:

"You must diligently serve the Buddha; for a Buddha is difficult to encounter in this age, and a bhikṣu of high conduct is difficult to find to serve. Your life hangs by a thread—do not follow the delusions of the world."
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The entire nation rejoiced and sighed in admiration, each upholding the six perfections and the most sublime conduct.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"The woman at that time was Maitreya;
Śakra, Lord of Devas, was my own self.
Such was the vigor and diligence of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve."

72. The Sūtra on a Woman’s Prayer [The Jātaka of the Woman] (72). The Sūtra on a Woman’s Prayer. "In the past, when the Bodhisattva was born as a woman, her husband was by nature fierce, foolish, and envious. Whenever he went abroad for trade, he would entrust his wife to a neighbor who was a widow; this woman observed the Buddha's precepts and practiced as a lay follower (*upāsikā*). "

At that time, when the Buddha entered the kingdom, the king, his ministers, and the common people all received the precepts; only the mother heard the sutra and returned to tell it to her daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law rejoiced and sighed, saying:
"This is indeed the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path, the Most Perfect Enlightenment."
Having heard of the Buddha from his mother, he immediately bowed his head toward her from afar.
On the day of the fast, his mother asked,
"Would you like to go and listen to the Dharma?"
The wife said joyfully, "Very well.
She then searched outside the city; suddenly, she felt jealous of her husband and became despondent and displeased, immediately returning home and reproaching herself.
"Is my transgression heavy?
Her mother returned and explained to her:

"The devas, dragons, ghosts, spirits, emperors, kings, ministers, and commoners listen to the sutras; some attain the four paths of the śramaṇa, while others receive the prediction of bodhisattvahood."
"A Buddha is difficult to encounter in this age, and the Dharma is difficult to hear; why then have you returned?
Hearing of the Buddha's virtues, the wife shed tears and fully explained her husband's jealous intentions.
The mother said,
"You may try going once.
The wife said:
"Respectfully accepted.

The next day, she followed her mother to see the Buddha; prostrating herself with her five limbs touching the ground, she stood back and composed her mind, gazing upon the Buddha’s marks and signs, reflecting on his purity, and realizing he was truly a Heavenly Honored One.
The Buddha asked the girl,
"What is your wish for coming here?
She immediately prostrated herself and replied:

"I have heard that the Buddha is the Unsurpassed, Truly Realized Way, the Most Perfectly Enlightened One, the Charioteer of the Dharma, and the Teacher of Gods and Humans; his virtue is like the sands of the Ganges and his wisdom is like empty space. Having attained the six supernormal powers and universal penetration, he has acquired all-encompassing knowledge. I come to request the Honored One’s presence; may the Buddha take pity on me."
The World-Honored One said, "The Buddha is the protector of all; fulfill whatever you wish.
The woman bowed her head to the ground and said:

"O Lady, those dwelling in this world who have not yet attained the state of fundamental non-existence all live as spouses because of desire; may I, throughout successive lifetimes, dwell as a spouse with one of supreme virtue, sharing the same aspiration and free from the conduct of jealousy."
Second, their conduct of body, speech, and mind is upright and transcends the world.

Third, from lifetime to lifetime they reverently serve the Triple Gem; the defilements of their minds diminish daily, and they advance toward the Way without weariness. Protected by the aid of all Buddhas, no malevolent forces can obstruct them; they will surely attain all-encompassing wisdom and rescue sentient beings from their hardships.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
May you attain it."
The wife was filled with great joy and, having prostrated herself, returned to her own dwelling.
Her husband, returning from his trade, was traveling by boat upon the water and was due to arrive on that very day.

Having observed the wife’s noble conduct and her peerless vow, Śakra, Lord of Devas, rejoiced and praised her virtue; he stirred up wind and rain to halt the progress of the boat, so that it did not reach its destination until the following day.

"After the woman’s life ended, her spirit was reborn into a family of the Way; her countenance was radiant and outshone the world. When she grew up, she married into a state Confucian scholar's household, and the nation acclaimed her as a woman of high virtue."

At that time, the husband entered the sea to gather treasures in order to relieve the destitute people, while his wife remained at home, guarding herself with propriety as if defending against invaders. The king, the queen, and the wives and concubines of the high ministers all looked up to her as a model; they gathered at her gate like clouds to receive instruction in the conduct of feminine virtue.
The wife woke from her sleep at night and contemplated the impermanence of the world:

"Prosperity and wealth are like illusions; who can attain eternal existence? My body is but a fragile boat upon which my spirit rides, much like one who gazes at the reflection of the moon while longing for the celestial jewels."
What benefit is there to oneself in toiling the mind and exhausting the body?
Dreams and illusions are all empty; even the gods and worldly glory shall return to such a state.
At dawn tomorrow, I shall seek the Unsurpassed, Right, and True One, the God among Gods, to be my teacher.

Upon rising at dawn, he beheld a stone stupa in the courtyard; the Buddha image radiated golden light, and scriptures were inscribed upon the carved walls. He marveled that the Buddha was the teacher of all sages, peerless throughout the three realms.
The wife sighed with joy and said, "This must be the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!

She immediately prostrated herself on the ground, circumambulated the temple three times, scattered flowers, burned incense, lit lamps, and hung silk banners; morning and night she remained solemn and devout, bowing her head in respectful worship.
The queen and the ladies of the court requested that they might receive the pure wind [of the Dharma] to repel the heterodox and honor the True.
A neighboring ruffian, Jia Feng, encountered the wife and her husband and said:

"Your wife has practiced sorcery; she has falsely established a temple to spirits and burns incense morning and evening, chanting curses and using malevolent charms, wishing for your death—this is most inauspicious."
When the husband returned home, his wife said to him: "Last night, I became aware of the impermanence of the world.

At dawn, I beheld the image of the Supreme, True, and Peerless Holy One, most wondrous and sublime, appearing in our courtyard. I have now made offerings to it—burning incense, lighting lamps, hanging silken banners, and presenting flowers; morning and evening I prostrate myself and take refuge in it. You, my husband, should attend to this matter, for it surely accords with the sacred principles."
The husband was greatly delighted; with single-minded reverence and solemnity, the people of the land, both great and small, all followed his example for eighty-four thousand years and more.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The woman at that time was I myself.”
The son-in-law at that time was Maitreya; the single mother was Śāriputra;
and the neighboring ruffian was Devadatta.
Such was the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s boundless resolve and his supreme diligence.

73. The Sūtra on Dīpaṃkara’s Bestowal of Prediction [The Jātaka of the Solitary Mother] (73) The Sūtra on Dīpaṃkara’s Bestowal of Prediction: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a woman. A young widow who maintained her virtue, she took refuge in the Triple Gem. Dwelling in poverty yet delighting in the Way, she practiced with tireless diligence. Having abandoned violent profits, she made her living by selling medicinal oils."

At that time, there was a śramaṇa in the latter part of his life whose aspirations were set upon lofty conduct; he had no leisure for literary studies, and those of a narrow-minded disposition called this lack of illumination (avidyā).

In matters of ritual reverence, there may be partiality, yet from beginning to end, nothing was ever neglected; she provided oil for alms to offer before the Buddha, her devotion as constant as the light of a lamp, never failing for a single day.
There was a certain *śrāmaṇera* who prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined, asked:
"This elderly *śrāmaṇera*, though his wisdom is slight, is complete in precepts and lofty in conduct. What merit shall he obtain in the future by offering lamps in worship?"
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent is this question!

This elder mendicant, after incalculable kalpas, shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfectly Enlightened One. With a radiant light upon his neck, he shall lead and guide the three realms; those sentient beings who attain deliverance through him shall be beyond counting."
Upon hearing this, the widow hurried to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated herself, and said:

“The oil for the ‘Alleviator of Hunger’ lamp was indeed what I offered. May he attain the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way, leading all sentient beings back to the fundamental non-being of the spirit, so that devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons may all find peace and joy.”
"I only pray that you will show me compassion and grant me the prediction of my future enlightenment.
The Buddha told the woman:

"A female body cannot attain Buddhahood, nor the path of a Pratyekabuddha, nor the status of Brahmā, Śakra, Māra, or a Cakravartin King. This supreme and majestic state is not something that can be achieved by one in a female body."
"To obtain that, one must discard this defiled body and receive a pure body.
The woman bowed her head and said,
"I shall now discard it."
Returning to his quarters, he bathed in purity and prostrated from afar, saying:
"This body is a composite of the four great elements; it is not something I can preserve forever.
He then ascended the tower and made this vow:
"By offering this impure body of mine to satisfy the hunger and thirst of sentient beings, I pray that I may obtain a male form and receive the prediction of my future Buddhahood.

If there are sentient beings in a turbid age who are blind and ignorant, turning their backs on the right path and following the wrong, and who do not know the Buddha, I shall rescue and deliver them in that world."
He threw himself down from a great height, and those who watched were struck with cold dread.

The Buddha, knowing his sincere intent, transformed the ground so that it became as soft as celestial silk; seeing that his body was unharmed, he immediately transformed into a male, and his joy was immeasurable.
He rushed to the place where the Buddha was and, leaping for joy, said:
"I have received the grace of the World-Honored One and have already attained a purified body.
I only pray that you will extend your compassion and grant me the prediction of my noble destiny."
The Buddha praised him, saying:

"Your valor is rare in this world; you shall certainly attain Buddhahood, of this have no doubt. When you become a Buddha after having offered lamps to eliminate hunger, he shall bestow a name upon you."

When the devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons heard that he would become a Buddha, they all bowed toward him in greeting and congratulation; returning to their abodes, they sighed in admiration and each redoubled their diligent practice.
At that time, the beings whom he exhorted and inspired were beyond counting.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The aged bhikṣu at that time was Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
The single mother was my own self."
"Such is the vigor of the Bodhisattva’s resolute will in the Perfection of Vigor.
*Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
*Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of the Kingdom of Kāñcī in Wu.
Chapter Five: The Perfection of Dhyāna (Dhyanapāramitā). This chapter contains nine sections.
[74] Attaining the Method of Dhyāna (74): "What is the perfection of dhyāna?"

Rectify the mind and unify the intent; gather all that is wholesome and internalize it within the heart. Regarding all defilements and evils, eliminate them with goodness. There are four stages of dhyāna (*dhyāna*):

the practice of the first dhyāna involves removing all that is greedily craved—the five seductive and perverse objects. When the eye beholds beautiful forms, the mind becomes lustful and frantic; one must likewise remove attachment to sounds heard by the ear, fragrances smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the mouth, and what is pleasing to the body. In the resolve for the Way, one must certainly distance oneself from these.
Furthermore, there are five hindrances:
the hindrance of covetousness for wealth, the hindrance of anger and resentment, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of sensual delight, and the hindrance of regret and doubt.

Whether the Way exists or not, whether a Buddha appears or not, whether the sutras exist or not, the mind-consciousness remains pure and stainless. With a clear mind, one perceives the truth and attains omniscience; neither devas, nagas, ghosts, nor demons can delude such a person.

It is like a person who has ten enemies and manages to escape from them, dwelling alone in the mountains where no one knows him and he has nothing further to fear; having distanced himself from sensual desires, his inner self is pure and his mind is tranquil—this is called the first dhyāna.

When the mind attains the first dhyāna and advances toward the second dhyāna, it is like a person fleeing an enemy: though dwelling in deep mountains, they fear the enemy will track them down and thus hide even more deeply. Likewise, although the practitioner has distanced themselves from the ten sensual desires, they still fear that the thieves of desire will come to destroy their resolve for the Way. Having attained the second dhyāna, sensual desires are somewhat further removed and can no longer defile them.
In the first dhyāna, when good and evil contend, one uses the good to eliminate the evil; thus evil recedes and the good advances.
In the second dhyāna, the mind of joy is stilled, so that one no longer relies on the abiding state of the good to eliminate that evil.
The two mental states of joy and goodness are both completely extinguished; the smoke of the ten unwholesome actions is cut off, and no external causes or conditions enter the mind.

It is like a high mountain whose peak has a spring: there is no inflow from without, nor does it rain down from dragons; rather, the water emerges spontaneously from within. The water is pure and the spring is full. Goodness emerges from within the mind, and evil no longer enters through the ears, eyes, nose, or mouth. Controlling the mind in this way, one then proceeds toward the third dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, the guarding of the mind is firm and steadfast; neither good nor evil enters it. The mind is as stable as Mount Sumeru, and no unwholesome states emerge.
External matters, whether good or evil, are extinguished and do not enter; the mind is like the root and stem of a lotus in water, with the flower closed and yet unopened, covered by the water.
The practice of the third dhyāna is as pure as a flower; having departed from all evils, both body and mind are at peace.
Controlling the mind in this manner, one then proceeds toward the fourth dhyāna.

Abandoning both good and evil, the mind neither thinks of good nor retains evil; the heart is bright and pure like a lapis lazuli bead. It is also like a man or woman who has bathed themselves clean, anointed their bodies with fine incense, and wears new inner and outer garments—fresh, superior robes, pure and fragrant both inside and out. When the Bodhisattva’s mind is upright, they attain that fourth dhyāna.
The multitude of evil influences and various defilements cannot obscure his mind; it is like a clean silk cloth that takes on whatever color it is dyed with.
It is also like a potter molding clay into vessels: as long as the mud is free of sand and gravel, it can be fashioned into any kind of vessel.
Furthermore, it is like a smith who has refined gold until it is pure; then, with hundreds of wonders and thousands of ingenuities, he can act according to his heart's desire.

When a Bodhisattva’s mind is pure and attains those four dhyānas, they may proceed according to their will: they may leap lightly into flight, walk upon water, divide their bodies and disperse their forms, manifest ten thousand transformations, pass through obstacles without hindrance, and exercise mastery over both existence and non-existence.

He grasps the sun and moon, moves heaven and earth, and possesses penetrating vision and hearing such that there is nothing he does not hear or see. With a pure mind and luminous contemplation, he attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). There is nothing among the changes undergone by sentient beings since the beginning of heaven and earth that he does not know: the thoughts currently dwelling in the minds of beings throughout the ten directions; events yet to sprout; and the souls of sentient beings as they become gods or humans, enter the realms of the Mount Tai (Pretas), hungry ghosts, or animals, receive retribution for their sins when their merit is exhausted, or receive blessings when their calamity ends—there is no distance too great for him to know.

Now, having attained the four dhyānas, if one desires to attain the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, or the supreme illumination of a Pratyekabuddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, it shall be obtained immediately upon seeking it.

Just as all things arise from the earth, so too everything from the wisdom of the five supernormal powers up to that of the World-Honored One is accomplished through the four dhyānas; it is like the actions of sentient beings, which cannot be established without the earth.
The World-Honored One further said:

"When sentient beings dwell in the world, even if they possess the clever and subtle wisdom of celestial emperors, immortals, and sages, if they do not behold this sutra and fail to attain the concentration of the four abandonments, they remain ignorant and deluded."
"Once one possesses wisdom and further maintains single-mindedness, one is close to transcending the world.
This is the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Dhyāna (Dhyanapāramitā); such is single-mindedness. 75.

[The Bhikṣu Attains Dhyāna] (75) "In the past, a bhikṣu, having finished his meal and rinsed his mouth, entered a deep mountain among graves and sat beneath a tree. With palms joined and head bowed, he focused his mind and extinguished all discursive thoughts."
Within his inner mind, he eliminated the five hindrances; once the five hindrances were extinguished, his mind became radiant, as darkness receded and clarity remained.

He looked with compassion upon gods, humans, and all classes of beings—those that fly, crawl, and wriggle—pitying their foolish delusions and how they harbor these five hindrances, which obstruct and cut off the heart of luminous goodness.

When the five hindrances are eliminated, all wholesome qualities become strong; it is like a poor man who takes out a loan to manage his livelihood, gains a profit, and returns that debt to the creditor, using the remaining wealth to improve his dwelling. As his daily income increases, his heart is filled with joy.

Furthermore, it is like a slave being released to become a free citizen, or one suffering from illness recovering their health; it is like the nine clans flourishing daily, or one facing heavy punishment in prison being released by amnesty.
It is also like finding precious treasures after crossing the sea and traversing perilous paths, returning home to see one's kin—the joy of which is immeasurable.

The mind harboring the five hindrances is like these five sufferings; when a bhikṣu perceives the truths and abandons the five hindrances, he is like that ordinary person who escapes the aforementioned five afflictions. As the hindrances recede and clarity advances, all evils are extinguished; with the resolve for the Path becoming powerful, he immediately attains the first dhyāna.
From the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna, there are generally three practices:
first, diligent effort; second, frequent mindfulness; and third, contemplation.
Through these three matters, one attains the fourth dhyāna: from the first dhyāna to the second, from the second to the third, and from the third to the fourth.
The fourth dhyāna surpasses the third dhyāna; the third dhyāna surpasses the second dhyāna; and the second surpasses the first.
In the first dhyāna, the ten unwholesome actions recede and the five wholesome actions advance.
What are the ten unwholesome actions?

Delighting in forms with the eye, sounds with the ear, fragrances with the nose, flavors with the tongue, and pleasant sensations with the body, together with the aforementioned five hindrances—these are called the ten unwholesome acts.
What are the five wholesome acts?
The first is calculation (*vitarka*), the second is reflection (*vicāra*), the third is affection (*prīti*), the fourth is joy (*sukha*), and the fifth is one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
These five wholesome factors reside within.

In the second dhyāna, there is no calculation and no reflection; the mind is restrained for internal contemplation, and wholesome conduct resides within. No longer do [mental states] enter or exit through the ears, eyes, nose, or mouth; the two types of conduct, good and evil, no longer interfere with one another, and the mind abides within in a state of pure joy alone.
In the practice of the third dhyāna, joy is eliminated; the mind remains pure, serene, and tranquil. The World-Honored One, the Buddha, said:
"Those who are able to extinguish desire and purify their minds will find their bodies perpetually at peace."
In the fourth dhyāna, the mind of joy departs and one attains tranquil concentration.

In the first dhyāna, the ear is disturbed by sound; in the second dhyāna, the mind is disturbed by thought; in the third dhyāna, the mind is disturbed by rapture; in the fourth dhyāna, the mind is disturbed by breathing.

In the first dhyāna, the sounds of the ears cease; progressing to the second dhyāna, discursive thought ceases; progressing to the third dhyāna, joy ceases; progressing to the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation cease, and one attains the concentration of emptiness.
"The Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Dhyāna consists of single-mindedness in this manner.
(76) [The Bodhisattva Attains Dhyāna] (76): "By how many factors does a Bodhisattva who is resolved upon the Path enable internal purity, one-pointedness of mind, and the attainment of dhyāna?"
Or, seeing an elder with white hair, fallen teeth, and an altered physical form, one perceives this and attains awakening, thinking:
"This will certainly happen to me later.
With single-minded focus, one attains *dhyāna*.
Or, seeing a patient whose body and mind were tormented by pain as if being flogged with a staff,
he realized with regretful awakening:
"This will surely be my fate later."

With a single-minded heart, he attained dhyāna. He beheld sentient beings whose lifespans had come to an end, their breath stilled and their warmth departed; their spirits had transmigrated and their bodies grown cold. Their kin abandoned them, casting them far away into the wilderness. Within ten days, they became bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, or were devoured by foxes, dogs, and various birds. Worms grew upon their flesh and muscles, which in turn devoured their own bodies. Pus, blood, and foul secretions flowed in torrents across the ground. The skeletal remains fell apart, with each joint separated from its place: the feet, ankles, shins, and thighs; the buttocks, spine, ribs, and arms; the head, teeth, and skull—each part separated from the others.
The practitioner thought to himself:
"All who are born must die; human beings and things are like illusions. Meeting implies separation, for when the spirit departs, the body disperses.
How could I remain here alone and not be like them?"
Beholding this, he was moved with deep sorrow and attained meditative concentration with single-minded focus.
At other times, he saw the bodies of those who had died long ago, their bones decayed and reduced to dust, indistinguishable from the earth and soil.
He reflected deeply within himself, saying:
"I am of such a nature," he thought, and with single-minded focus attained dhyāna.

Some, upon hearing of the poisonous torments of boiling water and fire in Mount Tai, the cruel and piercing pains thereof, the exhaustion of hungry ghosts suffering from years of famine, or the agony of animals being slaughtered, flayed, and mangled—retaining these images with startled awe—attained dhyāna with single-minded focus. Others saw those who were impoverished, frozen, or starving to death, or saw those who had committed transgressions being executed by the king’s law.
The practitioner thought to himself:
"This man encountered such calamity because he lacked the will for the Way; if I do not practice with diligence, I shall surely meet the same fate as him.
With a single-minded focus, he attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Reflecting deeply in internal contemplation, he realized that below he was oppressed by excrement and urine, while above he was tormented by cold and heat; perceiving the body as loathsome, he attained dhyāna with a single-minded focus.

Or one may see a year of calamity when the five grains do not flourish; the people, impoverished, rise in rebellion and engage in mutual combat, with corpses strewn everywhere. Seeing this, one feels sorrowful and thinks:
"If I do not practice the Way, I shall surely return to such a state."
"By unifying his mind, he attained dhyāna.

He beheld that prosperity inevitably declines and wealth is difficult to preserve; that youth gives way to old age and illness, and life is as fleeting as a flash of lightning. Recalling this, he was struck with awe, and by unifying his mind, he attained dhyāna."
The majesty of the Buddha’s physical marks is peerless; all arise from purity to become the refuge of the multitude. To maintain this with joy and unify the mind leads to dhyāna.
To contemplate the profound meaning of the sūtras and the lofty conduct of śramaṇas, and to unify the mind, leads to dhyāna.
Only by practicing good deeds with the body and accumulating merit over time can one unify the mind and attain dhyāna.

Only the ignorant pursue that which contradicts the Buddha’s luminous Dharma; they labor in vain and only increase their transgressions. The various devas dwelling in the world observe the precepts and maintain the fasts, thereby attaining rebirth in heaven for themselves, where their glory and longevity are immeasurable, having unified their minds to attain dhyāna.

Having received the profound sutras of the Buddha, he reflected upon them repeatedly; as he instructed and guided the multitude, his heart was filled with joy, and by unifying his mind, he attained dhyāna.

Contemplating that sentient beings are constantly formed and then destroyed, and that their destruction brings nothing but suffering, he was moved to deep sorrow; by unifying his mind, he attained dhyāna.

The nature of sentient beings cannot preserve itself; facing the transformations at the beginning of existence, the practitioner of the Way fears for himself. When life comes to its end, it arrives suddenly; one may fall into the evil realms. Viewing worldly glory and pleasure as true or false like a dream, he sets his will on profound awakening, unifies his mind, and attains dhyāna.

All food that enters the mouth is drenched with mucus and saliva; though it appears attractive on the outside, it is foul-smelling within and transforms into excrement and urine. To contemplate this as loathsome and to unify the mind therein leads to *dhyāna*.

While the child is in the mother’s womb, it is initially like thick congealed gruel; as it gradually grows larger, after thirty-eight weeks, its body is fully formed. At the time of birth, the perils are many and safety is rare.

Once born, all manner of illnesses advance against one; whether they be one, ten, fifty, or even reach a hundred, all must age and die, and none can escape this affliction. One is no different; by unifying the mind, one attains dhyāna.

That which exists perishes immediately; when sought, it leaves no trace. The three realms are all empty; let your resolve be free from craving and attachment. Pitying sentient beings who do not behold the Buddha’s scriptures—obstructed by perverse desires and ignorant that all things are impermanent—I vow to rescue and deliver them, unifying my mind to attain meditative concentration.

"His resolve was firm and his conduct sublime; he harbored the four immeasurable minds to compassionately nurture all sentient beings, just as a loving mother pities and protects her infant. While the child plays joyfully with his peers, the mother, out of her compassionate heart, goes forth seeking; she sees that the child has been soiled by mud and dust, crying out from hunger and thirst."

Beholding her child in such a state, she wept with grief and took him home; she bathed him, provided him with food and clothing, and as his body became healthy and his mind joyful, the compassionate mother rejoiced. She cherished and protected him with such affection that she could not bear to let him go, remaining by his side just as before.

The path-maker’s compassion and protection of sentient beings surpass even that of a loving mother; he teaches all people throughout the world—including those that fly, crawl, and wriggle—to revere the Buddha, behold the sutras, and draw near to the assembly of śramaṇas. They should adopt and uphold the Buddha’s precepts, cherishing them in their practice, and remain far removed from the three evil realms. With minds focused on the good, speech directed toward the good, and deeds performed with goodness, they shall suppress the aforementioned three evils and forever promote the three virtues, ensuring that they never again fall into the wretched and perilous states of the Mount Tai (Yama) hell, the hells, the hungry ghosts, or the animals.

I established for him a hall of boundless blessings, yet I soon followed this by offering admonitions, fearing that while dwelling in such fortune he might become arrogant and dissolute, allowing his evil mind to run wild and return to the three miserable realms; thus, I used the perils of honor and emolument as a warning against the transformations of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
He exhorted them to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), with an intention like that of a compassionate mother who protects her children.
"Contemplate sixteen matters and unify your mind to attain dhyāna.
What are these sixteen?"

One knows for oneself whether the breath is long or short; one knows for oneself when the breath moves the body; one knows for oneself whether the breath is subtle or manifest; one knows for oneself whether the breath is pleasant or unpleasant; one knows for oneself whether the breath is still or running; one knows for oneself whether the breath is joyful or sorrowful. One knows for oneself through the breath that all things are impermanent; one knows for oneself through the breath that past things cannot be recovered; one knows for oneself through the breath that one has abandoned internal thoughts and cast aside all deliberation; one knows for oneself through the breath whether one is relinquishing the life of the body or not relinquishing it.

The practitioner reflects deeply: if this exists, then that is obtained; if this does not exist, that is not obtained. Indeed, birth is inevitably accompanied by the affliction of old age and death; if the soul-spirit is not extinguished, one will again receive a body.
Where there is no birth, there is no aging; where there is no aging, there is no death. By contemplating this as one, the mind attains dhyāna.

When a practitioner of the Way observes the cycle of birth and death in the world with the eye of wisdom, they do so solely through the twelve links of dependent origination. By contemplating this as one, the mind attains dhyāna.
“A practitioner of the Way observes his own physical form through five matters:

first, he observes that the features of his face frequently change; second, that suffering and pleasure frequently shift; third, that his will and intentions frequently turn; fourth, that his physical form frequently alters; and fifth, that his virtues and vices frequently change.”
These are called the five matters.
Their enumeration undergoes change, just as flowing water follows one after another; by contemplating this, one unifies the mind and attains dhyāna.
How should a practitioner of the Way contemplate dhyāna?

One observes a dead person from head to foot, contemplating and scrutinizing them with focused attention; whether walking, sitting, lying down, rising, eating, drinking, or engaged in any of the ten thousand activities, one should constantly maintain this mindful focus to solidify one’s resolve, thereby attaining mastery over meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) regarding whatever is contemplated.

It is like a person cooking several pecks of rice who wishes to know whether it is cooked or not; he simply takes a single grain of rice, crushes it between his fingers, and examines it. If that one grain is cooked, it is clear that the rest are all cooked.

When one's aspiration for the Way is such as this, the mind’s wandering is like the flow of water; the practitioner of the Way focuses his thoughts on a single matter, so that the mind is stilled and the will is pure, responding to the true Way in accordance with its ritual form, whereby nirvana may be attained.
"Is it possible to attain the first dhyāna and become an Arhat?
He replied: 'Among them, some can attain it and some cannot. By what practice can one attain it? "
What practice fails to attain [the goal]?
Within a single dhyāna, if there is mindfulness accompanied by craving, the Way will not be accomplished.

Heaven and earth are impermanent; even empty space is difficult to preserve. Exhaust all internal defilements and be free from thoughts of greedy attachment. When one’s resolve is pure in this manner, the state of an Arhat can be attained.
From the second or third up to the fourth dhyāna, one should maintain the mind as in the first dhyāna.

If one’s resolve is fixed on the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the corresponding fruit, at the end of life one may proceed upward to the seven heavens of the first dhyāna to receive a lifespan of one kalpa;
if one dies while in the second dhyāna, one proceeds upward to the eleven heavens of the second dhyāna to receive a lifespan of two kalpas.
At the end of the third dhyāna, one is reborn in the upper fifteen heavens with a lifespan of eight kalpas;
at the end of the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn in the upper nineteen heavens with a lifespan of sixteen kalpas.

The practitioner observes for himself that the impurities within his own body are entirely unclean: hair, skin, skull, and flesh; eyes, blinking, mucus, and saliva; sinews, veins, muscle, and marrow; liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach; heart, gallbladder, spleen, and kidneys; feces, urine, pus, and blood—only through the combination of these various filthinesses does one become a human being.
It is like a sack filled with the five grains; one with eyes may empty the sack and examine it, seeing that each variety is distinct.

A person of clarity contemplates their body in this way: the four great elements each have their own names, yet together they constitute no person. By observing through non-desire, they perceive original emptiness and unify the mind to attain dhyāna.
“The practitioner deeply contemplates and distinguishes the four great elements of the body—earth, water, fire, and wind.
Hair, body hair, bones, teeth, skin, flesh, and the five viscera constitute the element of earth.”
Tears, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, sweat, fat, marrow, brain, and urine—these are water.
That which generates internal warmth and governs digestion is fire.
The panting of the breath is, in itself, wind.
It is like a butcher who slaughters an animal and carves it apart, clearly understanding its every detail as he divides it into four parts.

When a practitioner observes internally and discriminates the four great elements—this earth, that water, and likewise fire and wind—he realizes they are entirely devoid of a person. By contemplating this with a tranquil mind and unifying his thoughts, he attains dhyāna.

The practitioner of the Way naturally perceives the length and brevity of his breaths, distinguishing their slowness or speed, and their coarseness or subtlety; just as a person carving wood knows the depth of the cut, he contemplates the breath in this manner, unifies his mind, and attains dhyāna.
"Such is the single-mindedness of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of dhyāna. 77.
[The Prince Attains Dhyāna] (77): When the Prince went out on an excursion, the King issued a decree throughout the kingdom that no impurities should be allowed upon the royal road.
As the Prince was leaving the city, Śakra, the Lord of the Second Heaven, transformed himself into an old man and stood before his chariot, with white hair, a hunched back,
leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps. The Prince asked, "What is this man?"
The messenger replied,
"He is an old man!
[The King asked,] "What is meant by 'old'?"
He replied, "The four great elements have matured; there is little life remaining.
The Prince said:
"Shall I too grow old in the future?
He replied, "Since antiquity there have been those who grew old; no sage has ever escaped this."
The Prince said,
"I thought that nobility and honor were different from those of the common folk, yet since neither can escape [suffering], what benefit does such honor bring to oneself?
He returned to the palace and kept this in mind, attaining meditative concentration with single-minded focus.
The king asked his attendant,
"Is the prince pleased with his excursion and the sight of the kingdom?
He replied:
“Observing the old man on the road and realizing that life is impermanent, his heart felt no joy.

Fearing that the Prince would leave the kingdom, the King increased the number of musicians and deluded him with worldly splendor and confused him with manifold sounds, wishing to destroy his resolve for the Way so that he would remain in the honored position.
Later, as he went out on another excursion, the King issued a strict command, saying:
"Let no one who is weak or aged remain by the roadside.

The former śramaṇa again transformed himself into a sick man, his body exhausted and his breath faint, his flesh wasted away until he was but skin and bone, with foul secretions coating his body, leaning against the side of a gate.
He asked,
"Who is this person again?
He replied:
"He is ill. [The other] asked,
"What do you mean by 'ill'?"
“Because of irregularity in eating and drinking, and lack of constancy in sleeping and rising, one contracts this illness, sometimes recovering and sometimes dying.
He asked:
“I too eat and drink without moderation and am irregular in my sleep and rising; shall I also fall ill?”
He replied, "As long as there is a body, there is illness; none can escape this affliction.
The Prince said:
"I shall not escape this calamity; hereafter it will surely be the same for me.
Returning to the palace, he kept this thought in mind and entered meditative concentration with single-minded focus.
Later, upon emerging from meditation, Śakra Devendra again transformed himself into a dead man being carried on a litter with a funeral banner raised, while mournful wailing filled the roads.
He asked,
"Who is this person again?
He replied:
"A dead person.
"What is meant by death?
"The end of life and the departure of the spirit; the physical frame disperses, and one is forever separated from kin—a painful state, difficult to endure."
The Prince asked,
"Is it so for me as well?
They replied:
"Even the pure virtue of the supreme sage cannot escape such calamities.
He turned his carriage back to the palace and entered meditative concentration with single-minded focus.
Later, he went out again on a journey to the royal fields and lodgings, where he sat beneath a tree.
Seeing those who plow the fields, he observed the soil being turned over, where insects emerged—some wounded and some dead—and were pursued and eaten by birds.
His heart was filled with sorrow, and he sighed deeply, saying:
"Alas! Sentient beings are so restless and troubled; their suffering is difficult to endure."
Reflecting thus with deep sorrow, he entered meditative concentration with a single-minded focus.
At that time, as the sun rose high and shone upon the Prince’s body, the trees bent their branches down so as not to let the sun scorch him.

The king followed the direction it had taken and, from afar, beheld the spiritual presence of the unsurpassed, holy virtue; overcome by a mingling of sorrow and joy, he did not know how to cast himself down, but prostrated himself in worship, and the Prince likewise bowed his head to the ground.
When the father and son had finished their parting words, the King returned to the palace, and the Prince entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with single-minded focus.
Such was the Bodhisattva’s single-mindedness in the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). 78.
[The Prince Attains Meditative Concentration] (78): When the Prince was first born, the King ordered a master to examine his marks. The master said:
"If he remains in the kingdom, he will surely become a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin);
if he renounces the world to become a śramaṇa, he shall become a Teacher of Gods and Men.

The King constructed the Three Seasons Palace, with distinct palaces for each season—spring, summer, and winter. Each palace housed five hundred female musicians, neither fat nor thin, their height beyond reproach, their complexions as radiant and clear as fresh blossoms, all as beautiful as peach and plum flowers. Each possessed several arts, their graceful charms captivating the wise, so as to entertain the Prince.

In front of the hall, sweet fruits were planted in rows, their fragrant blossoms wafting with exquisite perfume; there was a pure bathing pool containing various flowers, where birds of diverse species sang in harmonious chorus.

The sound of the palace gates opening and closing could be heard for forty li; loyal ministers and guards patrolled tirelessly, while the birds of watch—cormorants, mandarin ducks, and ruddy sheldrakes—let out a continuous chorus of alarm.
At the age of seventeen, there was no scripture the Prince did not master; his teacher, in turn, bowed to receive instruction from him.
The King took a consort for him, whose name was Gopī; her beauty was so radiant that she rivaled celestial maidens, and her physical strength could instantly repel sixty massive elephants.

When he reached the age of nineteen, the Prince gathered all his courtesans—numbering fifteen hundred in total—and had them reside together in a single hall, where they indulged in the utmost musical performances.
He intended that once they were exhausted from sleep, they would leave him alone; however, Heaven caused all the musicians to fall asleep as if unconscious.

The Crown Prince pondered deeply as he gazed upon the musicians; they were like wooden puppets, all their joints hollow within like the nodes of bamboo. Their hands and feet dangled toward the ground, tears flowed from their eyes, and saliva fouled their cheeks. They lay prostrate over the drums with disheveled hair. The musicians all wore famous earrings and dangling *bu-yao* ornaments that shone with brilliance; they were adorned with pearls, necklaces, jade rings, and various exquisite trinkets. Their fine garments, embroidered silks, and upper robes were strewn about, while lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, horns, and pipes lay scattered across the floor.
The birds on guard and the sentries fell instantly into a deep sleep, unconscious.

With his unobstructed eyes, the Prince surveyed the bodies of all those around him, and then looked back at his own consort. He saw her hair, skull, bones, teeth, nails, and fingers; her skin, flesh, pus, blood, marrow, and brain; her tendons, veins, heart, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, intestines, stomach, and the cavities of her eyes; her excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva. Looking inward, she was like a withered bone; looking outward, she was like a bag of flesh—not a single part was worthy of esteem.

In a place of impurity and stench, the mere sight and memory of it causes one to feel nausea; yet it is like a mask made of indigo cloth, adorned with colorful patterns and perfumed on its surface, while its interior is filled with excrement, urine, pus, and blood. The fool believes in its outward appearance, but the wise person beholds its inner reality and would close their eyes even from ten thousand li away.
The Crown Prince beheld them as being like illusions, difficult to preserve for long; dwelling in the world is merely a temporary loan that must inevitably be returned to its owner.
Seeing those who lay prostrate and sprawled about like corpses, he became even more disillusioned and focused his mind single-mindedly on dhyāna.

Emerging from his meditative awakening, he looked up at the shimmering stars; the night was already half-past, and the various devas were so densely packed that they filled the air. With palms joined in reverence, they offered incense, flowers, and manifold music, their heads raised in boundless devotion. Seeing the devas prostrating themselves, the Prince immediately spoke this sutra:

"Lust and dissipation are the most evil; they cause one to become mad and intoxicated. One slanders the correct and praises the perverse, mistaking darkness for light. For this reason, the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats do not praise them as good; one should swiftly distance oneself from them."
Reflecting thus again and again, he called to Chandaka, saying,
"Quickly saddle Kanthaka.
He then reflected once more within himself:
“The opening and closing of the city gates can be heard for forty *li*; what do you say to this?
The devas all replied in unison:
“We respectfully accept.”
“World-Honored One!
We shall guard the gates so that they make no sound.

The palace attendants were unaware; the horse’s hooves were silent, not a whisper could be heard. As the Prince mounted his horse, ten billion Śakras, four hundred billion Caturmahārājas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits escorted and led him, leveling and smoothing the roads.
The celestial music sang in verse:

"How sublime and lofty! We have encountered such a birth; we behold the numinous radiance that dispels the dust and toil of the mind. May it never decline throughout eternity! Alas, how painful it is that those in the eight difficulties are far removed from the Honored One—how pitiable!"
He spoke again, saying:
"How fortunate it is that we have met by chance!
Just as the horse was beginning to leave the gate, the gate made a sound.
The horse choked with emotion and neighed piteously, its tears streaming down its cheeks.
The gods concealed the King so that none in the kingdom would know.
The reason for this was their desire to enable the Prince to attain the Way of the Buddha as soon as possible.

The Crown Prince abandoned the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King and his seven treasures; enduring all manner of suffering to deliver sentient beings, the Bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is such that his single-mindedness is thus.

79. [The Crown Prince Attains Meditation] (79): Before the Crown Prince had attained the Way, he took stalks of grass from the ground and sat upright beneath a tree with palms joined, casting off all defiled thoughts, purifying his mind, and unifying his will.
He thought to himself:
"From this day forward, even if my flesh and sinews wither and rot, I shall not rise from this spot until I have attained Buddhahood.

The Bodhisattva immediately attained the first dhyāna, then the second, third, and fourth; in a single night, he attained the *ṛddhi-vidyā* (knowledge of supernormal powers) and came to know his parents, brothers, wives, and nine generations of kin throughout countless kalpas.

Within two nights, he attained the two *ṛddhis* (supernatural powers) and came to know for himself the poverty, wealth, nobility, meanness, longevity, shortness of life, fairness, and darkness [of complexion] throughout incalculable kalpas; he knew all that was thought and unthought within the minds of sentient beings, such that there was nothing he did not know.
Within three nights, he attained the three *siddhis*, and the three poisons were completely extinguished.
As the night was turning toward dawn, he had perfected the Way of the Buddha.
He reflected deeply within himself, saying:
"I have now attained Buddhahood; it is most profound, most profound, difficult to know, and difficult to comprehend—the subtlest of the subtle, the most wondrous of the wondrous.
Now that I have perfected the Way of the Buddha, there is nothing I do not know."
He rose and went to the place where the dragon lived; the dragon’s name was Muḷāla. At the edge of the water where Muḷāla dwelt, there was a tree, and the Buddha sat beneath it and said:
"In the past, Dīpaṃkara Buddha granted me the prediction of my exaltation, saying that I would become Śākyamuni Buddha. Just as I have heard it to be true, I have now attained Buddhahood."

Since incalculable kalpas past, through the vows accumulated by practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, I have now finally attained this supreme honor; as the destination of my virtuous merit, my labors shall not go to waste.
As soon as the Buddha thought of this, he entered the perfection of dhyāna.
Standing by the water’s edge, his radiance shone through to the place where the dragon dwelt.
When the dragon beheld the light and shadow, the scales upon its body all stood on end.
The Dragon once beheld three Buddhas:
Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha; when these three Buddhas attained the Way, they all sat upon this very seat.
The light clearly illuminated the dragon’s abode, and when the dragon beheld the radiance, he thought to himself:
"This light is identical in brilliance to that of the three previous Buddhas; could it be that another Buddha has appeared in the world?"

The dragon was greatly delighted; emerging from the water, he looked left and right and beheld the Buddha sitting beneath the tree, his body endowed with the thirty-two marks and a purple-golden hue. His radiance was brilliant, surpassing the moon and exceeding the sun, and his sublime features were as perfectly beautiful as a tree in full bloom.

The dragon approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head touching the ground, and circumambulated the Buddha seven times. Remaining forty *li* away from the Buddha, he covered the Buddha with his seven heads.

The dragon joyfully produced wind and rain for seven days and seven nights; yet the Buddha sat upright, unmoving, unshaking, neither breathing nor resting, having attained Buddhahood without eating for seven days, his mind joyful and entirely free of conceptual thought.

The dragon was greatly delighted; for seven days he did not eat, yet he had no thought of hunger or thirst. When the seven days were over, the wind and rain ceased, and the Buddha awoke from his meditation.
The dragon transformed himself into a young brahmin wearing fresh garments; kneeling long with palms joined, he bowed his head to the ground and asked:

"Are you free from cold and heat, and free from hunger and thirst? With merit and blessings gathered together, and no poisonous influences afflicting you, you dwell in the world as a Buddha, uniquely honored throughout the three realms—is this not a source of joy?"

The Buddha told the dragon: “The sutras of the Buddhas of the past state that it is a joy for sentient beings to leave the three evil realms and obtain human birth; it is a joy to dwell in seclusion within the world and maintain one’s resolve in the Way. It is a joy to have now attained all that was previously heard; it is a joy to dwell in the world with compassion, not harming any living being. It is a joy for the heavy poisons of the heavenly Māras to all subside; it is a joy to be dispassionate and desireless, not longing for glory. Having attained the Way in the world, one becomes a Teacher of Gods and Humans, with a mind fixed in the concentrations of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.”

"When one who possessed a body due to various desires returns the spirit to its original non-being, abiding eternally in tranquility and forever severing ties with suffering— this is the unsurpassed joy.
The Dragon bowed his head and said,
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma."
The Buddha told the dragon, "In the future there will be many sages;
their vows shall accord with the proper rites as they seek to eliminate the suffering of the hungry ghosts (preta), and you should likewise take refuge in them in advance.
The dragon said:
"So be it," they replied,
and returned to the community of *śrāvakas*.
Among the animals, those who first took refuge in the Buddha were converted by him, with this dragon at their head.
The Bodhisattva’s perfection of dhyāna is such that his single-mindedness is thus. 80.

[The Buddha’s Attainment of Dhyāna] (80): The Buddha traveled along a narrow path where there was a tree; he sat beneath it together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, entering meditative concentration with a single mind.
As five hundred chariots passed by, the Buddha was overcome with intense thirst and said to Ānanda:
"Go fetch some water; I wish to drink it.
He replied:
"Five hundred chariots have just passed by, making the water turbid and unfit for drinking.
He further commanded him again:
"My thirst is extreme; go quickly and fetch some water."
This was repeated up to three times.
Ānanda said, "There is a stream named Kukudvāra; it is clear, pure, and beautiful, suitable for bathing and drinking."
Before the Buddha had finished speaking these words to Ānanda, there was a man named Pāveyya who served as a disciple to Sañjaya; Sañjaya’s name was Rājagiriya.

Kauśika beheld the Buddha’s spiritual radiance; his body was the color of purple-gold, and his marks and signs were most extraordinary, such as had rarely been seen among the sages of antiquity. His heart overflowed with joy, and with hands folded in reverence, he stepped forward directly, prostrated himself, and said:
"Just now, five hundred chariots passed by this way; did the World-Honored One hear or see them?"
He replied,
“I have neither heard nor seen it.
Pao-chieh said:
"Is the World-Honored One lying down?
He replied,
"I am sitting in meditation, having attained the concentration of one-pointed mind."
Pao-chieh sighed and said:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—how profound and deep is his meditative concentration! Even to this extent?

Previously, your carriage shook the kingdom; you personally covered yourself in dust, yet your resolve for the Way remained unyielding, neither hearing nor seeing anything. Though heaven and earth might be moved, such a will is difficult to overturn."
"When my teacher was alive, he also attained meditative concentration beneath a tree by the side of a road. At that time, five hundred chariots passed before him, and someone asked him:
'Did you hear or see anything?'"
He replied,
"I have neither heard it nor seen it.
The other man said:
"Did you fall asleep at the hour of the rat?
He replied, "I unified my mind to attain pure and tranquil concentration; therefore, I did not hear it."
The man said, "The resolve for the path of an Arhat is so profound that it is just like this:
as the carriage passed before me, my body was covered in dust, yet I was not aware of it."
The man, beholding that his resolve was profound and mysterious, served him as a teacher for the rest of the year.
Pāṭaliputra said:

"The Buddha’s tranquil concentration and his non-reliant resolve are like those of my former teacher. From this day forward until the end of my life, I shall uphold the Five Precepts of the Buddha and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), never daring to commit any evil."
The Buddha asked Pāveyyaka,
"How does the sound of five hundred chariots compare to the roar of thunder?
He replied:
“The sound of a thousand chariots is not even comparable to a small peal of thunder during rain, let alone the roar of a wrathful lightning bolt.
The World-Honored One said:

“In the past, when I was staying beneath a thatched hut in the district of Āṭaṇḍā, I sat contemplating the root of birth and death. At that time, a violent storm with wind, rain, hail, and lightning struck, killing four bulls and two brothers who were plowing.”
The common people of that district were very numerous in their numbers as they watched.
At that time, I went out for a walk, and a certain man came to where I was.
I asked him, "What is this great crowd watching?"
The man related the matter exactly as it had occurred.
The other person asked,
"Where did the Buddha go at that time?"
He replied,
"I am alone beneath the eaves.
The man said:
"Is the Buddha lying down now?
He replied, "No."
The man said:
"How could there be one who has awakened and yet does not hear?

My resolve for the Way is most profound; from this day forward, I wish to serve the World-Honored One as a teacher, uphold the five pure precepts as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), and maintain the truth throughout my life."
Upon hearing this, Pāveyyaka’s mind was opened and his fetters were untied; his joy was immeasurable. Turning to his attendants, he commanded them, saying:
"In my inner treasury there are a thousand garments woven with gold thread. Select the finest ones and bring them here; I wish to offer them to the Buddha."
The attendant, having received these instructions, returned home to fetch it. The Cīna-bāṣpa (胞罽) personally draped the garment over the Buddha’s body, then withdrew, prostrated himself, and said:

"From this day forth, I pray that the World-Honored One will deign to extend his august presence to the abodes of the faithful lay devotees in my village, and likewise grace my own home with a visit. There, every member of my clan, great and small, shall personally provide offerings to the Buddha."

To serve and nourish the heavenly dragons, ghosts, spirits, and all classes of creatures—whether flying, crawling, or wriggling—with a heart of supreme reverence throughout one's entire lifespan as long as heaven and earth lasts, is not equal to feeding a single śramaṇa for a single day; how much less so would it be for the Unsurpassed, Truly Real Buddha?
"I pray that you will bestow upon me your vast compassion and grant me infinite merit.
The World-Honored One said,
"Excellent!"
Such was the aspiration of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of dhyāna. 81.
[The Jātaka of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita] (81): The World-Honored One himself related that when he was a bodhisattva, his name was Sadāprarudita.
The Bodhisattva Constant Sorrow always walked with tears streaming down his face.

At that time, there was no Buddha in the world and the scriptures had all perished; he did not behold the assembly of śramaṇas, sages, and noble ones, yet he constantly longed to see the Buddha and hear the sublime purport of the sutras.
The age was defiled and turbid; people turned their backs on the right path and followed the deviant, seeking profit through artifice and falsehood like moths delighting in fire.

While the Four Immeasurables and the Six Perfections are the eternal abode of peace, the world abandoned these teachings of the Buddha and pursued those dangerous calamities, thereby destroying themselves. Thus, overcome by grief and desolation, he walked along in mournful lamentation.
In the past, there was a Buddha named King of the Stainless Dharma-Reflection Tathāgata. He entered parinirvāṇa long ago, and his teachings have long since been exhausted.
The Bodhisattva Constant Compassion once saw that Buddha in a dream preaching the Dharma to him, saying:

"Be careful not to be arrogant. As for the conduct of a scholar, remove the defilement of mental attachment and affection; do not cling to the dust and toil of the six sense-faculties; do not leave behind even a hair’s breadth of any worldly love."
"Store this within your heart; the cessation of all discursive thoughts is what constitutes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

When the Bodhisattva heard this Dharma from the Buddha, he was like a starving man who has obtained sweet food; his joy was immeasurable, the defilements of his mind were removed, and he entered into pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*).

He immediately abandoned his home and left behind his wife and children, entering the deep mountains to dwell in seclusion. Sustaining himself with mountain fruits and gourds, he stood in the mountains, beating his breast with his hands and wailing piteously, saying:
"Alas for my life! What a grievance!"

Not having encountered the era of a Buddha nor heard the Buddha’s sutras, I pray that the World-Honored Ones of the Ten Directions—the Truly Realized Ones of the present, who see through and hear through all things, possessing complete knowledge and whose radiant influence reaches everywhere—even though they appear only as faint and indistinct visions—may you manifest your venerable spirits so that I may behold the Buddha and hear the ultimate path of the Great Way’s vast pattern.
As soon as his lamentation ended, a celestial deity descended and said:
"O Wise One, do not wail any longer; the Buddha possesses a Great Dharma called the Radiance of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā)."

All Buddhas of the past, those of the present, and those yet to come, have all achieved their realization through this. You must therefore seek it out, recite and study its text, contemplate and master its meaning, and practice it with devotion; in this way, you will surely attain the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Your body is the color of purple-gold, and the radiance from your neck is boundless.

Among the scriptures and paths of the ten directions, you are the enlightened sovereign; the most honored among all sages and the teacher of gods and humans—such majestic deportment is something that no other Buddha lacks.
The Bodhisattva Sadāśoka looked up and replied,
"From whom shall we hear this sublime Dharma?
By what means shall we go to which land?"
"What is the name of his clan? The celestial being replied: "From here, proceed due east.

Do not think of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not think of suffering or pleasure, good or evil, nor of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, body, mind, or self; nor of what was experienced by people in past lives or what will happen in future lives; do not think of earth, water, fire, wind, or space; nor of blue, yellow, white, black, or any other colors; nor of greed, lust, anger, hatred, delusion, jealousy, or envy; nor of men and women, the nine clans, left or right, front or back, high or low, slow or fast."
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, whether there is the Way of the Sūtras or no Way of the Sūtras, whether there are worthies and sages or no worthies and sages—it is all empty;
thus, set aside your thoughts and sever all vows. Let your grasping mind not contradict my teaching as you now behold this sublime scripture of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Bodhisattva Changbei (Constant Compassion) looked up and said, "I respectfully accept;
I shall keep this in mind from beginning to end.
The celestial being spoke again:
"Maintain this with diligence.
Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.
The Bodhisattva, having received these instructions, straightened his mind and purified his inner being, then traveled eastward to seek him out.
After several days, he ceased [his practice] and reflected deeply within himself, saying:

"My past merit has been meager; I was born at a time when I did not encounter a Buddha. In this world there are no śramaṇas, and both ruler and subjects are muddled and confused, with none who know the Buddha."
"The Perfection of Wisdom, the Honored Teacher who dispels darkness—how many *li* is he from here that I have not yet beheld him?
With such intense grief in his heart, he proceeded while wailing; the utmost sincerity of his devotion moved all the Buddhas.

A Buddha from the upper direction arrived, flying before him; his body was the color of purple-gold, his marks and signs were most sublime, his face was like the full moon, and his neck was radiant as the sun. Attended by the various devas, with jeweled canopies and flowered parasols, they played music and scattered flowers, joining their palms and bowing their heads.
The Buddha praised the bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Your agility is marvelous and rarely seen in the world."
When the Bodhisattva saw the Buddha, he was both filled with joy and sorrow; prostrating himself, he said:
"I pray that the Buddha will have pity on me, sever my bonds, untie my knots, open my blindness, and heal my illness by preaching the sutra for me."
The Buddha told him: "The three realms are all empty;
that which exists is entirely non-existent. All things are like illusions, arising and ceasing in a single moment, just like bubbles on water; such is the nature of observing the world."
Reflect upon this: I shall expound the sutra for you; focus your mind and listen attentively, and take care not to forget it.

From here, traveling eastward twenty thousand *li*, there is a land named Gandhāva, the city of all Bodhisattvas. Within that entire country, there are only those of superior capacity and no ordinary people. I wish to expound for them the virtues of the Bodhisattvas; though the kalpas have already come to an end, their virtues remain inexhaustible.

There is a Most Honored Bodhisattva of Supreme Virtue named Dharmodgata; among those holy ones, he is like the moon among the stars. He cherishes all the scriptures, his brilliance being limitless, as he expounds the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and repeatedly instructs others. Among the bodhisattvas there are those who receive the sūtra, those who recite it, those who copy it, and those who investigate its original source—go and see him, for he will surely become your teacher.
"I exhort you to seek the Buddha; hasten toward him, and he shall naturally expound for you the sublime majesty of the Inner and Outer Infinite Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Upon hearing the Buddha praise the name and virtue of that bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Constant Sorrow entered into the joy of the Dharma and attained the concentration of the present. All mental constructions were stilled, and he beheld all the Buddhas expounding the virtues of the Infinite Perfection of Wisdom for his sake. Praising his own merit of diligent progress in seeking the Buddha, they all exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"You have attained the very same resolve for Buddhahood that I possessed when I first set my mind upon it in the past.
All the Buddhas of the past, the future, and the present have sought it in precisely this manner."
"You shall surely attain Buddhahood and deliver all living beings.
When the Bodhisattva Changbei emerged from his samādhi, he looked around him left and right but no longer beheld the Buddhas. He was immediately overcome with grief and, shedding tears, said:
"From where did the spiritual radiance of the Buddhas come?"
"Now, where has he gone?
Thus was the Bodhisattva’s single-mindedness in the Perfection of Dhyāna.

82. [The Jātaka of the Brahmin Nārada] (82): "In the past, there were two Bodhisattvas whose resolve was pure and whose conduct was clean; they were inwardly tranquil and free from desire, appearing like celestial gold. Having left behind the crowds of the defiled and turbid, they dwelt in mountain marshes, carving out caves in the rock for their dwellings."

Dwelling in seclusion with a tranquil mind, he wore garments of *gāmbhārī* grass and sat upon mats of straw; eating fruits and drinking from springs, he was pure and non-active, his will as vast as empty space. Having fully mastered the four dhyānas, he attained the wisdom of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*):

first, the power of clairvoyance, by which he could see all things without exception; second, the power of clairaudience, by which he could hear all sounds without exception; third, the power of levitation, by which he could fly and pass through obstacles without hindrance; fourth, the power of telepathy, by which he could know the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings throughout the ten directions; and fifth, the power of recollecting past lives, by which he could know for himself all that had transpired throughout incalculable kalpas.
Brahmā, Śakra, seers, sages, and all the devas, nāgas, and ghosts—all bowed their heads in reverence.

Having dwelt in mountains and marshes for over sixty years, he took pity on sentient beings who wander through ignorance and darkness, failing to see that committing evil brings heavy calamity in the future; thus they were urged to restrain their emotions, renounce desire, and reverently serve the Triple Gem, so that when blessings arrive like an echo, they shall surely attain glory.
There were two brahmins:
the first was named Tikiḷa and the second was named Nala.

Tikiḷa rose at dawn to recite the scriptures; exhausted, he fell asleep and lay down. At that time, Nala was also reciting the scriptures and inadvertently stepped upon Tikiḷa’s head. Tikiḷa immediately rose and said:
"Whoever treads upon my head, when the sun rises at dawn tomorrow, shall have their own head split into seven pieces—is this not good?
Nalāi said, "I have merely trodden upon you by mistake; why such a heavy oath?"
Even common earthenware vessels of such inferior quality still collide with one another; how much more so for humans living together—how could they avoid error and loss throughout their entire lives?
Your words are ever truthful; when the sun rises tomorrow morning, my head shall surely be split into seven pieces.
"I shall restrain the sun so that it does not rise.
Thereupon, it did not emerge.

For five days, the entire kingdom was shrouded in darkness; people sought one another with torches, the officials neglected their duties, and both ruler and subjects were filled with confusion. They assembled the various ministers and invited Daoist masters.
The King asked,
"If the sun does not rise, where lies the fault?
Among the Daoist practitioners, one who possessed the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) replied:
"The mountain immortals have had a slight dispute between them; therefore, I have established this daily decree so that they do not emerge.
The King asked, "Is there a specific cause for their dispute?"
The Daoist related the matter from beginning to end to the king in detail.
The king said, "What can be done?"

He replied, "If Your Majesty leads the officials and the people, great and small alike, to hasten there and prostrate yourself in a gesture of reconciliation, he will surely respond with compassion and harmony.
The King then issued a decree according to the Daoist's instructions; they went to the mountain marshes and prostrated themselves, saying:
"When the state was prosperous and the people were at peace, it was due to the grace of the Two Honored Ones; yet now there is no harmony, and all within the realm have lost their place.
The blame lies with me, while the common people are without fault; I pray that you will grant them amnesty."
Narada said, "If Your Majesty diligently understands his intention, and he is convinced by it, I shall release the sun.
The King proclaimed Narada’s message at the place of Jivaka.
The king then said,
"Let him release the sun while his head is smeared with mud.
As soon as his head was smeared with mud, it split into seven pieces, leaving Nala without a body.

The king, his ministers, and the common people were all filled with joy. The two practitioners extensively expounded for the king the governance of a state, teaching that he should employ the four immeasurable and boundless acts of compassion, encourage the observance of the five precepts, and practice the ten virtuous deeds.
The king, along with his ministers and subjects, all received the precepts in unison.
Upon returning to his kingdom, the king issued an edict, saying:
"Regardless of rank, whether high or low, let every person carry the Sūtra of the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds, and let this serve as the basis for the administration of the state."

From that time forth, the King’s benevolence reached even the grasses and trees; loyal ministers were sincere, pure, and yielding; fathers followed the Way and mothers set the standard for propriety within the household, each upholding these virtues; they maintained the Dao with integrity and faithfulness, and every family had filial sons.
The World-Honored One said:

"The two bodhisattvas saw that the ruler of that land did not know the Triple Gem, and his ministers and subjects were muddled, obscuring themselves with false views, like those walking with their eyes closed in the darkness."
"Out of pity that his followers were dying without beholding the Buddha's sutras, he manifested this transformation, desiring that they might behold the light.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Narada was my own self."
"He who was named Jīva was Maitreya.
Such was the single-mindedness of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).
— *Ṣaḍpāramitā-samuccaya Sūtra*, Volume Seven.
The Compendium of the Six Perfections, Volume Eight, translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Senghui of Kangju during the Wu Dynasty.
Chapter Six: The Immeasurable Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā). This chapter contains nine sections.
83. [The Jātaka of Prince Śūra] (Eighty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas, all seated together.
The foremost disciple, Śāriputra, came forward, prostrated himself, knelt, and said:
"What meritorious deeds did Chandaka perform in his past lives?

While the Bodhisattva was at home, he was destined to become a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), yet [Chandaka] exhorted him to abandon his kingdom and enter the mountains to study the Way, leading him to personally attain Buddhahood, to rescue and deliver sentient beings, and to achieve such towering merit as even unto his final Nirvana."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal its origin for us.
The Buddha praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Śāriputra, your question is most excellent!
Candaka’s meritorious achievements over successive lifetimes are immeasurable; listen attentively, and I shall explain them.
They replied:
“Yes, indeed.
The Buddha said:
“In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I was in the kingdom of Nikhaba. Its king heard:”
"Some people ascend to heaven by practicing the Way, while others ascend to heaven by serving the shrines of the gods.
Since his childhood, the King has constantly aspired to ascend to heaven, yet he did not know the means by which it might be achieved.
In the kingdom there were more than forty thousand brahmins;
the king showed them [this matter] and said, "I wish to ascend to heaven;
by what means shall I do so? An elder replied:
"Excellent your question!
Do you intend, O King, to ascend to heaven with this very body,
or by means of the soul?"
The king said,
"Sitting like this, one desires to ascend to heaven.
He replied:
"One should perform a great sacrifice, and one may obtain it.
The King was immeasurably delighted and bestowed two thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* of gold and silver upon him.
Having obtained the treasure, the Brahmin returned home and enjoyed himself to his heart's content; when the treasure was exhausted, they deliberated, saying:

"Command the King to provide one hundred boys and girls whose radiance surpasses all others, and one hundred of each kind of elephant, horse, and miscellaneous beast. First feed us, and afterwards kill these humans and animals; using their flesh and bones as steps, we shall ascend to heaven."
He reported the matter to the King, who said, "Excellent!

The King immediately commanded his outer ministers to quickly prepare as instructed, and they all cast him into prison.
