Those who wept filled the roads, and the people of the land unanimously said, "For one to be a king and yet turn his back on the Buddha’s true transformation to promote demonic sorcery is to destroy the very foundation of the state."
The Brahmin spoke again:
"If we do not kill this living king and attain rebirth in heaven, it is certain that we shall have his corpse executed in the marketplace.
They deliberated further, saying:
"Among the Gandhamādana Mountains there is a celestial maiden of the Heavenly King named Simharūpā-devī; she is divine and difficult to obtain, so we urge Your Majesty to seek her.
If she is not brought back, all our affairs will come to an end, and we shall be free from reproach."
Again, he went before the king and said:
"Within Mount Gandhamādana there are celestial music goddesses; one must obtain their blood and mix it with that of humans and animals to create steps, only then can one ascend to heaven."
The King, filled with profound joy, said:
"Why did you not state this earlier? It is now already the fourth month, and only now do you speak of it?
He replied:
"I shall explain the beginning and end of my art.
The King ordered all the common people within the realm to assemble, providing abundant rewards, wine, and music in full. He proclaimed, "Who among you today can capture the divine maiden?"
Among the people, there was one who knew and said:
"In the seventh mountain there are two Daoist masters, one named Śarī and the other named Upan.
They know the dwelling place of this goddess."
The King said, "Call him here!
The messenger received the command and, after several days, brought the Daoist back.
The king was delighted and provided wine for seven days of celebration, saying:
"Since you have brought the divine maiden for me, I shall ascend to heaven and bestow my kingdom upon you."
He replied, "I shall certainly exert myself.

He withdrew and sat down; after seeking for more than two months, he passed through seven layers of mountains and reached Mount Gandhamādana, where he beheld a great lake, thirty li in length and breadth.

On level ground by the side of the pond was a great city of precious jewels, eighty *li* in length, breadth, and height. Precious trees surrounded the city, their brilliant radiance illuminating the kingdom; within the pond were lotus flowers with a thousand petals, each emitting five-colored light that shone upon one another, while birds of various species sang in harmonious chorus.

The city gates were sevenfold, with towers, pavilions, and palaces following one another in succession; banners and streamers blazed with brilliance, and the five musical tones resounded from bells and chimes. The Lord of Devas dwelt in the center, while performers entertained him.
After seven days, he emerged from his seclusion to sport; having bathed in the pond and finished his enjoyment, he was about to ascend back to heaven.
At the foot of a tree by the side of the pond stood a holy brahmacārin, stainless within and without, who had attained the clarity of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The two Daoists stepped forward, bowed their heads to the ground, and said:
"This music has been lost to the world; for whom will it now provide delight?
He replied:
"The daughters of Māra, numbering over a thousand, were sporting here; they have only now come to offer their devotion, so you must withdraw at once.
Having received these orders, they withdrew and deliberated, saying:
"This brahmin possesses such spiritual power through his virtue and Way; by what means shall we bring celestial maidens to him?"

"You must simply employ sorcery to bind the grass and recite incantations over it before casting it into the water; this will cause the Brahmin’s physical strength to fail and the celestial maiden’s spiritual power to vanish.
He then bound the grass, cast it into the water, and recited the sorcery incantations.
As Śakra departed, all the other devas followed suit; only this goddess was unable to fly away. The two rishis entered the water, untied her upper garment, and bound her with it.
The woman asked,
"What do you intend to do with me?
They answered as previously stated.
Using bamboo as a walking staff, he traveled for seven days until he reached the kingdom.
He went to the palace in trepidation; the king was delighted and brought forth a woman to provide him with food. The king comforted the practitioner, saying:
"I have attained ascension to heaven; this kingdom is now a gift to you."

"The king’s eldest son was named Nalasi; he became the king of a foreign kingdom. His crown prince was named Surā, who from the outset was compassionate and benevolent, harmonious and luminous, and possessed great brilliance. From the beginning, he perceived the future events of sentient beings in this world; there was nothing obscure that he did not see, and nothing subtle that he did not penetrate. The six perfections and sublime practices never left his mind, as he vowed to seek the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Master of the Dharma, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Sugata, and the One in the World, reaching the state of Original Non-being."
The King said, "I am about to ascend to heaven; let me call my grandson to bid him farewell.
When the grandson arrived, he prostrated himself, and after receiving the King's parting words, he withdrew and took his seat.
The King asked,
"Are your relatives and the people at peace?
He replied:
"May you receive this moisture and attain universal peace. Sūna said:
"The reason I did not seek a heavenly maiden as my consort was that the King would surely have killed me had I done so."
He reported this to the king based on what he had heard from the man.
The king said,
"I shall use his blood to create steps for ascending to heaven."
Sun immediately ceased eating and withdrew to his bed in displeasure.
Fearing he might pass away, the King gave him the Consort as a wife.
Those both inside and outside the palace were filled with joy, and all their distress came to an end.
After four months, the brahmin heard it said again:
"One should dig a pit and kill various animals to fill it, take the blood of a divine maiden to smear upon it, and choose an auspicious day to sacrifice to Heaven."
The king said,
"Excellent! and commanded the elders of the various states, the officials, and the common people:
"One should establish this sacrifice.
Upon hearing this, the Grandson was despondent and displeased; he challenged the Brahmin, saying:
"From which sacred scripture does the method for this sacrifice originate?"
He replied,
"One who performs this sacrifice should be destined for ascension to heaven.
The Imperial Grandson Nan said:

Now, killing is to harm the life-force of sentient beings; he who harms the life-force of sentient beings is the foremost of the rebellious and evil. His calamity is boundless: as his soul undergoes successive transformations, they harbor mutual resentment and malice. They injure and poison one another, generation after generation, without respite. Upon death, they enter Mount Tai, where they are burned, boiled, roasted, and sliced; having endured every form of torment, they may emerge as animals, dying only to be subjected to further slaughter.
If they later become humans, they will suffer the retribution of having their corpses mutilated—this is the consequence of such cruelty and killing.
"How could there be anyone who ascends to heaven by practicing cruelty?
The Brahmin replied, "Your years have only recently begun; what wisdom could you possibly possess to challenge us?"
The Imperial Grandson said:
"In my past lives, for five hundred successive births, I was born into the families of brahmins; I studied your sacred scriptures, for which purity and truth are paramount."
"Your clever deceptions— how could they possibly accord with the purport of the scriptures?
The Brahmin said,
"If you know my Way, why do you not set it forth?"
The Imperial Grandson explained in detail: “The Brahmins set a lofty standard; their sacred path is supremely pure.

Yet you all are filthy and turbid, cruel and gluttonous. You falsely slaughter many people and animals under the pretext of heterodox sacrifices; you drink wine and engage in lewdness; you deceive the sovereign and exhaust the common people, causing them to turn their backs on the Buddha, violate the Dharma, distance themselves from the worthy, and cease their veneration. You spend all your wealth to provide for ghosts while neglecting your own kin to suffer hunger and cold—is this not contrary to the sacred path and the noble conduct of a śramaṇa?”
The Brahmans were filled with shame and, bowing their heads, withdrew.
The Grandson then became the King for his grandfather and set forth these words of supreme, true, and most perfect enlightenment, spoken with utmost sincerity:

"Now, those who wish to ascend to heaven should take refuge in the Three Honored Ones, awaken to the four transiencies, completely sever stinginess and greed, cultivate a pure resolve, sacrifice themselves to save the multitude, and extend their benevolence to all sentient beings—this is the first [requirement]."

To have compassion for all living beings, to extend one's own forgiveness to others, to maintain a constant will of contentment and not take what is not given, to preserve chastity without dissipation, to be trustworthy and not deceitful, and to regard alcohol as a disorderly poison that withers the way of filial piety—by reverently practicing these ten virtues and guiding one’s kin toward the right path, this constitutes the second [set].

To endure the insults of sentient beings; to feel compassion for those who are insane or intoxicated; to meet malice with sorrow and rescue others without harming them; to instruct them by means of the Three Honored Ones so that they may understand and rejoice in their liberation; and to nurture them with loving-kindness and equal protection, such that one's grace matches that of the two polarities of heaven and earth—these are the three.
To possess a keen resolve and diligent progress, aspiring to ascend to the higher practices—this is the fourth.
To abandon depravity and eliminate defilement, with a will as tranquil as space—this is the fifth.
To study extensively without limit, seeking all-encompassing wisdom—this is the sixth.
One who cherishes such vast virtue will remain free from fault from beginning to end; thus, one may attain the status of Dharma King of the three realms—how could ascending to heaven be difficult?

If, however, one violates the compassionate teachings of the Buddha, exalts that which is cruel and violent, slaughters the lives of sentient beings, indulges in lustful pleasures and heterodox sacrifices, one will be abandoned by Heaven while alive and fall into the three miserable paths after death, where they shall be further mutilated and slain, suffering endless calamities.
"By means of this fundamental evil, I hope to ascend to heaven, just as one who defies the king's command hopes to attain a high position.
The King said, "Excellent!"
"It is true! he exclaimed.
He opened the prisons and issued a general amnesty, banished all malevolent spirits, and immediately mobilized the national treasures to entrust to Sun Xingde.
The Imperial Grandson distributed these treasures among the destitute, and for seven days, there was no lack or insufficiency.
After performing acts of charity, he exhorted the people to observe the precepts; the entire realm was moved by his transformative influence, and there were none who did not follow and uphold them.
Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all unanimously praised his goodness, raining down famous jewels, various silks, and all kinds of grain.
The neighboring states admired his virtue and submitted to his rule, like myriad streams returning to the sea.

The Crown Prince and his consort took their leave of their parents and departed; upon returning to the state, they withdrew behind closed doors and neglected affairs of state for their mutual pleasure. The ministers reported this to the King, saying:
"If you do not remove his consort, the affairs of state will surely fall into decay."
The father-king said,
"Since she was given in marriage by our ancestral king, how can it be revoked?
He summoned her and confined her.
Upon hearing this, the consort was filled with shame; she flew back to her original dwelling on the Seventh Mountain, where she beheld Upananda and others and told them:
"When my husband comes, send him here for me."
"Leave behind this gold finger-ring as a token of faith.
When the father heard that the consort had departed, he sent his son back to the kingdom; not seeing his consort, he wept in sorrowful lamentation.
A deity guarding the palace said:
"Do not grieve; I shall show you the way.
Your consort is on the seventh mountain; if you seek her with haste, you may reach her.
Upon hearing this, the Imperial Grandson immediately donned his pearl-embroidered robes, girded his sword, and took up his bow; the radiance of his garments shone for forty *li*.

The next day, he arrived at Mount Qishan and saw his consort having broken off tree branches and cast them on the ground as markers; proceeding forward, he encountered two Daoist masters and asked them, "Has my consort passed through this place?"
He replied,
"Yes. He gave him the ring and they traveled together, with [the king] attending upon him.

He constructed a bridge of wood to cross the small stream and ascended Mount Aṣṭapada. There he beheld a brahmin practicing the four dhyānas; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage and said:
"Have you seen my consort pass this way?"
He replied,
"I have passed through here.
Sit for a moment, and I shall show you the way."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, transformed himself into a monkey whose majestic spirit shook the mountains, causing the Great Grandson to be struck with great fear.
The Brahmin said, "Do not be afraid; he has come to offer you worship."
When the monkey saw the three practitioners, it hesitated and did not move forward.
The brahmin said,
"Proceed."
The monkey immediately stepped forward and offered the fruit as an act of worship; the brahmin accepted it.
The four of them shared it together and said to the monkey, "Take these three people to the shrine of the deity who has the form of a human."
He asked, "Who is this person who has caused him to ascend to heaven?
The brahmin replied:

"The crown prince of kings, the foremost among bodhisattvas, shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, a guide of the Dharma; all sentient beings shall receive his grace and return to the fundamental non-being."
The monkey sighed and said,
"Excellent! When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, I beg to become his horse."
The two Upans— one wishing to become a slave and the other wishing to become an arhat—
the bodhisattva said:
"Excellent!"
They immediately ascended to heaven together.

On the way, they encountered five hundred Pratyekabuddhas who were bound by past affinities; they all passed by them and paid their respects. They sent the monkey back to fetch flowers to scatter over the various Buddhas, making this vow: "May I swiftly attain Perfect Enlightenment, so that I may lead sentient beings to extinguish birth and death, and cause their spirits to return to original non-being."
The three men again made their wishes as before, and having prostrated themselves before all the Buddhas, they departed.
Upon reaching the exterior of the city gate of Śiśumāragiri, which resembled a human form, the monkey prostrated himself and withdrew, while the three men sat down together.
At that time, a maidservant came out to draw water, and the bodhisattva asked her,
"What will you do with this water?
She replied:
"Give the princess a bath.

The Bodhisattva removed his finger-ring and threw it into the water. When the goddess saw the ring, she immediately stopped bathing and said to her kinsmen, "My husband has come seeking me; he is here now."
The father, named Tuo-mo (Sumana), joyfully came out quickly and met him.
The Bodhisattva prostrated himself in the manner of a son-in-law, and the two rishis likewise prostrated themselves and withdrew.

The king invited him into his inner chambers and personally bestowed his daughter upon him; with more than a thousand handmaidens and celestial music for their mutual delight, he remained there for seven years.
As he spoke of the care and nurturing provided by his parents, his voice choked with emotion; he then took his leave and returned to his own country.
The Heavenly King said, "The multitude of people in this country is vast; now that I have entrusted it to you, why do you wish to depart?
The Bodhisattva again declined as he had before.
The King said,
"Stay for seven days more, so that we may enjoy ourselves in full delight.
After seven days had passed, a great divine king came to the place where the Heavenly King was and offered his congratulations, saying:
"Since my deceased daughter has returned and furthermore secured a holy son-in-law," the Heavenly King said, "my daughter was of humble station, yet she has obtained a holy and heroic husband.
She wishes to return to support her parents; I trouble you to escort her back."

The King of Ghosts respectfully assented and immediately used celestial jewels to construct a palace, with seven-tiered towers and various precious heavenly musical instruments rarely seen in the world. The King of Ghosts personally escorted it to its native land, prostrated himself, and withdrew.
When the Bodhisattva saw his father, he addressed him with full sincerity and devotion; the King-Grandfather was delighted and abdicated the throne in his favor.
No one among the celestial maidens, ghosts, or dragons failed to praise this excellence.

He issued a general amnesty for all crimes and bestowed gifts throughout the land; from the commoners of the four quarters down to all living beings, he relieved their poverty and destitution, granting them whatever they desired.

The sentient beings leaped for joy, all of whom sighed in admiration, praising the Buddha’s benevolent transformation as more moistening and nourishing than heaven and earth. From the eight directions, they came to the kingdom to seek his grace, like young children relying on a compassionate mother; when the ancestral king reached the end of his life, he was immediately reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The royal grandson was I myself;
the brahmin of the four dhyānas was Śāriputra."
Upananda is now Maudgalyāyana; Śāriputra is now Chandaka;
and Śakra, Lord of Devas, is now Kātyāyana.
The father-king was Kāśyapa;
the grandfather-king is the present King Śuddhodana;
and the mother was my own mother, Māyādevī.
The queen was Gopī.
For many years, the Bodhisattva practiced the four immeasurables with vast compassion and the six perfections to no end, rescuing and delivering sentient beings beyond the reach of calculation.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly of disciples, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the *zhiliang* spirits were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
84. The Sūtra on the King of Cera (The Previous Life of the Prince) Once upon a time, the chief queen of the King of Cera had no heir. The king was deeply grieved and commanded her, saying:
"Return to the female deities to seek the means of obtaining an heir; when you return, I shall not reproach you."
Later, she wept as she took her leave, vowing to sacrifice her life by throwing herself from a perilous mountain precipice; she then departed for the forests and marshes.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was moved and said:
"This king’s principal consort was my sister in a former life; now, because she has no heir, she is casting away her body from a mountain precipice."
Filled with compassion and pity for her, he suddenly descended and, placing fruit in a vessel, handed it to her, saying:
"Sister, swallow this fruit; you shall surely have a holy offspring who will become a hero of the world."
"If Your Majesty has any doubts, I shall show you the vessel.
This is the divine vessel of the Heavenly King, the supreme proof.
Thereupon, the Queen looked up to heaven and swallowed the fruit; suddenly, she no longer saw where the Heavenly Emperor had gone.
As the time drew near, her body became heavy; returning to the palace, she beheld the king and reported the matter to him in full sincerity.
When the term was complete, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was exceedingly ugly, such as had rarely been seen in the world.

In his early childhood, he was brilliant and possessed vast understanding; his wisdom and strategy were peerless. His strength could topple an elephant, and he could run to seize a soaring hawk. When he let out a cry, its resonance shook like the roar of a lion; his fame spread far and wide, and people from all eight directions sighed in admiration.
The king took as his consort a daughter from a neighboring kingdom named Candraprabhā; she was upright, elegant, and possessed every worldly excellence.
He also had seven younger brothers, who were likewise handsome and refined.
Later, fearing the Moonlight and loathing the Prince’s appearance, she falsely said:
"According to the ancient customs of my country, members of a household do not see one another during the day; this is a matter of profound etiquette."
"The Consort shall not fail in her decorum.
She replied, "I respectfully accept; I dare not disregard your honorable instruction."
From that time forth, whenever the Prince went out or came in, he never failed to observe the situation, reflecting deeply:
"My native land is at enmity with the seven kingdoms; they contend by force without respite, and the myriad people sigh in lamentation!"
"I shall employ expedient means to bring peace.
He thought to himself: "My body is most humble;
if my consort beholds it, she will surely depart. If she departs, the world will be at peace and the myriad people will find rest."
Delighted, he addressed the Queen, wishing to behold the Consort once and observe her appearance.
The Queen said,
"Your form is ugly."
"The Consort’s beauty and radiance are equal to those of a celestial maiden;
yet once you have awakened and departed, you will end as a widower.
The Prince repeated his refusal, and the Queen, pitying him, immediately acceded to his wish.
As the consort was inspecting the horses, the Prince feigned being a cowherd;
when the consort saw him, she said, "Is this cowherd ugly?
The Queen replied:
"He was the herdsman of the former kings.
Later, when she was about to observe the celestial signs, the Consort saw him again and, feeling doubtful, said:
"I have seen this man wherever I travel; could he be the Crown Prince?"
The consort said,
"I wish to behold the radiant countenance of the Crown Prince.
The King then devised a stratagem, ordering his brothers to go forth and travel through the kingdom, with the Prince’s officials attending and escorting him as guards.
When the consort observed this, her heart was slightly pleased.
Later, as they entered the garden again, the Crown Prince climbed a tree and threw fruit at her back;
the consort said, "This is the one destined to be the Crown Prince."
At night, he waited for her to fall asleep and silently shone a light upon her; beholding her form, he was struck with fear and fled back home.
Later, the King said in anger, "How could you allow the Consort to return?"
He replied, "The departure of the Consort is the foundation for the ultimate peace of the world; the people will finally find rest in their kin.
He bowed in farewell and sought her out.
Upon arriving at the Queen’s country, he feigned being a potter and hired himself out to make earthenware; his vessels were so exquisitely crafted that they surpassed anything in the land.
When the master potter beheld their excellence, he took them to present to the King.
The king, delighted upon obtaining the vessel, bestowed it upon his youngest daughter, who then presented it to her elder sisters.
Candraprabhā, knowing what her husband had done, threw it to the ground and smashed it to pieces.

She then entered the city to hire herself out as a dyer of various colors; she knotted together a single bolt of cloth and fashioned it into many exquisite and ingenious designs, filled with diverse crafts such as were rarely seen in the world.
The dyers were delighted by its uniqueness and presented it to the king.
The king was greatly pleased and showed it to his eight daughters.
Candraprabhā recognized it and cast it away, refusing to look at it again.
Furthermore, he served as a minister and was hired to tend horses;
when the horses were well-fed and well-trained, [the king] asked, "What skills do you possess? He replied:
"The various delicacies of the Grand Cook's Office are already prepared.
Your servant has had a meal prepared to present to the Great King.
The King said:
"Who prepared this food?
The minister answered truthfully.
The King appointed him as Grand Cook (Taiguan) to oversee and manage all the various delicacies and meals.

He took the soup inside to offer it to the king’s eight daughters; wishing to employ a skillful means, he feigned spilling it over his own body. The daughters were struck with alarm and fear, yet Candraprabha did not look at them.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, joyfully exclaimed:
"Has the Bodhisattva reached such a state of concern for the salvation of sentient beings?"
"I shall employ a stratagem to assist him.
He summoned the seven rival states to assemble at his capital; only then would the great calamity of the myriad people cease.
He transformed this into a letter from King Moonlight’s own hand and gave it to him as a wife.
The seven states established rites and created ceremonies for the bridegroom’s personal reception; they all gathered together to offer their greetings, asking:
"Why have you come soaring here?
Each replied: [as follows].
"He has betrothed his daughter named Candraprabhā.
The litigation raged on as each produced their own hand-written documents; their grievances rose in unison:
"We shall exterminate your lineage; of this there is no doubt."
He dispatched an envoy with a reply letter, which all [the lords] read and interrogated him, saying:
"You have used one of your daughters to toy with our seven states; we resent the might of Qi's army, and the ruin of your state lies right before us."
The father king, filled with fear, said:
"This calamity is vast.
Is it perhaps summoned by the consequences of past deeds?"
He said to Candraprabhā:
"As you have become a consort to a man, whether your husband is wise or foolish, auspicious or inauspicious, handsome or ugly—all these result from past karma; who can avert them?"
"Yet you were not steadfast and single-minded in fulfilling filial piety and honoring your elders.
Now that your son-in-law has returned to his own country, the calamity has reached this point.
I shall now divide your corpse into seven portions to offer as an apology to the seven kings."
Moonlight wept and said, "I pray you grant me a brief interval of time to seek out a man of wisdom; there must surely be one capable of repelling the threat posed by the seven kingdoms."
The King immediately issued a proclamation, saying:
"Whoever is able to avert this calamity shall be wedded to Candraprabhā and provided with the support of Prabhūtadhana.
The Crown Prince said:
"Build a high observation tower quickly; I shall perform a ritual to avert this.
When the tower was completed, the Crown Prince’s illness temporarily abated as he took a few steps, but then he fell to the ground, saying:
"I must wait for the moonlight to carry me; only then will I repel the enemy."
Candraprabha was terrified and fearful of being slaughtered; supporting himself on another’s arm, he climbed onto the terrace and managed only just to stand.
The Prince called out in a loud voice to the seven kings, his voice resonating far like the roar of a lion, instructing them with the Buddha’s teachings:
"As rulers of the people under Heaven, you should employ the Way of Benevolence; yet now you have given rise to anger, and when anger is excessive, calamity follows."
"Calamity strikes and the person perishes.
Now, does the loss of one's person and the ruin of one's state arise from name-and-form?
Thereupon, the masters of the seven kingdoms, all of whom had been prostrate on the ground, rose at once and, after a brief moment, wished to return to their own lands.
The Crown Prince addressed the King, saying:
"In the way of marriage alliances, none is better than those with the various kings.
Why not betroth our seven daughters to those seven kings?"
With sons-in-law as his frontier guardians and protectors, the King shall be secure!
His ministers and subjects shall find rest!
His parents shall receive their nourishment!
The King said: "Excellent!
This joy is truly great!"
He then commanded the seven kings to give their daughters as wives to him.
The eight sons-in-law were honored with abundant ceremonies, and both the ruler and the people rejoiced.

At this, the king, along with his ministers and subjects, first learned that the Crown Prince was the former husband of Candraprabhā; they immediately selected excellent ministers and warriors to escort them, ordering each to return to his own kingdom.
The nine kingdoms were harmonious and at peace, and the myriad people clapped their hands in joy; they all praised him, saying:
"Heaven has sent us a father!
Indeed, the sagely ruler's skillful means are beyond the perception of ordinary men."
When his virtue was accumulated and his merit perfected, he then shone brightly, free from further censure or slander.
After many years had passed since his return to the kingdom, the Great King passed away, and the Crown Prince succeeded him to the throne.
He granted a general amnesty for all crimes and taught the myriad people through the five precepts, the six perfections, the eight fast-day observances, and the ten wholesome actions.

Calamities and afflictions were entirely stilled; the nation became abundant and the masses lived in peace. His great transformation spread far and wide, and all venerated the Three Honored Ones. As his virtue flourished, blessings returned; all illnesses were extinguished, and their complexions and radiance shone brilliantly, surpassing even the peach blossom.

Why was this so? It was because in a past life, when the Bodhisattva and his wife were both plowing their fields together, he sent his wife to fetch food. He waited for her return, but she did not come back for a long time; instead, she was seen walking along with a Pratyekabuddha, hidden by the mountain slope.
Doubt arose in his mind, and he was moved to anger; seizing a hoe, he intended to go and strike him.
When he arrived, however, he saw his wife dividing her own food to offer it to the śramaṇa, after which she withdrew and stood with her hands joined in reverence.
When the śramaṇa had finished eating, he tossed his alms bowl into the air; it shone with brilliant radiance as he flew away.

The husband felt remorse and shame, thinking: "It is because my wife possesses such virtue that she has brought about this honor; I, however, am burdened by grave folly and shall surely suffer its calamity."
He then said to his wife, "The merit of your offering, I shall share with you.
Let us eat the remaining rice together; you shall have no fault."
When their lives came to an end, they were each reborn into royal families.
The wife possessed the grace of pure compassion; thus, she was beautiful from birth.
The husband was first wrathful and later compassionate; therefore, he was initially ugly and subsequently handsome.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When a person performs actions, if they first give and later take back, they will be born into a wealthy and noble family in their next life, but will become impoverished as they grow up;
if they first take back and later give, they will receive the results in their next life by first being poor and lowly, and later becoming wealthy and noble."
The Crown Prince was my own self; his wife was Gopī;
and the King, his father, was King Śuddhodana.
The mother was my own mother, Śrīmatī;
the Lord Śakra was Maitreya. Throughout successive lifetimes, this Bodhisattva has been concerned for sentient beings, rescuing them from the mire of suffering and the flames of calamity.
"Thus did the Bodhisattva practice the Perfection of Universal Wisdom through the giving of light. 85.

The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Separating from the Ghost Wife by Means of Light [The Jātaka of an Ordinary Man] (85) "The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Separating from the Ghost Wife by Means of Light: 'In the past, the Bodhisattva was an ordinary man. At the age of sixteen, his intellect and character were open and penetrating; his learning was broad and his vision vast, such that there was no scripture he had not mastered with profound depth.'"
He reflected:
"Among the various scriptures and paths of practice, which scripture is the most true?
Which path is the most secure?"
Having reflected thus, he sighed deeply and said:
"Only the Buddha’s sutras are most true; only the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is most peaceful.
He spoke again:
"I shall cherish the truth and abide in peace.
When his parents wished to take a wife for him, he said with regret, "No calamity of seduction is greater than physical beauty;
if such demonic enticements arrive, one's Way and Virtue will perish."
"If I do not flee and depart, shall I be swallowed by a wolf?
Thereupon, he went to a foreign land and supported himself by hiring out his labor.

At that time, there was an old farmer who, being aged and childless, found a girl while walking through the weeds; her beauty was unsurpassed in the land, so he joyfully raised her as his heir. He sought a son to be her mate, but throughout the entire country, no one was suitable.
The old man had hired the Bodhisattva for five years; observing his conduct from its subtle beginnings until its manifest perfection, he esteemed him from the bottom of his heart and said:
"Young man!..."
"I have sufficient means to support you; I shall give my daughter to you as a wife so that she may become my successor.
The woman possessed divine virtue, which deluded the Bodhisattva’s mind.
Not long after he had taken her, he suddenly attained self-awakening and said:
"I have observed the enlightened transformations of the Buddhas: they regard form (*rūpa*) as fire and man as a moth.

Just as a moth covets the color of the flame and its body is consumed by the burning, so too does this old man burn my person with the fire of form, bait me with the lure of wealth, and ruin my virtue with the filth of household life."
That night, he fled in silence, traveling over a hundred li until he stayed overnight in an empty pavilion.
The person staying in the pavilion asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am seeking lodging.

As the innkeeper led him inside, he beheld a magnificent bed with bedding and various precious objects that dazzled his eyes; there was a woman whose appearance resembled his own wife, who captivated the Bodhisattva’s heart and caused him to dwell with her for five years.
Mingxin Jue said: "Lust is like a silkworm that devours its own body and endangers its life.
This is why I fled to seclusion; yet even in my decline, I have encountered it again."
He departed in silence and hastened away, yet he again beheld the palace treasures and women as before; once more his mind was deluded, and he lived with them for ten years.
Then his mind became enlightened, and he said:
"My calamity is grave indeed."
Fleeing yet unable to escape, he made a solemn vow within himself, saying:
"I shall never stay overnight.
He then fled once more.
Seeing a large house from afar, he avoided it and traveled through the grass.
The gatekeeper asked,
"Who is traveling at night?"
He replied:
"The destinies and the intermediate state. He asked:
"There is a prohibition, yet no one observes it.
The palace attendants called forward what they had previously seen, as described above.
The wife said:
"Since incalculable kalpas past, I have vowed to be your wife.
Where will you go now that you flee? How can you find peace?
Thus the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"The root of desire is difficult to uproot; it is indeed like this!
He then gave rise to the four reflections on impermanence, saying:

"I wish to extinguish all the defilements of the three realms through the meditative concentrations on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; why then can these impurities alone not be eradicated?"
As he gave rise to these four foundations of mindfulness, the ghost-wife immediately vanished. His heart became bright and clear, and he beheld the Buddhas standing before him.
He emerged from the concentrations of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, received the śramaṇa precepts, and took the Unconquerable One as his teacher.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Perfection of Universal Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) through the giving of light was carried out.
86. The Sūtra on the Prediction to Māṇava [The Jātaka of the Brahmin Māṇava] "Long ago, the Bodhisattva was born in the kingdom of Padma."
At that time, he was a brahmin named Jou-t'ong (Māṇava).

He petitioned his teacher to study, and as he gazed upward at the celestial phenomena and delved into the various books of diagrams and prophecies, he mastered everything upon hearing or seeing it. He maintained the truth and honored filial piety; thus, the scholars of the land praised him.
The Master said, "Your Way is complete and your arts are sufficient; why do you not travel abroad with your aspirations to begin the sprouting of transformation and instruction?
He replied:
"Because I have long been impoverished and lack goods with which to repay your kindness, I did not dare to withdraw.
My mother’s illness is particularly grave, and I have no means to provide medical treatment; I beg to go out to work as a hired laborer so that I may provide for the cost of her medicine."
The Master said, "Excellent!

He bowed his head in prostration and withdrew, traveling through the neighboring kingdoms. There he saw five hundred brahmins who had assembled in a lecture hall and prepared a high seat. A single beautiful woman and five hundred silver coins were provided; she would ascend the high seat and engage the scholars in debate, and whoever was seen to possess profound and vast knowledge would be honored with the gift of the woman and the money.
The Bodhisattva observed them and saw that their wisdom was shallow; as they struggled to respond and were left speechless, he said to the assembly of scholars:
"I too am the son of a Brahmin; may I join the discussion?"
They all said in unison, "Yes.
He then ascended the high seat; the scholars posed shallow challenges, yet his responses were profound, and their questions were narrow, yet his explanations were vast.
The Confucian scholars said, "One whose Way is lofty, brilliant, and far-reaching may be taken as a teacher.
They all bowed their heads to the ground in prostration. The Bodhisattva declined and withdrew, whereupon the scholars all said:
"Although he possesses lofty wisdom, he is a man from a foreign land; it is not fitting that he should receive a maiden from my country. I shall increase his gift with more money.
The Bodhisattva replied, "He whose Way is lofty has profound virtue. I seek the Way of desirelessness; therefore, such treasures are what I truly desire."

To transmit the spirit through the Way and to bestow sagehood through virtue—wherein the divine and the sagely pass it on to one another, their transformative influence remaining imperishable—can this not be called having a worthy heir?
Yet you wish to fill up the source of the Way and cut down the root of virtue; can this not be called having no progeny?
Having finished speaking, she withdrew immediately; the assembly of scholars were abashed and felt ashamed.
The woman said, "That man of high character is my true gentleman."

Lifting her robes and traveling on foot, she followed his tracks across various kingdoms; her strength was exhausted and her feet were wounded, so she paused to rest by the roadside until she reached the kingdom of Patma.
Its king, named Jisheng (Victorious), was touring the borders of his realm when he saw the woman resting from her fatigue.
He asked,
"Who are you that are by the side of the road?
The woman related to him in detail the circumstances of her situation.
The King rejoiced at her resolve and felt profound pity for her;
he commanded his daughter, saying, "Follow me back to the palace, and I shall take you as my own daughter.
The girl replied:
"How can one eat the food of a different surname in vain?
I wish to hold office and shall follow Your Majesty.
The King said:
"You gather famous flowers to adorn me.
The woman immediately gave her respectful assent; she followed the king back to the palace and every day gathered famous flowers for the king's use.
When Mañjuśrī returned to his kingdom, he saw the people on the roads bustling about, filling in the ruins and sweeping away the filth from the ground.
He asked a passerby, "The common folk are so joyful; is there some celebration to come?"
He replied:
"Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, will come in the future to teach and transform us; therefore, the multitude rejoices with great joy."
The Confucian youth felt joy in his heart; he entered meditative absorption, his mind pure and free from defilement.
Seeing that the Buddha was approaching, he encountered on the road the aforementioned woman gathering flowers, who carried a flask under her arm; he requested some flowers from her.
He obtained five flowers.
While the queen and the common people all personally cleared the path, the Bodhisattva requested a small portion of the ground and cleared it himself.
The people said:
“There is another small stream, but its waters are turbulent and swift, and the soil and stones cannot remain.
The Bodhisattva said,
“May I use the power of my dhyāna to bring down those small stars to fill it?”
He further thought to himself:
"In the ritual of making offerings, one should personally perform good deeds through the toil of the four great elements.
He then set down the stone of the star-carriage and filled it with his own physical strength, remaining steadfast through the power of dhyāna.

While the rest were still slightly delayed by the moat, the Buddha arrived; he took off his deerskin garment and laid it upon the damp ground, then scattered five flowers over the Buddha. The flowers remained suspended in mid-air, as if they had been sown by hand and their roots had taken hold in the earth to sprout.
The Buddha told him:

"In the ninety-first kalpa hence, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, and Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām. In that world, things will be inverted; fathers and sons will become enemies, and the royal administration will harm the people as if raining down a multitude of blades. Though the people seek to avoid it, they cannot escape its calamity."
"You shall then deliver sentient beings there; those who attain liberation at that time will be beyond calculation.
Joyful in heart, the youth Ruci leaped into the air to a height of seven *ren* above the ground. Descending from the sky, he spread his hair upon the earth, commanding the Buddha to tread upon it.
When the World-Honored One had finished crossing, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not tread upon this ground. Why is this so?"
"The place where one receives the prediction of enlightenment is supreme and unsurpassed; if a wise person establishes a *stūpa* here, it is equivalent to receiving the prediction.
All the devas then responded in unison, saying:
"We shall each establish a *stūpa*."
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Bhadrika, who stuck a small twig into the ground and said,
"My realm is already established.
The devas looked at one another and said:
"How could an ordinary commoner or a mere youth possess the wisdom of a supreme sage! he thought.
He immediately had a multitude of treasures carried up and erected a *stūpa* (a sacred pillar) at the summit. Bowing his head, he said:
"I pray that I may receive the Buddha's teaching and transformation just as you have now; what merit would there be in this *stūpa* I have erected?"
The World-Honored One said:
"When the Youth becomes a Buddha, you shall receive your prediction [of enlightenment].
The Buddha then addressed Śāriputra:
"The Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta was myself.
The girl selling flowers is now Kuṭi.
The son of the elder is now Nālada here in this assembly."
Pūraṇa immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction:
"In the future you shall become a buddha, named Kṣipradarśin."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the disciples of the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, were filled with joy; they prostrated themselves and departed.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Infinite Perfection of Wisdom through the giving of light.
87. The Sūtra of King Māndhātṛ [The Jātaka of King Nanda] (87). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Anavatapta, sitting beneath a tree. His countenance was radiant and brilliant, surpassing refined gold; he smiled with joy, and the light from his mouth shone in five colors.
At that time, all who witnessed it were filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
they all sighed in unison, saying, "Truly, he is what is called the God among Gods.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated himself, and said:
“The smile of the World-Honored One must surely intend to deliver sentient beings from the darkness.
The World-Honored One said:
“Excellent!”
"It is truly as you say; my laughter was not in vain, for it arose from the Dharma.
Do you wish to know the meaning of my smile?
Ānanda replied:
"Those who hunger for the scriptures will truly never be satiated.
The World-Honored One said:

"In the past, there was a sage-king named Māndhātṛ, who at that time was a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents. His mind was upright and his conduct impartial; the people had no sense of theft or resentment. He possessed kindness, compassion, joy, and protection, and his intent was like that of Śakra."
At that time, the lifespan of the people was eighty thousand years.

The Emperor possessed the seven treasures: the purple-gold wheel-turning jewel, the flying white elephant, the dark-blue divine horse, the bright moon divine pearl, the jade-like virtuous queen, the noble minister who presides over treasures, and the noble minister who commands the army.

The Emperor had a thousand sons, who were handsome, benevolent, and serene; they were well-versed in the past and possessed foreknowledge of the future, such that among all conscious beings there were none who did not revere and admire them.

When the Emperor desired to travel and observe the lands of the east, west, south, or north, as soon as his intention was formed in his mind, the golden wheel would appear before him, leading him wherever he wished to go; the seven treasures were likewise so, flying to guide the Holy King.
The devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits all provided protection; they scattered various precious flowers and proclaimed his immeasurable longevity.
The Emperor commanded his close attendants in charge of his grooming:
"When you see white hairs growing on my head, you must inform me immediately."
"The fact that my hair has turned white is a clear sign of approaching death.
I wish to cast off the burdens of this defiled world and its vulgar customs, and instead pursue a life of purity and detachment.
His close attendants acted according to his command; later, when they saw his hair had indeed turned white, they immediately reported it to him.
The Emperor’s heart was gladdened, and he summoned the Crown Prince, saying:
"My head has grown white; that it is white is indeed proof of impermanence. It is not fitting to let one's thoughts wander in this world of no benefit."
"I now establish you as Emperor to preside over the four quarters of the world; the lives of your ministers and subjects depend upon you, so you must have compassion for them.
If you practice the Dharma as I do, you may escape the evil realms;
when your hair turns white, you shall renounce the kingdom and surely become a śramaṇa."
"In establishing the teaching for my son, I shall prioritize the four immeasurables, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions.

As soon as he had finished these instructions, he renounced his kingdom and, beneath a tree on this very site where the hut stands, shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma robes, and became a śramaṇa.
The ministers and the common people mourned with such intensity that they leaped and wailed, their grief so profound it caused their hearts to knot.
"For one thousand and eighty-four generations, the lineage of the Dharma Prince Mādhava has been passed down; now, at the end of the Holy Sovereign’s True Dharma, it is about to perish."

King Māndhātṛ again relinquished his celestial realm and descended with his spirit to be born from the king of the final age; he likewise became a Cakravartin Emperor, named Nanda, and the True Dharma flourished once more.

He issued a clear decree to the Empress and the ladies of the palace, ordering them to observe the eight precepts and the six monthly fasts: first, to exercise compassion and love for all living beings;
second, to be cautious against theft and to use wealth to relieve the poor;
third, to maintain chastity and purity while guarding their true nature.
Fourth, one should maintain trustworthiness in speech according to the Buddha's teachings;
fifth, one should exhaustively practice filial piety so that wine never passes one's lips;
sixth, one must not sleep on high beds or within embroidered curtains.
Seventh, do not eat in the evening or at dusk;
eighth, be careful never to let perfumes, flowers, or cosmetics come near your body, and do not defile yourself with lewd songs or depraved pleasures.
The mind shall be free from discursive thought, the mouth shall be free from speech, and the body shall be free from action.
He commanded all his holy ministers, the exemplary scholars who lead the way, down to the common people:
