Widowers, widows, the young and weak, and beggars shall be provided for and rescued; the sick shall be supplied with medicine, and the needy with food and clothing. Those who suffer from lack and have nothing shall be permitted to go to the palace gate to request what they lack. Those who do not comply with this transformation shall be subjected to heavy corvée labor. By placing one such family among five families of the virtuous, let the five transform the one; those who first comply shall be rewarded, and ministers shall be selected for their virtue rather than their noble lineage.
Since the King’s enlightened laws were implemented, the people of the four continents have looked upon one another with kindness and harmony, and the intent to kill has been extinguished.
They practice constant yielding; they do not close their doors at night; they are chaste and pure, desiring no woman who is not their wife.
One does not speak of two; the teachings issued forth are benevolent and compassionate. Observing that things are not constant, one’s words are not flowery or ornate.
Seeing others attain prosperity and good fortune, the heart rejoices and speaks of assistance; thus the Great Way transforms and spreads, and malevolent poisons are extinguished.
He believed in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Śramaṇas, and his words were free from further doubt or entanglement.
"The King of the South is compassionate and nurturing; his bounty reaches everywhere, and there is none among the eight directions, above or below, who does not praise his virtue."
On the following day, Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the sun, moon, and stars, the oceanic dragons, and the terrestrial deities gathered together to deliberate:
"The human kings of this world possess the four immeasurables of compassion and kindness; the reach of their benevolence exceeds that of the various devas."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the gods:
"Would you like to see King Nanda?
The gods replied:
"Your long-cherished wish is indeed fulfilled by your enlightened instruction.
Then, in the time it takes to extend one's arm, Śakra arrived at the Hall of Compassionate Benevolence in King Nanda’s palace. Seeing King Nanda, he said:
"The Sage King possesses such magnificent virtue that the various devas have been parched with longing to see you, wishing for this day after day."
"How could the Holy King not wish to see the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where everything exists spontaneously and there is nothing that cannot be obtained through mere wishing?
The King of the South said, "Excellent!
I desire to go and sport there."
Śakra returned there and called his charioteer, named Mālu, saying:
"Go and welcome King Nanda with the precious chariot drawn by a thousand horses that I ride.
The charioteer received the command and went to welcome King Nanda with the celestial chariot.

When the carriage arrived and stopped beneath the palace gate, the assembled ministers and the common people were all struck with amazement; they marveled at this auspicious omen of the Sage King as something unprecedented, proclaiming it to one another until the entire realm was filled with joy.

"His Majesty’s universal compassion reaches all sentient beings; he personally observes the six monthly fasts and the eight precepts, and further teaches them to his people. These virtues are so profound that they have caused the Lord of Devas to regard him with reverence and affection, coming to welcome him."
King Namban ascended the chariot, and both the vehicle and the horses flew upward; he hovered slowly and circled about so that the people might see him clearly. The King said to his charioteer:
"Take me now to observe the two realms of the wicked—hell and the realm of hungry ghosts—those places where beings are burned, boiled, and tortured for the karmic retribution of their past offenses."
The charioteer followed these instructions, and upon their completion, [the King] ascended to heaven.
Śakra Devānām Indra, filled with joy, descended from his throne to welcome him, saying:

"You have labored your mind to weave the fabric of the world and have taken concern for the salvation of sentient beings. These are the great undertakings of a Bodhisattva—the four immeasurables and the six perfections—and the various devas long to behold you."
Śakra approached him of his own accord, took him by the arm, and sat with him.
The King of the South’s physical form underwent a transformation, becoming fragrant and pure; the radiance of his countenance was so upright and handsome that it was no different from Śakra’s.
He then manifested the music named "Joy," its sounds being immeasurable; he scattered precious flowers and incense such as had never been seen in the world.
Śakra spoke again:
"Be careful not to cherish longing for your former abode in the human world; the manifold delights of the heavens are yours, O Holy King."
Nan Wang’s will was set upon transforming the ignorant and deluded, extinguishing their various heterodox minds, and causing them to know the Triple Gem; he replied to Śakra Devendra, saying:
"It is like borrowing someone else's property: one must eventually return it to its owner."

This celestial throne is not my permanent dwelling; I shall temporarily return to the world to instruct my descendants, so that they may govern the state with a rectified mind through the Buddha’s luminous Dharma, ensuring that filial piety is passed down in succession, that their precepts are complete and their conduct sublime, and that they relinquish human existence to be reborn in the heavens to enjoy the delights of the Śakras.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The King of the South was my own self.
My descendants have transmitted the lineage for one thousand and eighty-four generations; they established their sons as kings while their fathers went forth to become śramaṇas."
Ānanda rejoiced and, bowing his head in prostration, said:

"The World-Honored One’s compassion for sentient beings is so profound that his grace and nourishment are such as this; his merit is imperishable. Now he has indeed attained Buddhahood and become the Honored One within the three realms, whom all devas, immortals, seers, and sages do not fail to revere."
The bhikṣus rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed. 88.
The Sūtra of Ariṣṭanemi [The Jātaka of the Elder Ariṣṭanemi]. (88) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the village of Uruvilvā.
At that time, after the midday meal, the bhikṣus were seated in the lecture hall and discussed among themselves:
"Human life is exceedingly short; there is little physical security before one must depart for the next world."
Among gods and humans, no being is born without dying.

Yet those who are ignorant and mired in darkness are stingy and greedy, refusing to practice charity; they do not honor the Way of the scriptures, claiming that good deeds bring no merit and evil deeds entail no grave retribution.
"If one indulges the mind and satisfies the will, there is no evil to which one will not resort; to violate the Buddha's teaching—what benefit is there in regret thereafter?

With his divine ear, the Buddha heard from afar the bhikṣus discussing these extraordinary and unsurpassed matters. The World-Honored One immediately rose and went to where the bhikṣus were, took a seat, and said:
"What was it that you were discussing just now?"
He knelt with his right knee on the ground and replied:
"Shortly after our meal, we were discussing how human life is transient and fleeting, and that one must soon pass into the next world.
He spoke as described above.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
How most delightful!"
When you have left home to study the Way, your resolve must be pure, and you should contemplate only that which is good.
A bhikṣu, whether sitting or rising, should keep two matters in mind:
first, the recitation of the sūtras; second, meditative stillness.
"Would you like to hear the sutra?
He replied, "Indeed,
I would most gladly wish to hear it."
The World-Honored One then said:

"In the past, there was a king named Kṛkin. In his kingdom there was a tree called the Śubhakṛtsna, with a circumference of five hundred and sixty *li*. Its roots spread four hundred and eighty *li* beneath the ground, it rose four thousand *li* high, and its branches extended two thousand *li* in each of the four directions."

The tree has five sides: on one side, the king and his court ladies eat together; on two sides, the hundred officials eat; on three sides, the common people eat; on four sides, śramaṇas and practitioners eat; and on five sides, birds and beasts eat.
The fruits of those trees were as large as two-dou measures of jars; their flavor was as sweet as honey, and there were neither guardians nor mutual encroachment.
At that time, the lifespan of all people was eighty-four thousand years, and they suffered from exactly nine kinds of ailments:
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the need for excretion and urination, desire, overeating, and the physical frailty of old age—these were the nine ailments they possessed.
Women do not marry until they are five hundred years old.
At that time, there was an elder named Ariṣṭanemi, whose wealth was beyond counting.
Ariṣṭanemi thought to himself:

"Life is exceedingly brief; there is no birth without death. Wealth is not one's own possession and frequently brings about calamities and afflictions. It is better, therefore, to practice giving to relieve the poor and destitute."
Though worldly glory may be pleasant, nothing endures forever; it is better to abandon the household life, cast off defilement and turbidity, uphold purity, don the *kāṣāya*, and become a *śramaṇa*.
He immediately went to the assembly of the worthy to receive the śramaṇa precepts.

When ordinary people saw that Mianmi had become a śramaṇa, more than several thousand of them heard of his holy transformation and all realized impermanence: that prosperity is followed by decline, and nothing that exists fails to perish; only the Way is truly noble. They all became śramaṇas, following his teaching and transformation.
“Nianmi preached the sutra to his disciples, saying:
‘Human life is exceedingly short; it is fleeting and impermanent. One must cast off this body and proceed to the next world.’”
If there is no birth, there is no death; how then could there be permanence?
For this reason, one should sever the mind of stinginess and greed, practice giving to the poor and destitute, restrain the emotions and control desires, and refrain from committing any evil.
When people dwell in this world, the flow of their destiny is exceedingly swift; human life is like the dew upon the morning grass, falling in an instant.
Since human life is thus, how could it possibly endure for long?
Human life is like raindrops falling from the sky that form bubbles and vanish instantly; the swift flow of life is even more rapid than that of bubbles.
Human life is like a flash of lightning, vanishing in an instant; the swift flow of life is even more rapid than that of lightning.
Human life is like striking water with a stick; as soon as the stick is removed, the water closes back together. The flow of life passes even more swiftly than this.
Human life is like a small amount of oil placed on a blazing fire; it is consumed and burned away in an instant. The departure of life is swifter than that small amount of oil.

Human life is like the threads on a loom; as they are gradually exhausted, so too does the span of one's allotted destiny diminish day and night. With such abundant anxiety and heavy suffering, how could it endure for long?

Human life is like leading an ox to the slaughterhouse: with every step the ox takes, it draws closer to death. A person gaining even a single day is like the ox taking a single step; the flow of life passes away even more swiftly than this.

Human life is like water flowing down from a mountain; it advances day and night with such speed that it does not stop for even a moment. The passing of human life is even more rapid than this; it hastens toward death day and night, advancing swiftly without pause.

When people dwell in this world, they undergo great toil and hardship and are beset by many anxieties; since human life is so difficult to obtain, one should therefore uphold the Right Path, observe the precepts and the sūtras without violating or damaging them, and practice giving to those in poverty, for among those born into this world, there is none who does not die.
Nianmi instructed his disciples in this manner, further saying:

"I have abandoned greed, lust, anger, hatred, delusion, song, dance, music, sleep, and deviant thoughts; I have attained the pure mind, distanced myself from craving and desire, cast off all evil conduct, washed away the defilements of the inner mind, and extinguished all external thoughts. Seeing good, I do not rejoice; encountering evil, I do not grieve. With no duality between suffering and pleasure, I purify my conduct; with a single unmoving mind, I attain the fourth *dhyāna*."

With a mind of loving-kindness, I teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to know the path of goodness so that they may ascend to birth in the heavens; out of compassion and pity, I grieve for them, fearing they might fall into evil realms.
When I behold the four dhyānas and the various concentrations of emptiness, there is nothing I do not clearly perceive, and my heart is filled with joy;
using what I have seen, I transform all things, leading them to perceive the profound Dharma.
Regarding the Buddha-work of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), if there are those who attain it, one also rejoices in their success.

One nurtures and protects all things as if protecting one’s own body; practicing these four matters with a mind of perfect equanimity, one remains unaffected by the various forms—coarse or beautiful—perceived by the eye; the sounds of praise or abuse heard by the ear; fragrances, whether sweet or foul, and flavors, whether bitter or pungent; textures, whether smooth or coarse; and by pleasant desires that accord with the heart or distressing troubles that oppose it; remaining neither elated by what is liked nor resentful toward what is disliked.
By observing these six practices, one attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way.
You all should likewise practice these six practices in order to obtain the Way of the Arhat.
"Aniruddha is the most venerable teacher among the holy ones of the triple world; his wisdom is wondrously penetrating, such that there is nothing obscure it does not illuminate.
Although his disciples have not yet attained the path of Arhatship, at the end of their lives they will all be reborn in the heavens."

Those whose minds are tranquil and whose wills are detached, who still cherish meditative concentration, are all reborn in the Brahma Heaven; next, they are reborn in the Heaven of Emanated Transformation and Sound; next, in the Heaven of Delight Without Arrogance; next, in the Tuṣita Heaven; next, in the Yāma Heaven; next, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; next, in the Heaven Above the First; and finally, they are reborn into the families of worldly kings and nobles.

High conduct brings high reward; low conduct brings low reward. Whether one is poor or wealthy, noble or humble, long-lived or short-lived—all these result from past karma. By reverently observing the *Mii* precepts, one ensures that one’s suffering will not be in vain.
“Maitreya is my own self.
All śramaṇas who practice with diligence and exertion can be liberated from the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, and affliction, and attain the Great Way of true cessation and nirvāṇa;
those who cannot practice it fully may yet attain the path of the non-returner, the once-returner, or the stream-enterer.”
The wise reflect deeply that human life is impermanent; it is fleeting and brief, lasting at most a hundred years, which may or may not even be attained.
Within those hundred years, one undergoes three hundred seasons—each of the months of spring, summer, and winter accounting for one hundred.
One undergoes twelve hundred months—four hundred months each for the periods of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
There are thirty-six thousand days in a lifetime: twelve thousand days in spring, and twelve thousand days each for the heat of summer and the cold of winter.
Throughout a hundred years, if one eats twice a day, there are a total of seventy-two thousand meals: twenty-four thousand meals each in spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Furthermore, excluding those times when one is an infant who has not yet been weaned from nursing and cannot eat solid food; or when, being startled, one does not eat; or during illness; or when feeling anger; or while practicing meditation or observing a fast; or when impoverished and lacking food—these instances are all included within the seventy-two thousand meals.

Within a hundred years of life, fifty years are spent sleeping at night; ten years are lost during infancy; ten years are lost in illness; and twenty years are spent managing domestic affairs and other such matters. Thus, of a hundred-year human lifespan, one obtains only ten years of true happiness.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "I have already spoken of human life;

I have spoken of years, months, days, meals, and the span of life. That which I ought to say for the sake of the bhikṣus has all been said. What I sought in my resolve is now fully accomplished; you, bhikṣus, should likewise bring your own aspirations and pursuits to completion."

"Whether in the mountains and marshes or in ancestral temples, you must lecture on the sutras and contemplate the Way without falling into indolence; those who seek only their own pleasure will surely have cause for regret later.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bhikṣus were filled with joy and, having paid homage to the Buddha, departed.
89. The Sūtra of King Ādarśamukha [The Jātaka of King Ādarśamukha] (89). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the bhikṣus took up their alms bowls at the time for eating and entered the city to seek food, the sun had not yet reached midday. They thought together:
"We have entered the city very early; would it not be well for us all to go to the lecture hall of the heterodox brahmins and sit there for a short while?"
They all said in unison, "So be it.
They then went together to that place, exchanged greetings with the various brahmins, and took their seats.
At that time, the brahmins disputed the scriptures among themselves; their knots of attachment arose and remained unresolved, as they turned upon one another with slander and resentment, saying:
"I know this Dharma; what Dharma do you know?"
"What I know accords with the Path; what you know does not accord with the Path.
My Dharma can be put into practice; your Dharma is difficult to approach.

What was said before is contradicted by what is said after; much that is taught is erroneous. You cannot lift the heavy burden placed before you; though I explain the meaning for you, you cannot understand it. Your knowledge is empty; you possess nothing at all; being thus constrained, what more can be done?"
They countered one another with the spears of their tongues, mutually inflicting harm; for every single poison they received, they retaliated with three.

When the bhikṣus heard such evil words from the groups of disciples, they neither spoke ill of those disciples nor did they testify to the correctness of their claims; each rose and sat down to go to Śrāvastī in search of alms.
When the meal was finished, he put away his almsbowl and returned to the Jeta Grove. He paid homage to the Buddha, sat down to one side, and related everything exactly as it had happened.
He thought to himself, "These brahmins subject themselves to such hardship in their studies; when will they ever attain liberation?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These followers of heterodox paths have not been deluded and ignorant for only a single lifetime,
bhikṣus!"

In the distant past, there was a king on this land of Jambudvīpa named Ādarśamukha (Mirror-Face), whose wisdom was like the sands of the Ganges. Although he recited the essential sutras of the Buddha, his ministers and subjects for the most part did not recite them;

they carried small books as if bound in chains, placing their faith in the light of fireflies while doubting the far-reaching vision of the sun and moon. They took the blind man as their metaphor, desiring to make him abandon the puddles of the roadside to travel across the great ocean.
The Emperor commanded his messengers, ordering them to travel throughout the realm to collect all those born blind and bring them to the palace gates.
Having received the mandate, the ministers traveled through the kingdom and brought all the sightless people to the palace, reporting:
"We have found all the blind; they are now before Your Majesty."
The king said,
"Take him away and show him the elephant. The minister,
obeying the king's command, led the blind man to the place where the elephants were and took him by the hand to show them to him.

Among them were those who held the elephant’s feet, its tail, the base of its tail, its belly, its flanks, its back, its ears, its head, its tusks, and its trunk; these blind men contended over the elephant in great confusion, each asserting that their own perception was true and the others’ false.
The messengers led him back and took him to the king's presence.
The king asked him,
"Did you see the elephant?"
They replied, "We all saw it.
The king said:
"What kind of creature is this elephant?
The foot-holders replied,
"O Illustrious King!"
The elephant was like a lacquered tube. The one holding its tail said it was like a broom;

the one holding the base of the tail said it was like a staff; the one holding its belly said it was like a drum; the one holding its flanks said it was like a wall; the one holding its back said it was like a high stool; the one holding its ears said it was like a winnowing basket; the one holding its head said it was like a ladle; the one holding its tusks said it was like horns; and the one holding its trunk replied: "O Wise King!..."
"The elephant is like a great rope.
Then, before the king, they contended together, saying:
"Great King!..."
"An elephant is like true thusness," I said.
King Jingmian laughed at this and said, "Blind! Oh, how blind!"
"You still have not seen the Buddha's sutras.
He then spoke in verse:
"For those who are now like the blind, They argue in vain, each claiming their own view is the truth."
"Seeing one thing, they claim all else is not; they sit upon a single elephant while harboring mutual resentment.
It is further said:
"To be preoccupied solely with minor texts, without beholding the true Dharma of the Buddha—which is vast and boundless, lofty and unsurpassed—is like being without eyes!"
"Then, both the noble and the humble recited the Buddha’s scriptures together.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The King Mirror-Face was none other than myself."
The man without eyes was none other than the Brahmin of the lecture hall.
At that time, his sons were devoid of wisdom; because they were blind, they fell into dispute.
Now their dispute is likewise in darkness; to persist in dispute is of no benefit.
At that time, the Buddha thoroughly examined this fascicle and instructed his disciples to explain it:
"To provide illumination for future generations and to ensure that my teachings and the Way endure for a long time, I have spoken this *Arthavargīya-sūtra*."
"Claiming oneself to be enlightened while others fall short, when will the sun of wisdom break through the darkness of delusion?
Deeming oneself without the Way while claiming all others are thus learned, when will this inverted confusion and lack of practice be resolved?"
Always self-awakened, one practices the honored conduct; having personally heard and seen, one’s practice is peerless.
Though already fallen into the five dwellings bound to the world, one may through exquisite conduct surpass them.
Clinging to folly while dwelling in hope for the good, one may attain deliverance through false learning;
yet though one hears and sees with earnest attention and maintains the precepts, do not say that this is sufficient.
Do not follow all the worldly practices you see; though they may seem clever, they are merely such practices.
Maintain them with equal respect as those [wholesome] practices, and do not harbor thoughts that they are inferior or excessive.
Therefore, severing the subsequent [fetters], they are also exhausted; having abandoned conceptualization, one attains solitary wandering.
Do not seek self-knowledge to achieve cleverness; though there is seeing and hearing, practice only contemplation.
Completely free from aspiration regarding both sides, with the womb and its union likewise distanced,
and abiding nowhere in either place, one observes all phenomena and attains right stillness.

The mind experiences what is seen and heard; when one eliminates wrong thoughts and does not dwell on the trivial, observing phenomena with wisdom and contemplating them with the mind, one thereby attains equanimity and the emptiness of the world.
Since there is nothing from the outset, what is there to depend upon?

One originally practices the Dharma to seek the ultimate truth; yet merely guarding the precepts does not constitute wisdom—only through the Perfection of Wisdom does one ultimately attain non-retrogression.

90. The Sūtra of King Sūkṣma [The Jātaka of King Sūkṣma] (90) The Sūtra of King Sūkṣma: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king named Sūkṣma. His will was pure and his conduct stainless; he took refuge solely in the Triple Gem. He studied the Buddhist sūtras and maintained a tranquil mind focused on the meaning of the Dharma. He deeply perceived that the origin of human beings is fundamentally non-arising."

That which is strong in vital energy (qi) becomes earth; that which is soft becomes water; that which is warm becomes fire; that which is mobile becomes wind. When these four are in harmony, consciousness arises.
The above clarifies the capacity for awakening: by ceasing desire and emptying the mind, one returns the spirit to its original non-being.

Thereupon, he made this vow: "I shall awaken those who do not yet wake. The spirit relies upon the four states of existence: those of great benevolence become heavenly beings; those of lesser benevolence become human beings; and those whose various defiled and mixed actions result in the classes of crawling, flying, and wriggling creatures. Through their conduct they receive bodies, whose forms are of ten thousand varieties. Consciousness and the primal qi are subtle and difficult to perceive; the form has no tethering hair—whom could one possibly grasp?"
"Thus, while the old [teachings] are explained, the new are received; this cycle continues from beginning to end without end.

The King, considering that the spiritual essence transforms according to impermanence and revolves through the five realms of existence in an unceasing stream, sought to explain the intent of his ministers. Yet the masses remained shrouded in darkness and difficult to awaken, still harboring doubts, and said:
"The body dies and the spirit is born, receiving a different form in each life. We, your subjects, are many, yet few among us have knowledge of past lives."
The King said:
"If your discourse has not yet established its fundamental principles, how can you claim to know the events of successive generations?
If one's vision does not perceive even what is decaying before one's eyes, who could possibly see the transformations of the soul?"
On a day of leisure, the king went out through a private gate, dressed in coarse clothing and walking on foot, to visit an old man who mended shoes. He said to him in jest:
"Among all the people under heaven, who is happy?"
The old man said,
"Only kings find such joy.
He asked:
"What is his joy? The old man replied, "The hundred officials reverently serve him, and the myriad people present their offerings; that he may immediately follow his heart's desires—is this not joy?"
The king said, "It is exactly as you have said.
He immediately gave him wine to drink; once he was intoxicated and unconscious, the king cast him into the palace.
He said to the primary consort:
"This old man of the soles says:
'The King is happy.'"
"I shall now play a joke upon him.
I will clothe him in royal vestments and have him take charge of the administration of the state,
so that the people will not be startled."
The consort replied,
"I respectfully agree.
On the day he awoke, a handmaid feigned this speech:
“The Great King’s neck is stiff with intoxication and his affairs have accumulated in great confusion; he ought to examine them calmly before proceeding to preside over the government.

The Hundred Ministers urged him to attend to these matters, yet he remained dim-sighted and bewildered, unable to discern east from west. The court historian recorded his failings and his ministers offered mutual admonition; though he sat upon his throne all day long, his body was racked with pain, food no longer tasted sweet, and he grew thin and haggard by the day.
The palace lady feigned surprise and said,
"Great King, why has your radiance been diminished?
He replied:
"I dreamed that I became an old man mending soles, toiling with my own person to seek food; it was said to be extremely difficult, and for that reason I suffer from this ailment.
There was no one among the crowd who did not laugh at him in secret.
Sleepless throughout the night, tossing and turning from side to side, he said:
"Am I this man who filled his boots?
Or am I truly the Son of Heaven?"
If you were a son of heaven, why is your skin so coarse?
Originally a beggar mending shoes, by what cause did you dwell in a royal palace?
My mind is utterly bewildered.
"The pupils are disoriented!
With bodies in two places, who can discern which is real?
The senior consort feigned surprise and said:
"The Great King is displeased," they said.
They provided him with all manner of music and entertained him with wine; once he was heavily intoxicated and unconscious, they restored him to his former garments and sent him back to a coarse bed.
When he sobered from the wine and awoke, he saw his humble room and coarse garments as they were before; yet all his joints ached as if he had been flogged with a whip.
Several days later, the King visited him again, and the old man said:
"When you drank my wine previously, you were intoxicated and unconscious; only now have you finally awakened."

While dreaming that he occupies the royal throne, oversees the various officials, and has his national history recorded, he is scrutinized by his subordinates; inwardly filled with trepidation, the pain in his hundred joints exceeds even that of being flogged.
"If even a dream is like this, how much more so when one truly becomes a king?
My previous argument was certainly not wrong.
When the king returned to his palace, he discussed this matter with his ministers, and those who laughed filled his ears.
The King said to his ministers:

"Regarding this single body, what it has experienced through sight and hearing since its very beginning, it still does not know of itself; how much more so for one who leaves the old and receives the new in another life, undergoing manifold hardships, being struck by malevolent spirits and afflicted by the distress of illness—how difficult would it not be to claim that one wishes to know where the transformation of the spirit goes and the land in which the next body is received?"
The Sūtra says:

"The fool harbors various heterodox desires and seeks to behold the soul; it is like one walking in darkness looking up at the stars and moon. Exhausting his body until the end of his days, when could he ever see them?"

Thereupon, the ministers and the common people of the land first perceived that the soul and the primal qi unite, beginning and then returning to the beginning, revolving without end; they thus believed in the existence of birth and death, and the destinies of calamity and fortune.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was my own self.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s infinite perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in bestowing light."
91. The Brahmāyu Sūtra (91). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you cultivate virtue and practice all manner of goodness, you will surely obtain great fortune.

It is like a farmer who possesses fertile fields from long ago; when the plowing is thorough and the soil well-prepared, and the rain falls with harmonious moderation, if he sows the seeds at the proper time, they will sprout according to the seasons."
When weeds and filth are cleared away and there are no further calamities, why fear that one will not reap the harvest?

In the past, before I was a Buddha, my heart was vast and universal in its love, and I took pity upon and rescued sentient beings, just as a compassionate mother nurtures her infant. For seven years I practiced in this manner, and thus the merit of my benevolence became manifest.
When his life ended, his soul ascended to become a Brahmā-rāja, named Brahmā-maheśvara, occupying that celestial station.

He underwent seven cycles of the formation and destruction of heaven and earth; whenever the world was about to be destroyed, I would ascend to the fifteenth heaven, the Ābhāsvara (Luminous) Heaven. After the subsequent reformation of the world, he returned to the Brahmā Heaven, pure and free from desire, existing spontaneously wherever he was.
Thereafter, he descended thirty-six times as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; in his palaces of the seven treasures, food, drink, clothing, and music were all spontaneous.
Later, he returned once more to the world as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), followed by a retinue of the seven treasures:

first, a purple-gold wheel; second, a divine moon-bright pearl; third, a white elephant capable of flight; fourth, a dark-blue horse with crimson manes; fifth, a jade-like woman as his consort; sixth, a minister in charge of treasures; and seventh, a sage counselor.
In every matter there were eighty-four thousand [details].
The king had a thousand sons, all of whom were handsome, pure, benevolent, and valiant; each one was equal to a thousand men.
At that time, the king governed by means of the five teachings, never wronging the people.

First, to be compassionate and benevolent, refraining from killing, so that one's kindness extends to all living beings; second, to be pure and yielding, refraining from theft, relinquishing one's own interests to aid the multitude; third, to be chaste and pure, refraining from lust and not violating any desires; fourth, to be sincere and trustworthy, refraining from deception, so that one’s speech is free from flowery embellishment; fifth, to honor filial piety, refraining from intoxication, so that one’s conduct remains unstained.

At that time, prisons were not established and the whip or staff was never employed; wind and rain were harmonious, the five grains ripened in abundance, and calamities did not arise. The world was at peace, and the people of the four continents led one another by the Way.
"Faith in the good brings blessings, while evil brings heavy calamity; upon death, all shall ascend to heaven, with none entering the three evil realms.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In a former life, I practiced the four immeasurable minds for seven years. By this merit, I became a Brahmā King above and Śakra Devendra below. Returning again to the world, I became a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents for many hundreds and thousands of lifetimes. My merits accumulated and my virtue was perfected; all evils were extinguished and all virtues gathered together. Abiding in the world as a Buddha, I am uniquely supreme, speaking alone and walking solitary within the triple realm."
The bhikṣus, having heard this sutra, rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha before departing.
Such was the practice of the Bodhisattva’s Infinite Perfection of Wisdom regarding the giving of light.
